            .Neurological PT Examination - Worksheet
                .Observation
                    .History
                        Specific comments
                            -Information gathered from chart review or patient interview present complaint, HPI, PMH, pertinent health information, social support (home environment)
                        Example Outcome measures
                        Clinical relevance
                            Allows you to gather data, clarify information, establish baseline, make appropriate referrals
                    .Review of Systems
                        Specific comments
                            Series of brief tests that provide an overview of the specific system of interest.
                        Example Outcome measures
                        Clinical relevance
                            -Used to determine the need for a further detailed examination.
                            -Rule out or differentiate specific system involvement.
                            -Identify system-related impairments that contribute to activity limitations and participation.
                            -Determine if there are RED flags and if referral is warranted.
                Mental Status: Basic mental functions
                    Level of Consciousness (LOC): Alertness
                        Specific comments
                            Be specific in documenting level of alertness:
                                able to follow commands such as
                                    1) eye movements/responses
                                    2) motor responses
                                    3) verbal responses
                        Example Outcome measures
                            Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)
                        Clinical relevance
                            LOC is the most sensitive indicator of change in neurological status.
                            Common terms to describe assessment of LOC:
                                Alert, drowsy, obtunded, comatose
                    Orientation
                        Specific comments
                            Ask for patient's
                                1) full name, age, birthplace
                                2) where they are now, type of place, city they are in
                                3) the date, day of week, what time it is, season
                        Example Outcome measures
                            The Mini-Mental State Exam (MMSE)
                            Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA)
                        Clinical relevance
                            Disorientation to time appears before disorientation to place then self.
                Mental Status: Complex mental functions
                    Language
                        Specific comments
                            Assess both receptive and expressive language
                        Example Outcome measures
                            MMSE
                            MoCA
                        Clinical relevance
                            Different language impairments are caused by lesions in the dominant frontal lobe and left temporal and parietal lobes
                            Aphasia- communication deficits
                                Receptive
                                Expressive
                                Global
                    Memory
                        Specific comments
                            -Assess immediate recall and STM by naming 3 objects, having the patient repeat the 3 objects immediately and then sometime later. Provide distracters during the delay to prevent the patient from rehearsing. Assess working memory by Serial 7's or WORLD backward
                        Example Outcome measures
                            MMSE
                            MoCA
                        Clinical relevance
                            Treatment considerations-Keeping things in writing and helping the patient refer to them can help.
                            Using environmental aids (calendars, clocks, schedules, cell phones) can help to recall
                    Visuospatial Functions
                        Specific comments
                            Have patient bisect a line Clock drawing
                        Example Outcome measures
                            MMSE
                            MoCA
                        Clinical relevance
                            Impaired visuospatial function is more severe with damage to the right (parietal lobe) hemisphere
                            Hemineglect (unilateral) inattention to one side that is not due to a primary sensory or motor impairment
                Mental Status: Meta-cognitive functions
                    Higher level cognitive functions
                        Specific comments
                            Meta-cognitive deficits consist of:
                                -Inability to divide attention
                                -Inability to generalize
                                -Decreased safety awareness and judgment
                                -Poor insight to condition
                                -Problem-solving deficits
                                -Impaired executive function
                                -inability to prioritize or select a behavior that is appropriate to the situation
                                -inhibit inappropriate behaviors
                                -to maintain focus to a task despite distractions
                        Example Outcome measures
                        Clinical relevance
                            Individuals must learn to do what their brains did automatically before
                            Consider compensating
                Cranial Nerves
                    I - Olfactory
                        Specific comments
                            Do not use noxious odors as they stimulate pain fibers from
                        Example Outcome measures
                        Clinical relevance
                            Anosmia-loss of the sense of smell
                    II - Optic
                        Specific comments
                            Visual acuity
                            Visual fields
                            Pupillary light reflex (afferent)
                        Example Outcome measures
                        Clinical relevance
                            -Damage anywhere in the visual pathway from the eye to the visual cortex can cause specific visual fields impairments in one or both eyes.
                    III, IV, VI
                        Specific comments
                            Extraocular movements
                            Note: III also involved with pupillary light reflex, convergence, and elevation of the eye lid
                            Smooth pursuit-ability to follow a slow-moving object across full range of vertical and horizontal eye movements
                            Saccades- eye movements used to rapidly re-fixate from one object to another
                        Example Outcome measures
                            H-test (screen for AROM)
                            Parts of the
                                Vestibular
                                Oculomotor
                                Screening
                                (VOMS)
                        Clinical relevance
                            Testing can identify pathology in the muscle, CN, pathways in the cortex and brainstem that control eye movements
                            Deficit is an inability to shift gaze
                    V - Trigeminal
                        Specific comments
                            Sensation of the face
                                -Light touch
                                -Pain and temperature
                            Muscles of mastication
                        Example Outcome measures
                        Clinical relevance
                            Deficits would include loss of sensation to face, and/or impaired movement of the jaw
                    VII - Facial
                        Specific comments
                            Muscles of facial expression and taste
                        Example Outcome measures
                        Clinical relevance
                            -Facial weakness can be caused by lesions of UMN in the contralateral motor cortex, or LMN in the ipsilateral facial nucleus or exiting nerve fibers
                    VIII - Vestibulocochlear
                        Specific comments
                            Hearing: Whisper or snap test
                        Vestibular:
                            Vestibular-Ocular reflex (VOR)
                        Example Outcome measures
                            Head Impulse Test
                            Part of the Vestibular/Ocular Screenin (VOMS)
                            Dizziness Handicap Inventory (DHI) - self report measure
                        Clinical relevance
                            -One sign of vestibular impairment is nystagmus which is a quick jerk-like movement of the eyes. If hearing loss is suspected, the patient should be referred for an audiogram.
                            -If vestibular loss is suspected, further testing should be conducted including:
                                VOR testing
                                Positional testing
                    IX-X Glossopharyngeal and Vagus
                        Specific comments
                            Taste
                            Pharyngeal movements
                            Gag reflex
                        Example Outcome measures
                        Clinical relevance
                            Dysphagia - difficulty with swallowing
                    XI - Spina1 Accesso
                        Specific comments
                            Trapezius
                            SCM
                        Example Outcome measures
                        Clinical relevance
                    XII - Hypoglossal
                        Specific comments
                            Motor to tongue
                        Example Outcome measures
                        Clinical relevance
                            -Fasciculations and atrophy are signs of LMN lesions. Unilateral tongue weakness causes the tongue to deviate to the weak side
                            -Dysarthria- motor speech disorder
                Sensory
                    Light touch
                        Specific comments
                            Use cotton wisp
                            Apply gentle touch (not pressure)
                            Eyes are closed and the patient reports YES, every time he erceives the stimulus
                        Example Outcome measures
                        Clinical relevance
                            Combined ALS and DCML systems
                    Pain & Temperature
                        Specific comments
                            Use cold reflex hammer handle
                            Ask the patient if they perceive the handle as cold
                        Example Outcome measures
                        Clinical relevance 
                            Primary sensation: anterolateral spinothalamic system 
                    Joint Position Sense
                        Specific comments
                            Eyes closed (EC)
                            Hold the digit lightly by the sides while moving the patient's finger or toes up or down.
                            Ask the patient to report after each movement the direction of the movement
                        Example Outcome measures
                        Clinical relevance
                            Primary sensation:
                                DCML system
                    Kinesthesia/Joint Movement Sense
                        Specific comments
                            Patient describes the direction of limb movement while in motion
                        Example Outcome measures
                        Clinical relevance  
                    Vibration
                        Specific comments
                            Apply stimulus (128 Hz vibration fork) over a bony prominence
                            Ask the patient to report whether they feel the vibration sense and then to report when it stops.
                        Example Outcome measures
                        Clinical relevance  
                            Primary sensation:
                                DCML system
                    Combined Cortical sensation EX: Stereognosis
                        Specific comments
                            Eyes closed
                            Place an item such as a coin, key, paper clip in the hand of the patient.
                            The patient is to manipulate the stimulus and identify the item
                        Example Outcome measures
                        Clinical relevance
                            Cortical sensation- test for lesions of the sensory cortex
                Motor
                    Observation: Muscle mass
                        Specific comments
                            Inspect bulk, girth
                        Example Outcome measures
                            Tape measure
                        Clinical relevance
                    Observation: Involuntary movements
                        Specific comments
                            Inspect for:
                                Tremors Fasciculations
                        Example Outcome measures
                        Clinical relevance 
                    Passive movement
                        Specific comments
                            Assess soft tissue limitations and tone
                        Example Outcome measures
                            Goniometry
                        Clinical relevance 
                            Alters functional mechanics
                    Tone
                        Specific comments
                            -Ask to patient to relax. Move each limb passively at several joints to get a feel for any resistance or stiffness that may be present
                        Example Outcome measures
                            Modified Ashworth scale (MAS) — spasticity only
                        Clinical relevance 
                            -Spasticity is a manifestation of UMN lesion, it may be a little as a "catch" or a very stiff limb that cannot be moved passively (velocity -dependent).
                            -Rigidity is "lead pipe or cogwheel" resistance to passive movement and is seen with disorders such as Parkinson's disease.
                            -Hypotonia is seen with LMN.
                    Strength
                    Active movement/AROM
                        Specific comments
                            Force production capacity
                            Functional strength
                        Example Outcome measures
                            MMT
                            Dynamometry
                            5TSTS
                        Clinical relevance
                            Conscious patient usua y Invo ves grading of strength
                            Unconscious patient usually involves observation of spontaneous movements
                    Motor Control of movement:
                    Motor coordination for selective motor control (see movement analysis section)
                        Specific comments
                            -Involves coordination of muscle groups for movement during functional activities i.e., selective motor control, appropriate timing and sequencing of muscle activation & coordination of muscle groups for stability during functional activities
                        Example Outcome measures
                            Task analyses and active examination observes patient performance
                        Clinical relevance
                            Abnormal Synergist patterns-disturbed organization of synergisticvoluntary movement patterns.
                            Usually defined as movements that are primitive and highly stereotyped.
                            Selective movement control (isolated movement) is commonly impaired.
                    Reflexes
                        Specific comments
                            Assessment o reflexes
                            Assessment of pathologic reflexes/UMN signs
                        Example Outcome measures
                        Clinical relevance
                            UMN lesion: Hyperreflexia; presence of pathological reflexes
                            LMN lesion: H oreflexia
                Coordination
                    Finger to nose
                    Heel to shin
                    Rapid alternating Movement: Supination/pronation Toe/finger tapping
                        Specific comments
                            Evaluation of task requires reversal of movements and accuracy in touching the targets
                            Quantification of performance is achieved by noting the time to complete a number of repetitions or vice versa
                            Qualitative assessment is descriptive, noting movement disorders
                        Example Outcome measures
                        Clinical relevance
                            -Coordination is affected due to multiple systems/disorders.
                            -Limb ataxia is usually caused by lesions of the cerebellar hemispheres and the associated pathways while truncal ataxia is often caused by a lesion in vermis
                            -Dysmetria- inability to judge distance or range of movement
                            -Dysdiadochokinesis-difficulty with reversal of movements
                            -Ataxia- uncoordinated movement
                Balance
                Static Standing balance
                    Sensory
                    Organization / CNS Integration
                        Specific comments
                            Ask the patient to maintain standing with EO/ EC on floor
                            EO/EC on foam
                        Example Outcome measures
                            Berg Balance Test m-CTSIB
                            Mini-BESTest
                        Clinical relevance
                            Assess the ability to utilize sensory input
                    Reactive postural control
                        Specific comments
                            Ask the patient to maintain a posture or steady oneself with perturbation
                        Example Outcome measures
                            Applications of perturbations
                            Mini-BESTest
                        Clinical relevance
                            Assess the motor responses (postural strategies) used to maintain balance along with the timing of response.
                            Note the amount of assistance if needed to maintain balance
                Dynamic standing Balance
                    Voluntary (self-generated) postural control
                        Specific comments
                            Ask the patient to while standing to perform a voluntary activity
                        Example Outcome measures
                            Berg Balance Test
                            Reach Tests
                            Mini-BESTest
                        Clinical relevance
                            -Impaired anticipatory postural control results in instability during weight shifting activities and can be observed in the AP and lateral directions
                Walking balance
                    Walking Balance (walking)
                        Specific comments
                            Ask the patient to perform various walking activities
                        Example Outcome measures
                            FGA
                            Mini BESTest
                        Clinical relevance
                            The effects of attentional demands on postural control is important
                    Balance Self-efficacy
                        Specific comments

                        Example Outcome measures
                            Activities-specific

                        Clinical relevance

                    Sitting Balance

                        Example Outcome measures

                .Case vignettes (see solutuons at page 18) (See Q&A doc for these cases)
                    .Discuss and demonstrate specific tests and measures that you would use to assess your patient’s chief complaints and functional limitations. Make sure you thoroughly examine your patient (i.e., assess both sides of the body and/or body segment [LE/UE]).
                        Case 1: Your patient is reporting stiffness in his or her calf when trying to move fast- such as when he/she is “hustling”
                        to open the front door when the doorbell rings.

                        Case 2: Your patient is reporting decreased “feeling” in the right hand and reports dropping items when not looking at
                        his/her hand.

                        Case 3: Your patient is c/o double vision.

                        Case 4: Your patient reports difficulty remembering recent events.

                        Case 5: Your patient c/o difficulty maintaining balance in the dark or dimly lit areas.

                        Case 6: Your patient demonstrates irregular and inaccurate upper limb movements during activities such as bringing a cup to his/her mouth.

                        Case 7:  Your patient presents with an inability to smile symmetrically.

                        Case 8: Your patient demonstrates an inability to reach out for a “protective response” when perturbation in sitting.

                        Case 9: Your patient tells you that he has fallen last week while walking outdoors, no injuries, and has an extensive past medical history with multiple co-morbidities.

                        Case 10: Your patient had a sudden loss of hearing on the left side and experienced acute dizziness. They are now having difficulty with their balance when they turn their head while standing and walking.

            .International Standards for the Classification of Spinal Cord Injury - Motor Exam Guide

                .C5 Elbow Flexors | Biceps Brachii, Brachialis
                    Grade 3 
                    -Patient Position: The shoulder is in neutral rotation, 
                    neutral flexion/extension, and adducted. The elbow is fully 
                    extended, with the forearm in full supination. The wrist is in 
                    neutral flexion/extension.
                    -Examiner Position: Support the wrist.
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Bend your elbow and try to reach your 
                    hand to your nose.”
                    -Action:The patient attempts to move through the full range of 
                    motion in elbow flexion.

                    Grades 4 & 5
                    -Patient Position: The shoulder is in neutral rotation, neutral 
                    flexion/extension, and adducted.  The elbow is flexed to 90° and 
                    the forearm is fully supinated.
                    -Examiner Position: Place a stabilizing hand on the anterior 
                    shoulder. Grasp the volar aspect of the wrist and exert a pulling 
                    force in the direction of elbow extension. 
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Hold your arm. Don’t let me move it.”
                    -Action:The patient resists the examiner’s pull and attempts to 
                    maintain the elbow flexed at 90°.

                    Grade 2
                    -Patient Position: The shoulder is in internal rotation and
                    adducted with the forearm positioned above the abdomen, just 
                    below the umbilicus. The elbow is in 30° of flexion. The forearm 
                    and wrist are in neutral pronation/supination. Sufficient flexion of 
                    the shoulder must be permitted to allow the forearm to 
                    comfortably move over the abdomen.
                    -Examiner Position: Support the arm.
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Bend your elbow and try to bring your 
                    hand to your nose.”
                    -Action:The patient attempts to move the elbow through a full 
                    range of motion in elbow flexion.

                    Grades 0 & 1
                    Patient: The patient is in the grade 2 position with the shoulder in 
                    internal rotation and adducted.  The palm and ventral forearm are 
                    positioned above the abdomen. The elbow is in 30° of flexion. 
                    The forearm and wrist are in neutral pronation/supination. 
                    Sufficient flexion of the shoulder must be permitted to allow the 
                    forearm to comfortably move over the abdomen.
                    -Examiner Position: One hand supports the forearm while the 
                    other hand palpates the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa.  The 
                    belly of the biceps brachii muscle may also be palpated or 
                    observed for movement. 
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Bend your elbow and try to bring your 
                    hand to your nose.”
                    -Action:The patient attempts to move the elbow through a full 
                    range of motion in elbow flexion.

                C6 Wrist Extensors | Extensor Carpi Radialis Longus, Extensor Carpi Radialis Brevis
                    Grade 3
                    -Patient Position: The shoulder is in neutral rotation, neutral 
                    flexion/extension, and adducted.  The elbow is fully extended, the 
                    forearm is fully pronated, and the wrist flexed.
                    -Examiner Position: One hand supports the distal forearm to
                    allow the wrist to be pre-positioned in sufficient flexion for testing. 
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Bend your wrist upwards. Lift your 
                    fingers toward the ceiling.”
                    -Action:The patient attempts to extend the wrist through a full 
                    range of motion.

                    Grades 4 & 5
                    -Patient Position: Same as grade 3, except the wrist is 
                    fully extended.
                    -Examiner Position: Grasp the distal forearm to stabilize the 
                    wrist.  Apply pressure across the metacarpals in a downward 
                    direction toward flexion and ulnar deviation.
                    The force applied should be angled toward the ulnar side of the 
                    wrist rather than directly downward, since it is the radial wrist 
                    extensors that are being tested.  
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Hold your wrist up. Don’t let me 
                    push it down.”
                    -Action:The patient resists the examiner’s push and attempts to 
                    maintain the wrist in the fully extended position.

                    Grades 0, 1 & 2
                    -Patient Position: Position the patient with the arm resting on the 
                    exam table.  The shoulder is in neutral flexion/extension, neutral 
                    rotation, and adducted.  The elbow is fully extended. The forearm 
                    is in neutral pronation-supination and the wrist fully flexed
                    The patient may also be positioned with the shoulder in slight 
                    flexion, internal rotation, and adducted, with the patient’s arm 
                    above the abdomen. The elbow is flexed to 90° and the forearm 
                    is in full supination.  The wrist is flexed.
                    -Examiner Position: Support the forearm and ask the patient to 
                    bend the wrist backwards into extension.  For trace function,
                    palpate the radial wrist extensors just proximal to the wrist, on 
                    the radial aspect of the distal forearm. Observe the muscle belly 
                    for movement.  
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Bend your wrist backwards.”
                    -Action:The patient attempts to extend the wrist though a full 
                    range of motion in wrist extension.

                    C6 Common Muscle Substitution
                    Wrist extension can be mimicked by forearm supination and the use of gravity.  The examiner needs to make sure the 
                    forearm is stabilized and is in proper position.

                C7 Elbow Extensors | Triceps
                    Grade 3
                    -Patient Position: The shoulder is in neutral rotation, adducted, 
                    and 90°of flexion.  The elbow is fully flexed with the palm of the 
                    hand resting by the ear.
                    -Examiner Position: Support the upper arm.
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Straighten your arm.”
                    -Action:The patient attempts to move through the full range of 
                    elbow extension.

                    Grades 4 & 5
                    -Patient Position: Same as grade 3, except the elbow is in 
                    45° of flexion.
                    -Examiner Position: Support the upper arm. Grasp the wrist 
                    and apply resistance to the distal forearm in the direction of 
                    elbow flexion. 
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Hold this position. Don’t let me bend 
                    your elbow.”
                    -Action:The patient resists the examiner’s pressure and attempts 
                    to maintain the position of the elbow in 45° of flexion.

                    Grade 2
                    -Patient Position: The shoulder is in internal rotation and 
                    adducted, with the forearm positioned above the abdomen. The 
                    forearm is in neutral pronation/supination.   The elbow is fully 
                    flexed.  When checking Grade 2, sufficient flexion of the shoulder 
                    must be permitted to allow the forearm to clear and move over 
                    the chest and abdomen.
                    -Examiner Position: Support the patient’s arm.
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Straighten your arm.”
                    -Action:The patient attempts to move through the full range of 
                    elbow extension.

                    Grades 0 & 1
                    -Patient Position: Maintain the grade 2 position with the shoulder 
                    in internal rotation and adduction, and the forearm positioned
                    above the abdomen. The forearm is in neutral 
                    pronation/supination and the elbow is in 30° of flexion. 
                    -Examiner Position: Support the arm. For trace function,
                    palpate the distal triceps at its insertion on the olecranon. 
                    The belly of the triceps muscle may also be palpated and 
                    observed for movement.
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Straighten your arm.”
                    -Action:The patient attempts to fully extend the elbow. 

                    C7 Common Muscle Substitution
                    Elbow extension can be mimicked by externally rotating the shoulder, by quickly flexing the elbow and then relaxing, 
                    and with spasticity of the triceps.  These substitutions can be minimized by maintaining the correct position for testing, 
                    correct instructions to the patient, and avoiding elbow flexion.  Palpation of the triceps should be done to confirm the 
                    patient is using the correct muscle for the test.

                C8 Long Finger Flexors | Flexor Digitorum Profundus
                    Grade 3
                    -Patient Position: The shoulder is in neutral rotation, neutral 
                    flexion-extension, and adduction.  The elbow is fully extended 
                    with the forearm fully supinated. The wrist is in neutral flexion-
                    extension.  The metacarpal phalangeal (MCP) and proximal 
                    interphalangeal joints (PIP) are stabilized in extension. 
                    -Examiner Position: Using two hands grasp the patient’s hand 
                    and stabilize the wrist In neutral.  Secure the PIP and MCP joints 
                    in extension with both hands while isolating the middle finger for 
                    testing. Stabilize the volar aspect of the 3rd middle phalanx with 
                    the thumb of the opposite hand.   
                    As an alternate method, 1 hand may be used to stabilize instead 
                    of 2.  The PIP and MCP joints are stabilized as previously 
                    described, with the thumb of the stabilizing hand now securing 
                    the middle phalanx.
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Bend the tip of your middle finger.”
                    -Action:The patient attempts to flex the distal interphalangeal 
                    (DIP) joint through the full range of motion in flexion.

                    Grades 4 & 5
                    -Patient Position: The same as grade 3, except the DIP joint is 
                    fully flexed. 
                    -Examiner Position: Stabilize the wrist, MCP and PIP joints as in 
                    grade 3.  Apply pressure with the tip of the finger or thumb 
                    against the distal phalanx of the patient’s middle finger.
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Hold the tip of your finger in this bent 
                    position.  Don’t let me move it.”
                    -Action:The patient attempts to maintain the fully flexed position 
                    of the DIP joint, and resist the pressure applied by the examiner 
                    in the direction of finger extension.

                    Grades 0, 1 & 2
                    -Patient Position: The shoulder is in neutral rotation, neutral 
                    flexion-extension, and adduction.  The elbow is fully extended.  
                    The forearm is in neutral pronation-supination and the wrist in 
                    neutral flexion-extension. The MCP and PIP joints are stabilized 
                    in extension.
                    -Examiner Position: Stabilize the wrist in neutral and the MCP 
                    and PIP joints in extension.  For trace function, palpate the 
                    tendons of the long finger flexors or observe the muscle belly for 
                    movement. 
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Bend the tip of your middle finger.”
                    -Action:The patient attempts to flex the distal interphalangeal 
                    (DIP) joint through the full range of motion in flexion.

                    C8 Common Muscle Substitution
                    When testing grades 1 through 3, the wrist must be carefully stabilized.  Involuntary movement of the distal phalanx 
                    can occur in the presence of active wrist extension. This tenodesis movement could be misinterpreted as voluntary 
                    contraction of the long finger flexors.  
                    While testing grades 4 and 5, the proximal phalanges must be well stabilized.  This will avoid misinterpretation of 
                    distal phalanx movement caused by contraction of the hand intrinsics or the flexor digitorum superficialis.

                T1  Small Finger Abductor | Abductor Digiti Minimi
                    Grade 3
                    -Patient Position: The shoulder is in internal rotation adducted, 
                    and at 15° flexion.  The elbow is at 90° flexion, the forearm is 
                    pronated, and the wrist is in neutral flexion/extension.
                    -Examiner Position: Support the patient’s hand, taking 
                    care to assure that the MCP joints are stabilized to 
                    prevent hyperextension.
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Move your little finger away from your 
                    ring finger.”
                    -Action:The patient attempts to move the little finger through the 
                    full range of motion in abduction. 

                    Grades 4 & 5
                    -Patient Position: Same as grade 3, except the little finger 
                    is fully abducted.
                    -Examiner Position: Support the patient’s hand, taking care to 
                    assure that the MCP joints are stabilized to prevent 
                    hyperextension. Use the index finger to apply pressure against 
                    the side of the patient’s distal phalanx.
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Hold your little finger away from your 
                    ring finger.  Don’t let me push it in.”
                    -Action:The examiner exerts a pushing force against the side of 
                    the distal phalanx, and the patient attempts to resist the 
                    examiner’s force and keep the little finger fully abducted.

                    Grades 0, 1 & 2
                    -Patient Position: The shoulder is in neutral rotation, neutral 
                    flexion/extension, and adducted.  The elbow is in full extension.  
                    The forearm is in full pronation and the wrist in neutral flexion-
                    extension.  The MCP joint is stabilized. 
                    An alternate position is with the shoulder in internal rotation, 
                    adducted, and neutral flexion/extension. The elbow is in 90° of 
                    flexion, the forearm and wrist are in neutral flexion /extension,
                    and the MCP joint is stabilized.
                    -Examiner Position: Stabilize the dorsal wrist and hand by 
                    pressing down lightly on the back of the hand. Be sure that the 
                    MCP joints are stabilized to prevent hyperextension. Palpate the 
                    abductor digiti minimi muscle and observe the muscle belly 
                    for movement.
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Move your little finger away from your 
                    ring finger.”
                    -Action:The patient attempts to abduct the little finger through the 
                    full range of motion.

                    T1 Common Muscle Substitution
                    Finger extension can mimic 5th finger abduction. Proper positioning and stabilization will minimize this error.

                L2 Hip Flexors | Iliopsoas
                    Grade 3
                    -Patient Position:  The hip is in neutral rotation, neutral 
                    adduction/abduction, with both the hip and knee in 15° of flexion. 
                    -Examiner Position: Support the dorsal aspect of the distal thigh 
                    and leg.  Do not allow flexion beyond 90° when examining acute 
                    thoraco-lumbar injuries due to the kyphotic stress placed on the 
                    lumbar spine.
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Lift your knee towards your chest as far 
                    as you can, trying not to drag your foot on the exam table.”
                    -Action:The patient attempts to flex hip to 90° of flexion.

                    Grades 4 & 5
                    -Patient Position: The hip is in 90° of flexion with the 
                    knee relaxed. 
                    -Examiner Position: Brace the anterior superior iliac spine 
                    on the opposite side and place a hand on the distal anterior 
                    thigh, just above the knee.  Pressure is applied in the direction of 
                    hip extension
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Hold your knee in this position.  Don’t 
                    let me push it down.”
                    -Action:The patient attempts to resist the examiner’s push and 
                    keep the hip flexed at 90°.

                    Grade 2
                    -Patient Position: Place the patient in the gravity eliminated 
                    position with the hip in external rotation and 45°of flexion. The 
                    knee is flexed at 90°.
                    -Examiner Position: Support the leg.
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Try to bring your knee out to the side,”
                    or “Try to flex your thigh toward the side of the body.”
                    -Action:The patient attempts to move through the full range of 
                    motion in hip flexion.

                    Grades 0 & 1
                    -Patient Position: Place the patient in the grade 3 position, with 
                    the hip in neutral rotation, neutral adduction/abduction and the hip 
                    and knee flexed to 15°. 
                    -Examiner Position: Support the thigh to eliminate friction while
                    palpating the superficial hip flexors just distal to the anterior 
                    superior iliac spine.
                    -Instructions to Patient: Ask the patient to “lift your knee towards 
                    your chest as far as you can.”
                    -Action: The patient attempts to flex the hip.
                    Note: For Grade 1, the examiner is actually palpating the more
                    superficial hip flexors, i.e. sartorius and rectus femoris rather than 
                    the iliopsoas. The insertion of the iliopsoas is too deep to be
                    seen or felt when it possesses only Grade 1 strength. When 
                    examining a patient with an acute traumatic lesion below T8, the 
                    hip should not be allowed to flex passively or actively beyond 90°.  
                    Flexion beyond 90° may place too great a kyphotic stress on the 
                    lumbar spine.

                    L2 Common Muscle Substitution
                    Any muscle of the trunk that can elevate or rotate the pelvis can trick the examiner into thinking that the hip flexor 
                    muscles are active.  This could include the rectus abdominus, the adductor muscles, obliques, or the quadratus 
                    lumborum.  With accurate palpation, correct patient instructions, and observation of any trunk movement, this 
                    substitution can be avoided.

                L3 Knee Extensors | Quadriceps
                    Grade 3
                    -Patient Position: The hip is in neutral rotation, neutral 
                    adduction/abduction and 15° of flexion. The knee is in 30° 
                    of flexion.
                    -Examiner Position: Place the arm under the tested knee and 
                    rest the hand on the patient’s distal thigh. This causes the tested 
                    knee to flex to approximately 30°.
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Straighten your knee.”
                    -Action:The patient attempts to straighten the knee through the 
                    full range of motion in extension.

                    Grades 4 & 5
                    -Patient Position: Same as grade 3, except the knee is in 15° 
                    of flexion.
                    -Examiner Position: Place the arm under the tested knee and 
                    rest the hand on the patient’s opposite thigh. Grasp the leg to be 
                    tested, just proximal to the ankle.
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Hold this position. Don’t let me bend 
                    your knee.”
                    -Action:Examiner exerts downward force into knee flexion while 
                    the patient attempts to hold the knee in 15 degrees of flexion.

                    Grade 2
                    -Patient Position: The hip is in external rotation and 45°of flexion. 
                    The knee is flexed at 90°.
                    -Examiner Position: Support the distal thigh and leg.
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Straighten your knee.”
                    -Action:The patient attempts to move through the full range 
                    of motion.

                    Grades 0 & 1
                    -Patient Position: Place the patient with the hip in neutral 
                    rotation, neutral adduction/abduction with both the hip and knee 
                    in 15° of flexion.  
                    -Examiner Position: Support the leg. Palpate the patellar tendon 
                    or the belly of the quadriceps muscle for trace function.   The 
                    muscle belly may also be observed for movement.
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Straighten your knee.” 
                    Note:  In this position, asking the patient to push the back of the 
                    knee downward toward the exam table may be better to elicit 
                    trace contraction in the quadriceps.
                    -Action:The patient attempts to straighten the knee.

                L4 Ankle Dorsiflexors | Tibialis Anterior
                    Grade 3
                    -Patient Position: The hip is in neutral rotation, neutral 
                    adduction/abduction, with the hip and knee slightly flexed. The 
                    hand may be placed under the knee of the tested leg to 
                    incorporate slight flexion. The ankle is plantarflexed. 
                    -Examiner Position: At the patient’s side. Support the leg.
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Pull your toes upward toward your 
                    head, letting your ankle bend.”
                    -Action:The patient attempts to dorsiflex ankle through a full 
                    range of motion.

                    Grades 4 & 5
                    -Patient Position: Same as grade 3, except the ankle is 
                    fully dorsiflexed.
                    -Examiner Position: In the grade 3 position, place
                    the hand on the dorsum of the foot and apply pressure downward 
                    in the direction of plantarflexion.
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Hold your ankle in this position. Don’t 
                    let me push it down.”
                    -Action:The patient attempts to resist the examiner and maintain 
                    the ankle in full dorsiflexion.

                    Grade 2
                    -Patient Position: The hip is in external rotation and 45° of 
                    abduction. The knee is flexed, and the ankle is fully 
                    plantar flexed.
                    -Examiner Position: Support the leg.
                    Instruction to Patient: “Lift the toes upward toward the head, 
                    allowing the ankle to bend.”
                    -Action:The patient attempts to dorsiflex ankle through the full 
                    range of motion.

                    Grades 0 & 1
                    -Patient Position: Place the hip in neutral rotation, neutral 
                    adduction/abduction, and neutral flexion/extension.  The knee is 
                    fully extended and the ankle slightly plantarflexed.
                    -Examiner Position: Palpate the proximal lower leg over the 
                    tibialis anterior muscle belly or on the tendon of the tibialis 
                    anterior muscle as it crosses the anterior ankle. Observe the 
                    muscle belly for movement.
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Bring your toes upward toward your 
                    head, letting your ankle bend.”
                    -Action:The patient attempts to dorsiflex the ankle.

                    L4 Common Muscle Substitution
                    Ankle dorsiflexion can be mimicked by the long toe extensors, particularly the extensor hallucis longus.  Correct 
                    stabilization and observation along with proper patient instruction and palpation can eliminate this substitution.

                L5 Long Toe Extensors | Extensor Hallucis Longus
                    Grade 3
                    -Patient Position:  The hip is in neutral rotation, neutral 
                    adduction/abduction, and neutral flexion/extension.  The knee is 
                    fully extended.
                    -Examiner Position: At the patient’s side. Support the foot.
                    -Instructions to Patient:  “Lift your big toe upwards toward 
                    your knee.”
                    -Action:The patient attempts to move the great toe through the 
                    full range of motion.

                    Grades 4 & 5
                    -Patient Position: Same as grade 3, except the toe is 
                    fully extended.
                    -Examiner Position: At the patient’s side. Place the thumb on the 
                    distal phalanx of the great toe and apply pressure downward in 
                    the direction of toe flexion.
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Keep your toe lifted upward. Don’t let 
                    me push it down.” 
                    -Action:The patient attempts to resist the examiner and maintain 
                    the great toe in full extension.

                    Grade 2
                    -Patient Position: The hip is in external rotation, 45° abduction.  
                    The knee is flexed.  The ankle and long toe are in a relaxed, 
                    neutral position.
                    -Examiner Position: Support the leg.
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Lift your big toe upwards toward 
                    the knee.”
                    -Action:The patient attempts to extend the great toe through the 
                    full range of motion.

                    Grades 0 & 1
                    -Patient Position: Place the patient in the grade 3 position.
                    -Examiner Position: Support the leg and palpate the extensor
                    tendon of the long toe for trace function.
                    -Instructions to Patient:  “Lift your big toe upwards toward 
                    your knee.”
                    -Action: The patient attempts to extend the great toe.

                    L5 Common Muscle Substitution
                    Great toe extension can be facilitated by plantarflexion. If a patient actively plantar flexes the entire foot, passive 
                    extension of extensor hallucis longus can be achieved during the active plantarflexion of the foot. This is a type of 
                    tenodesis for the foot and can be avoided by proper stabilization to eliminate foot and ankle movement.
                    Another possible muscle substitution for L5 can occur when the patient actively flexes the big toe and then relaxes. 
                    Passive relaxation into a neutral position can be perceived as active extension.

                S1 Ankle Plantarflexors | Gastrocnemius, Soleus
                    Grade 3
                    Note: Checking for Grades 3-5 is significantly different 
                    from what is described in standard manual muscle testing texts.  
                    This departure is required for examining patients in the 
                    supine position.
                    -Patient Position: 
                    The hip is in neutral rotation and 45° of flexion, with the knee fully 
                    flexed and ankle in full dorsiflexion.
                    -Examiner Position: Place one hand behind the knee to assist in 
                    stabilizing the leg.  The other hand is positioned under the sole of 
                    the patient’s foot, pushing the foot into dorsiflexion. The patient’s 
                    heel remains resting on the exam table.
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Push your foot down into my hand and 
                    lift your heel off the table.”
                    -Action:The patient pushes the forefoot downward into the 
                    examiner’s hand and raises the heel off the exam table, through a 
                    full range of motion in plantarflexion.

                    Grades 4 & 5
                    -Patient Position: The hip is in neutral rotation, neutral flexion-
                    extension, and neutral abduction-adduction. The knee is fully 
                    extended and the ankle is in full plantarflexion.
                    -Examiner Position: Place one hand on the distal lower leg while 
                    the other hand grasps the foot across the plantar surface of 
                    metatarsals.  Apply pressure on the bottom of the foot in the 
                    direction of dorsiflexion.
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Hold your foot pointed down. Don’t let 
                    me push it up.”
                    -Action:Examiner gives pressure on the plantar aspect of the 
                    metatarsals in the direction of dorsiflexion. The patient attempts 
                    to resist the examiner by maintaining the foot and ankle in 
                    full plantarflexion.

                    Grades 0, 1, & 2
                    Patient Position The hip is in external rotation and 45° of flexion. 
                    The knee is flexed.
                    -Examiner Position: Support the lower leg. For trace function 
                    palpate either the gastrocnemius muscle belly or the achilles 
                    tendon, or observe the muscle belly for movement.
                    -Instructions to Patient: “Point your toes downward like a 
                    ballet dancer.”
                    -Action:The patient attempts to plantar flex the foot through a full 
                    range of motion.

                    S1 Common muscle substitution
                    Visually monitor the hip flexors to assure that these muscles are not being used to facilitate plantarflexion.

            .Practice and Feedback Lab
                Lab Objectives:
                    -Apply motor learning strategies to drive skill acquisition and recovery of function.
                    -Design effective practice paradigms to promote motor learning and skill acquisition.
                    -Describe various types of feedback and apply these when teaching a motor skill.
                    -Demonstrate the ability to perform a neurologic PT examination, establish a prognosis and plan of care using evidence-based therapeutic interventions for clients with a
                    neurologic diagnosis.
                    -Apply a core set of outcome measures in clinical settings to assess gait, balance, and function for persons with neurologic diagnoses.

                Lab Schedule:
                    Introduction and round robin
                    Review using cases (stations rotate every 60 minutes)
                    Break
                    Review using cases (stations rotate every 60 minutes)
                    Discussion and wrap up

                (See Q&A doc for these cases) ↓

                Station 1: A 47-year-old man who sustained a Right hemorrhagic stroke while at work 4 weeks ago. His goals are to be able to return to his role as a postal worker. This requires him to drive, walk independently in the community, and carry and sort packages and letters.
                    Upon gait analysis you observe that the patient:
                        Walks independently without a cane but only in a familiar environments/level surfaces
                        Reports fear of falling when walking in unfamiliar situations/uneven surfaces
                        Presents with decreased strength and walking efficiency limiting his participation
                            Gait pattern: reduced stance time on LEFT
                            Wide BOS throughout gait cycle
                            Reduced heel strike on LEFT
                            Tends to overuse the cane when outside or when fatigued

                    A. Identify limitations in body structures/function, activity limitations, participation restrictions.

                    B. Design 3 stations that he will train through in a supervised setting. Note: the patient will be supervised by an experienced physical therapist to ensure safety 100% of the time. Formulate treatment activities that are: challenging, salient, address his impairments that interfere with capacity to walk. Remember to prioritize functional activities when developing your intervention. Provide rationale for your choices.

                    C. How will you measure the response to your intervention and/or if the intervention is too challenging or too easy for the individual?

                    D. Provide ideas for progression and regression for I of your interventions.

                    E. Teach the 'patient' the exercises using professional language and appropriate feedback given this is the first time they are attempting the exercise.

                    F. Structure the practice for each intervention (blocked, random, massed, distributed, etc.).

                    G. Identify what type of feedback you would use (knowledge of performance, results, feedback schedules, etc.).

                    H. Describe which outcome measure(s) you will use to determine the effectiveness of your treatment selection and how the results from the outcome measure (s) will be interpreted (e.g., minimal detectable change; minimally clinically important differences; and/or cut-off values for the specific outcome measure). Practice assessing your patient using one outcome measure that you choose.

                Station 2: A female is admitted to inpatient rehab for evaluation and treatment for a stroke in the posterior fossa referred to as Wallenberg's Syndrome. Upon reading her history, you note that she suffered a rapid onset of vertigo, nausea/vomiting, and gait unsteadiness in association with head-motion intolerance and nystagmus-secondary to an infarct in the left PICA. She works in an office and would like to return to work as soon as possible. She enjoys walking outdoors and playing with her grandchildren. She notes imbalance particularly on uneven surfaces and when moving her head while walking.

                    How would you proceed with the neurological PT examination for the given diagnosis?

                        A. List which systems you would emphasize during your PT examination and which you may not prioritize given the pathology.

                        B. Provide rationale to why you would emphasize the system you selected and why you may decide to not prioritize certain ones.

                        C. Perform the specified tests and measures that you selected in A on your 'patient.'

                        D. What outcome measures would you select to measure gait and balance function? How often would you measure these outcome measures in a clinical setting?

                        E. Perform one of the specified outcome measures with your patient.

                        F. Develop an intervention to address gait instability/unsteadiness.

                        G. Teach the 'patient' the exercises using professional language and appropriate feedback.

                Station 3: A male patient presents to outpatient rehab with a reduced ability to maintain his balance when he lifts heavy objects, leans over to retrieve objects from the floor, steps up onto a surface without support or when he turns his head and trunk. He has difficulty recovering a stable standing posture following perturbation. He expresses that he has difficulty performing activities while walking safely and is fearful that he may fall. He currently has not fallen. The patient presents with weak quadriceps and tight heel cords and no sensory deficits or cerebellar impairments. His Berg Balance Score is 49/54 and his Functional Gait Assessment (FGA) is 18/30. His goal is to return to fishing on his boat.

                    A. Using a patient-centered approach, design 3 stations that he will train through in a supervised setting that include interventions to improve balance.

                    B. Teach the 'patient' the exercises using professional language and appropriate feedback given this is the first time they are attempting the exercise.

                    C. Structure the practice for each intervention (blocked, random, massed, distributed, etc.).

                    D. Provide an example of how you would direct the patient's attention to the movement effect (external attentional focus) for at least 1 intervention.

                    E. Demonstrate how you will promote self-efficacy during your treatment.

                    F. Provide an example of how you would incorporate opportunities for patient autonomy.

                    G. Write a short term and long-term goal for this patient keeping in mind the patient, task, and environment.

            Department of Physical Therapy

            Summer 2025 
            Credits: 4

            COURSE DESCRIPTION & METHODS OF INSTRUCTION 
            The first unit of this course provides a knowledge foundation for the principles that drive 
            neurological rehabilitation, which will then be applied to the clinical management of specific 
            neurologic diagnoses that are discussed throughout the course series. The students will be 
            introduced to the structure of a PT neurological examination that can be applied when 
            evaluating clients with neurologic diagnoses and disorders. We will focus on the Hypothesis-
            Oriented Algorithm for Clinicians (HOAC) framework for clinical decision making that will provide 
            a foundation for client management. Information will be presented regarding motor behavior and 
            motor control as it relates to normal and abnormal movement and function. Students will learn 
            strategies to improve motor function and skill acquisition (motor control and motor learning) 
            utilizing knowledge of recovery and neuroplasticity processes following an insult to the CNS.   
              
            The second unit of this course will apply the foundational knowledge, gained in unit 1, to the 
            management of clients with vestibular and balance disorders. The anatomy, physiology and 
            function of the vestibular system will be reviewed. We will provide an overview of the etiology, 
            pathophysiology and clinical manifestations of typical vestibular disorders. The students will 
            learn to identify and describe common functional impairments, activity limitations and 
            participation restrictions, which can be the result of a vestibular diagnosis. Students will learn 
            evidence-based examination procedures used to evaluate clients with vestibular and balance 
            disorders, based on current best practice. Students will use findings from clinical examination 


            skills to establish a patient-centered, individualized plan of care. The role of the physical 
            therapist in the management of patients/clients with vestibular and balance diagnoses and 
            interventions to optimize function, activity and participation will be provided to optimize care.  
      

            COURSE RATIONALE 
            This is the first of a three-part series of courses which introduces the student to the principles of 
            neurological rehabilitation. In this course, students will learn the neurologic PT assessment and 
            motor learning principles that will carry through to Neuromuscular PT 2 and 3. The course series 
            will culminate with a comprehensive practical exam that will prepare students to enter clinical 
            practice.

            COURSE LEARNING OBJECTIVES (CLOS) 
            Upon completion of this course, you should be able to:  


             

             

            7 

             

            • Integrate knowledge from anatomy, biomechanics and neuroscience to make clinical 
            decisions to perform and interpret findings from a well-integrated and individualized 
            examination for clients with neurological diagnoses.  
            • Develop an individualized treatment plan for clients with neurologic diagnoses using 
            information gathered from the neurological PT examination, best evidence and the 
            client’s unique goals and characteristics.  
            • Describe and apply current theories of motor learning, motor control and neuroplasticity 
            to the evaluation and treatment of clients with neurologic disorders while considering 
            unique personal and environmental factors.  
            • Demonstrate the ability to perform a PT examination, establish a prognosis and plan of 
            care using evidence-based therapeutic interventions for clients with a vestibular and/or 
            balance disorder.  

             

            ONLINE COURSE POLICIES 
            Late Work 
            Work that is submitted late will be deducted according to assignment grading rubrics or 
            instructions.  

             

            Course Communication  
            Students should log into Canvas daily to work through learning modules. Course 
            announcements will be used to post timely changes from the instructor.  
              
            Students are expected to check their official University of Pittsburgh email (pitt.edu) on a 
            frequent and consistent basis to remain informed of University communications, as some may 
            be time sensitive. Students’ official University email address should be used for all course 
            communications.  
              
            The most effective way to reach the instructor is through their University of Pittsburgh email or 
            office telephone number. Instructor contact information can be found on the course overview 
            page. Emails should be titled with the course number for clarity.  

             

            Synchronous Online Session Attendance  
            Synchronous live sessions will be held weekly through Zoom. Login details will be provided 
            within each course module. Sessions may be recorded at the discretion of the instructor.  
              
            Attendance at live sessions is a course requirement. If you are unable to attend a weekly live 
            session, please contact your instructor prior to your absence to make arrangements. Multiple 
            absences may negatively impact your overall course grade.

            8 

             

            contributing to the discussion.

            Course Disclaimer  
            The practice of physical therapy involves many techniques that require touch. In all cases, this 
            is done in the context of an examination/evaluation and in the context of treatment/healing. In 
            some situations, this may involve hand placement over areas of the body (e.g. chest, buttocks, 
            thighs, etc.) that may seem uncomfortable and/or awkward, but nevertheless necessary to 
            achieve the desired effect of managing the condition. At all times there is an expectation that 
            you respect your practice partner and communicate about the specific technique(s) you 
            will be practicing and explicitly state how/where you will be placing your hands.  

             

            If an individual is uncomfortable at any time, they can discuss acceptable alternatives with 
            the Course Instructors; however, please note that all students are expected to master the 
            didactic information and clinical skills commensurate with the course objectives.   

             

            We expect all faculty and students to practice skills in a professional manner. If you feel 
            that a fellow classmate or instructor is acting unprofessionally during any classroom or lab 
            session, please notify the lead instructor (course coordinator) or the Department Chair (Dr. 
            Irrgang). Please find additional information on actionable items on the University of Pittsburgh 
            Office for Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion webpage.

            If the situation is life-threatening, please call 911 or  988.  “988” is a suicide hotline recently 
            launched in the US.  It works the same as “911,” but dialing or texting “988” will connect a 
            person directly to the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. You do not have to be suicidal to reach out to 
            988.  The trained counselors can help you through whatever mental health challenges you are 
            experiencing.

                1. Purpose

                evaluation purposes. This policy reflects the academic standards outlined in the Commission 
                on Accreditation in Physical Therapy Education (CAPTE) Standards & Required Elements and 
                the Physical Therapy Code of Ethics, ensuring integrity, fairness, and professionalism in the 
                assessment process of rigorous physical therapy education. This policy also encourages 
                students to strive for academic excellence and mastery of the material, ensuring adequate 
                preparation to meet the demands of professional practice.  
                2. Policy 
                This written examination policy is applicable to all major written examinations throughout 
                the DPT program.  This document establishes the rules and procedures regarding 
                examination retake/remediation, scheduling, and student conduct for major written 
                examinations. 
                3. Definitions 
                Major examination: Any written examination or quiz administered to a student in a 
                proctored environment.  
                4. Major Written Examination Retake/Remediation 
                There is no opportunity for retake or formal remediation of written examinations. 
                       4.1      Course instructors may present different opportunities for students to demonstrate 
                understanding of course content.

                5. Examination Scheduling 
                5.1. The course instructor will provide the date and time of each written examination in 
                the course syllabus.

                non-class time that allows for full cohort participation. 
                Examinations scheduled during non-class time should remain between 10:00 AM – 
                6:00 PM Eastern US time. 
                Exceptions to the examination schedule may be made for students with an approved 
                excused absence.  In this case, an alternative examination schedule will be arranged 
                by the course instructor and the student. Exceptions to the examination schedule 
                will not be made for an unexcused or an unapproved absence. 
                5.3. Within a given course, all major examinations must be administered to all students 
                at the same time, and in a proctored environment (In-person/Proctorio/Zoom).  
                The length of time provided to complete an examination should not exceed the 
                scheduled class time.  
                5.3.1. All students are expected to begin the major examinations at the designated 
                start time scheduled by the course instructor. 
                5.3.2. Students are expected to refer to the course syllabus and/or Canvas 
                materials to confirm the examination start time. 
                5.3.3. Failure to begin the examination within 15 minutes of the designated start 
                time may result in a zero-grade for the examination. 
                5.4. Alternative testing arrangements recommended by the Office of Disability Resources

                6.3. Skeletons or other course related models MUST be removed from the room.

                6.4. For online testing, all students are expected to keep their laptop computers

                6.4.1. Students are required to use a camera for all online proctored examinations 
                as an added measure of security; cameras must be positioned such that the

            .Course Description 
                The first unit of this course provides a knowledge foundation for the principles that drive neurological rehabilitation, which will then be applied to the clinical management of specific neurologic diagnoses that are discussed throughout the course series. The students will be introduced to the structure of a PT neurological examination that can be applied when evaluating clients with neurologic diagnoses and disorders. We will focus on the Hypothesis-Oriented Algorithm for Clinicians (HOAC) framework for clinical decision making that will provide a foundation for client management. Information will be presented regarding motor behavior and motor control as it relates to normal and abnormal movement and function. Students will learn strategies to improve motor function and skill acquisition (motor control and motor learning) utilizing knowledge of recovery and neuroplasticity processes following an insult to the CNS.  

                The second unit of this course will apply the foundational knowledge, gained in Unit 1, to the management of clients with vestibular and balance disorders. The anatomy, physiology and function of the vestibular system will be reviewed. We will provide an overview of the etiology, pathophysiology and clinical manifestations of typical vestibular disorders. The students will learn to identify and describe common functional impairments, activity limitations and participation restrictions, which can be the result of a vestibular diagnosis. Students will learn evidence-based examination procedures used to evaluate clients with vestibular and balance disorders, based on current best practice. Students will use findings from clinical examination skills to establish a patient-centered, individualized plan of care. The role of the physical therapist in the management of patients/clients with vestibular and balance diagnoses and interventions to optimize function, activity and participation will be provided to optimize care. 

            .Course Communication 
                You should log into Canvas several times per week to work through learning modules. Course announcements will be used to post timely changes from the instructor. You are expected to check your official University of Pittsburgh email (pitt.edu) on a frequent and consistent basis to remain informed of University communications, as some may be time sensitive. Your official University email address should be used for all course communications. The most effective way to reach your instructor is through their University of Pittsburgh email or office telephone number. Instructor contact information can be found above. Emails should be titled with the course number for clarity. 

            .Course Outcomes 
                Upon completion of the course the student will be able to:
                    Integrate knowledge from anatomy, biomechanics and neuroscience to make clinical decisions to perform and interpret findings from a well-integrated and individualized examination for clients with neurological diagnoses. 
                    Develop an individualized treatment plan for clients with neurologic diagnoses using information gathered from the neurological PT examination, best evidence and the client’s unique goals and characteristics. 
                    Describe and apply current theories of motor learning, motor control and neuroplasticity to the evaluation and treatment of clients with neurologic disorders while considering unique personal and environmental factors. 
                    Demonstrate the ability to perform a PT examination, establish a prognosis and plan of care using evidence-based therapeutic interventions for clients with a vestibular and/or balance disorder.

        Unit 1 Overview
        //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
