                    .Introduction to Neurorehabilitation

                    .Course Objectives
                        • Describe and apply current theories of motor learning, motor control 
                        and neuroplasticity to the evaluation and treatment of clients with 
                        neurologic disorders while considering unique personal and environmental 
                        factors.
                        • Integrate knowledge from anatomy, biomechanics and neuroscience to 
                        make clinical decisions to perform and interpret findings from a well-integrated 
                        and individualized examination for clients with neurological diagnoses.
                        • Develop an individualized treatment plan for clients with neurologic 
                        diagnoses using information gathered from the neurological PT examination, best 
                        evidence and the client’s unique goals and characteristics.
                        • Demonstrate the ability to perform a PT examination, establish a prognosis 
                        and plan of care using evidence-based therapeutic interventions for clients with 
                        a vestibular and/or balance disorder.

                    .Course Objectives
                        • Describe and apply current theories of motor learning, motor control                          and neuroplasticity to the evaluation and treatment of clients with                          neurologic disorders while considering unique personal and environmental                          factors.

                    .Neurological Rehabilitation
                        • Main objective: Functional Competence
                        • How do we accomplish this?

                        • We help patients to:
                            Learn to identify constraints to the movement system
                            Develop strategies to accomplish tasks to achieve desired outcomes
                            Practice these strategies to refine motor skills
                            Provide motivation to promote self-efficacy

                    .Neurorehabilitation: An evolving field
                        • Neurofacilitation
                        • Muscle re-education
                        • Task-oriented motor learning

                    .Biomedical vs. Biopsychosocial Models
                        Pathology
                        ↓
                        Impairment
                        ↓
                        Functional Limitations
                        ↓
                        Disability

                        ('') (Γ)
                            ### Diagram Transcription

                            #### Top Level: Health Condition
                            - Health condition (disorder or disease):  
                              - Cerebrovascular accident (CVA)

                            #### Middle Levels: Body Functions and Structures, Activity, Participation
                            1. Body functions and structures:  
                               - Muscle weakness  
                               - Abnormal muscle tone  
                               - Impaired motor control  
                               - Sensory loss  
                               - Vertigo  

                            2. Activity:  
                               - Unable to feed self  
                               - Dependent transfers  
                               - Inefficient and unsafe ambulation that requires assistance  

                            3. Participation:  
                               - Can’t complete job  
                               - Unable to join family or social events  
                               - Engage in shopping  
                               - Attend church  

                            #### Bottom Level: Contextual Factors
                            - Environmental factors:  
                              - External elements such as physical barriers, accessibility, and societal attitudes.

                            - Personal factors:  
                              - Internal elements such as motivation, coping strategies, and personal beliefs.

                    .Neuroplasticity 1
                        • Historically, it was thought that CNS could not be regenerated 
                        if lesioned
                        • However, we now know that the brain can change!

                    .Neuroplasticity 2 (!!E).Lv3
                        • Neuroplasticity: “the brain’s capacity to be shaped or molded by experience and the ability to reorganize and recover after injury” (Johnston, 2003)
                        • Neuroplasticity can occur by:
                            Modification of synapses
                            Sprouting of new fibers
                            Neurotransmitter and receptor changes

                    .Neuroplasticity in Intact and Pathological CNS
                        BOX 1-2 Evidence of Activity-Induced Neural Plasticity in the Unimpaired and Impaired 
                        Nervous System​
                        Studies in Unimpaired Nervous System​
                        ■ Following increased use of fingers in monkeys (Jenkins, 1990)​
                        ■ With skilled Braille reading in humans with the enhanced sensory feedback (Pascual-Leone, 1993)​
                        ■ Following amputation, perhaps because of increased use of remaining portion of the limb (Hall, 1990)​
                        ■ Following practice of a novel task (three-ball cascade juggling) (Draganski, 2004)​
                        Studies in Impaired Nervous System​
                        ■ CVA: Following challenging practice of a motor task (Nudo, 2003; Hosp, 2011)​
                        ■ CVA: Following constraint-induced movement therapy (Liepert, 2000; Ishida, 2015)​
                        ■ CVA: Following virtual reality in chronic stroke (You, 2005)​
                        ■ SCI: Supralesional and sublesional reorganization of spinal cord locomotor pattern 
                        generators following body weight-supported treadmill training in spinal cord injury (Grasso, 2004)​
                        ■ SCI: Neuroplasticity after spinal cord injury (review article) (Behrman, 2006)​

                    .Principles of Neuroplasticity (Kleim, 2008) (!!E).Lv1
                        Γ(See 'Q&A doc::EXPLANATION 2' for this section)
                        TABLE 14-2 Principles of Experience-Dependent Plasticity​
                            PRINCIPLE​ + DESCRIPTION​
                                1.Use It or Lose It:
                                    Failure to drive specific brain function can lead to functional degradation.​
                                2.Use It and Improve It:
                                    Training that drives a specific brain function can lead to an enhancement of that function.​
                                3.Specificity​:
                                    The nature of the training experience dictates the nature of the plasticity​
                                4.Repetition:
                                    Matters​ Induction of plasticity requires sufficient repetition.​
                                5.Intensity:
                                    Matters​ Induction of plasticity requires sufficient training intensity.​
                                6.Time Matters​:
                                    Different forms of plasticity occur at different times during training.​
                                7.Salience Matters​:
                                    The training experience must be sufficiently salient to induce plasticity.​
                                8.Age Matters​:
                                    Training-induced plasticity occurs more readily in younger brains.​
                                9.Transference​:
                                    Plasticity in response to one training experience can enhance the acquisition of similar behaviors.
                                10.Interference​:
                                    Plasticity in response to one experience can interfere with the acquisition of other behaviors.​

                    .Use it or Lose it & Use it and Improve it
                        • Constraint-induced movement therapy
                            Restricting use of uninvolved limb                          to emphasize the use of the                          involved limb

                    .Specificity
                        • Motor skill acquisition rather than ‘use’ is necessary for changes in neuronal activity
                        • Skilled vs. unskilled movement
                        • Performance of functional tasks

                    .Repetition Matters
                        • How many reps does it take to make changes in the brain?
                        • Lang et al., 2009: Dosing and Participation: How many reps are actually being done?
                        o Mobility: 121 walking steps/OT session & 370 walking steps/PT session
                        o Upper limb functional repetitions: 41 functional reps/OT session & 12 functional reps /PT session

                    .Time Matters
                        • “…time windows in which therapy is particularly effective in directing the lesion 
                        induced reactive plasticity.”
                        • Intervene in the acute phase if medically stable
                        oAssociated with greater functional gains than delayed treatment
                        oDelays in treatment also associated with development of 
                        compensatory strategies that may interfere with treatment

                        • Caution for overuse in early vulnerable periods

                    .Salience Matters
                        • Making practice meaningful
                        • Motivation and attention are required to engage in a task

                    .Age Matters
                        • Mechanisms of neuroplasticity are reduced in the aging brain
                        • The brain can still change with experience, but may be slower and/or not as 
                        significant in older versus younger brains
                        • Training should still involve complex motor skills, aerobic exercise, and varying 
                        environments

                    .Transference and Inference
                        • Transference: plasticity within one set of neural circuits promotes concurrent 
                        or subsequent plasticity
                        oExercise promotes angiogenesis and the expression 
                        of neurotrophins to enhance neuronal growth and survival
                        • Interference: plasticity within a given neural circuitry to impede the induction 
                        of new, or expression of existing, plasticity within that same circuitry
                        oCompensatory strategies developed in the absence of rehabilitation 
                        may interfere with functional recovery
                        oExplicit cueing and instruction may interfere with learning in some individuals

                    .Translating Principles of Neuroplasticity to Practice (Winstein, 2015) ('') (!!E).Lv1
                        Γ Venn diagram
                            Be Challenging
                            Motivation and Active Participation
                            Progressive and Adaptive

                    .Summary
                        • The goal of neurorehabilitation is to restore or maintain 
                        functional competence
                        • Principles of neuroplasticity are used to drive our clinical decision-
                        making and plans of care
                        • The main principle of the task-oriented motor learning approach to 
                        neurorehabilitation is that patients must explore and practice motor 
                        tasks, self-assess, and self-correct errors

                    .Motor control and motor learning in clinical practice
                        • Every mover is unique, and each patient presents with a 
                        unique movement problem 
                        • Knowledge and understanding of motor control, motor 
                        learning and motor development is foundational for 
                        developing effective movement analysis skills, effective 
                        instruction, and effective practice environments

                    .Motor control
                    • “How the neuromuscular system functions (cooperatively) to activate and 
                    coordinate the muscles and limbs involved in the performance of a motor skill” 
                    (Magill, 2006)
                    • “Ability to regulate or direct the mechanisms essential to movement” 
                    (Shumway – Cook et al., 2012)
                    • “How the nervous system is organized so that the many individual muscles 
                    and joints become coordinated during skill execution” (Schmidt et al., 2019)
                    • You cannot see motor control! It is the underlying processes that contribute 
                    to performance, you infer whether motor control is normal/abnormal from 
                    performance (!!E.f)


                    .Movement versus skill
                    • Motor skill is goal-oriented, voluntary, and developed as a result 
                    of practice
                    oSkills are made up of movements
                    oSkills may be difficult to coordinate at first
                    oWith practice and learning, skills become more effortless
                    oMay change with conditions: stress, environment


                    .Skill classification – a continuum
                    • Gross vs fine motor: size of primary musculature required
                    • Continuous, discrete, serial: beginning and ending of the skill
                    oDiscrete: recognizable beginning and ending (kicking a ball, swinging a baseball 
                    bat)
                    oContinuous: no recognizable beginning/end; skill initiated by performer and 
                    ended by performer; rhythmic, repetitive (cycling, walking, running, swimming)
                    oSerial: discrete movements strung together (playing a piano piece, gymnastics 
                    routine)
                    • Open vs Closed: stability of the environment
                    oOpen: supporting surface, objects, people in motion (tennis, steering a car)
                    oClosed: supporting surface, object, people are stationary (when seated, picking 
                    up a cup)

                            ### Transcription of the Image: Specificity of Motor Skills

                            The image illustrates the classification of motor skills based on two primary dimensions:

                            1. Specificity of Where Actions Begin and End
                            2. Stability of the Environmental Context

                            #### 1. Specificity of Where Actions Begin and End

                            - Continuous Motor Skills  
                              - Definition: Arbitrary beginning and end of the action; repetitive movements.  
                              - Examples:  
                                - Steering a car  
                                - Walking  
                                - Swimming  

                            - Discrete Motor Skills  
                              - Definition: Specified beginning and end of the action; single movement.  
                              - Examples:  
                                - Flipping a light switch  
                                - Hitting a piano key  
                                - Depressing the clutch pedal in a car  

                            - Serial Motor Skills  
                              - Definition: Continuous series of discrete movements.  
                              - Examples:  
                                - Playing a song on the piano  
                                - Typing a sentence on a computer keyboard  
                                - Shifting gears in a standard-shift car  

                            ---

                            #### 2. Stability of the Environmental Context

                            - Open Motor Skills  
                              - Definition: Supporting surface, objects, and/or other people in motion.  
                              - Examples:  
                                - Driving a car  
                                - Catching a thrown ball  
                                - Walking on a crowded sidewalk  

                            - Closed Motor Skills  
                              - Definition: Supporting surface, objects, and/or other people stationary.  
                              - Examples:  
                                - Picking up a cup  
                                - Buttoning a shirt  
                                - Shooting a free throw in basketball  

                            ---

                            ### Organigram Flow and Interconnections

                            The diagram is structured to show how these classifications intersect based on the specificity of actions and environmental stability:

                            1. Intersection Between Continuity and Seriality:  
                               - Continuous Motor Skills are distinct from Serial Motor Skills, as continuous skills involve arbitrary beginnings and endings with repetitive movements, while serial skills involve a sequence of discrete movements.

                            2. Intersection Between Open and Closed Skills:  
                               - Open Motor Skills differ from Closed Motor Skills based on the stability of the environment. Open skills occur in dynamic environments (e.g., driving), while closed skills occur in stable environments (e.g., buttoning a shirt).

                            3. Combining Dimensions:  
                               - Skills can belong to multiple categories depending on their characteristics. For example:
                                 - Driving a car is both an Open Motor Skill (dynamic environment) and a Continuous Motor Skill (arbitrary beginnings and endings).  
                                 - Picking up a cup is both a Closed Motor Skill (stable environment) and a Discrete Motor Skill (specified beginning and end).  

                            ---

                            ### Summary Table

                            | Dimension                          | Category               | Definition                                                                 | Examples                                                                 |
                            |----------------------------------------|----------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
                            | Specificity of Where Actions Begin and End | Continuous Motor Skills | Arbitrary beginning and end of the action; repetitive movements                  | Steering a car, Walking, Swimming                                           |
                            |                                        | Discrete Motor Skills   | Specified beginning and end of the action; single movement                      | Flipping a light switch, Hitting a piano key, Depressing the clutch pedal in a car |
                            |                                        | Serial Motor Skills     | Continuous series of discrete movements                                          | Playing a song on the piano, Typing a sentence on a computer keyboard, Shifting gears in a standard-shift car |
                            | Stability of the Environmental Context | Open Motor Skills       | Supporting surface, objects, and/or other people in motion                         | Driving a car, Catching a thrown ball, Walking on a crowded sidewalk           |
                            |                                        | Closed Motor Skills      | Supporting surface, objects, and/or other people stationary                      | Picking up a cup, Buttoning a shirt, Shooting a free throw in basketball     |

                            ---

                            ### Reflection and Interconnections
                            - Overlap Between Categories: Some skills may fit into multiple categories. For example, driving a car is both Continuous (steering and repetitive movements) and Open (dynamic environment). Similarly, buttoning a shirt is both Discrete (single movement) and Closed (stationary environment).
                            - Clinical Relevance: Understanding these classifications helps tailor interventions to match the specific demands of the task. For instance:
                              - Continuous Skills (e.g., walking) require practice in rhythmic, repetitive patterns.
                              - Discrete Skills (e.g., flipping a light switch) benefit from focused, isolated training.
                              - Serial Skills (e.g., typing) demand practice in sequences of coordinated movements.
                              - Open Skills (e.g., driving) necessitate training in dynamic, unpredictable environments.
                              - Closed Skills (e.g., picking up a cup) can be practiced in controlled settings.

                            By considering both the specificity of actions and the stability of the environment, clinicians can design more effective rehabilitation programs that align with the principles of neuroplasticity and functional recovery.

                    .Motor performance
                    • The movement/action that you see
                    • You can measure it:
                    oBy the outcome, overall result
                    oBy the quality of the motion, by assessing the coordination pattern
                    oExample: gymnastics skill
                    ▪ Outcome: stay on the beam? 
                    ▪ Pattern: is the head where it’s 
                    supposed to be? Hands? Looking
                    where she’s supposed to?


                    .Coordination
                    • The patterning of head, body and/or limb motions relative to the 
                    environmental context (e.g., walking on dry surface vs. ice).
                    • Space-time pattern
                    • Generally, we talk of intralimb coordination (reach to grasp) and 
                    interlimb coordination (walking)


                    .Motor equivalency
                    • The capability of the motor control system to enable a person to 
                    perform a skill in a variety of different ways; multiple ways to achieve 
                    the same goal
                    oYou can write your signature: preferred hand, non-preferred 
                    hand, held in your mouth by your teeth. Your signature won’t 
                    look exactly the same, but you can do it


                    .Motor development
                    • Process of change that a person passes through as they grow 
                    and mature (Utley et al. 2008)
                    • ‘Adaptive change towards competence’ (Keogh 1985, referring to 
                    child motor development)
                    • The study of human development from infancy to old age with 
                    specific interest in issues related to either motor learning or motor 
                    control (Magill 2006)


                    .Theories of motor behavior 1
                    • Perception-Action Theory (Gibson) 
                    oMotor behavior is tied to a performer-environment interface
                    oWe perceive and interact with the world in relation to our own personal 
                    attributes/morphology
                    oThe perception of the individual within the environment determines the 
                    behavior that emerges
                    oTake home: patients should be engaged in familiar, functional tasks so 
                    that they can learn (or relearn) the appropriate scaling and movements 
                    required to complete the task and optimize functional competence


                    .Theories of motor behavior 2
                    • Biomechanics (Bernstein) 
                    oMotor performance arises from an infinite variety of possible combinations 
                    (degrees of freedom) of joints, muscles, and nerves
                    oMotor tasks are guided by an internal representation of an intended action 
                    reflecting external forces and internal characteristics
                    oTake home points:
                    ▪ Motor skills can be performed in a variety of ways
                    ▪ Optimal degrees of movement variability exist within our movements
                    ▪ Planning and performance of motor skills are tied to environmental context


                    .Theories of motor behavior 3
                    • Dynamic Pattern Theory
                    oCoordinated movement patterns are the primary elements of human motor 
                    behavior
                    oA preferred coordinated movement pattern may be shifted depending on the 
                    conditions of the task and/or environment
                    oVelocity of forward translation: step, walk, run
                    oTake home: motor variability may be normal if transitioning between 
                    coordinated movement patterns and may not indicate error in movement


                    .Theories of motor behavior 4
                    • Dynamic Systems (Thelan)
                    oCoordinated movement patterns reflect the interaction of numerous 
                    underlying subsystems
                    oEach subsystem, including environment, may act as a control parameter for 
                    an observed motor behavior
                    oTake home points: 
                    ▪ Perceptual processes, biomechanical influence, cognitive processing, force 
                    production capacity, sensory processing, and emotional state are all potential 
                    contributors to motor behavior
                    ▪ Evaluation of multiple subsystems and the environmental context is necessary 
                    prior to designing a therapeutic intervention for persons with neurologic disorders

                    (Γ).Theories of motor behavior 1, .Theories of motor behavior 2, .Theories of motor behavior 3, .Theories of motor behavior 4 (!!E).Q&A

                    .Motor learning
                    • “Understanding how movements are learned” (Schmidt et al., 2019)
                    • “The study of the acquisition of motor skills, or the reacquisition of skills 
                    that are difficult to perform or cannot be performed due to injury or 
                    disease” (Magill/Shumway–Cook)
                    • “Set of processes brought about by practice or experience that leads to a 
                    relatively permanent change in the capability to produce a skilled action 
                    (Schmidt & Lee, 2005)
                    • You can’t see learning, you can’t measure learning directly, measure it only 
                    indirectly via performance (!!E.f)


                    .Performance characteristics typically observed with learning
                    • Improvement – performance of the skill shows improvement over a period of 
                    time
                    • Consistency – as learning progresses, performance becomes increasingly 
                    more consistent
                    • Stability – as learning progresses, internal and external perturbations have less 
                    of an influence on performance
                    • Persistence – as the person progresses in learning the skill, the improved 
                    performance capability lasts over increasing periods of time (i.e., changes in 
                    performance become more permanent)
                    • Adaptability – the improved performance becomes adaptable to a variety of 
                    performance characteristics i.e., the skill becomes more generalizable


                    .Motor learning: long term change
                    • Consolidation - the process by which motor skills are transformed from an 
                    initial fragile state, in which they are especially prone to being disrupted or 
                    lost, to a more solid or permanent state

                    • Generalization -use of past learning in present situations of learning if the 
                    conditions in the situations are regarded as similar
                    oTransfer of knowledge onto new situations 


                    .Summary (!!E).Q&A
                    • Understanding motor control and motor learning will serve as the 
                    foundation for your examination of how someone moves, how to 
                    facilitate normalization of movement through practice and instruction
                    • A motor skill is goal-oriented, voluntary, and developed as a result of 
                    practice
                    • Motor skills need to adapt to environmental context (open → closed)

                    1:04
                    activate and coordinate the muscles and
                    1:07
                    limbs involved in the performance of a motor skill.
                    1:10
                    Although in clinical practice we evaluate
                    1:13
                    motor control, it is not something that we can actually see.
                    1:16
                    It is the underlying processes that contribute to performance.
                    1:20
                    By our observations, we infer whether motor control is
                    1:25
                    normal or abnormal from the patient's performance of the motor skill.
                    1:29
                    What is a motor skill?
                    1:34
                    Is simply moving the same as performing a skill?
                    1:36
                    No. A motor skill is
                    1:40
                    a goal-oriented voluntary action that is developed as a result of practice.
                    1:43
                    Skills are made up of movements but are not synonymous with movement.
                    1:49
                    Skills may be difficult to coordinate at first,
                    1:54
                    but with practice and learning,
                    1:57
                    motor skills become more effortless.
                    1:59
                    Motor skills may change with conditions such as stressors or environmental constraints.
                    2:02
                    Skills can be classified on a continuum.
                    2:08
                    Skills can be gross or fine motor. For example,
                    2:13
                    swinging a golf club is an example of a gross motor skill.
                    2:17
                    Playing the piano is an example of a fine motor skill.
                    2:21
                    Skills can be classified as continuous, discrete, or serial.
                    2:25
                    Discrete skills have a defined beginning and end.
                    2:31
                    For example, swinging a baseball bat.
                    2:35
                    Continuous skills have no recognizable beginning or end
                    2:38
                    and are initiated and ended by the performer.
                    2:43
                    These are typically rhythmic or repetitive skills such as cycling, walking, or swimming.
                    2:46
                    Serial skills are discrete movements that are strung together in a particular order,
                    2:52
                    such as when you're completing a gymnastics routine.
                    2:58
                    Skills can also be categorized as open or
                    3:02
                    closed based on the stability of the environment.
                    3:06
                    In open environments,
                    3:10
                    there is less stability.
                    3:12
                    The support surface, objects,
                    3:14
                    or people in the environment may be in motion,
                    3:16
                    such as when we're driving a car or playing tennis.
                    3:19
                    In closed environments, the support surface, objects,
                    3:22
                    and people in the environment are stationary,
                    3:26
                    for example, when sitting at a table drinking a glass of water
                    3:28
                    or getting dressed in your bedroom.
                    3:33
                    Here you can see the continuums of motor skills
                    3:38
                    based on where the actions begin and end
                    3:42
                    and on the stability of the environment.
                    3:45
                    This is important to think about when teaching our patients motor skills.
                    3:48
                    If a novice learner is learning a new skill,
                    3:52
                    we likely want to start in
                    3:56
                    a more closed environment and then may progress to a more open environment.
                    3:58
                    Depending on the individual and the skill,
                    4:03
                    we may break up serial motor skills into
                    4:06
                    discrete parts when we are first teaching the patient a new skill.
                    4:10
                    Motor performance is the movement or action that you see or observe.
                    4:15
                    You can measure motor performance and we all do this in clinical practice.
                    4:20
                    You can measure the outcome or overall result of
                    4:25
                    the performance by determining if the patient was able to complete the motor skill.
                    4:28
                    We can do this using clinical outcome measures,
                    4:33
                    and this may provide us with normative data.
                    4:36
                    We can also evaluate the quality of a movement by assessing the coordination pattern.
                    4:39
                    For example, for a gymnastics routine,
                    4:45
                    you may assess the outcome by determining if
                    4:48
                    the gymnast was able to complete the routine while staying on the beam.
                    4:51
                    You may assess the quality or pattern of movements by
                    4:55
                    determining if each body part is where it should be during the routine.
                    4:58
                    To expand on coordination,
                    5:03
                    this is the patterning of the head,
                    5:06
                    body, and/or limb movements relative to the environment.
                    5:09
                    The patterns of motions of our limbs may change based on
                    5:13
                    whether we are walking on a dry sidewalk versus an icy sidewalk.
                    5:17
                    Motion takes place in space and time
                    5:22
                    so can be coordinated across time and through space.
                    5:25
                    Generally, we think about
                    5:31
                    intralimb coordination or coordinating joints across one body segment,
                    5:33
                    such as when we reach to grasp an object.
                    5:38
                    We also think about interlimb coordination,
                    5:41
                    or multiple limbs coordinating together, like we do when we walk.
                    5:45
                    Motor equivalency is the capability of a motor control system to enable
                    5:50
                    a person to perform a motor skill or achieve a goal in a variety of different ways.
                    5:56
                    For example, you can write your signature with your dominant hand,
                    6:01
                    with your non-dominant hand,
                    6:05
                    or with the pen held in your mouth by your teeth.
                    6:07
                    Your signature will not look the same,
                    6:10
                    the same quality is not there,
                    6:13
                    but you know how to achieve the goal or how to complete the motor skill in various ways.
                    6:15
                    Moving on to motor development,
                    6:20
                    this is the process of change that a person goes through as they grow and mature.
                    6:23
                    Or the study of human development from infancy to old age with
                    6:29
                    specific interests in issues related to motor learning and motor control.
                    6:33
                    Now we will review several theories of
                    6:39
                    motor behavior and their application to clinical practice.
                    6:42
                    It is important to understand the underlying principles by exploring these theories
                    6:46
                    so that you can understand the rationale behind what we do in neurologic rehabilitation.
                    6:50
                    First, the perception-action theory proposes that
                    6:55
                    motor behavior is tied to a performer environment interface.
                    6:59
                    We perceive and interact with the world in relationship
                    7:05
                    to our own personal morphology or physical attributes.
                    7:09
                    For example, we can determine how high a curb is in relationship to our own bodies.
                    7:13
                    The perception of the individual within the environment
                    7:19
                    is what determines the motor behavior that emerges.
                    7:23
                    A take-home point for the perception-action theory is that patients
                    7:26
                    should be engaged in familiar functional tasks similar to those that they would
                    7:31
                    encounter or perform in real life so that they
                    7:36
                    can learn or re-learn the appropriate movements
                    7:39
                    and accurate scaling of movement required to complete
                    7:43
                    the task so that we can optimize functional competence.
                    7:47
                    In structuring practice, the environment should be set up in
                    7:51
                    a similar way to what the individual needs to do on a day-to-day basis.
                    7:55
                    The biomechanics theory suggests that motor performance arises from
                    8:00
                    an infinite variety of possible combinations of joints, muscles, and nerves.
                    8:05
                    This is termed degrees of freedom.
                    8:11
                    Motor tasks are guided by an internal representation of an intended action
                    8:15
                    reflecting both external forces and internal biomechanical characteristics.
                    8:20
                    Some take-home points to remember,
                    8:27
                    are that motor skills can be performed in a variety of ways
                    8:30
                    that optimal degrees of movement variability exist within our movements,
                    8:34
                    and remembering that planning and performance of
                    8:40
                    motor skills are tied to the environmental context.
                    8:43
                    Our movements need to be somewhat variable in order
                    8:46
                    to adapt to changing task conditions and environments.
                    8:50
                    The dynamic pattern theory states that
                    8:55
                    coordinated movement patterns are the primary elements of human motor behavior.
                    8:59
                    A preferred coordinated movement pattern
                    9:04
                    may be shifted depending on the conditions of the task and/or environment.
                    9:08
                    For example, with changes in velocity of forward translation are preferred pattern of
                    9:13
                    movement changes from taking a single step to walking slowly,
                    9:18
                    to walking quickly to running.
                    9:24
                    A take-home message to remember here is that motor variability may be
                    9:26
                    normal if we are transitioning between different coordinated movement patterns
                    9:31
                    based on the conditions of the task and/or environment and
                    9:35
                    that variability may not necessarily indicate error in movement.
                    9:40
                    The dynamic systems theory states that coordinated movement patterns reflect
                    9:46
                    the interaction of numerous underlying subsystems,
                    9:52
                    and that each of these subsystems,
                    9:56
                    including the environment,
                    9:58
                    may act as a control parameter for an observed motor behavior.
                    9:59
                    Take-home points are that perceptual processes,
                    10:05
                    biomechanical influence, cognitive processing,
                    10:10
                    force production capacity, sensory processing,
                    10:14
                    and emotional state are all potential contributors to motor behavior.
                    10:17
                    The evaluation of multiple subsystems and the environmental context is
                    10:23
                    necessary prior to designing
                    10:29
                    a therapeutic interventions for persons with neurologic disorders.
                    10:31
                    We mentioned motor learning several times during this lecture,
                    10:36
                    but what is motor learning?
                    10:40
                    Again, there are many different definitions.
                    10:42
                    Motor learning can be described as the study of the acquisition of motor skills or
                    10:44
                    the reacquisition of skills that are difficult to
                    10:50
                    perform or cannot be performed due to injury or disease.
                    10:53
                    It is the set of processes brought about by practice and experience that leads
                    10:57
                    to a relatively permanent change in the capability to produce a skilled action.
                    11:03
                    Again, you can't see learning or measure it directly,
                    11:08
                    but we measure it indirectly via performance of motor skills.
                    11:13
                    What exactly about motor performance indicates to us
                    11:19
                    that motor learning is taking place?
                    11:24
                    It may be through improvement, for example,
                    11:26
                    improvement of walking may be indicated by
                    11:30
                    a faster gait speed or a more normal gait pattern.
                    11:32
                    We may observe consistency.
                    11:36
                    As the patient practices the motor skill,
                    11:39
                    they become more consistent and make less errors.
                    11:42
                    We may observe stability or the ability to perform a motor skill
                    11:45
                    despite internal or external perturbations that may influence performance.
                    11:50
                    We may observe persistence or the ability of the individual to demonstrate
                    11:56
                    improved performance over increasing periods
                    12:01
                    of time as the changes in their performance becomes more permanent.
                    12:04
                    For example, we may observe that the patients still demonstrates
                    12:08
                    improvement in performance at their weekly follow-up visits.
                    12:12
                    Finally, we may observe adaptability or if
                    12:16
                    the improved motor performance is generalizable
                    12:20
                    across different performance and/or environmental contexts.
                    12:23
                    Over time, long-term changes due to motor learning occur via consolidation,
                    12:28
                    where motor skills are transformed from an initial state to a more permanent state.
                    12:35
                    Over time, we will also see generalization or the use of
                    12:42
                    past learning in present situations if the situations are similar.
                    12:46
                    In other words, experts in a certain motor skill will be able to
                    12:50
                    perform that skill across different situations and/or environments.
                    12:55
                    In summary, understanding motor control and motor learning will serve
                    13:00
                    as the foundation for your examination of how someone moves,
                    13:04
                    how to facilitate normalization of movement through practice and instruction.
                    13:08
                    A motor skill is goal-oriented,
                    13:14
                    voluntary, and developed as a result of practice.
                    13:17
                    Motor skills need to adapt to environmental context.
                    13:21

                    .Motor Learning
                    • Change in capability to perform a skill inferred from relatively 
                    permanent improvement in performance as a result of practice 
                    or experience (Magill)

                    • Set of (perceptual/cognitive/motor) processes associated with 
                    experience or practice leading to relatively permanent change in 
                    capability to produce skilled action (Shumway-Cook & Woollacott)

                    How do we know learning has occurred based on performance?
                    How can you tell a beginner from an expert based on performing a skill?


                    .Requirements for Motor Learning (!!E)
                        • Key features – measureable change in behavior of a motor skill; 
                        result of practice/experience; relatively permanent
                        oImprovement – noted change occurs over time
                        oConsistency – regular performance (trial to trial)
                        oStability – less variability with internal or external disruption 
                        oPersistence - permanent change in performance
                        ▪Retention – assessed after period of no practice
                        oAdaptability – adjusts to performance context; generalizable


                    .Improvement: Amount of Practice
                        • Performance changes due to practice
                        ('')
                            Experience/Practice
                            Performance
                            Retention Period


                    .Persistence: Retention Period ('')
                    • Retention – ability to demonstrate skill over time and after 
                    a period of no practice
                    oImproved performance last over longer periods

                    .Performance: Movement Variability
                    • Consistency – low variability each attempt
                    oExhibits stable performance trial to trial
                    • Stability – resistance to perturbation
                    oExhibit stable performance with internal or external disruptions
                    oCan manage stress, environmental conditions, etc.
                    • Adaptability – modifiable with context
                    oExhibit ability to generalize the skill to changes in task, 
                    environment or personal demands
                    oMay modify a task to perform a similar one


                    .Adaptability: Transfer ('')

                    .Explicit and Implicit Learning
                        Explicit learning
                        • Declarative knowledge about the 
                        activity that they are practicing
                        • Able to verbalize how they should 
                        solve a problem relating to 
                        kinematic variables of movement
                        • Cognitive demand is high
                        • Large elements of the movement 
                        being performed consciously

                        Implicit learning
                        • Procedural learning
                        • Acquisition of a skill without the 
                        concurrent acquisition of knowledge 
                        about the performance of that skill
                        • Results from large amounts of 
                        practice, often without conscious 
                        recollection of the individual 
                        components being learned


                    .Stages of Learning - Fitts & Posner 
                    • Cognitive (early – novice)
                    oHigh concentration; Self-talk
                    oNeed to understand the goal of task
                    oLots of errors; highly variable performance
                    • Associative (mid)
                    oLink environmental cues with movements
                    oLess variability in performance
                    oRefining movement; begin to detect errors
                    • Autonomous (late – expert)
                    oLess attention needed; almost automatic
                    oMay multi-task


                    .Changes with learning ('')
                    • Knowledge structure of skill
                    • Attentional demands
                    • Focus of visual selective attention
                    • Ability to detect/correct errors


                    .Motor performance: interaction of intrinsic and extrinsic constraints ('')
                    • Intrinsic constraints: inherent 
                    biomechanical, psychological, and 
                    neuromuscular attributes
                    • Extrinsic constraints: spatial and 
                    temporal regulatory features of tasks 
                    and environments
                    oSpatial: surface, available space, 
                    size and location of objects
                    oTemporal: time limits


                    • Facilitating learning relies on 
                    task analysis
                    • Two major dimensions
                    oEnvironmental context 
                    (closed/open)
                    oFunctional role (skill): 
                    stability/mobility
                    • Four components within each 
                    dimension
                    oSimple to complex
                    oTrial variability
                    oManipulation (of objects)

                    .Gentile’s Taxonomy of Tasks ('')


                    .Challenge Point
                    • Nominal task difficulty: characteristics of the task
                    • Functional task difficulty: how challenging a task is in relation to the skill level of the 
                    performer and the learning conditions
                    oDepends on:
                    ▪ Nominal difficulty of the motor task
                    ▪ Skill level of learner
                    ▪ Age of learner (child or older adult)
                    ▪ Neurological health of learner
                    • Key Points: 
                    oChallenge the motor skills of patients by exposing them to many different types of 
                    tasks
                    oIncorporate manipulation of spatial and temporal constraints of those tasks
                    oTask progressions can occur within rather than across tasks (consider open/closed 
                    and variable environments)

                    .Summary
                    • Practice should be tailored to the learner and their stage of learning
                    • Earlier stages of learning require more cognitive attention to complete 
                    the task compared to learners in later stages of learning
                    • Task analysis is important to facilitate learning and can be modified 
                    by functional roles and environmental context

                    .Attention Defined
                    • “Characteristics associated with consciousness, awareness, and 
                    cognitive effort as they relate to the performance of skills, with 
                    particular reference to the limitations associated with these 
                    characteristics on the simultaneous performance of multiple skills, 
                    and the detection of relevant information in the environment” 
                    (Magill, ch. 9, pg. 195)
                    • “Attention may refer to task and environment monitoring, scope or 
                    breadth of physical and other cues relevant to task performance, the 
                    skill or ability to control concentration despite conflicting inputs or 
                    distraction, as well as concentration on content regarding particular 
                    movement-relevant cues.” (Wulf & Lewthwaite) (!!E).Lv1


                    .Attention
                    • As PTs we need to be intentional about how we direct our 
                    patient’s attention
                    • When we go above our limited capacity there is interference

 
                    .Focusing Attention
                    • Directing resources to specific aspects of performance or the environment
                    • Attentional focus has both width and direction:
                    oWidth: amount of information and size of perceptual field
                    ▪ Can be either broad – where the performer needs to attend to a large quantity of 
                    information
                    ▪ Narrow - attention is directed to 1 or 2 locations or cues
                    ▪ Example: Ultimate Frisbee: scanning field for open opponent needs broad attentional 
                    focus, once a teammate is selected a narrow focus of attention (just on that individual ) is 
                    needed to complete the pass
                    oDirection: 
                    ▪ External = attends to information in environment
                    ▪ Internal = internal thoughts, feelings

                    
                    .Attentional Focus
                    • Is it better to focus the patient’s attention on their own movements 
                    (internal) or on the effect of their movement (external)?

                    • When the performer’s attention is directed to the movement effect 
                    (external focus), compared with the actual movement (internal focus), 
                    the result is typically greater movement accuracy and efficiency for 
                    the performer

                    
                    .Action Effect Hypothesis
                    • Actions are best planned and controlled by their intended effects
                    • In other words, focus should be on the outcome rather than the 
                    specific steps of the action
                    • Examples
                    oWhere you want to throw something
                    oJump toward target
                    oThink of golf club as a pendulum
    

                    .Attentional demands are different in stages of learning
                        • Automated through practice
                        • As the learner progresses through the stages of motor 
                        learning, there is less demand on attentional capacity
                        • In late stages of learning, may challenge attentional capacity 
                        by considering dual task training


                    .Types of attention
                    • Selective: the ability to attend to important/relevant information while 
                    ignoring other sources of information
                    • Divided: the ability/inability to perform more than one task at a time. 
                    Referred to as the ‘dual-task’ paradigm
                    • Attention switching/Alternating attention: the ability to 
                    quickly/seamlessly switch between 2 tasks or sources of information
                    • Sustained attention: ability to remain attentive over a period of time. 
                    Also called ‘vigilance.’


                    .Attention in Children
                    • ↓ Attentional Capacity
                    oMaturation of CNS increases capacity
                    • Selective Attention
                    oInfants – prefer faces, sharp contrasts, colors
                    o2-5 year-olds – narrow – they exclude info
                    o6-11 year-olds - too broad – they take in too much
                    ▪Do not know relevant from irrelevant
                    ▪Too much information to process
                    oEarly adolescence: adult-like patterns (relevant info)


                    .Attention and Older Adults
                    • Decreased Capacity -- Decreased # of brain cells
                    oLess automated
                    • Decreased Dividing attention between multiple display items
                    • Decreased Inhibition of distracters (Stroop)
                    • Decreased Difficulty switching between situations
                    • Decreased Executive processing (prefrontal lobe)


                    .Motivation and Self-Efficacy
                    • Self-efficacy: “Feeling confident about one’s ability to attain a specific level of 
                    performance in a given environment”
                    oMajor predictor of activity and participation
                    • Social Cognitive Theory (Bandura)
                    oPatients need to have early task success to build confidence and a sense of 
                    achievements
                    oBut also need to be sufficiently challenged to develop frustration tolerance
                    oSocial persuasion (praise from PT) provides motivation to patients and builds 
                    confidence
                    • OPTIMAL Theory (Wulf and Lewthwaite)
                    oConsiders the social-cognitive, affective, and attentional influences on behavior
                    oEmphasizes the importance of priming the social cognitive and affective motivational 
                    state of the patient prior and during therapeutic activities
                    Patient-centered, task-oriented training = Higher levels of self-efficacy (!!E)


                    .Optimizing Performance Through Intrinsic Motivation and Attention for Learning (The OPTIMAL theory) (!!E).Lv2
                        • Learning is enhanced when patients are provided: 
                        oOpportunities for autonomy
                        oEnhanced expectations for achieving outcomes
                        oFocus on the task goal instead of movements i.e., external focus of attention
                        oFeedback on performance success instead of feedback on errors
                        oPositive normative feedback is beneficial to automaticity, efficiency, and self-
                        perceived confidence in abilities 
                        oFeedback describing the task as a ‘learnable skill’


                    .Translating Science into Practice: Active Ingredients (Winstein, 2015) (!!E)
                        ΓVenn Diagram
                            Challenge

                            Progressive 
                            and Adaptive

                            Solicit Intrinsic 
                            Motivation for 
                            Active 
                            Participation


                    .Motivation & Active Participation
                    • Active and engaged
                    • Motivation
                    • Salient and meaningful


                    .Motivation & Promotion of Self-Efficacy
                    • Instructions can influence motor behavior
                    • Specificity of feedback
                    • Use outcomes!
                    • Promote autonomy
                    • Let the patient chose
                    • Patient-driven goals


                    .Motivational Interviewing (Emmons & Rollnick, 2001)
                    • Open-ended questions
                    • Affirmations – listen and comment on positive behaviors
                    • Reflection – active listening
                    • Summary


                    .Summary
                    • Be aware of the feedback you provide and how that may affect the 
                    development of the motor skill by drawing attention to internal or 
                    external focus
                    • Attentional demands will vary based on the individual patient and 
                    their stage of motor learning
                    • Self-efficacy can be promoted by allowing the patient to have 
                    autonomy, providing feedback on success, and incorporating task-
                    specific training

                Module 1 Summary 
                    Well done! You have completed the first of five modules for Unit 1. Before moving on to the next module, remember to review these three key learnings: 

                    Theories of motor control should be used to guide physical therapy interventions and provide evidence for using varied practice opportunities and for task-specific practice. 
                    The stages of motor learning range from early stages (novice or cognitive) to later stages (autonomous or expert) with early stages requiring more attention to complete the task. 
                    The acquisition and performance of a motor skill is impacted by attention and can be directed by the therapist by providing feedback and cues. 

                Learning Outcomes
                    After completing this module, you can now: 

                    Demonstrate an understanding of current theories of motor control and motor learning. 
                    Identify variables that affect neuroplasticity and how to create an environment to optimize skill acquisition. 
                    Apply motor learning strategies to drive skill acquisition and recovery of function.
