                    Neuromuscular 1

                    .Traditional Approaches to Neurologic Rehabilitation

                    University of Pittsburgh Department of Physical Therapy 

                    Jasmine Edwards, PT, DPT, NCS


                    .Objectives
                        • Discuss the key traditional approaches to neurological rehabilitation.
                        • Relate the traditional approaches to contemporary concepts for neurologic 
                        rehabilitation.


                    .Traditional Approaches
                        • Goal of neurologic PT is to improve 
                        our patient’s function
                        • Neurofacilitation approaches: 
                        developed for those with abnormal 
                        sensorimotor function or muscle tone
                        • Created a foundation for current 
                        approaches
                        • Based on reflex and hierarchical 
                        theories of motor control

                        Reflex Theory

                        Hierarchy Theory


                    .Rood Approach ('')
                        • Developed by Margaret Rood 
                        • Sensory stimulus is used to determine motor responses
                        • Use of developmental sequences
                        • Neuromuscular function is related to:
                        • Mobility
                        • Light work or phasic muscles
                        • Stability 
                        • Heavy work or tonic muscles


                    .Rood Approach, continued 1 ('') (!!E).Q&A
                        • Motor developmental sequences
                        • Vital function sequence
                        • Skeletal function sequence
                        • 4 levels of motor control
                        • Mobility (Level I): free active motion 
                        that translates body through space
                        • Stability (Level II): fixes body part to 
                        allow for weightbearing
                        • Controlled Mobility (Level III): 
                        weightbearing position where 
                        proximal part moves on fixed distal 
                        part
                        • Skill (Level IV): non-weightbearing 
                        position where free distal part is 
                        moving

                        Fell, Dennis. Lifespan Neurorehabilitation. Available from: VitalSource Bookshelf, F. 
                        A. Davis Company, 2017.


                    .Rood Approach, continued 2
                        (Γ)
                            ### Transcription as a Table

                            | SENSORY STIMULATION TECHNIQUES | APPLICATION OF TECHNIQUE                                                                 |
                            |-------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
                            | Light Touch                         | Quick light strokes over a muscle using either fingers, cotton, or a brush to facilitate contraction of the underlying muscle. |
                            | Tapping                             | Brisk taps with fingertips over the tendon or muscle belly of the involved muscle to facilitate phasic contraction of this muscle. |
                            | Quick Stretch                       | Quick over-elongation of a muscle (often applied at its lengthened range) to facilitate contraction. |
                            | Quick Ice                           | Quick stroking with ice on the skin over the muscle belly facilitates contraction of the underlying muscle. |
                            | Traction                            | Manually applied distraction to a joint or limb segment for muscle relaxation and to promote movement. |
                            | Approximation                       | Compression of a joint or body segment stimulates co-contraction of muscles around the body segment and promotes stability. |
                            | Resistance                          | Manual application of force away from the axis of motion at the joints as the patient is asked to move or to stabilize. |

                            ---

                            ### Transcription as an Outline

                            1. Rood Approach, continued
                               - Sensory Stimulation Techniques
                                 1. Light Touch
                                    - Application: Quick light strokes over a muscle using either fingers, cotton, or a brush to facilitate contraction of the underlying muscle.
                                 2. Tapping
                                    - Application: Brisk taps with fingertips over the tendon or muscle belly of the involved muscle to facilitate phasic contraction of this muscle.
                                 3. Quick Stretch
                                    - Application: Quick over-elongation of a muscle (often applied at its lengthened range) to facilitate contraction.
                                 4. Quick Ice
                                    - Application: Quick stroking with ice on the skin over the muscle belly facilitates contraction of the underlying muscle.
                                 5. Traction
                                    - Application: Manually applied distraction to a joint or limb segment for muscle relaxation and to promote movement.
                                 6. Approximation
                                    - Application: Compression of a joint or body segment stimulates co-contraction of muscles around the body segment and promotes stability.
                                 7. Resistance
                                    - Application: Manual application of force away from the axis of motion at the joints as the patient is asked to move or to stabilize.

                            ---

                            ### Key Points
                            - The Rood Approach utilizes sensory stimulation techniques to enhance motor control and muscle activation.
                            - Each technique targets specific physiological responses:
                              - Light Touch: Facilitates muscle contraction through light tactile stimulation.
                              - Tapping: Promotes phasic contractions by stimulating the muscle tendon or belly.
                              - Quick Stretch: Uses rapid elongation to trigger reflexive muscle contraction.
                              - Quick Ice: Utilizes cold stimulation to induce muscle contraction.
                              - Traction: Applies manual distraction to relax muscles and improve joint mobility.
                              - Approximation: Compresses joints to stimulate co-contraction and stability.
                              - Resistance: Provides manual resistance to challenge muscle strength and control.

                            This structured approach ensures that each technique is applied precisely to address specific therapeutic goals, such as improving muscle activation, enhancing stability, or promoting movement efficiency.

                    .Rood Approach, continued 3
                        ### Transcription as a Table

                        | SENSORY STIMULATION TECHNIQUES | APPLICATION OF TECHNIQUE                                                                 |
                        |-------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
                        | Prolonged Stretch                   | Slow passive lengthening of a muscle to inhibit its contraction.                           |
                        | Deep Pressure                       | Manual pressure across the longitudinal axis of the muscle tendon to cause relaxation.      |
                        | Neutral Warmth                      | Wrapping of body or limb in blanket, towel, or air splint for purpose of general relaxation. |
                        | Slow Stroking                       | Slow stroking with the hand along midline of the back, near the posterior rami, for 3 to 5 minutes leads to calming of patient. |
                        | Prolonged Cold                      | Application of an ice pack or ice massage over a muscle leads to its relaxation and reduction of pain. |

                        ---

                        ### Transcription as an Outline

                        1. Sensory Stimulation Techniques
                           - Prolonged Stretch
                             - Application: Slow passive lengthening of a muscle to inhibit its contraction.
                           - Deep Pressure
                             - Application: Manual pressure across the longitudinal axis of the muscle tendon to cause relaxation.
                           - Neutral Warmth
                             - Application: Wrapping of body or limb in blanket, towel, or air splint for purpose of general relaxation.
                           - Slow Stroking
                             - Application: Slow stroking with the hand along midline of the back, near the posterior rami, for 3 to 5 minutes leads to calming of patient.
                           - Prolonged Cold
                             - Application: Application of an ice pack or ice massage over a muscle leads to its relaxation and reduction of pain.

                        ---

                        ### Key Takeaways
                        - Prolonged Stretch: Used to inhibit muscle contraction by slowly lengthening the muscle passively.
                        - Deep Pressure: Applies manual pressure along the muscle tendon to promote relaxation.
                        - Neutral Warmth: Uses general warming techniques like blankets or air splints to relax the body or limb.
                        - Slow Stroking: Calms the patient through slow, soothing strokes along the midline of the back.
                        - Prolonged Cold: Reduces pain and promotes muscle relaxation using ice packs or ice massages.

                        These sensory stimulation techniques are valuable tools in physical therapy, each targeting specific physiological responses to enhance relaxation, reduce pain, and improve overall function.

                    .Rood Approach, continued 3 & .Rood Approach, continued 4 Q&A
                        ### Test Questions Based on the Provided Content

                        #### Section 1: Rood Approach, continued 2

                        1. Which sensory stimulation technique involves quick light strokes over a muscle using either fingers, cotton, or a brush to facilitate contraction of the underlying muscle?
                           - A) Prolonged Stretch
                           - B) Light Touch
                           - C) Deep Pressure
                           - D) Quick Ice

                           Correct Answer: B) Light Touch

                           Rationale:  
                           - Light Touch is specifically described as using quick, light strokes over a muscle to facilitate contraction. This technique targets the superficial cutaneous receptors, which can enhance motor control and muscle activation.
                           - Prolonged Stretch (Option A) is used for inhibiting muscle contraction by slowly lengthening the muscle passively, not facilitating contraction.
                           - Deep Pressure (Option C) applies manual pressure across the longitudinal axis of the muscle tendon to cause relaxation, not facilitation.
                           - Quick Ice (Option D) uses cold stimulation to induce muscle contraction but does so through a different mechanism than light touch.

                        2. What is the primary purpose of the Tapping technique in the Rood Approach?
                           - A) To promote phasic contractions by stimulating the muscle tendon or belly.
                           - B) To inhibit muscle contraction by applying prolonged stretch.
                           - C) To reduce pain through application of ice.
                           - D) To enhance stability by compressing joints.

                           Correct Answer: A) To promote phasic contractions by stimulating the muscle tendon or belly.

                           Rationale:  
                           - Tapping involves brisk taps with fingertips over the tendon or muscle belly, which stimulates the muscle spindles and promotes reflexive phasic contractions. This technique is designed to activate specific muscles quickly.
                           - Inhibiting muscle contraction (Option B) is achieved through techniques like Prolonged Stretch, not tapping.
                           - Reducing pain (Option C) is associated with techniques like Prolonged Cold, not tapping.
                           - Enhancing stability (Option D) is achieved through Approximation, not tapping.

                        3. Which technique involves manually applied distraction to a joint or limb segment for muscle relaxation and to promote movement?
                           - A) Resistance
                           - B) Traction
                           - C) Approximation
                           - D) Slow Stroking

                           Correct Answer: B) Traction

                           Rationale:  
                           - Traction involves manually applying distraction to a joint or limb segment, which helps relax muscles and improve joint mobility. This technique is distinct from others because it focuses on mechanical distraction.
                           - Resistance (Option A) involves manual application of force away from the axis of motion, not distraction.
                           - Approximation (Option C) compresses joints to stimulate co-contraction and stability, not distraction.
                           - Slow Stroking (Option D) calms the patient through slow, soothing strokes along the midline of the back, not distraction.

                        4. What is the purpose of the Approximation technique in the Rood Approach?
                           - A) To facilitate muscle contraction through quick light strokes.
                           - B) To promote phasic contractions by tapping the muscle tendon.
                           - C) To stimulate co-contraction of muscles around a body segment and promote stability.
                           - D) To reduce pain through application of ice.

                           Correct Answer: C) To stimulate co-contraction of muscles around a body segment and promote stability.

                           Rationale:  
                           - Approximation involves compression of a joint or body segment, which stimulates co-contraction of muscles around that segment, enhancing stability.
                           - Facilitating muscle contraction through quick light strokes (Option A) is the purpose of Light Touch, not Approximation.
                           - Promoting phasic contractions by tapping the muscle tendon (Option B) is the purpose of Tapping, not Approximation.
                           - Reducing pain through application of ice (Option D) is the purpose of Prolonged Cold, not Approximation.

                        5. Which technique involves manual application of force away from the axis of motion at the joints as the patient is asked to move or stabilize?
                           - A) Traction
                           - B) Resistance
                           - C) Quick Stretch
                           - D) Neutral Warmth

                           Correct Answer: B) Resistance

                           Rationale:  
                           - Resistance involves manually applying force away from the axis of motion, challenging the patient’s muscle strength and control. This technique is distinct from others because it focuses on providing an external load.
                           - Traction (Option A) involves manually applied distraction to a joint or limb segment, not resistance.
                           - Quick Stretch (Option C) involves rapid elongation of a muscle to trigger reflexive contraction, not resistance.
                           - Neutral Warmth (Option D) involves general warming techniques like blankets or air splints, not resistance.

                        ---

                        #### Section 2: Rood Approach, continued 3

                        6. Which sensory stimulation technique involves slow passive lengthening of a muscle to inhibit its contraction?
                           - A) Quick Stretch
                           - B) Prolonged Stretch
                           - C) Deep Pressure
                           - D) Slow Stroking

                           Correct Answer: B) Prolonged Stretch

                           Rationale:  
                           - Prolonged Stretch is specifically described as slowly lengthening a muscle passively to inhibit its contraction. This technique targets the Golgi tendon organs, which respond to sustained stretch.
                           - Quick Stretch (Option A) involves rapid elongation of a muscle to trigger reflexive contraction, not inhibition.
                           - Deep Pressure (Option C) applies manual pressure across the longitudinal axis of the muscle tendon to cause relaxation, not inhibition.
                           - Slow Stroking (Option D) calms the patient through slow, soothing strokes along the midline of the back, not inhibition.

                        7. What is the primary purpose of the Deep Pressure technique in the Rood Approach?
                           - A) To inhibit muscle contraction by slowly lengthening the muscle.
                           - B) To promote relaxation by applying manual pressure across the longitudinal axis of the muscle tendon.
                           - C) To calm the patient through slow stroking along the midline of the back.
                           - D) To reduce pain through application of ice.

                           Correct Answer: B) To promote relaxation by applying manual pressure across the longitudinal axis of the muscle tendon.

                           Rationale:  
                           - Deep Pressure involves manual pressure across the longitudinal axis of the muscle tendon, which promotes relaxation by activating mechanoreceptors that inhibit muscle tone.
                           - Inhibiting muscle contraction by slowly lengthening the muscle (Option A) is the purpose of Prolonged Stretch, not Deep Pressure.
                           - Calming the patient through slow stroking along the midline of the back (Option C) is the purpose of Slow Stroking, not Deep Pressure.
                           - Reducing pain through application of ice (Option D) is the purpose of Prolonged Cold, not Deep Pressure.

                        8. Which technique involves wrapping the body or limb in a blanket, towel, or air splint for the purpose of general relaxation?
                           - A) Prolonged Stretch
                           - B) Deep Pressure
                           - C) Neutral Warmth
                           - D) Slow Stroking

                           Correct Answer: C) Neutral Warmth

                           Rationale:  
                           - Neutral Warmth involves general warming techniques like blankets, towels, or air splints to relax the body or limb. This technique provides a calming effect through thermal stimulation.
                           - Prolonged Stretch (Option A) involves slow passive lengthening of a muscle to inhibit contraction, not general relaxation.
                           - Deep Pressure (Option B) applies manual pressure across the longitudinal axis of the muscle tendon, not general relaxation.
                           - Slow Stroking (Option D) calms the patient through slow, soothing strokes along the midline of the back, not general relaxation.

                        9. What is the primary purpose of the Slow Stroking technique in the Rood Approach?
                           - A) To inhibit muscle contraction by slowly lengthening the muscle.
                           - B) To promote relaxation by applying manual pressure across the longitudinal axis of the muscle tendon.
                           - C) To calm the patient through slow, soothing strokes along the midline of the back.
                           - D) To reduce pain through application of ice.

                           Correct Answer: C) To calm the patient through slow, soothing strokes along the midline of the back.

                           Rationale:  
                           - Slow Stroking involves slow, soothing strokes along the midline of the back near the posterior rami, which calms the patient by activating parasympathetic responses.
                           - Inhibiting muscle contraction by slowly lengthening the muscle (Option A) is the purpose of Prolonged Stretch, not Slow Stroking.
                           - Promoting relaxation by applying manual pressure across the longitudinal axis of the muscle tendon (Option B) is the purpose of Deep Pressure, not Slow Stroking.
                           - Reducing pain through application of ice (Option D) is the purpose of Prolonged Cold, not Slow Stroking.

                        10. Which technique involves the application of an ice pack or ice massage over a muscle to lead to its relaxation and reduction of pain?
                            - A) Quick Ice
                            - B) Prolonged Cold
                            - C) Neutral Warmth
                            - D) Slow Stroking

                            Correct Answer: B) Prolonged Cold

                            Rationale:  
                            - Prolonged Cold involves the application of an ice pack or ice massage over a muscle to reduce pain and promote relaxation. This technique targets nociceptors and reduces inflammation.
                            - Quick Ice (Option A) uses cold stimulation to induce muscle contraction, not relaxation.
                            - Neutral Warmth (Option C) involves general warming techniques like blankets or air splints, not cold application.
                            - Slow Stroking (Option D) calms the patient through slow, soothing strokes along the midline of the back, not cold application.

                    .Brunnstrom’s Approach
                        - Developed by Signe Brunnstrom
                        - Observed abnormal synergy patterns following stroke

                        #### Flexion Synergy
                        - Upper Extremity
                          - Scapula: retraction and elevation
                          - Shoulder: abduction and external rotation
                          - Elbow: flexion
                          - Forearm: supination
                          - Wrist: flexion
                          - Fingers/Thumb: flexion and adduction
                        - Lower Extremity
                          - Pelvis: elevation and retraction
                          - Hip: flexion, abduction, external rotation
                          - Knee: flexion
                          - Ankle: dorsiflexion and inversion
                          - Toe: dorsiflexion

                          ¦Bàsicament contragut i cap a fora; prova-ho físicament (!!E)

                        #### Extension Synergy
                        - Upper Extremity
                          - Scapula: protraction and depression
                          - Shoulder: adduction, internal rotation
                          - Elbow: extension
                          - Forearm: pronation
                          - Wrist: flexion or extension
                          - Fingers/Thumb: flexion and adduction
                        - Lower Extremity
                          - Hip: extension, adduction, internal rotation
                          - Knee: extension
                          - Ankle: plantar flexion and inversion
                          - Toes: plantar flexion

                    .Brunnstrom’s Approach, continued 1 (!!E).Lv1.Q&A.Questions(!!Blind).Do the quiz
                        • Incorporated the use of developmental reflexes
                            • Body positions can be used to inhibit or facilitate a response
                        • Stages of motor recovery after stroke
                            • Stage 1: Extremities are flaccid (no movement and decreased tone)
                            • Stage 2: Spasticity begins to develop, gradual voluntary movements
                            • Stage 3: Voluntary movements through partial ROM of synergy pattern
                            • Stage 4: Begin to move out of synergy, spasticity starts to decline
                            • Stage 5: Synergies lose dominance
                            • Stage 6: Isolated movement is possible, coordination near normal

                    .Brunnstrom’s Approach, continued 2 (!!E).Lv2.Questions(!!Blind).Do the quiz
                        • Clinical Beliefs:
                        • Have to move through all stages of recovery
                        • When a limb is flaccid movement is performed using reflexes
                        • To move out of a synergistic pattern they must have active movement in 
                        flexion and extension synergies
                        • For complex movement the weaker synergy pattern must be strengthened

                    .Neurodevelopmental Treatment (NDT)
                        • Developed by Berta and Karl Bobath
                        • Normal postural reflex mechanisms are necessary for motor skills
                        • A “living” concept with change occurring as new evidence emerges
                        • Incorporated a focus on the task and environment
                        • Interventions are based on the individual’s needs
                        • Key points of control is an important component of interventions
                        • Limit practice of abnormal patterns
                        • Begins with postural alignment

                    .Neurodevelopmental Treatment (NDT), continued
                        • Goals of treatment
                        • Modify abnormal tone
                        • Facilitated automatic postural reactions
                        • Use developmental positions to facilitate recovery
                        • Provide normal sensory – motor experience
                        • Use of key points of control
                        • Use of biomechanical and postural alignment
                        • Emphasis on handling patient for intrinsic feedback
                        • Improve quality of movement during functional tasks

                    .Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation (PNF)
                        • Developed by Herman Kabat, Margaret Knott, & Dorothy Voss
                        • Used in examination and intervention for patients with musculoskeletal or 
                        neuromuscular dysfunction
                        • Goals:
                        • Increase the patient’s ability to move or remain stable
                        • Help the patient achieve coordinated motion
                        • Increase the patient’s stamina and avoid fatigue

                    .Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation (PNF), continued 1
                        • Basic procedures:
                        • Manual Contacts
                        • Body Position and Body Mechanics
                        • Quick Stretch 
                        • Appropriate Resistance
                        • Verbal Command
                        • Visual Stimuli
                        • Traction
                        • Approximation
                        • Timing

                                    Flexion/Abduction/ER D2
                                Extension: 
                                    Extension/Abduction/IR D1
                                    Extension/Adduction/IR D2
                            LE
                                Flexion
                                    Flexion/Adduction/ER D1

                    .Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation (PNF) 3 (!!E).Lv2.Questions(!!Blind).Do the quiz
                        ('')
                            #### Technique
                            - Rhythmic Initiation
                              - PROM → AAROM → AROM → Resisted ROM
                              - Initiate movement; facilitate improvement in speed, direction, quality of movement

                            - Agonist Reversals
                              - Concentric → eccentric → concentric contractions of agonistic muscle repeated
                              - Increase joint ROM; improve strength and coordination of movement

                            - Repeated Contractions
                              - Isotonic contraction of agonist
                              - Increase active ROM, strength, & endurance of the agonist, and relaxation of the antagonist

                            - Slow Reversals
                              - Concentric contractions of antagonistic muscle groups without relaxation between reversals
                              - Increase agonist motion; strengthen agonist/antagonist

                            - Alternating Isometrics
                              - Isometric of agonist then antagonist
                              - Increase isometric strength of postural muscles of trunk and proximal muscles

                            - Rhythmic Stabilization
                              - Simultaneous isometric of agonist/antagonist
                              - Improve postural control, balance, and stability in various functional, weight-bearing positions

                            - Contract Relax
                              - PROM of the limb to ROM limitation in the agonist pattern and then a max isotonic contraction of the antagonist is performed and resisted
                              - Relaxation of muscles antagonistic to active muscle group to increase ROM into the agonist movement pattern

                            - Hold Relax
                              - Isometric contraction of muscle then relaxation and elongation during the relaxation phase
                              - Relaxation and increased ROM

                    .Sensory Integration Theory
                        • Developed by Jean Ayres
                        • “the neurological process that organizes sensation from one’s own body and 
                        from the environment and makes it possible to use the body effectively within the 
                        environment” 
                        • Integration of sensory systems for movement
                        • Processing of sensory information followed a developmental sequence
                        • “stand-alone problem” 
                        • Team approach for interventions

                    .Summary
                        • Traditional approaches are based on the reflex and hierarchy theories of motor 
                        control.
                        • They laid the foundation for current treatment approaches.
                        • Many are incorporated into contemporary interventions and are still widely used 
                        in the clinic.

                    4:24
                    this occurs when there is a contraction of agonist and
                    4:26
                    antagonist that allows for the body to be fixed in a position for weight bearing.
                    4:30
                    Control mobility or level 3,
                    4:35
                    it builds upon level 2 and it allows for
                    4:38
                    the proximal segments of the body to be moved over the fixed distal body part.
                    4:42
                    Then there's finally skill or level 4,
                    4:47
                    where the distal body part is freely moving on the stable proximal body part.
                    4:50
                    The figure on the right provides a visual of Rood sequence of
                    4:56
                    motor development and how a patient would move through the previously described levels.
                    5:01
                    A physical therapist would identify the component of the sequence which was missing and
                    5:07
                    work to restore it in the order in which it would
                    5:13
                    naturally be acquired for learning to occur.
                    5:15
                    To either facilitate or inhibit patient responses,
                    5:20
                    Rood use sensory stimulation techniques.
                    5:24
                    There are a number of techniques used within this approach and
                    5:27
                    the ones listed on this slide within the table are considered faciliatory.
                    5:31
                    Light touch consists of quick light strokes over a muscle using either fingers,
                    5:35
                    cotton or a brush to facilitate contraction of the underlying muscle.
                    5:41
                    Tapping occurs when there is brisk taps with the fingertips over the tendon or
                    5:46
                    muscle belly of the involved muscle to facilitate that phasic contraction of the muscle.
                    5:51
                    An example is tapping the triceps muscle to
                    5:57

                    6:00

                    6:05

                    6:09
                    which excite afferent resulting in firing of
                    6:12
                    Alpha motor neurons and contraction of
                    6:16
                    the triceps and simultaneous inhibition of the biceps.
                    6:18
                    Quick stretch occurs when there's this quick over elongation of
                    6:23
                    a muscle typically performed when it's
                    6:28
                    in this lengthen range to facilitate a contraction.
                    6:31
                    Quick ice is where there's quick stroking with ice on the skin over
                    6:35
                    the muscle belly which facilitates contraction of the underlying muscle and traction.
                    6:39
                    You may actually be familiar with this technique from musculoskeletal courses,
                    6:46
                    especially in reference to the neck.
                    6:50
                    That's where it's manually applied distraction to
                    6:53
                    a joint or limb segment for muscle reheatelaxation and to promote movement.
                    6:56

                    7:01
                    a joint or body segment that stimulates
                    7:06
                    co-contraction of muscles around that body segment for stability.
                    7:09
                    This can be used for lower extremity weight bearing and standing.
                    7:14
                    An example could be approximation of the pelvis down into the thigh.
                    7:19
                    Resistance is where there's manual application of force away
                    7:24
                    from the axis of motion at the joints as the patient is asked to move or to stabilize.
                    7:30
                    The techniques listed on this slide within this table are inhibitory of
                    7:36
                    abnormal reflex activity and hypertonicity by
                    7:42
                    shifting the balance of the autonomic nervous system from sympathetic to parasympathetic.
                    7:45
                    Prolonged stretch occurs when there is
                    7:51

                    7:53

                    7:58

                    8:01

                    8:05

                    8:08

                    8:12

                    8:17

                    8:22

                    8:27

                    8:30

                    8:35

                    8:41

                    8:46

                    8:50

                    8:55

                    9:12

                    9:24

                    9:28
                    Brunnstrom's approach was created by Signe Brunnstrom in
                    9:34

                    9:39

                    9:46

                    9:49
                    After a lesion or an injury to the central nervous system,
                    9:56

                    10:00

                    10:05

                    10:11

                    10:15
                    A flexion synergy of
                    10:18

                    10:21

                    10:26

                    10:31

                    10:33

                    10:35
                    If the lower extremity,
                    10:42

                    10:44

                    10:50

                    10:54

                    10:56

                    11:00

                    11:02

                    11:13

                    11:16

                    11:22

                    11:27

                    11:31

                    11:33

                    11:45

                    12:04

                    12:09

                    12:13

                    12:21

                    12:23

                    12:29

                    12:32

                    12:35
                    The Brunnstrom stages of motor recovery after stroke are still widely used in the clinic.
                    12:39

                    12:45

                    12:49

                    12:55

                    13:01

                    13:04

                    13:08

                    13:13

                    13:18

                    13:22

                    13:28

                    13:31

                    13:37

                    13:39

                    13:43

                    13:50

                    13:55

                    14:02

                    17:46

                    17:52

                    18:07

                    18:38

                    18:47

                    18:56

                    19:00

                    19:05

                    19:09

                    19:14

                    20:07

                    20:10

                    21:54

                    21:58

                    .Challenge Point Hypothesis 1
                        • Optimal level of information that helps learner learn

                        • Keep the learner challenged

                        • Adjust task and practice environment so there is some 
                        success while still challenging the learner


                    .Challenge Point Hypothesis 2
                    • Begin with “nominal task difficulty”

                    • Adjust functional task difficulty through adaptive practice
                    oUse of assistive device
                    oPractice as a closed vs. open skill
                    oLess info to process; fewer parts
                    oSize of racquet; size of bat; size of ball; speed of object, etc.

                    • Even better if the learner chooses when to adjust difficulty of the task
                    • Beware of excessive adaptations

                    .Challenge Point Hypothesis 3
                    • What is the functional task difficulty?
                    • Depends on:
                    oNominal difficulty of the motor task
                    oSkill level of learner
                    oAge of learner (child or older adult)
                    oNeurological health of learner
                    • Frequency of and type of feedback
                    • Type and structure of practice

                    .Practice (!!E).Lv2
                    • Manipulation of practice condition
                    oDistribution of practice
                    oPractice order
                    oVariability of practice
                    oEnvironment of practice

                    .Distribution of Practice
                    • Massed practice: repetition of a motor task with minimal rest 
                    between trials or between practice sessions
                    • Distributed practice: repetition of a task with trials, blocks of trials, 
                    or practice sessions spaced out over time

                    • The effects of performance and rest schedules seem different for 
                    discrete and continuous tasks

                    .Evidence for Distributed Practice
                    • Learning to type (Baddeley & Longman, 1978)
                    oDistributed Practice
                    • Why?
                    oFatigue, cognitive effort
                    oMemory consolidation (sleep)
                    oSpecificity of practice


                    .Part vs. Whole Practice 1
                    • Part practice: a task is broken into component parts and practiced 
                    oWorks best when the actions of one part does not influence the actions of the 
                    next part
                    oEffective if the parts being practiced are naturally occurring subdivisions of 
                    the task
                    oIt is not beneficial to practice parts of continuous tasks (ambulation) (!!E)


                    .Part and Whole Practice 2
                    • Phases of locomotion cycle may represent inseparable portions of a rapid short 
                    duration task
                    oWhole task practice is more effective for tasks involving continuous motion
                    oWeight-shifting practice improved standing weight shifting but not weight 
                    shifting during gait (Winstein)
                    For all part practice: Make sure learner knows the big picture


                    .Observational Learning & Mental Practice ('')
                        • Observation of others (or self) 
                        completing a task promotes 
                        learning
                        • Imagining rehearsal of the task 
                        can be an adjunct to physical 
                        practice

                        ('')
                            (Γ)
                                Here is the exact word-for-word transcription, structured to reflect the organigram flow and interconnections between its elements:

                                ### Organigram Flow Transcription
                                #### Main Process
                                1. Assess mental capacity
                                2. Establish nature of mental practice
                                3. Teach imagery technique
                                4. Embed and monitor
                                5. Develop self-generated treatments

                                #### Interconnections and Refinements
                                - Incorporating a new activity (linked to multiple stages)
                                - Refining (continuous improvement across the entire process)

                                Each step logically leads into the next, creating a structured flow from assessment to self-generated treatments, with refinement and new activity incorporation playing ongoing roles in the system.

                    .Mental Practice
                    • Practicing the sequence – mental practice

                    • Imaging doing skill – mental imagery
                    o Vividness – controlling the image
                    o Internal perspective; external perspective


                    .Mental Practice – When?
                    • First stage: mental + physical
                    • Motor component
                    o Need some physical experience first
                    • Cognitive component 
                    o Prior to physical practice

                    • OVERALL RULE: 
                    oPhysical practice better than mental, and mental better than 
                    none
                    oMental practice may be used as an adjunct to physical

                    .Guided Practice 
                    • Helps with performance, not learning (!!E)
                    • Can help beginner
                    • Can help if dangerous
                    • Don’t overuse → will become dependent

                    .Guided Discovery Training
                        • Directed by the patient with some therapist support/input
                        • Generally yields better skill acquisition, retention, and generalization compared to 
                        physical guidance or training with high therapist control (!!E)
                        • Less prevalent in clinical practice
                        • Patient involved in selection of activities, assessment of performance, 
                        determining strategies to complete the task, directs practice, and summarizes 
                        learning (!!E)
                        • May not be appropriate for all – particularly individuals with cognitive impairment

                    .The Role of Error in Learning
                    Errorless learning
                    • Implicit learning through repetitive 
                    task-specific training without the 
                    experience of error
                    • Tasks may be broken into parts and 
                    each part practiced before 
                    completing the whole task
                    • Feedback typically provided 
                    frequently at first and then may be 
                    faded over time
                    • May allow for less generalization

                    Errorful learning 
                    • Implicit learning through skill 
                    execution without a prior instruction
                    • Feedback is typically withheld and 
                    learning occurs through practice
                    • Allows for self correction and learning 
                    from mistakes
                    • Therapists can elicit patient analysis 
                    of performance after the fact to 
                    generate adaptations for future 
                    performance


                    .Limitations of Task-Specific Training (!!P)
                    • May not be appropriate for all patients
                    oSelection is dependent on degree of recovery
                    ▪ Medically unstable
                    • Severity of motor and/or cognitive deficits
                    ▪ Limited voluntary movement require hand-on approach
                    ▪ Limited motor learning capabilities 


                    .Summary
                    • Practice should include tasks that are sufficiently challenging
                    • Whole task practice should be used for most tasks; if part practice is 
                    used, the whole task should be kept in mind
                    • Physical practice is superior to mental practice only; but mental 
                    practice may be used in conjunction with or if physical practice is not 
                    possible
                    • Allowing for errors in learning and guided discovery training is 
                    associated with greater skill acquisition, retention, and generalization

                    0:41

                    0:44

                    0:47

                    0:51

                    0:55

                    1:39

                    1:43

                    1:54

                    1:57

                    2:03

                    2:07

                    2:10

                    2:14

                    2:19

                    2:23

                    2:26
                    to identify intrinsic and external constraints of the task,
                    2:30
                    creating a motor plan and modifying or refining that motor plan.
                    2:34

                    2:38

                    2:41

                    2:46

                    2:48

                    2:49

                    2:52

                    2:56
                    a motor task with minimal rest between trials or between practice sessions.
                    3:00

                    3:05
                    trials or blocks of trials spaced out over time.
                    3:10
                    Tasks that are more discreet and simple can
                    3:14

                    3:18
                    However, providing rest to allow for
                    3:21

                    3:25
                    Braddeley and Longman conducted a study to determine the optimal length
                    3:30

                    3:36
                    As you can see from the table,
                    3:41
                    the participants who practiced one hour per day over the course of
                    3:43
                    12 weeks learned the keyboard in the fewest number of hours overall
                    3:47

                    3:53
                    Those who practiced more intensively with more hours per day,
                    3:59
                    but for fewer weeks,
                    4:03

                    4:05
                    Why might this be?
                    4:11
                    Well, after an hour of training,
                    4:13
                    the participants may have been fatigued from the physical and/or cognitive effort.
                    4:16
                    They may not have had the capacity to attend to the task for longer than an hour.
                    4:20
                    Also, we know that sleep is important for memory consolidation,
                    4:25
                    so maybe those who were given more opportunities to
                    4:30

                    4:33
                    to have consolidation of the motor task because they
                    4:36

                    4:39
                    Finally, we know that specificity of practice is important.
                    4:42
                    It may not be likely that someone is typing for two hours straight,
                    4:46

                    4:50

                    4:53
                    Another type of practice structure that we may
                    4:59
                    use is part practice versus whole practice.
                    5:02
                    Part practice is when we take a task and break it down
                    5:06
                    into its component parts and then those parts are practiced.
                    5:09
                    This type of practice works best when the actions of one part
                    5:14
                    does not necessarily influence the action of the next part of the task.
                    5:18
                    It is also most effective to use part practice when
                    5:22
                    the parts of the task are naturally occurring subdivisions.
                    5:26
                    It is not beneficial to practice parts of a continuous skill such as ambulation.
                    5:30
                    This is because phases of the locomotion cycle are not meant to be separated.
                    5:37
                    The biomechanics change when you only practice
                    5:42
                    a single-step rather than continuous locomotion.
                    5:45
                    Therefore, utilizing whole practice is more beneficial for continuous skills.
                    5:48
                    In a study by Winstein,
                    5:54
                    they found that practicing weight shifting
                    5:56
                    improved weight shifts that were utilized in standing,
                    5:58
                    but not weight shifts during an ambulation cycle.
                    6:02
                    Therefore, to improve weight shifting during ambulation,
                    6:05

                    6:09
                    In addition, whenever utilizing part practice,
                    6:13
                    the learner should know the big picture and should keep in mind the entire task.
                    6:17
                    Observational learning can be helpful to learn a motor skill.
                    6:23
                    This is when the patient has the opportunity to
                    6:28
                    either observe someone else completing the task
                    6:30
                    or observe themselves completing a task.
                    6:33
                    It is especially helpful when someone is able to
                    6:36

                    6:39

                    6:42

                    6:45

                    6:48

                    6:51
                    or having two patients that are around
                    6:55
                    the same skill level work together on the same task.
                    6:57
                    Mental imagery can also be used as an adjunct to physical practice and has demonstrated
                    7:01
                    enhanced effects for learning
                    7:07
                    functional activities and generalization of learned activities.
                    7:08
                    Functional imaging shows us that brain activation for patients who are
                    7:13

                    7:17

                    7:22

                    7:25
                    Braun and colleagues suggests the framework
                    7:28

                    7:31

                    7:34

                    7:37

                    7:41
                    It should be embedded and monitored by the physical therapist.
                    7:45

                    7:50

                    7:54
                    It can be helpful to ask the patient to rehearse
                    8:02

                    8:05

                    8:09

                    8:14

                    8:19

                    8:24

                    8:28

                    8:29
                    Or they can imagine the task from an external perspective,
                    8:32
                    or imagining watching themselves completing
                    8:37
                    the task similar to watching a video of themselves.
                    8:40
                    When is mental practice helpful?
                    8:44
                    It may be helpful as a first stage,
                    8:47
                    but it is always a good idea to have some physical practice
                    8:50
                    first that allows for more focus and specific mental practice.
                    8:53
                    It can be helpful as an adjunct to physical practice when
                    8:59
                    the patient is unable to participate in physical practice,
                    9:03
                    maybe due to safety concerns or some other reason.
                    9:06
                    A good rule of thumb is that physical practice is better than mental practice.
                    9:10
                    But mental practice is better than no practice at all.
                    9:15
                    Again, mental practice may be used as an adjunct to physical practice.
                    9:18
                    Guided practice refers to practicing a task with manual assistance.
                    9:24
                    As physical therapists, we are often providing
                    9:30
                    manual or physical guidance for safety or to allow for completion of a task.
                    9:32
                    However, beware of providing patients with
                    9:38
                    too much manual guidance because they may become reliant on having assistance.
                    9:41
                    Providing manual assistance to someone else while they complete
                    9:47
                    a task changes the biomechanics of that task.
                    9:50
                    In addition, the patient may become reliant on external manual cueing,
                    9:54
                    rather than that intrinsic feedback
                    9:59
                    that is necessary to appropriately complete the task.
                    10:02
                    Manual guidance may be used with caution when there is
                    10:06
                    a safety concern or for just learning a task.
                    10:09
                    But the patient should be generating their own movement strategies and
                    10:13
                    patterns and should not be relying solely on external inputs.
                    10:17
                    With guided discovery training,
                    10:23
                    this is a type of strategy training where the therapist has less control over practice.
                    10:26
                    The practice is largely directed by the patient with
                    10:32
                    some therapists support or queuing from the therapist for patient engagement.
                    10:35
                    This generally leads to better skill acquisition, retention,
                    10:39
                    and generalization compared to
                    10:44
                    physical guidance or training with high therapists control.
                    10:46
                    Guided discovery is currently less prevalent in clinical practice,
                    10:50
                    but really can be beneficial to promote
                    10:55
                    motor learning because of high levels of patient engagement.
                    10:57
                    The patient is involved in the selection of activities,
                    11:01
                    assessment of their performance,
                    11:04
                    determining strategies to complete the motor task,
                    11:06
                    directing their practice, and summarizing their learning.
                    11:09
                    Guided discovery may not be appropriate for all patients,
                    11:13
                    particularly those with significant cognitive impairment.
                    11:17
                    This brings us to discuss the role of error in learning.
                    11:22
                    In guided practice where we're providing manual or physical guidance,
                    11:26
                    there is less error because the patient is being manually queued on how to move.
                    11:31
                    In guided discovery, there is more room for
                    11:37
                    errors and for the patient to learn from their errors.
                    11:39
                    With errorless learning, implicit learning occurs through
                    11:43
                    repetitive task specific training without the experience of error.
                    11:46
                    Usually, this is through high therapists control by breaking down
                    11:51
                    a task into parts and repetitively practicing each component until it is mastered.
                    11:56
                    Feedback is typically provided frequently,
                    12:01
                    but then maybe faded over time.
                    12:04
                    This type of training may allow for less generalization because
                    12:07
                    the feedback and practice is very specific to the task that is being mastered.
                    12:12
                    In errorful learning, implicit learning occurs
                    12:18
                    through skill execution without prior instruction.
                    12:21
                    Feedback is typically withheld and learning occurs through practice.
                    12:25
                    This allows for self-correction and learning from mistakes or trial and error.
                    12:30
                    For generalization, therapists can elicit
                    12:35
                    patient analysis of their own performance and allow them to
                    12:39
                    reflect on how the performance of the task may need to
                    12:43
                    change based on other task or environmental constraints.
                    12:46
                    This allows for generalization.
                    12:51
                    Task-specific guided discovery may not be appropriate for all patients.
                    12:54
                    Patients should be medically stable and cleared
                    13:00
                    by their physician to start rehabilitation.
                    13:02
                    If there are very severe motor and/or cognitive deficits,
                    13:05
                    the patient may require more of a guided practice approach and may
                    13:08
                    not benefit as much from errorful learning due to decrease capacity to learn.
                    13:13
                    In summary, practice should include tasks that are sufficiently challenging.
                    13:20
                    Whole task practice should be used for most tasks, particularly continuous tasks.
                    13:25
                    If part practice is utilized,
                    13:32
                    the whole task should be kept in mind.
                    13:34
                    Physical practice is superior to mental practice only.
                    13:37
                    But mental practice may be used in
                    13:41
                    conjunction with or if physical practice is not possible.
                    13:43
                    Allowing for errors and learning and guided discovery training is
                    13:47
                    associated with greater skill acquisition, retention, and generalization.
                    13:52

                .('08 PT2261 Module 2 Part 2 Effective Practice.pdf')
                    .Designing Effective Practice 2

                    .Objectives
                        • Compare and contrast constant, variable, blocked, and 
                        random practice
                        • Identify when different practice schedules may be beneficial 
                        to learning
                        • Describe how contextual interference affects learning

                    Γ.Important terms
                        constant practice vs variable practice

                        Practice Sequence
                           blocked practice
                           random practice
                           Hybrid practice

                        Intensity of Practice
                        Specificity of Practice
                        Practice Order
                            Blocked order
                            Serial order
                            Random older

                        Blocked vs. Random Practice
                            Open or closed skill
                            Low vs. High complexity

                        Contextual Interference
                            Reconstruction hypothesis
                            Elaboration hypothesis

                        Performance Error

                        Practice based on stage of learning
                            Cognitive stage
                            Associative stage
                            Autonomous stage

                    .The more practice the better
                    • True or False?

                    .True, but
                    • Practice with patient engagement
                    • Keep learner challenged
                    • Keep target context in mind​
                    • Strategically use: constant, variable, random, blocked practice​
                    • Distribute practice
                    • Incorporate mental practice appropriately​
                    • Incorporate guided practice wisely


                    .Practice should be Challenging
                    • Optimal level of information 
                    that helps learner learn
                    • Keep the learner challenged
                    • Adjust task and practice 
                    environment so there is so 
                    there is some success while 
                    still challenging the learner

                    .Intensity of Practice
                    • Intensity Matters
                    • Hours of training/day
                    • Increased resistance
                    • Increased cardiovascular workload 
                    (heart rate, RPE)
                    • Challenging balance programs

                    • Beware of high intensity too early
                    • Consider fatigue level
                    • Allow for success
                    • Enjoyment of tasks/salient practice


                    .Specificity of Practice
                    • Practice should be similar to performance situation
                    oMotor/biomechanical characteristics
                    oInformation processing
                    oEnvironmental conditions
                    • The closer your practice resembles the task the better for 
                    skill acquisition!

                    
                    .Practice Order
                    • Blocked order: repeated practice of a task or group of tasks in a specified order
                    • Serial order: practice of a task or group of tasks in a predictable repeating order
                    • Random order: practice of a non-repeating and unpredictable group of tasks


                    .Practice Sequence: Blocked vs. Random 
                    • Blocked Practice
                    oPractice sequence in which one 
                    repeatedly rehearses the same 
                    task
                    oAllows the learner uninterrupted 
                    time to concentrate on the tasks at 
                    hand
                    oOne skill is practiced and refined 
                    before going to the next

                    • Random Practice
                    oPractice sequence where the 
                    learner performs a number of 
                    different tasks or variation of a task 
                    in no particular order
                    oAvoiding or minimizing consecutive 
                    repetitions of any single tasks


                    .Blocked vs. Random Practice 1
                    • Random practice is generally more beneficial for learning than the blocked 
                    practice
                    oSkilled performance is delayed initially 
                    oImproved retention and generalization
                    oHigh contextual inference: depth of cognitive processing
                    ▪ Reconstruction hypothesis
                    ▪ Elaboration hypothesis
                    • Random practice of task variations rather than different types of tasks (variable 
                    practice)
                    • Beware of too much variation that may cause interference and/or confusion to 
                    the patient


                    .Contextual Interference ('')

                    • Shea and Morgan (1979)
                    oThree tasks
                    oBlocked practice
                    oRandom practice
                    oRetention trials
                    oRandom group exhibited 
                    better retention

                    .Blocked vs. Random Practice 2
                    • Hybrid practice structure may be appropriate for some patients 
                    oBlocked practice may be more beneficial for learning a new skill 
                    during the cognitive stage of learning
                    oWhen the learner understands the movement strategy practice 
                    should shift to random practice


                    .Blocked vs. Random Practice 3
                    • Task characteristics
                    oOpen or closed skill
                    oLow vs. High complexity
                    • Learner
                    oStage of learning
                    oAge of learner
                    oIntellectual capacity


                    .Variable vs. Constant Practice
                    • Constant practice
                    oRepeat same skill, same parameters​
                    oOnly one variation of the task during a session
                    • Variable practice
                    oRepeat same skill, different parameters


                    .Performance Error
                    • Variable practice leads to more error
                    • Good or bad for learning? 


                    .Constant, Variable, Blocked, Random
                    • Constant vs. Variable Practice: 
                    oSame skill, different parameters
                    • Blocked vs. Random Practice: 
                    oDifferent skills


                    .Practice based on stage of learning
                    • Cognitive stage: blocked – more repetition, then shift to semi-
                    blocked late in this stage, early in next (for example, three trials of 
                    one skill, then switch)
                    • Associative stage: semi-blocked – three trials of one skill, then 
                    switch -- mid to late in this stage, random
                    • Autonomous stage: random – switching from one skill to another
                    Continuum


                    .Summary
                    • The learner should be actively involved, sufficiently challenged, and 
                    practicing specific tasks to promote learning
                    • Different practice schedules may be appropriate based on the 
                    individual, the task, and the stage of motor learning
                    • Variable and random practice leads to performance error, which is 
                    important for learning (errorful vs. errorless practice)

                    4:56

                    4:59

                    5:03

                    5:07

                    5:14

                    5:18

                    6:14

                    6:18

                    6:24

                    6:28

                    6:34

                    6:49

                    6:57

                    7:01

                    7:07

                    7:12

                    7:19

                    7:22

                    7:28

                    7:33

                    7:36

                    7:41

                    7:46

                    7:50

                    7:54

                    8:00

                    8:02

                    8:05

                    8:08

                    8:22

                    8:26

                    8:41

                    8:48

                    8:54

                    9:00

                    9:05

                    9:13

                    9:17

                    9:21
