                    a new skill when the patient is in the cognitive stage of learning.
                    9:31
                    Once they have an understanding of the movement strategy,
                    9:35
                    practice can then shift to random variations of
                    9:38
                    the task to promote consolidation and retention.
                    9:41
                    When should we use blocked practice and when should we use random practice?
                    9:45
                    It may depend on the skill you are teaching the patient,
                    9:50
                    whether it is an open versus closed skill or
                    9:53
                    the skill has a low complexity versus a high complexity.
                    9:56
                    It may be very difficult to effectively structure random practice of
                    10:01
                    a highly complex skill without being overly complicated and confusing to the learner.
                    10:05
                    Use of random versus blocked practice may depend on
                    10:12
                    the individual patient and what stage of learning that they are in,
                    10:16
                    as well as the age of the learner and their intellectual capacity.
                    10:19
                    Blocked practice may be better for very early stages of learning for
                    10:23
                    very young or very old patients and those with less capacity to learn.
                    10:28
                    However, this is not always the case so it is
                    10:33
                    important to structure practice for the individual task and the individual person.
                    10:36
                    Remember, an optimal practice schedule is one that engages the patient,
                    10:40
                    but does not overwhelm them.
                    10:45
                    We talked a little bit about varying the task parameters with random practice.
                    10:48
                    This is also referred to as constant versus variable practice.
                    10:54
                    Constant practice is when you ask a patient to practice
                    10:58
                    the same skill under the same parameters whereas variable practice,
                    11:01
                    the learner rehearses the same skill under different parameters.
                    11:06
                    Variable practice will lead to more error,
                    11:11
                    which we know can be beneficial for learning.
                    11:15
                    Like random practice, variable practice can also
                    11:18
                    benefit retention and generalization of performance of the motor skill.
                    11:21
                    Just pulling all of these different types of practice together,
                    11:26
                    constant practice generally refers to
                    11:30
                    practicing the same skill under the same condition.
                    11:33
                    Variable practice refers to practice of the same skill under different conditions.
                    11:37
                    An example of variable practice may be practicing a sit to stand transfer
                    11:42
                    from different chair heights or different surfaces such as from a soft chair or a couch.
                    11:47
                    Blocked practice refers to practicing
                    11:52
                    the same skill over and over again within one practice session.
                    11:55
                    This overlaps with the idea of constant practice.
                    12:00
                    Random practice refers to practicing
                    12:04
                    different skills in a random and unpredictable order.
                    12:07
                    This is just an example of how you may utilize
                    12:11
                    these various practice schedules based on the stage of learning that the learner is in.
                    12:15
                    In the early cognitive stage,
                    12:21
                    this is when you may utilize blocked practice scheduling.
                    12:23
                    Then later in the cognitive stage,
                    12:27
                    you may shift to a more hybrid practice schedule
                    12:29
                    using some blocked and some random practice,
                    12:33
                    or use some variable practice,
                    12:36
                    so practicing the task under different conditions.
                    12:39
                    In the associative stage,
                    12:42
                    you may use a hybrid form of practice and then move to a random form of practice.
                    12:44
                    In the autonomous stage,
                    12:49
                    the practice should be random or variable as the learner has now mastered the skill.
                    12:51
                    These are just suggestions and may not be true for every learner,
                    12:58
                    and as we said,
                    13:02
                    it will depend on the characteristics of the learner
                    13:04
                    and the characteristics of the task.
                    13:07
                    In summary, the learner should be actively involved,
                    13:10
                    sufficiently challenged, and practicing specific tasks in order to promote learning.
                    13:14
                    Different practice schedules may be appropriate based on the individual,
                    13:20
                    the task, and the stage of motor learning.
                    13:24
                    Variable and random practice leads to performance error,
                    13:27
                    which is important for learning.
                    13:31

                    .Stages of Learning (!!E)
                        • Cognitive or Novice Stage
                        oNeed assistance to detect errors
                        • Associative or Advanced Stage 
                        oCan error detect
                        • Autonomous or Expert Stage
                        oCan error detect & correct

                    .Feedback – Why? (!!E).Q&A
                        • Function
                        oMotivate or Energize (compare to goal)
                        oReinforce (use positive reinforcement)
                        oInform
                        ▪Descriptive (their errors)
                        ▪Prescriptive (how to correct)

                    .Feedback (!!E)
                        • Types
                        oIntrinsic – inherent through movement
                        ▪Somatosensory or visual information; 
                        auditory, tactile
                        ▪Indications about accuracy, success
                        oExtrinsic (“Augmented Feedback”)
                        ▪Supplemental information
                        ▪May be verbal, visual, or manual

                    
                    .Augmented Feedback 1
                    • Outcome of movement related to the goal
                    oObjective/measurable
                    oQualitative feedback to focus attention on body 
                    movement
                    ▪ Explains organization of action for early learning 
                    stages
                    ▪ Refine coordination or technique for later learning 
                    stages
                    oQuantitative feedback can be used about the movement
                    ▪ Motivational, can guide temporary performance

                    .Augmented Feedback Types (!!E)
                    • Knowledge of results (KR): given to the learner about the outcome of his 
                    performance
                    oPromotes an external focus of attention
                    • Knowledge of performance (KP): feedback about quality of the movement
                    oPromotes an internal focus of attention

                    .Augmented Feedback 2
                    • How essential is augmented feedback for learning?
                    o“Depends”
                    oCan help, hinder, or have no effect
                    oConsider the task
                    oConsider the individual

                    .Augmented Feedback 3
                    • Usable & interpretable
                    • Prioritize
                    oSkill analysis
                    oCoordination of task (space-time pattern)
                    oPromote learner engagement

                    Attention –
                    External Focus!

                    .Focus of Augmented Feedback
                    • Internal Focus - May disrupt automaticity of movement/motor 
                    control 
                    • External Focus (goal-directed)
                    oResearch shows may enhance retention; works across specialties!
                    oGolf – “push against the ground” vs. “shift weight onto front foot” 
                    o“RUN SOFTER” vs. “more knee bend”
                    oSit to stand - “Stand up without touching the back of your legs to the chair” 
                    vs. “scoot forward and learn forward more as you stand”

                    .Feedback Schedules 1
                    • When?
                    oImmediate: feedback presented immediately following movement
                    oConcurrent: feedback provided during movement
                    oSummary (terminal)
                    ▪ Occurs after the event or set number of trials 
                    oDelayed: feedback given after a brief period of time
                    ▪ Time for self-assessment (practice error detection & estimation)
                    ▪ Do not delay too long OR fill with another task/skill

                    .Feedback Schedules 2
                    • How often? NOT 100% of the time!!
                    • Faded: decreasing frequency
                    oDecreased dependency on feedback
                    • Bandwidth: feedback only when performance is outside of a predetermined error 
                    range
                    • Self-Selected – based on learner’s request (help)
                    oTends to fade
                    oAfter good trial (confirmatory)
                    oBegin to self-identify error

                    .Stages of Learning & Feedback (!!E)
                    • Cognitive or Novice Stage
                    oHigh concentration; self-talk 
                    oLearning task goal, developing strategies & understanding important 
                    environmental features
                    • Associative or Advanced Stage 
                    oRefining movement, less variability in performance 
                    oMore consistent & efficient performance
                    • Autonomous or Expert Stage
                    oLess attention needed; may multi-task 
                    oOptimize movement for environmental constraints; fixing closed 
                    skills/diversifying open skills

                    .Goals 1 (!!E)
                    • Individual ---------Task -------- Environment
                    (Actor/Audience) – (Behavior & Degree) – (Condition)
                    oConsider individual, task, and environment
                    oConsider feedback available/required
                    • Examples:
                    oPatient will perform STS from standard height (18”) chair with verbal cues 
                    for safety awareness in 1 week. (activity STG)
                    oPatient will perform STS from rocker/recliner independently in 3 weeks. 
                    (activity LTG)

                    How do these goals impact the feedback you will provide?


                    .Goals 2 (!!E)
                    • Individual --–--- Task ---–------ Environment
                    (Actor/Audience) – (Behavior & Degree) – (Condition)
                    oEvaluate task complexity
                    • Examples:
                    oPT will ambulate on level surfaces with a wheeled walker and step-to pattern 
                    for 150 ft in 1 week. (activity STG)
                    oPT will ambulate outdoors on varied surfaces with a wheeled walker and step-
                    through pattern for distances up to 500 ft in 3 weeks. (activity LTG)
                    oPT will attend bi-weekly church activities using wheeled walker in 1 month. 
                    (participation goal)
                    How do these goals (or stage of learning) impact the feedback you will provide?
                    How do these goals (or stage of learning) impact the practice paradigms you design?


                    .Best practices for promoting learning in neurorehabilitation (!!E)
                    • Presence of a clear goal to learning
                    • Relevance or salience of the goal to the client
                    • Sufficient and increasing complexity/challenge of the skill being learned 
                    • Use of repetitive task-specific practice with the experience of error 
                    • Manipulation of practice and feedback
                    oUse of variable practice
                    oExplicit/implicit cues

                    .Summary
                    • Feedback can be used as reinforcement, motivation, and/or 
                    information to the patient regarding the motor skill
                    • It is important to think about when to provide feedback, how often to 
                    provide feedback, and what type of feedback you will provide to 
                    enhance motor learning
                    • The type of feedback and the feedback schedule will vary depending 
                    on the specific patient and their personal characteristics, the 
                    environment, and the stage of motor learning

                    3:09

                    3:16

                    3:23

                    3:28

                    3:33

                    3:40

                    3:44

                    3:47

                    3:58

            2.7. Module 2 Summary
            //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
            //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

                Well done! You have completed the second of five modules for Unit 1. Before moving on to the next module, remember to review these three key learnings: 
                    -Practice should be challenging and task-specific for the learner and the practice schedule should be tailored for the patient and task. 
                    -The learner should be actively involved in practice and the practice should allow for error (variable practice). 
                    -Feedback can function to motivate, reinforce, and/or inform the patient in regard to completing a motor skill. 
                    -Learning Outcomes

                After completing this module, you can now: 
                    Apply motor learning strategies to drive skill acquisition and recovery of function. 
                    Design effective practice paradigms to promote motor learning and skill acquisition. 
                    Describe various types of feedback and apply these when teaching a motor skill.

            3.0. Module 3 Introduction
            //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
            //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

                Introduction
                    Welcome to Module 3 of Unit 1. This week, you will learn some of the components of the neurologic physical therapy (PT) exam as well as some common abnormal findings with neurological conditions. The neurologic PT exam will be used throughout the Neuromuscular Course series and serves as the foundation for examination and evaluation of individuals with neurologic disorders. 

                Learning Objectives
                    By the end of this week, you will be able to: 
                        Demonstrate the ability to perform a neurologic PT examination, establish a prognosis and plan of care using evidence-based therapeutic interventions for clients with a neurologic diagnosis. 
                        Recognize what patient/client problems are beyond the scope of physical therapist practice and know when to make an appropriate referral to another health practitioner.   
                        Evaluate data from the PT examination to drive clinical decision making for the plan of care that is patient -centered, evidence-based and personalized to the client’s capabilities.

                    Modified Ashworth Scale ('Modified Ashworth Scale Instructions (2).docx')
                        Modified Ashworth Scale Instructions
                        General Information (derived Bohannon and Smith, 1987):
                        Place the patient in a supine position
                        If testing a muscle that primarily flexes a joint, place the joint in a maximally flexed position and move to a position of maximal extension over one second (count "one thousand one”)
                            If testing a muscle that primarily extends a joint, place the joint in a maximally extended position and move to a position of maximal flexion over one second (count "one thousand one”)
                            Score based on the classification below


                        Scoring (taken from Bohannon and Smith, 1987):

                        0   No increase in muscle tone

                        1   Slight increase in muscle tone, manifested by a catch and release or by minimal resistance at the end of the range of motion when the affected part(s) is moved in flexion or extension
                        1+  Slight increase in muscle tone, manifested by a catch, followed by minimal resistance throughout the remainder (less than half) of the ROM
                        2   More marked increase in muscle tone through most of the ROM, but affected part(s) easily moved
                        3   Considerable increase in muscle tone, passive movement difficult

                        4   Affected part(s) rigid in flexion or extension

                        Patient Instructions:
                        The patient should be instructed to relax.
                         
                        Modified Ashworth Scale Testing Form
                        Name:   Date:   

                        Muscle Tested   Score



                        Elbow Flexors
                             

                        Start position: elbow fully flexed, forearm neutral, 
                        Movement: Extend elbow



                        Wrist Flexors
                             

                        Start position: elbow extended, forearm pronated, 
                        Movement: Extend wrist


                        Ankle Planter Flexors
                             

                        Start position: [Gastrocnemius] Supine, ankle plantar flexed, hip in neutral flexion and rotation 
                        Movement: Dorsiflex ankle

                        Reference for test instructions:
                        Bohannon, R. and Smith, M. (1987). "Interrater reliability of a modified Ashworth scale of muscle spasticity." Physical Therapy 67(2): 206.

                    Cranial Nerve Exam (from PT 2232) ('PT 2232_Mod 6_Cranial Nerve Exam (1).pdf')


                         

                         

                        PT 2232 Treatment Progression 1 

                         

                        PT 2232: Musculoskeletal PT 2 

                        Department of Physical Therapy 

                         

                         

                         

                        Cranial Nerve Exam 
                        A cranial nerve exam is important for assessing mental (cognitive) status and should be a routine part of a 
                        comprehensive neurological exam.  Certain tests and measures have been established for cranial nerves I-
                        XII.  The test and measurements seek to examine sensory and motor systems, reflexes, and coordination 
                        and balance.  A functional exam can also be used to test motor functions (or the ability to learn or 
                        demonstrate the skillful assumption, maintenance, modification and control of voluntary postures and 
                        movement patterns).  

                         

                        Please review the components of clinical examination for the 12 cranial nerves outlined below. 

                         

                        Cranial Nerve I: Olfactory Nerve 
                        • Clinical examination involves testing: 
                        o Olfaction (sense of smell) 
                        § Procedure: 
                        • Assess each nostril separately 
                        • Have patient close one nostril 
                        • Have the patient report if they can smell a non-noxious odorant 

                         

                        Cranial Nerve II: Optic Nerve 
                        • Clinical examination involves testing: 
                        o Visual acuity- Assessing the sharpness or clarity of vision (usually at distance of 20 ft). 
                        § Procedure: 
                        • Test each eye separately. 
                        • Wear eyeglasses if they normally wear them ask patient to read chart with 
                        uncovered eye. 
                        • May use a Snellen Eye Chart. 
                        o Visual field- The total area in which objects can be seen in the side (peripheral) vision as you 
                        focus your eyes on a central point. Note that there is overlap of the medial (nasal) fields. 
                        § Procedure: 
                        • You should be nose-to- nose with patient, separated by ~8-12”. 
                        • Each eye is assessed separately. 
                        • You cover one eye, and the patient covers the opposite eye. The open eye is 
                        staring directly at one another. 
                        • You move your hand out towards the periphery of your VF on the side where the 
                        eyes are open.  Your finger should be equidistant from both you and the patient. 
                        • You then move your finger in towards the face, along an imaginary line drawn 
                        between you and the patient.  Both you and the patient should detect the finger 
                        at the same time. 
                        • Your finger is then moved out to the diagonal corners of the field and moved 
                        inward from each of these directions (test all 4 quadrants of the visual field). 
                        • The other eye is tested following the same method. 
                        § Responses: 


                         

                         

                        PT 2232 Cranial Nerve Exam 2 

                        • Look for “field cuts” or areas where the patient loses the ability to see. 

                         

                        o Pupillary light reflexes - Afferent axons for constriction of the pupil due to increase light 
                        intensity 
                        § Procedure: 
                        • Bring penlight from the side of the patient’s head into the eye 
                        • Both eyes should constrict direct light reflex and indirect (consensual) reflex 
                        § Responses: 
                        • In a normal response, the eye which the light is shined has pupillary constriction 
                        (direct reflex) AND the contralateral pupil also constricts (indirect or consensual 
                        reflex).  
                        • An abnormal response is no pupillary constriction. 

                         

                        • Diseases of the optic nerve may include: 
                        o Disturbance and loss of visual acuity- ipsilateral blindness, bilateral blindness 
                        o Visual field deficits 
                        o Pupillary abnormalities 

                         

                        Cranial Nerves III, IV, & VI: Oculomotor, Trochlear, & Abducens Nerves 
                        • Recall that CNs III, IV, & VI provide innervation to the extraocular eye muscles. 
                        o When one of the muscles is weakened or paralyzed the eyeball will be misplaced causing 
                        visual impairments. 
                        • Clinical examination involves testing: 
                        o Ocular movements- Proper function and movement of the extraocular muscles for gaze. 
                        § Procedures: 
                        • Conjugate movements are tested by asking the patient to voluntarily shift 
                        gaze without moving the head. 
                        o Observed with the H-test. 
                        • Patient follows a moving target (slowly). 
                        o “Smooth pursuits”- the ability of the eyes to smoothly follow a 
                        moving object (slowly) 
                        § In seated position 
                        § Examiner holds a target (fingertip) ~3’ from patient 
                        § Patient is instructed to maintain focus on the target as the 
                        examiner moves the target smoothly in a horizontal direction 
                        • 1.5’ to the right and left of midline 
                        • Target moves at a rate that requires ~ 2 seconds to go 
                        fully from right to left and vice versa  
                        § Repeat with the examiner moving the target in the vertical 
                        direction 
                        • 1.5’ above and 1.5” below midline 
                        • Patient quickly looks at targets between 2 points. 
                        o “Saccade”- quick, involuntary small movements of both eyes 
                        simultaneously occurs when the eyes fix on one point after another 
                        in the visual field. 
                        § While keeping the head still the patient looks quickly between 
                        two points 


                         

                         

                        PT 2232 Cranial Nerve Exam 3 

                        § Test both horizontal and vertical movements 
                        § Both eyes should accurately move together to the target 
                        • Near point convergence (NPC) 
                        o NPC- Observe for ocular adduction and pupil constriction 
                        o Tested by asking the patient to focus both eyes on a target (~ 14-
                        point font size). 
                        o Patient focuses on the target at arm’s length and slowly brings it to 
                        the tip of their nose. 
                        o Patient is instructed to stop moving the target when they see 2 
                        distinct images or when the examiner observes outward deviation of 
                        one eye.  
                        o Pupillary light reflex (efferent limb) (see CN II tests) 
                        o Elevation of the upper eye lid 
                        § Looking for proper elevation via levator palpabre superioris with no drooping. 
                        • Disorders may include: 
                        o Strabismus- Disorder of the eyes where one eye does not turn normally so the person’s gaze 
                        appears divergent.  
                        o Ptosis- Drooping of the eyelid. 
                        o Diseases of the ocular nerves produce disturbances of ocular motility (ocular palsy), and in 
                        the case of the oculomotor nerve itself, pupillary alterations as well. 

                         

                         

                        Cranial Nerve V: Trigeminal Nerve 
                        • Clinical examination involves testing: 
                        o Sensory portion: 
                        § Facial sensation--Face, head, cornea, mucosa of nose, mouth, hard and soft palate, 
                        and tongue. 
                        • V1 ophthalmic division 
                        • V2 maxillary division 
                        • V3 mandibular division 
                        o Procedure: 
                        § Sensory testing to face 
                        • Respect the 3 divisions (V1,2 and 3) 
                        § Corneal reflex (not usually assessed in PT exam) 
                        • Afferent limb 
                        o Procedure: 
                        § Lightly touch the lateral corner of the eye with a cotton swab. 
                        § The patient’s eye should close. 
                        o Motor portion: 
                        § Muscles of mastication (chewing) 
                        • Masseter 
                        • Temporalis 
                        o Procedure: 
                        § Palpation of muscles of mastication 
                        • Have patient bite down on a tongue depressor or to 
                        clench their jaw 
                        • Palpate muscles 


                         

                         

                        PT 2232 Cranial Nerve Exam 4 

                        Cranial Nerve VII: Facial Nerve 
                        • Clinical examination involves testing: 
                        o Observation of gestures and facial movements 
                        o Self-reports of taste changes 
                        § Sensory portion: 
                        • Taste to anterior 2/3 of tongue (not usually assessed in PT exam) 
                        o Procedure: 
                        § Have patient slightly protrude their tongue with the eyes 
                        closed 
                        § Place a small amount of salt or sugar on the lateral side of the 
                        tongue using a tongue depressor 
                        § Ask the patient to identify the substance 
                        § OR have the patient tell you of any taste changes 
                        • Corneal reflex (not usually assessed in PT exam) 
                        o Efferent limb (see CN V for procedure) 
                        § Motor portion: 
                        • Muscles associated with facial expression 
                        o Procedure: 
                        § Have the patient: 
                        • Smile - buccinator 
                        • Show teeth- levator labii superioris 
                        • Close eyes tightly- orbicular oculi, 
                        • Elevate eyebrows – frontal belly of occipitofrontalis 
                        (epicranius) 
                        • Contract platysma- platysma 
                        • Treatment consideration: 
                        o Bell’s Palsy- A weakness of the muscles on one side of the face. Damage to the facial nerve 
                        causes that side of the face to droop and difficulty closing the eye. Damage to the nerve may 
                        also affect sense of taste and the production of tears and saliva. 

                         

                        Cranial Nerve VIII: Vestibulocochlear Nerve 
                        • Clinical examination involves testing: 
                        o Cochlear (organ of Corti) portion: 
                        § Procedure: 
                        • Whisper test or Finger rub test 
                        o Examiner whispers questions or commands near ear from behind 
                        the patient to prevent lip reading; Alternatively, you can gently rub 
                        your fingers together near the patient’s ear 
                        o Procedure is repeated on opposite side 

                         

                        o Vestibular (semicircular canals, utricle, saccule) portion: 
                        § Procedures: 
                        • Observation 
                        o Nystagmus- a series of automatic, back and forth oscillations of the 
                        eye(s).  Usually a sign of disease in the posterior fossa or peripheral 
                        vestibular apparatus  


                         

                         

                        PT 2232 Cranial Nerve Exam 5 

                        o Coordination/Balance 
                        • Head Impulse Test (HIT): 
                        o The patient is asked to focus on a close target (usually the examiner’s 
                        nose). The examiner passively moves the patient’s head out to the 
                        side and then quickly moves the head toward midline (the ‘impulse’) 
                        o A positive test includes the presence of a refixation saccade or 
                        corrective saccade and would indicate a peripheral vestibular 
                        hypofunction (can be present unilaterally or bilaterally) 

                         

                        Cranial Nerves IX & X: Glossopharyngeal and Vagus Nerves 
                        • Recall that the: 
                        o Glossopharyngeal nerve provides: 
                        § Sensory innervation - Taste to the posterior 1/3 of the tongue, pharynx, and soft 
                        palate 
                        § Motor innervation to stylopharyngeus muscle 
                        o Vagus nerve provides: 
                        § Motor to the pharynx, larynx, and involuntary mm of alimentary tract and air 
                        passages 
                        • Clinical examination involves: 
                        o Observing the movement of the uvula and soft palate with phonation and elicitation of the 
                        pharyngeal reflex 
                        § Procedure: 
                        • Ask the patient to say “AHHH!” with the mouth open 
                        • Observe the back of the throat 
                        • Uvula will deviate to the stronger side 
                        • Treatment considerations: 
                        o Lesion symptoms include: 
                        § Loss of taste 
                        § Loss of gag reflex 
                        § Dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) 

                         

                        Cranial Nerve XI: Spinal Accessory Nerve  
                        • Recall that the spinal accessory nerve: 
                        o Provides motor innervation to trapezius and SCM muscles 
                        § Disorder characterized by muscle atrophy and/or shoulder droop 
                        o Clinical examination involves: 
                        § AROM and strength assessments of the trapezius and SCM muscles 

                         

                        Cranial Nerve XII: Hypoglossal Nerve  
                        • Clinical examination involves: 
                        o Appearance of the tongue 
                        § Procedure: 
                        • Observe for deviation of the tongue 
                        o A minimal deviation of the tongue <1 cm is not clinically significant 
                        o The tongue will deviate to the weaker side 
                        o Movement/strength of tongue

                    Motor Exam for SCI (from PT 2262) ('PT2263_Mod1_Motor_Exam_Guide.pdf')
                        June 2008 page 1

                        International Standards for the Classification of Spinal Cord Injury
                        Motor Exam Guide

                        C5 Elbow Flexors | Biceps Brachii, Brachialis
                        Grade 3 
                        Patient Position: The shoulder is in neutral rotation, 
                        neutral flexion/extension, and adducted. The elbow is fully 
                        extended, with the forearm in full supination. The wrist is in 
                        neutral flexion/extension.
                        Examiner Position: Support the wrist.
                        Instructions to Patient: “Bend your elbow and try to reach your 
                        hand to your nose.”
                        Action: The patient attempts to move through the full range of 
                        motion in elbow flexion.

                        Grades 4 & 5
                        Patient Position: The shoulder is in neutral rotation, neutral 
                        flexion/extension, and adducted.  The elbow is flexed to 90° and 
                        the forearm is fully supinated.
                        Examiner Position: Place a stabilizing hand on the anterior 
                        shoulder. Grasp the volar aspect of the wrist and exert a pulling 
                        force in the direction of elbow extension. 
                        Instructions to Patient: “Hold your arm. Don’t let me move it.”
                        Action: The patient resists the examiner’s pull and attempts to 
                        maintain the elbow flexed at 90°.

                        Grade 2
                        Patient Position: The shoulder is in internal rotation and
                        adducted with the forearm positioned above the abdomen, just 
                        below the umbilicus. The elbow is in 30° of flexion. The forearm 
                        and wrist are in neutral pronation/supination. Sufficient flexion of 
                        the shoulder must be permitted to allow the forearm to 
                        comfortably move over the abdomen.
                        Examiner Position: Support the arm.
                        Instructions to Patient: “Bend your elbow and try to bring your 
                        hand to your nose.”
                        Action: The patient attempts to move the elbow through a full 
                        range of motion in elbow flexion.


                        International Standards for the Classification of Spinal Cord Injury
                        Motor Exam Guide

                        June 2008 page 2

                        Grades 0 & 1
                        Patient: The patient is in the grade 2 position with the shoulder in 
                        internal rotation and adducted.  The palm and ventral forearm are 
                        positioned above the abdomen. The elbow is in 30° of flexion. 
                        The forearm and wrist are in neutral pronation/supination. 
                        Sufficient flexion of the shoulder must be permitted to allow the 
                        forearm to comfortably move over the abdomen.
                        Examiner Position: One hand supports the forearm while the 
                        other hand palpates the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa.  The 
                        belly of the biceps brachii muscle may also be palpated or 
                        observed for movement. 
                        Instructions to Patient: “Bend your elbow and try to bring your 
                        hand to your nose.”
                        Action: The patient attempts to move the elbow through a full 
                        range of motion in elbow flexion.

                        C 6 Wrist Extensors | Extensor Carpi Radialis Longus, Extensor Carpi Radialis Brevis 
                        Grade 3
                        Patient Position: The shoulder is in neutral rotation, neutral 
                        flexion/extension, and adducted.  The elbow is fully extended, the 
                        forearm is fully pronated, and the wrist flexed.
                        Examiner Position: One hand supports the distal forearm to
                        allow the wrist to be pre-positioned in sufficient flexion for testing. 
                        Instructions to Patient: “Bend your wrist upwards. Lift your 
                        fingers toward the ceiling.”
                        Action: The patient attempts to extend the wrist through a full 
                        range of motion.


                        International Standards for the Classification of Spinal Cord Injury
                        Motor Exam Guide

                        June 2008 page 3

                        Grades 4 & 5
                        Patient Position: Same as grade 3, except the wrist is 
                        fully extended.
                        Examiner Position: Grasp the distal forearm to stabilize the 
                        wrist.  Apply pressure across the metacarpals in a downward 
                        direction toward flexion and ulnar deviation.
                        The force applied should be angled toward the ulnar side of the 
                        wrist rather than directly downward, since it is the radial wrist 
                        extensors that are being tested.  
                        Instructions to Patient: “Hold your wrist up. Don’t let me 
                        push it down.”
                        Action: The patient resists the examiner’s push and attempts to 
                        maintain the wrist in the fully extended position.

                        Grades 0, 1 & 2
                        Patient Position: Position the patient with the arm resting on the 
                        exam table.  The shoulder is in neutral flexion/extension, neutral 
                        rotation, and adducted.  The elbow is fully extended. The forearm 
                        is in neutral pronation-supination and the wrist fully flexed
                        The patient may also be positioned with the shoulder in slight 
                        flexion, internal rotation, and adducted, with the patient’s arm 
                        above the abdomen. The elbow is flexed to 90° and the forearm 
                        is in full supination.  The wrist is flexed.
                        Examiner Position: Support the forearm and ask the patient to 
                        bend the wrist backwards into extension.  For trace function,
                        palpate the radial wrist extensors just proximal to the wrist, on 
                        the radial aspect of the distal forearm. Observe the muscle belly 
                        for movement.  
                        Instructions to Patient: “Bend your wrist backwards.”
                        Action: The patient attempts to extend the wrist though a full 
                        range of motion in wrist extension.

                        C6 Common Muscle Substitution
                        Wrist extension can be mimicked by forearm supination and the use of gravity.  The examiner needs to make sure the 
                        forearm is stabilized and is in proper position.


                        International Standards for the Classification of Spinal Cord Injury
                        Motor Exam Guide

                        June 2008 page 4

                        C7 Elbow Extensors | Triceps
                        Grade 3
                        Patient Position: The shoulder is in neutral rotation, adducted, 
                        and 90°of flexion.  The elbow is fully flexed with the palm of the 
                        hand resting by the ear.
                        Examiner Position: Support the upper arm.
                        Instructions to Patient: “Straighten your arm.”
                        Action: The patient attempts to move through the full range of 
                        elbow extension.

                        Grades 4 & 5
                        Patient Position: Same as grade 3, except the elbow is in 
                        45° of flexion.
                        Examiner Position: Support the upper arm. Grasp the wrist 
                        and apply resistance to the distal forearm in the direction of 
                        elbow flexion. 
                        Instructions to Patient: “Hold this position. Don’t let me bend 
                        your elbow.”
                        Action: The patient resists the examiner’s pressure and attempts 
                        to maintain the position of the elbow in 45° of flexion.

                        Grade 2
                        Patient Position: The shoulder is in internal rotation and 
                        adducted, with the forearm positioned above the abdomen. The 
                        forearm is in neutral pronation/supination.   The elbow is fully 
                        flexed.  When checking Grade 2, sufficient flexion of the shoulder 
                        must be permitted to allow the forearm to clear and move over 
                        the chest and abdomen.
                        Examiner Position: Support the patient’s arm.
                        Instructions to Patient: “Straighten your arm.”
                        Action: The patient attempts to move through the full range of 
                        elbow extension.


                        International Standards for the Classification of Spinal Cord Injury
                        Motor Exam Guide

                        June 2008 page 5

                        Grades 0 & 1
                        Patient Position: Maintain the grade 2 position with the shoulder 
                        in internal rotation and adduction, and the forearm positioned
                        above the abdomen. The forearm is in neutral 
                        pronation/supination and the elbow is in 30° of flexion. 
                        Examiner Position: Support the arm. For trace function,
                        palpate the distal triceps at its insertion on the olecranon. 
                        The belly of the triceps muscle may also be palpated and 
                        observed for movement.
                        Instructions to Patient: “Straighten your arm.”
                        Action: The patient attempts to fully extend the elbow. 

                        C7 Common Muscle Substitution
                        Elbow extension can be mimicked by externally rotating the shoulder, by quickly flexing the elbow and then relaxing, 
                        and with spasticity of the triceps.  These substitutions can be minimized by maintaining the correct position for testing, 
                        correct instructions to the patient, and avoiding elbow flexion.  Palpation of the triceps should be done to confirm the 
                        patient is using the correct muscle for the test.

                        C8 Long Finger Flexors | Flexor Digitorum Profundus
                        Grade 3
                        Patient Position: The shoulder is in neutral rotation, neutral 
                        flexion-extension, and adduction.  The elbow is fully extended 
                        with the forearm fully supinated. The wrist is in neutral flexion-
                        extension.  The metacarpal phalangeal (MCP) and proximal 
                        interphalangeal joints (PIP) are stabilized in extension. 
                        Examiner Position: Using two hands grasp the patient’s hand 
                        and stabilize the wrist In neutral.  Secure the PIP and MCP joints 
                        in extension with both hands while isolating the middle finger for 
                        testing. Stabilize the volar aspect of the 3rd middle phalanx with 
                        the thumb of the opposite hand.   
                        As an alternate method, 1 hand may be used to stabilize instead 
                        of 2.  The PIP and MCP joints are stabilized as previously 
                        described, with the thumb of the stabilizing hand now securing 
                        the middle phalanx.
                        Instructions to Patient: “Bend the tip of your middle finger.”
                        Action: The patient attempts to flex the distal interphalangeal 
                        (DIP) joint through the full range of motion in flexion.


                        International Standards for the Classification of Spinal Cord Injury
                        Motor Exam Guide

                        June 2008 page 6

                        Grades 4 & 5
                        Patient Position: The same as grade 3, except the DIP joint is 
                        fully flexed. 
                        Examiner Position: Stabilize the wrist, MCP and PIP joints as in 
                        grade 3.  Apply pressure with the tip of the finger or thumb 
                        against the distal phalanx of the patient’s middle finger.
                        Instructions to Patient: “Hold the tip of your finger in this bent 
                        position.  Don’t let me move it.”
                        Action: The patient attempts to maintain the fully flexed position 
                        of the DIP joint, and resist the pressure applied by the examiner 
                        in the direction of finger extension.

                        Grades 0, 1 & 2
                        Patient Position: The shoulder is in neutral rotation, neutral 
                        flexion-extension, and adduction.  The elbow is fully extended.  
                        The forearm is in neutral pronation-supination and the wrist in 
                        neutral flexion-extension. The MCP and PIP joints are stabilized 
                        in extension.
                        Examiner Position: Stabilize the wrist in neutral and the MCP 
                        and PIP joints in extension.  For trace function, palpate the 
                        tendons of the long finger flexors or observe the muscle belly for 
                        movement. 
                        Instructions to Patient: “Bend the tip of your middle finger.”
                        Action: The patient attempts to flex the distal interphalangeal 
                        (DIP) joint through the full range of motion in flexion.

                        C8 Common Muscle Substitution
                        When testing grades 1 through 3, the wrist must be carefully stabilized.  Involuntary movement of the distal phalanx 
                        can occur in the presence of active wrist extension. This tenodesis movement could be misinterpreted as voluntary 
                        contraction of the long finger flexors.  
                        While testing grades 4 and 5, the proximal phalanges must be well stabilized.  This will avoid misinterpretation of 
                        distal phalanx movement caused by contraction of the hand intrinsics or the flexor digitorum superficialis.


                        International Standards for the Classification of Spinal Cord Injury
                        Motor Exam Guide

                        June 2008 page 7

                        T1  Small Finger Abductor | Abductor Digiti Minimi
                        Grade 3
                        Patient Position: The shoulder is in internal rotation adducted, 
                        and at 15° flexion.  The elbow is at 90° flexion, the forearm is 
                        pronated, and the wrist is in neutral flexion/extension.
                        Examiner Position: Support the patient’s hand, taking 
                        care to assure that the MCP joints are stabilized to 
                        prevent hyperextension.
                        Instructions to Patient: “Move your little finger away from your 
                        ring finger.”
                        Action: The patient attempts to move the little finger through the 
                        full range of motion in abduction. 

                        Grades 4 & 5
                        Patient Position: Same as grade 3, except the little finger 
                        is fully abducted.
                        Examiner Position: Support the patient’s hand, taking care to 
                        assure that the MCP joints are stabilized to prevent 
                        hyperextension. Use the index finger to apply pressure against 
                        the side of the patient’s distal phalanx.
                        Instructions to Patient: “Hold your little finger away from your 
                        ring finger.  Don’t let me push it in.”
                        Action: The examiner exerts a pushing force against the side of 
                        the distal phalanx, and the patient attempts to resist the 
                        examiner’s force and keep the little finger fully abducted.


                        International Standards for the Classification of Spinal Cord Injury
                        Motor Exam Guide

                        June 2008 page 8

                        Grades 0, 1 & 2
                        Patient Position: The shoulder is in neutral rotation, neutral 
                        flexion/extension, and adducted.  The elbow is in full extension.  
                        The forearm is in full pronation and the wrist in neutral flexion-
                        extension.  The MCP joint is stabilized. 
                        An alternate position is with the shoulder in internal rotation, 
                        adducted, and neutral flexion/extension. The elbow is in 90° of 
                        flexion, the forearm and wrist are in neutral flexion /extension,
                        and the MCP joint is stabilized.
                        Examiner Position: Stabilize the dorsal wrist and hand by 
                        pressing down lightly on the back of the hand. Be sure that the 
                        MCP joints are stabilized to prevent hyperextension. Palpate the 
                        abductor digiti minimi muscle and observe the muscle belly 
                        for movement.
                        Instructions to Patient: “Move your little finger away from your 
                        ring finger.”
                        Action: The patient attempts to abduct the little finger through the 
                        full range of motion.

                        T1 Common Muscle Substitution
                        Finger extension can mimic 5th finger abduction. Proper positioning and stabilization will minimize this error.

                        L2 Hip Flexors | Iliopsoas
                        Grade 3
                        Patient Position:  The hip is in neutral rotation, neutral 
                        adduction/abduction, with both the hip and knee in 15° of flexion. 
                        Examiner Position: Support the dorsal aspect of the distal thigh 
                        and leg.  Do not allow flexion beyond 90° when examining acute 
                        thoraco-lumbar injuries due to the kyphotic stress placed on the 
                        lumbar spine.
                        Instructions to Patient: “Lift your knee towards your chest as far 
                        as you can, trying not to drag your foot on the exam table.”
                        Action: The patient attempts to flex hip to 90° of flexion.


                        International Standards for the Classification of Spinal Cord Injury
                        Motor Exam Guide

                        June 2008 page 9

                        Grades 4 & 5
                        Patient Position: The hip is in 90° of flexion with the 
                        knee relaxed. 
                        Examiner Position: Brace the anterior superior iliac spine 
                        on the opposite side and place a hand on the distal anterior 
                        thigh, just above the knee.  Pressure is applied in the direction of 
                        hip extension
                        Instructions to patient: “Hold your knee in this position.  Don’t 
                        let me push it down.”
                        Action: The patient attempts to resist the examiner’s push and 
                        keep the hip flexed at 90°.

                        Grade 2
                        Patient Position: Place the patient in the gravity eliminated 
                        position with the hip in external rotation and 45°of flexion. The 
                        knee is flexed at 90°.
                        Examiner Position: Support the leg.
                        Instructions to Patient: “Try to bring your knee out to the side,”
                        or “Try to flex your thigh toward the side of the body.”
                        Action: The patient attempts to move through the full range of 
                        motion in hip flexion.

                        Grades 0 & 1
                        Patient Position: Place the patient in the grade 3 position, with 
                        the hip in neutral rotation, neutral adduction/abduction and the hip 
                        and knee flexed to 15°. 
                        Examiner Position: Support the thigh to eliminate friction while
                        palpating the superficial hip flexors just distal to the anterior 
                        superior iliac spine.
                        Instructions to Patient: Ask the patient to “lift your knee towards 
                        your chest as far as you can.”
                        Action:  The patient attempts to flex the hip.
                        Note: For Grade 1, the examiner is actually palpating the more
                        superficial hip flexors, i.e. sartorius and rectus femoris rather than 
                        the iliopsoas. The insertion of the iliopsoas is too deep to be
                        seen or felt when it possesses only Grade 1 strength. When 
                        examining a patient with an acute traumatic lesion below T8, the 
                        hip should not be allowed to flex passively or actively beyond 90°.  
                        Flexion beyond 90° may place too great a kyphotic stress on the 
                        lumbar spine.

                        L2 Common Muscle Substitution
                        Any muscle of the trunk that can elevate or rotate the pelvis can trick the examiner into thinking that the hip flexor 
                        muscles are active.  This could include the rectus abdominus, the adductor muscles, obliques, or the quadratus 
                        lumborum.  With accurate palpation, correct patient instructions, and observation of any trunk movement, this 
                        substitution can be avoided.

                        L3 Knee Extensors | Quadriceps
                        Grade 3
                        Patient Position: The hip is in neutral rotation, neutral 
                        adduction/abduction and 15° of flexion. The knee is in 30° 
                        of flexion.
                        Examiner Position: Place the arm under the tested knee and 
                        rest the hand on the patient’s distal thigh. This causes the tested 
                        knee to flex to approximately 30°.
                        Instructions to Patient: “Straighten your knee.”
                        Action: The patient attempts to straighten the knee through the 
                        full range of motion in extension.

                        Grades 4 & 5
                        Patient position: Same as grade 3, except the knee is in 15°

                        Examiner Position: Place the arm under the tested knee and 
                        rest the hand on the patient’s opposite thigh. Grasp the leg to be 
                        tested, just proximal to the ankle.
                        Instructions to Patient: “Hold this position. Don’t let me bend 
                        your knee.”
                        Action: Examiner exerts downward force into knee flexion while 
                        the patient attempts to hold the knee in 15 degrees of flexion.

                        Grade 2
                        Patient Position: The hip is in external rotation and 45°of flexion.

                        Action: The patient attempts to straighten the knee.

                        L4 Ankle Dorsiflexors | Tibialis Anterior
                        Grade 3
                        Patient Position: The hip is in neutral rotation, neutral 
                        adduction/abduction, with the hip and knee slightly flexed. The 
                        hand may be placed under the knee of the tested leg to 
                        incorporate slight flexion. The ankle is plantarflexed. 
                        Examiner Position: At the patient’s side. Support the leg.
                        Instructions to Patient: “Pull your toes upward toward your

                        Grades 4 & 5

                        Examiner Position: In the grade 3 position, place

                        Instructions to Patient: “Hold your ankle in this position. Don’t

                        Action: The patient attempts to resist the examiner and maintain

                        Grade 2
                        Patient Position: The hip is in external rotation and 45° of 
                        abduction. The knee is flexed, and the ankle is fully 
                        plantar flexed.
                        Examiner Position: Support the leg.
                        Instruction to Patient: “Lift the toes upward toward the head, 
                        allowing the ankle to bend.”
                        Action: The patient attempts to dorsiflex ankle through the full 
                        range of motion.

                        Grades 0 & 1
                        Patient Position: Place the hip in neutral rotation, neutral

                        L4 Common Muscle Substitution
                        Ankle dorsiflexion can be mimicked by the long toe extensors, particularly the extensor hallucis longus.  Correct 
                        stabilization and observation along with proper patient instruction and palpation can eliminate this substitution.

                        L5 Common Muscle Substitution
                        Great toe extension can be facilitated by plantarflexion. If a patient actively plantar flexes the entire foot, passive 
                        extension of extensor hallucis longus can be achieved during the active plantarflexion of the foot. This is a type of 
                        tenodesis for the foot and can be avoided by proper stabilization to eliminate foot and ankle movement.
                        Another possible muscle substitution for L5 can occur when the patient actively flexes the big toe and then relaxes. 
                        Passive relaxation into a neutral position can be perceived as active extension.

                        S1 Ankle Plantarflexors | Gastrocnemius, Soleus

                        Perspective

                        Updated Integrated Framework for Making Clinical
                        Decisions Across the Lifespan and Health Conditions
                        Judith E. Deutsch, PT, PhD, FAPTA1,, Kathleen M. Gill-Body, PT, DPT, NCS, FAPTA2,
                        Margaret Schenkman, PT, PhD, FAPTA3
                        1Rivers Lab, Department of Rehabilitation and Movement Science, School of Health Professions, Rutgers University, Newark, New Jersey,
                        USA
                        2Rehabilitation Services, Newton-Wellesley Hospital, Newton, Massachusetts, USA
                        3Department of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, Physical Therapy Program, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, Aurora,
                        Colorado, USA
                        Address all correspondence to Dr Deutsch at: deutsch@rutgers.edu and @JudithDeutsch

                        Abstract
                        The updated Integrated Framework for Clinical Decision Making responds to changes in evidence, policy, and practice since
                        the publication of the ﬁrst version in 2008. The original framework was proposed for persons with neurological health
                        conditions, whereas the revised framework applies to persons with any health condition across the lifespan. In addition,
                        the revised framework (1) updates patient-centered concepts with shared clinical decision-making; (2) frames the episode
                        of care around the patient’s goals for participation; (3) explicitly describes the role of movement science; (4) reconciles
                        movement science and International Classiﬁcation of Function language, illustrating the importance of each perspective to
                        patient care; (5) provides a process for movement analysis of tasks; and (6) integrates the movement system into patient
                        management. Two cases are used to illustrate the application of the framework: (1) a 45-year-old male bus driver with low
                        back pain whose goals for the episode of care are to return to work and recreational basketball; and (2) a 65-year-old female
                        librarian with a fall history whose goals for the episode of care are to return to work and reduce future falls. The framework is
                        proposed as a tool for physical therapist education and to guide clinical practice for all health conditions across the lifespan.
                        Keywords: Decision-Making: Clinical, Movement Analysis of Tasks, Movement System, Shared Decision-Making

                        Downloaded from https://academic.oup.com/ptj/article/102/3/pzab281/6497836 by guest on 05 May 2025


                        2 Clinical Decision-Making Across Health Conditions

                        Introduction
                        The Integrated Framework for Clinical Decision Making,
                        published in 2006,1 innovated clinical reasoning in neurolog-
                        ical physical therapy by being explicitly patient centered and
                        combining both enablement2 and disablement3 perspectives
                        of health, with an emphasis on a person’s role in society.4 It
                        incorporated the Hypothesis Oriented Algorithm for clinical
                        decision-making5,6 and was organized using the Patient
                        Client Management from the Guide to Physical Therapist
                        Practice.7 The framework was based on knowledge at that
                        time regarding neural plasticity. Motor learning, included
                        as a critical component of rehabilitation and task analysis,
                        was identified as central to the examination process. This
                        framework has been used over the last 15 years to organize
                        curricula of selected academic physical therapy programs.8 In
                        addition, it has been used specifically to teach neurological
                        content in physical therapy programs and for regional
                        courses taught by the Academy of Neurologic Physical
                        Therapy.
                        Since 2006, substantive changes have occurred in knowl-
                        edge, evidence, policy, and practice that make it timely to
                        update the Integrated Framework for Clinical Decision Mak-
                        ing.First,in2013,theAmericanPhysicalTherapyAssociation
                        (APTA) adopted a new vision for the profession of physical
                        therapy and identified the human movement system as the
                        “coreofphysicaltherapistpractice,educationandresearch.”9
                        Second, the third edition of the Guide to Physical Therapist
                        practiceincorporatedtheInternationalClassificationofFunc-
                        tion (ICF).10 Next, APTA, through task forces, academies,
                        working groups, and summits, has advanced the definition
                        and application of clinical reasoning,11–14 the human move-
                        ment system,15–17 and diagnosis.18,19 These initiatives have
                        focused the profession to define specific approaches to exam-
                        iningandmanagingmovementsystemproblemsastheyrelate
                        to activity limitations and participation restrictions for all
                        individualsacrossthelifespan.Theimportanceofframingthe
                        plan of care to improve the patient’s ability to participate in
                        life roles also has come into sharper focus.
                        Literature on shared decision-making also has advanced
                        beyond patient-centered practice. In partnership with their
                        clinician, individuals are encouraged to consider the benefits
                        and harms of available treatment or management options,
                        communicate their preferences, and collaborate with clin-
                        icians to choose the course of action that best fits their
                        preferences.20,21 Taken into consideration are individual
                        preferences, abilities, self-efficacy, a person’s readiness to
                        change, and clinicians’ knowledge.22 Implementation of
                        shared decision-making into health care practice23 has
                        been adapted for physical therapy24 using evidence-based
                        strategies around communication, motivational interviewing,
                        and decision aids to increase the person’s knowledge and
                        options.25,26
                        Finally, the manner in which physical therapists use
                        evidence to guide practice has exploded with the publication
                        of physical therapy–specific clinical practice guidelines,27–29
                        clinical prediction rules,30,31 the integration of evidence-
                        based practice with clinical reasoning,32–35 and the growth
                        of knowledge translation and implementation efforts across
                        the profession.36,37 The availability of synthesis documents
                        and resources for practice (eg,EDGE task force materials for
                        examination,38,39 synthesis and implementation resources40)
                        has also aided in clinical reasoning.41

                        Figure 1. The Revised Integrated Framework illustrates the centrality of
                        the shared decision-making and the inﬂuence of both movement science
                        and the movement system in the reasoning process. The patient-client
                        management organizes the steps of the reasoning process. Hypothesis
                        generation occurs at each step. An episode of care may follow the steps
                        of the patient client management sequentially.

                        This manuscript describes the revised Integrated Frame-
                        work for Clinical Decision Making (Fig.1), identifies the
                        emerging concepts and evidence that led to the revisions,and
                        extends the framework to persons with all health conditions.
                        Each step in the process is illustrated using 2 case examples:
                        a bus driver with low back pain and a librarian with postural
                        instability and falls. For those aspects of the framework
                        that have not changed, the reader is referred to the original
                        manuscript for details.1 Specifically, the revised Integrated
                        Framework of Clinical Decision Making:

                        a) applies to persons with any health condition across the
                        lifespan,
                        b) updates patient-centered concepts with shared clinical
                        decision-making,
                        c) frames the episode of care around the patient’s goals for
                        participation,
                        d) explicitly describes the role of movement science,
                        e) reconciles movement science and ICF language,illustrat-
                        ing the importance of each perspective to patient care,
                        f) provides a process for movement analysis of tasks,and
                        g) integrates the movement system into patient manage-
                        ment.

                        History and Interview
                        A key change in this revised framework is a focus on shared
                        decision-making.Thisclient–therapistpartnershipbeginsdur-
                        ing the history and interview.The questions that the clinician
                        asks and the way they are phrased lays the groundwork for
                        collaboration.ThisapproachisinformedbytheICF,Gordon-
                        Quinn’sadaptationoftheICF,42 strategiesfrommotivational
                        interviewing,43–45 and an appreciation of a person’s “readi-
                        ness to change.”46,47 A major focus is to understand the
                        patient’s perception of their condition, goals related to the
                        episode of care,and meaningful benchmarks of progress.It is
                        important to gain an appreciation of existing life constraints
                        or resources such as health insurance, home support, job
