                        To fully share decision-making, the clinician needs to
                        appreciate the patient’s preferences regarding their roles
                        and activities while considering what might be realistic for
                        the patient. This exchange of information, which occurs
                        throughouttheepisodeofcare,providescontextualinsightto
                        the clinician regarding the individual’s specific situation and
                        provides insight to the person regarding likely expectations
                        and time frames.
                        Inparallelwithgatheringinformationduringtheinterview,
                        the physical therapist observes the person’s spontaneous
                        movement, which can inform tasks and tests/measures to be
                        included in the systems review and examination. Likewise,
                        observations and queries related to cognition, learning
                        style, and preferences are important for the scope of the
                        intervention.
                        Systems Review
                        The second major change in this revised framework is the
                        organization of the systems review using the 6 body sys-
                        tems that comprise the movement system (cardiovascular,
                        pulmonary, integumentary, musculoskeletal, endocrine, and
                        nervous).17 The systems review systematically rules out body
                        systems with which the physical therapist need not be con-
                        cerned, identifies those that are resources for the patient,
                        guideschoicesregardingwhichaspectsoftheremainingbody
                        systemsimpactmovement,andidentifiesifreferraltoanother
                        health care provider is indicated.10 An existing component of
                        the systems review, obtained for all patients, is the minimum
                        dataset(vitalsigns[heartrate,bloodpressure],height,weight,
                        orientation, attention, communication ability, and learning
                        style).10

                        The systems review must be tailored to each person and
                        includes information obtained from a variety of sources
                        (eg, medical record, health history questionnaire, subjective
                        report, direct assessment). Targeted questions during the
                        interview process can identify unknown or unreported
                        health conditions as well as signs and symptoms that could
                        suggest alterations in function in specific body systems.Some
                        examples of such targeted interview questions are provided
                        (Tab.2, middle column). Other information is obtained by
                        direct assessment; examples of useful tests/measures are
                        presented (Tab.2,right column).
                        The clinician determines the combination of targeted ques-
                        tionsandscreeningtestsandmeasuresthatareusefulforeach
                        patient. Because sources of information vary across individu-
                        als, the order of obtaining information is person specific. On
                        completion of the systems review, the clinician can generate
                        an initial hypothesis related to the patient’s movement limita-
                        tions and makes preliminary decisions regarding the specific
                        activitiesthatneedtobeexaminedandthetestsandmeasures
                        that will be included in examination.The history and clinical
                        reasoningduringsystemsreviewaredemonstratedfor2cases:
                        a bus driver with low back pain and a librarian who incurred
                        a recent fall and injury (Tab.3).

                        tasks. The purposes of the examination are to (1) collect
                        baseline data on participation and activity that will be used
                        to determine clinical outcomes of the episode of care and
                        (2) obtain data from movement observations-analyses and

                        tests/measures of activity and Body Function Structure (BFS)
                        that will inform the evaluation, diagnosis, and prognosis. In
                        this revised integrated framework, we explicitly reconcile the
                        differences in language that exist between the ICF and move-
                        ment science and clarify how each perspective contributes to
                        clinical decisions.
                        The World Health Organization proposed the ICF as the
                        current model of health in 2001.2 ICF concepts and language
                        wereincorporatedintothethirdeditionoftheGuidetoPhys-
                        ical Therapist practice, replacing the previous World Health
                        Organization disablement models and terminology found in
                        the first edition of the “Guide.”71
                        Movement science was proposed as a basis for physical
                        therapist practice by Carr and Shepherd72 in 1987 and is
                        informed by biomechanics,kinesiology,psychology,and neu-
                        roscience.73 Motor control and motor learning are distinct
                        areas of study within the field of movement science. Many
                        motor control theories have been described to guide the
                        examination of movement. A current theory, the “systems
                        theory,” frames motor control by examining the relation-
                        ship between internal attributes of the person (eg, cognition,
                        perception, and action) and how these interact with the envi-
                        ronmentandtheattributesofthespecificmovementortask.74

                        Movement science terminology provides useful language and
                        toolsforphysicaltherapythatarenotprovidedbytheICF.We
                        acknowledge the value of both sources. In this version of the
                        framework, we consider the words “tasks” (motor learning)
                        and “activities”(ICF) as synonyms.
                        To combine the ICF and movement science concepts into
                        the examination of goal-directed motor behavior,we propose
                        that clinicians follow this 3-step process (Fig.2).
                        The clinician’s first step is to dissect the person’s partici-
                        pation goal into relevant component activities (ICF) or tasks
                        (movement science) in the context of their personal factors,
                        identifying what the client is both able and unable to do.
                        Activities that the clinician identifies as resources (able to do)
                        need no further examination; those that are not performed
                        successfully or efficiently require movement observation and
                        are interpreted through a “movement analysis of tasks”
                        (Step 2).
                        Considerthepersonwithchroniclowbackpainwhowants
                        to participate in their role as a bus driver (case example 1,
                        Tab.3). Achievement of this goal requires that the person

                        In the second step,the physical therapist performs a move-
                        ment observation and analysis of the relevant tasks that

                        have been identified as important by the person and the
                        clinician (Fig.2, left side). The term “tasks” is used here
                        from movement science to be consistent with “task analysis”
                        and “task specific training.” Movement Analysis of Tasks
                        begins with movement observation, followed by interpreta-

                        of Gentile’s taxonomy was offered as a tool to examine
                        the patients’ movement (stationary or moving) relative to
                        the environment (stationary or moving); this approach
                        provided a systematic progression of complexity.1,75 We
                        now extend the environment construct to incorporate the
                        additional considerations (physical, social, and attitudinal)
                        included in the ICF. When feasible, movement analysis of
                        activities-tasks should be examined in the environmental
                        context in which the person executes them. For example, in
                        the case of the bus driver (Tab.3), examination of driving
                        could be performed in a simulated driving environment
                        to reproduce all the contextual cues. In the case of the
                        librarian (Tab.3), locomotion and reaching tasks can be
                        assessed in the clinic using a mobile cart, shelves, and light
                        objects.

                        10 Clinical Decision-Making Across Health Conditions

                        available, such as biomechanical analyses across the lifespan
                        and health conditions,76–81 the Motor Control Framework
                        (MCF),82 and, more recently, the Academy of Neurologic
                        Physical Therapy (ANPT) Framework.83
                        In the first iteration of the integrated framework, we used
                        the MCF described by Hedman and colleagues82 in combi-
                        nation with Gentile’s taxonomy75 to guide movement obser-
                        vation and analysis. In this iteration of the integrated frame-
                        work, we expand the movement analysis of the tasks to
                        also include the approach recently recommended by ANPT
                        MovementSystemDiagnosis-MovementAnalysisTaskForces
                        Framework (ANPT Framework).83 The ANPT Framework
                        expands the original taxonomy described by Hedman and
                        colleagues and furthermore defines specific “observable con-
                        structsofmovement”thatcanbeanalyzedacrosstasks.These
                        constructs of movement, when considered together, reflect
                        what we refer to as “movement control.” Of importance,
                        this concept of movement control goes beyond the BSF and
                        activity categories of the ICF and is integral to the role of the
                        physical therapist as the movement specialist.
                        To date, the ANPT Framework has been applied to assess
                        the performance of 6 core tasks (sitting, sit-to-stand, stand-
                        ing, step up/step down, walk and turn, and reach/grasp/-
                        manipulate), but it may also be applied to other tasks (eg,
                        those relevant to examining high-level athletic performance,
                        age-appropriate motor development, etc). In the case exam-
                        ples presented in Table 3, the MCF is primarily used for
                        the movement analysis of tasks for the bus driver, while a
                        combination of the ANPT/MCF frameworks is used for the
                        librarian.
                        The third step in the examination process is to identify
                        body function/structure limitations that may interfere with
                        optimal movement and activity-task performance. To this
                        end, the clinician generates hypotheses from the movement
                        analysis of tasks (Step 2). These hypotheses may be tested
                        by combining movement observations with modification to
                        the environment as well as conducting relevant tests/mea-
                        sures (right side of Fig.2). For example, the clinician may
                        change the height of the chair during sit-stand to differentiate
                        between a force generation deficit or a range of motion
                        limitation.Knownrelationshipsbetweenbodyfunctionstruc-
                        ture limitations and activity-task performance guide this pro-
                        cess.84,85
                        Tests and Measures
                        The use of tests and measures (right side of Fig.2) com-
                        plements the participation goal dissection and movement
                        analysis of tasks (left side of Fig.2). APTA and its academies
                        havecompiledandrecommendedstandardizedtests/measures
                        across multiple practice areas and clinical settings86–88
                        and health condition–specific clinical practice guidelines.
                        For example, the case example of a person with low back
                        pain (Tab.3) demonstrates application of recommendations
                        regarding activity, participation,89 and physical90,91 and
                        mental body function structure measures92 from the first
                        physical therapy–specific clinical practice guidelines on low
                        back pain.93
                        The proposed sequence of the examination process as
                        described above is not obligatory. For example, a person
                        in the ICU with multiple trauma from a car accident and
                        loss of consciousness may not be able to communicate or
                        move without maximum assistance. For this person, the
                        relevant participation goals may need to be negotiated with

                        the caretaker. The limitations of purposeful active movement
                        may lead the clinician to directly assess cognition and range
                        ofmotion,bypassingamovementanalysisoftasksduringthe
                        initial encounter. As the individual recovers, the clinician can
                        then assess those activities that the person can attempt and
                        that are consistent with their participation goals. A second
                        example is a person with an acute total hip arthroplasty; the
                        clinician may examine range of motion, strength, and edema
                        prior to examining bed mobility,sit-to-stand,and gait.
                        Throughout the examination process, clinicians continue
                        to refine hypotheses about the relationship between the par-
                        ticipation goal, activity requirements, movement analysis of
                        tasks, and contributing body function/structure limitations,
                        all within the context of environmental and personal factors.
                        The results of the examination combined with the history
                        and systems review guide the evaluation and diagnosis. The
                        hypothesesgeneratedthroughouttheexaminationprocessfor
                        2 cases are described in Table 3.
                        Evaluation
                        In this iteration of the revised framework, we focus on inte-
                        grating each person’s movement ability into the evaluation
                        process, an element of decision-making that, to our knowl-
                        edge, has not been described to date. To achieve this, the
                        clinician should first identify which of the 6 identified body
                        systems, as components of the movement system, contribute
                        to the patient’s activity/participation limitations, which body
                        systems are not involved, and which body systems may be
                        enhancing activity/participation.
                        Next, as outlined by the ICF2 and elaborated on by oth-
                        ers,94 it is imperative for the clinician to identify any rel-
                        evant personal or environmental factors that impact, in a
                        positive or negative manner, the person’s ability to achieve
                        their stated goal or participate fully in rehabilitation. The
                        assessment of task-activity performance, as described above
                        in examination, adds the movement observation of tasks
                        to identify underlying movement control limitations. The
                        movement control factors underlying the person’s difficulty
                        with performed desired tasks and roles must be specifically
                        identified.Factors proposed by the MCF and the ANPT Task
                        Force include movement accuracy, symmetry, sequence and
                        timing, speed, smoothness, and amplitude as well as stability,
                        verticality, body alignment, and symptom provocation.81–83
                        Additional factors that affect task performance may relate
                        to body function structure limitations such as the muscu-
                        loskeletal system (muscle performance,95 joint hyper/hypo-
                        mobility)orthecardiovascularorpulmonarysystems(activity
                        tolerance). It is also important to determine if the person’s
                        task performance is consistent or changes across various
                        environmental conditions. For example, a person post-total
                        knee replacement may demonstrate similar difficulty rising
                        to stand from a low seat at home or at the barber shop
                        if the factors underlying task performance are deficits in
                        muscleperformanceandkneeflexibility.Incontrast,aperson
                        with Parkinson disease may be able to walk safely within
                        a quiet, familiar environment but not in the community if
                        the key movement-related factors underlying walking are
                        decreasedmovementspeedandimpaireddual-taskabilityand
                        endurance.
                        This evaluation summary linking participation and activity
                        restrictions to movement control factors and impairments in
                        body structure/function is discussed with the person, rein-
                        forcing the ongoing shared decision-making. Analysis of the

                        Diagnosis
                        Perspectives related to diagnosis made by physical therapists
                        havechangedsubstantiallysincepublicationofthefirstframe-
                        work. These changes were driven by the profession arriving
                        at a definition of the human movement system, recognition
                        that movement analysis of tasks is a critical component of
                        the examination, and ongoing efforts to develop agreed on
                        movement system diagnoses, referred to as diagnostic labels.
                        To date,only a limited number of diagnostic labels have been
                        proposed30,31,96–104; further work will be required to arrive
                        at useful diagnostic labels that can be used in a consistent
                        manner by health professionals,for all health conditions,and
                        across the lifespan.105
                        Identifyingthemovementsystemdiagnosisforeachpatient
                        extends the clinical reasoning process because it requires
                        the clinician to consider all available information about the
                        person and clearly identify each person’s primary movement
                        control problem(s), independent of health condition or age.
                        This step in the clinical reasoning process differs from what
                        is currently reflected in the Guide to Physical Therapist Prac-
                        tice, which states that “a diagnosis is typically made at the
                        impairment, activity and participation levels.”10 In fact, we
                        areproposingthatthemovementsystemdiagnosismayreflect
                        both movement control attributes andunderlying body struc-
                        ture/function impairments. We acknowledge the importance
                        of linking together findings related to the person’s impair-
                        ments, activity, and participation as well as to the patient’s
                        goalsasdescribedintheevaluationsectionabove.Incontrast,
                        however, our use of the term movement system diagnosis
                        (label)identifiestheprimaryunderlyingcause(s)ofmovement
                        dysfunction,whichmayaffectmultipleactivities.Thischange
                        is important because the step of identifying and labeling
                        the primary causes of the movement problem focuses the
                        intervention clearly on those movement deficits (and their
                        underlying contributing factors) that are likely to have the
                        greatest impact on participation.
                        We envision that movement system diagnoses,as they con-
                        tinue to be developed, will be best labeled at the level of
                        movement control and/or at the level of impairments in body
                        structure/function, and that each diagnosis will be associated
                        with a clear description of the movement control charac-
                        teristics and body structure/function impairments associated
                        with the diagnosis. The diagnosis we propose for the bus
                        driverwithlowbackpainidentifiesdeficitsinbothmovement
                        control characteristics (ie, sequencing, asymmetry) and BSF
                        impairments (ie, force generation, neuromuscular endurance,
                        and pain). In contrast, the diagnosis proposed for the person
                        with frequent falls is solely at the level of movement control
                        (ie,deficit in anticipatory and reactive postural control).
                        Individuals with the same health conditions may present
                        with different movement system diagnoses. For example, the
                        person with frequent falls (case example 2, Tab.3) with a
                        diagnosis of “deficits in muscle performance”would lead the
                        clinician to choose intervention strategies primarily aimed at
                        improvingstrength.Inthisexample,interventionplanswould
                        be focused differently than what is outlined in Table 3, even
                        though the health condition and presenting history may be
                        the same.

                        Goals
                        Goals for rehabilitation should relate to the person’s partici-
                        pation in relevant life roles or activities and must be carefully
                        identified to target their reported concerns and participation
                        limitations. In this revision of the integrated framework, we
                        emphasize how to use a shared decision-making approach to
                        arriveatagreedongoals,emphasizingmeaningfulbenchmark
                        goalsthatindicateprogressatparticipationandactivitylevels.
                        In the context of shared decision-making, the clinician and
                        patient should revisit the person’s initially stated goals to
                        determine if they are realistic and appropriate. Information
                        obtained during the systems review and examination, includ-
                        ing movement analysis, guides this process along with acuity
                        and severity of the health condition and other comorbid con-
                        ditions.Inaddition,theclinicianandpatienttogethercarefully
                        considerthemainconcernsandaspirationsaswellasenviron-
                        ments in which the person functions and life circumstances
                        (eg, relevant personal and environmental factors) that might
                        impact their ability to participate in or respond to rehabilita-
                        tion. Early in the episode of care, the patient should identify
                        realistic “benchmark goals”or improvements in activity/par-
                        ticipation that they consider meaningful progress (Tab.3).
                        If a patient does not articulate the goals at the level of
                        participation (eg, goal is to walk, without any context), the
                        clinician assists them to relate their stated goals to important
                        life activities. If a patient’s stated goals are inappropriate or
                        unrealistic, the clinician assists them to identify additional
                        goals that are central to improving the person’s desired activ-
                        ity and participation or are preventative. Taking all these
                        factors into consideration,the clinician and patient may need
                        to renegotiate goals at this point in the episode of care to
                        arrive at mutually agreed on, meaningful to the person, and
                        realistic goals to achieve within the available time frame.
                        Examplesfromthecasespresentedinthisarticleincludegoals
                        for individuals related to both return to work and return to
                        recreational activities (Tab.3).
                        Tofacilitateshareddecision-making,thecliniciancanshare
                        data regarding best practice and typical outcomes related to
                        thepatient’scondition.Inaddition,agrowingbodyofhealth-
                        or condition-specific decision aids can assist individuals seek-
                        ing care to participate in an informed manner. For example,
                        the Ottawa Personal Decision Guide25 may help the person
                        with low back pain (Tab.3) prioritize the return to work
                        and sleep goals before the recreation goal. It should be noted
                        that many decision aids are still being vetted for quality and
                        efficacy.106–108

                        Prognosis
                        Prognosisisbasedonthepatient’sgoals,withanemphasison
                        those related to activity and participation. Prognosis should
                        bespecificforeachgoal(eg,goalofwalkinginthehousemay
                        haveadifferentprognosisthangoalofwalkinginthecommu-
                        nity). To determine prognosis for activity and participation,
                        the clinician synthesizes knowledge from the examination,
                        health condition, foundational knowledge, theory, evidence,
                        and experience.
                        Consider,forexample,apersonwhosustainedalowerlimb
                        amputation due to dysvascularity (eg,diabetes).The person’s
                        goalistoreturntoworkwithin4monthstoajobthatrequires
                        walking. Regarding the health condition, consideration is
                        given to the expected level and rate of recovery based on evi-
                        dence. Issues to consider include the nature of the pathology

                        Physical Therapist Practice. It incorporates the language of the

                        (inthiscase,dysvascularity)aswellasstage,acuity,andtissue

                        about morbidity and mortality associated with lower limb
                        amputation.109–112
                        To determine prognosis with regard to benchmark goals
                        related to activity (walking) and participation (return to
                        work), the clinician draws on available data such as those
                        related to likelihood and timing of achieving independent
                        ambulation within 1-year post amputation,113 likely average
                        daily steps, and114 likely overall level of disability.114–116
                        The clinician keeps these types of data in mind when
                        assessing likelihood that this person will have sufficient
                        walking capacity at 4 months to return to work but tempers
                        expectations with respect to important modifiers that may
                        be facilitators or barriers to recovery. These modifiers
                        may include presurgical activity and endurance, previous
                        engagement and success with physical therapy, access to
                        rehabilitation services, and support. The clinician also
                        considers resources and constraints based on personal factors
                        (eg, their social, emotional, and motivational status) and
                        environmental factors. Prognosis statements are provided for
                        both case examples in Table 3.

                        Plan of Care
                        The plan of care (POC) focuses on the patient’s participa-
                        tion goals and related activities and body function/structure
                        requirements and is based on results of the examination,
                        evaluation, and movement system diagnosis. Elements that
                        are new to this revised framework include (1) application of
                        evidence-based shared decision-making to identify and select
                        optionsforintervention;(2)useofthemovementsystemdiag-
                        nosis to guide intervention; (3) recommendation to include
                        wellness and prevention in every plan of care; (4) application
                        of task-specific training for all health conditions and across
                        the lifespan; and (5) intervention at the body function struc-
                        ture level guided by the physiology of tissue healing and the
                        Frequency, Intensity, Time and Type (FITT) principle117,118
                        (see Fig.3).

                        Evidence-based Shared Decision-Making
                        The shared decision-making conversation in the POC focuses
                        on the clinician identifying evidence-based options for treat-
                        ment that are then selected and agreed on with the patient.
                        Examplesofoptionsthatcanbeofferedtothepatientinclude
                        choices among different appropriate interventions,how often
                        to attend clinic-based visits, and how to best structure a
                        realistic home exercise program.24
                        Movement System Diagnosis to Guide Intervention
                        The shared decision-making conversation also includes the
                        explanation of the movement system diagnosis and how to
                        address it. Individuals with the same health condition may
                        have different movement system diagnoses. We include in
                        Table 3 possible diagnostic labels for the bus driver and
                        librarian case examples and then outline an appropriate POC
                        for each example based on the diagnosis. In the low back
                        pain case example, the person has a movement system diag-
                        nosisof“motorcontroldeficits.”Anotherindividualwiththe
                        same health conditions could present with a fear-avoidance
                        movement system diagnosis,and the POC might then include
                        activities to increase self-efficacy rather than strength and
                        endurance.

                        Prevention and Health Promotion-Wellness
                        Included in Every POC
                        Educationcomplementsthedirectinterventionsandisthekey
                        strategy for prevention and wellness.119 In the revised frame-
                        work, prevention and health promotion–wellness are recom-
                        mended in every episode of care. Prevention addresses both
                        patient-identified problems and non–patient-identified prob-
                        lems (Hypothesis Oriented Algorithm for clinical decision-
                        making) and relies on the clinician’s knowledge of the health
                        condition,potential complications,and movement system.
                        Health promotion–wellness is an addition to this revised
                        framework and reflects the expanded role of the physical
                        therapist.66,120 Prevention and health promotion–wellness
                        are administered through patient education, direct care, or
                        referral and collaboration with colleagues. The transtheo-
                        retical model of behavior change uses stages of readiness
                        to guide the wellness intervention.60,61 These elements of
                        the POC are especially relevant for persons with chronic
                        health conditions.121,122,123 Health promotion and wellness
                        and prevention may be delivered as a single intervention; for
                        example,promotionofphysicalactivityisaninterventionthat
                        can address both wellness and prevention.124
                        Task-Speciﬁc Training
                        Knowledge of movement science is used to organize activity-
                        task–specific training; this includes selection of the task and
                        the environment, practice schedule, type and frequency of
                        feedback provided to the patient, and dose. Principles of
                        exercisecomplementmovementscience.Thespecificityofthe
                        intervention (ie, how task-specific training is implemented
                        for each patient) is derived from the movement analysis of
                        tasks and hypotheses about the factors contributing to the
                        patient’s limitations. Evidence of the relevance of task speci-
                        ficity is extending beyond treating persons with neurological
                        conditions. For example, persons with chronic knee pain
                        due to osteoarthritis who had task-specific training improved
                        both their trained tasks (sit-stand, floor-to-stand, and stair
                        negotiation) and had pain reduction.125

                        Downloaded from https://academic.oup.com/ptj/article/102/3/pzab281/6497836 by guest on 05 May 2025


                        Deutsch et al 13

                        In this revised framework, there is a fundamental assump-
                        tion that plasticity occurs across the cardiovascular, neuro-
                        muscular, integumentary, and musculoskeletal systems and
                        plasticity can be augmented with training and stimulation.
                        Evidence supports plasticity across systems126 and requires
                        that interventions or training be task specific and of a high
                        enough duration and intensity to achieve both behavioral
                        and structural changes.127–129 For this reason, we restate the
                        importance of dose in task-specific training. As an example,
                        the delivery of rehabilitation using task-specific training at
                        the correct dose to achieve improved walking for a person
                        post stroke is achieved with the use of high-intensity interval
                        trainingonatreadmill.127 Thehigh-intensityintervaltraining
                        improves the cardiovascular and neuromusculoskeletal sys-
                        temsbyimprovingaerobiccapacity,130 balance126 andneuro-
                        muscular endurance,126 all of which contribute to achieving
                        improved ambulation (activity/task goal) that will enable the
                        person to return to their job as a security guard.

                        Body Function/Structure–Level Intervention
                        Interventions to address relevant alterations in body func-
                        tion/structure are guided by knowledge of physiologic recov-
                        ery, tissue healing, and the FITT principle. Inflammation and
                        tissue healing are important to understand in the selection of
                        interventions that may promote optimal restoration. These
                        approaches are well defined based on the understanding of
                        tissue repair phases based on physiology: inflammation, pro-
                        liferation, and maturation; and tissue-healing phases based
                        on time acute, sub-acute, and chronic.131,132 Foundational
                        knowledgeofthephysicaltherapistguidesselectionofmodal-
                        ities and interventions.132
                        The FITT principle provides a systematicwayto dose body
                        function/structure interventions across health conditions.For
                        example, strengthening guided by FITT principles has been
                        appliedtopersonspoststroke,133 postlungtransplant,134 and
                        withinflammatorymyopathy.135 Themovementsystemdiag-
                        nosisguidestheinterventionofthebodyfunction/structureas
                        illustrated by the driver with low back pain (Tab.3). In this
                        example,severalinterventionswilldirectlyaddressthelimita-
                        tions with joint and soft tissue mobility to complement the
                        trunk and lower extremity strengthening activities. Further,
                        interventions aimed at reducing deficits in body structure/-
                        functioncanbeperformedinthecontextoftherelevanttasks.
                        In the example of the librarian, lower extremity strengthen-
                        ing can be performed using repeated sit-to-stand tasks from
                        various height surfaces with different foot positions; this task
                        could also incorporate holding objects and reaching to place
                        them onto surfaces.

                        Summary of the Framework and Application
                        There isacriticalneed for aunifying clinicaldecision-making
                        framework in physical therapy to highlight our expertise
                        as movement specialists and enhance communication within
                        and outside of the profession. This paper offers a unifying
                        framework that responds to changes in evidence and practice
                        thatoccurredoverthelast15years.Itisorganizedaroundthe
                        patient-client management of the Guide to Physical Therapist
                        practiceandisframedbyshareddecision-makingbetweenthe
                        patient and the clinician. Goals that focus on participation
                        are emphasized as an organizing principle,and guidelines are
                        providedfordissectingparticipationgoalsintoactivities-tasks

                        that can be examined or simulated in the clinic. Approaches
                        to task dissection and movement observation of tasks are
                        presented as a critical component of examination to enable
                        specific deficits in movement control to be identified, recog-
                        nizing that these deficits are not included in the ICF concepts
                        of BSF or tasks/activities. Movement and exercise science
                        serveasthetheoreticalfoundation.ICFandmovementscience
                        terminology are integrated to link these distinct bodies of
                        knowledge. The human movement system is integrated into
                        thesystemsreview,evaluation,anddiagnosis.Throughoutthis
                        article, case examples are used to illustrate the application of
                        the framework across all health conditions. The framework
                        is proposed as a tool for physical therapist education and
                        guide for clinical practice for all health conditions across the
                        lifespan.

                    .Neuro Exam Part 1 - Introduction

                    .Objectives
                    • Describe the organization of the neurologic physical therapy examination
                    • Provide rationale for organization of the neurologic physical therapy examination
                    • Identify frameworks that support the organization of the neurologic physical 
                    therapy examination


                    .Neurological Examination
                    • Objective and quantifiable tests and measures
                    oIdentify impairments
                    oIdentify additional needs (referrals, adjunct treatment)
                    oMeasure recovery of function
                    oCreate realistic goals 
                    oAid in appropriate discharge planning
                    oAssess the effectiveness of our interventions


                    .PT Examination ('')
                        - PT Examination  
                            - Physical Therapist Decision Making  
                              - REFER  
                                - Other PTs  
                                - Other disciplines  
                                - MD/DO/DDS (etc)  
                                - NPs/PAs  
                                - Psychology  
                                - Social work  
                                - Nursing  
                              - CO-MANAGE  
                                - Other disciplines  
                                - MD/DO/DDS (etc)  
                                - NPs/PAs  
                                - Psychology  
                                - Social work  
                                - Nursing  
                              - CONSULT  
                                - Other PTs  
                                - Other disciplines  
                                - MD/DO/DDS (etc)  
                                - NPs/PAs  
                                - Psychology  
                                - Social work  
                                - Nursing  
                              - RETAIN  
                                - Direct/Supervise  
                                  - Physical Therapist Assistants  
                                  - Physical Therapist Aides/Technicians  
                                  - Physical Therapist  
                                    - Develops plan of care  
                                    - Retains accountability for the plan of care  
                                    - Defines boundaries within which others assisting with service delivery operate  
                                    - Always has the option to perform all elements or direct and supervise  

                    .International Classification of Functioning, Disability, and Health ('')
                        (Γ)- International Classification of Functioning, Disability, and Health  
                          - Health condition (disorder or disease)  
                            - A healthy person with no known disease  
                          - Body functions and structures  
                            - Normal body tissues/organs functions (motor control, muscle tone, normal sensation, etc.)  
                          - Activity  
                            - Tasks and skills as expected (independent, efficient, and safe ADLs, transfers, mobility, ambulation)  
                          - Participation  
                            - Fulfilling roles, engagement in community/society (social outings with family and friends, shopping at market, attending church)  
                          - Contextual factors  
                            - Environmental factors  
                            - Personal factors  

                    .Conceptual Basis for Outcome Measurement ICF (2001) – International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health ('')
                        (Γ).PLANTILLA.Conceptual Basis for Outcome Measurement  
                          - ICF (2001) – International Classification of Functioning, Disability, and Health  
                          - Health Conditions  
                            - Underlying diagnosis or pathology  
                            - Tissue level  
                            - Example: Stroke  
                          - Body Function  
                          - Body Structures  
                            - Impairments  
                            - Loss or abnormality in structure/function  
                            - Organ level  
                            - Examples:  
                              - Paralysis  
                              - Aphasia  
                              - Spasticity  
                          - Activity  
                            - Activity Limitation  
                            - Functional limitations in daily life  
                            - Person level  
                            - Examples:  
                              - Assistance needed for ambulation  
                              - Self-care  
                          - Participation  
                            - Participation Restriction  
                            - Involvement or restriction in life situations  
                            - Societal level  
                            - Examples:  
                              - Changes in work roles  
                              - Social roles  
                              - Leisure activities  

                    .Physical Therapy Evaluation Framework ('')
                        (Γ).PLANTILLA.Hypothesis-Oriented Algorithm for Clinicians II (HOAC II - Part 1)

                        1. Collect initial data
                           - Gather information from referral, medical records, observation prior to formal evaluation, and patient interview

                        2. Generate patient-identified problems (PIPs) list
                           - Problems are predominantly descriptions of functional limitations
                           - Problems described from the patient's perspective on abilities and disabilities

                        3. Formulate examination strategy
                           - Based on initial hypotheses drawn from available data and identified patient problems
                           - Consultation if necessary

                        4. Conduct examination, analyze data, refine hypotheses, and adjust evaluation procedures accordingly

                        5. Add non-patient-identified problems (NPIPs) to the problem list
                           - Problems identified by the therapist or collaborating healthcare professionals (including family members)
                           - Anticipated problems that could lead to disability and decreased health status if unaddressed

                        6. For each existing problem
                           - Generate hypotheses on underlying causes
                           - Hypotheses often identify impairments contributing to the problem
                           - Some hypotheses may pinpoint pathological processes causing impairments, functional limitations, or disabilities with measurable evidence
                           - Consultation if necessary

                        7. For each anticipated problem
                           - Provide rationale for why anticipated problems may develop without intervention
                           - Justification is based on analysis of potential pathologies, impairments, and their impact on function and participation
                           - Consultation if necessary

                        8. Refine problem list  
                           - Adjust and finalize problem identification based on further assessment and verification
                        ------------------------------------------------------------------------------

                            ### Functional Assessment
                            - Observations of Movement and Task Analysis

                        .Step 1
                            -Preparation prior to formal evaluation begins.
                            -Generate a list of expected impairments and activity limitations.
                            -Formulate an examination strategy and identify what information will be prioritized.

                        .Step 2
                            -Identify those aspects of the individual's presentation which are functionally limiting, based on the PT examination findings and movement analysis.
                        .Step 3
                            -Determine patient–centered goals within the individual’s physical and cognitive capacity
                            -Design an intervention plan that is aimed at treating or compensating for the impairments/activity limitations and improving activity participation, vocational and avocational activities, community integration, and quality of life.
                        .Step 4
                            -Guided by available literature, provide appropriate intervention tactics for optimal function i.e., chievement of goals.
                            -Reassess and adjust tactics as appropriate.
                        .Step 5
                            -Community Engagement: address opportunities to incorporate new skills within the community for activity participation
                            -Promote sustainability of acquired skill and encourages healthy lifestyle behaviors

                    .Step 2 of the Framework ('')
                        (Γ).PLANTILLA.Step 2 of the Framework
                            1. History, Observation, and Review of Systems

                            2. Sensory Exam  
                               - Light Touch screen  
                               - S/D  
                               - Proprioception  

                            3. Balance Exam  
                               - Standing (and Sitting) Balance:  
                                 - Static Standing Balance: Sensory orientation and reactive postural control  
                                 - Dynamic Standing Balance: Self-generated voluntary postural control  
                                 - Walking Balance  

                            4. Mental Status Exam  
                               - Basic Mental Functions, Complex Mental Functions, and Meta-cognitive Functions  

                            5. Motor Exam  
                               - Muscle Mass  
                               - ROM  
                               - Tone  
                               - Muscle Capacity (Strength [force production], Endurance, Power)  
                               - Motor Control of Movement/Stability  
                               - Observation of Involuntary Movements  

                            6. Functional Skills Exam and Movement Analysis  
                               - Changing and Maintaining Body Positions:  
                                 - Bed mobility  
                                 - Sit <-> Stand  
                                 - Transfers  
                               - Mobility:  
                                 - Walking (level surface and complex situations)  
                                 - Stairs  
                               - Hand and Arm Use  
                                 - Grasping & Object Manipulation  

                            7. Cranial Nerve Integrity Exam  

                            8. Coordination Exam  
                               - FTN  
                               - HTS  
                               - Alt. Movements  

                        .Why is it structured this way?

                    .Summary
                    • The purpose of the neurologic PT exam is to identify impairments and aid in 
                    decision-making for PT treatment
                    • Based on the findings of the neurologic PT exam, we can identify additional 
                    referral or consult to other disciplines
                    • The findings of the neurologic PT exam can be used to measure progress, to 
                    create goals, and to develop plans of care

                    3:12
                    generating an initial problem list,
                    3:18
                    formulating an examination strategy,
                    3:21
                    and conducting the examination.
                    3:23
                    In the box to the right,
                    3:26
                    you can see some of the specific components of the neurologic PT exam,
                    3:28
                    which we'll go into in more detail in Modules 3 and 4.
                    3:33
                    Dr. Josbeno uses this framework to guide neurologic rehabilitation.
                    3:39
                    Step 1 aligns with the first step in the HOAC model,
                    3:45
                    where we are collecting initial information.
                    3:49
                    We may start to generate initial hypotheses from this initial information.
                    3:52
                    Step 2, which will be the main focus of the following two modules,
                    3:58
                    includes conducting the neurologic PT examination, including movement analysis.
                    4:02
                    Step 3 is where we would determine the physical therapy diagnosis,
                    4:10
                    and treatment strategies that align with patient goals.
                    4:14
                    Step 4 then includes carrying out the plan of care using
                    4:19
                    evidence-based treatment to facilitate
                    4:23
                    functional recovery or to maintain functional competence.
                    4:25
                    We may also re-evaluate during this step to determine if our treatment is
                    4:29
                    effective or may need to be adjusted based on patient presentation.
                    4:33

                    4:39
                    This is an important part of physical therapy.
                    4:44

                    4:46
                    improvement or maintenance of the gains that
                    4:51
                    the patient has made with physical therapy treatment.
                    4:53
                    As I mentioned, we will focus on Step 2 of this framework in Modules 3 and 4.
                    4:57
                    The neurologic PT exam can be divided into different assessments,
                    5:05
                    all of which are important.
                    5:10
                    However, some components of the exam may be
                    5:12
                    prioritized more than others depending on the individual patient,
                    5:16
                    the diagnosis, their personal factors,
                    5:20
                    availability of background information and many other factors.
                    5:24
                    We suggest structuring the neurologic PT exam in this order.
                    5:29
                    Of course, the first step is to review the patient history,
                    5:34
                    conduct a review of systems,
                    5:38
                    assess vital signs, and start with an initial observation of the patient,
                    5:40
                    which can really tell you a lot.
                    5:45
                    We suggest starting with mental status because this allows us to determine
                    5:47
                    how well the patient will be able to participate
                    5:53
                    in the remainder of the neurologic exam.
                    5:55
                    Are they alert and oriented?
                    5:58
                    Can they follow commands?
                    6:00
                    Does the patient have any cognitive impairments that may
                    6:02
                    affect how we conduct the exam and subsequent treatments?
                    6:05
                    We then suggest assessing cranial nerve function.
                    6:10
                    This can also assist with determining
                    6:14
                    sensory and or motor impairments that may impact the exam,
                    6:17
                    such as; do they have a visual field loss,
                    6:21
                    or difficulty communicating,
                    6:23
                    or a hearing impairment?
                    6:25
                    Cranial nerve findings may also indicate central nervous system pathology and
                    6:27
                    this information may be used to determine
                    6:32
                    if a referral to another provider is necessary.
                    6:35
                    Next, we suggest assessing the sensory system,
                    6:38
                    including light, touch, pain,
                    6:42
                    and temperature, and proprioception.
                    6:44
                    Sensory loss can affect how we may conduct our motor coordination,
                    6:46
                    balance, and or functional exams.
                    6:50
                    We may observe abnormal movement that could be related to a loss of
                    6:53
                    joint position sense rather than a motor impairment,
                    6:57
                    so it is important that we know if there's a sensory loss to
                    7:01
                    identify if that is a component to movement dysfunction.
                    7:04
                    Then we move on to the motor exam,
                    7:09
                    including an assessment of range of motion,
                    7:12
                    tone, and force production.
                    7:14
                    After we have assessed sensation and motor systems,
                    7:16
                    we move on to the coordination exam.
                    7:20
                    Here we may find deficits related to coordination of movements such
                    7:23
                    as impairments that you may see in persons with cerebellar pathology.
                    7:27
                    Next, we assess balance and function,
                    7:31
                    to identify how the functional impairments may be affecting
                    7:35
                    the patient's ability to balance
                    7:38
                    and participate in functional movements and or mobility.
                    7:41
                    We will discuss each of these components of
                    7:45
                    the neurologic PT exam in detail in the subsequent lectures.
                    7:48
                    In summary, the purpose of the neurologic PT exam is to
                    7:53
                    identify functional impairments and to aid
                    7:58
                    in decision making for physical therapy treatment.
                    8:01
                    We also use the findings from the neuro PT exam to identify the need for additional
                    8:04
                    referral or console to other disciplines or to a colleague within the same discipline.
                    8:10
                    The findings of our neurologic PT exam, including outcome measures,
                    8:16
                    can be used to measure progress,
                    8:21
                    create goals, and develop plans of care.

                    Neuro Exam Part 2 – History and review of systems

                    .FRAMEWORK to guide care (Dr. Josbeno)

                    .Physical Therapy Evaluation Framework
                        (Γ)
                            Γ We are here → ### Examination Strategy
                            Γ We are here → - Observation and History Review of Systems (ROS)

                            Γ We are here → ### Review of Systems
                            - Tests and Measures
                              - Mental Status  
                              - Cranial Nerve Examination  
                              - Sensory Assessment  
                              - Motor/Reflexes Evaluation  
                              - Coordination and Balance Testing  

                            ### Functional Assessment
                            - Observations of Movement and Task Analysis

                    .Step 2 of the Framework

                    .History
                        • Demographics
                        • History of Present Illness (HPI)
                            o Chief complaint
                        • Past Medical History (PMH)
                            o Past surgical history
                        • Pertinent Health Information 
                            o Medication and Allergies
                            o Diagnostic Tests
                            o Precautions
                        • Prior level of function
                        • Social History
                            o Home environment and caregiver support
                            o Work/Social engagement
                        • Client goals 
                            o What would they like to get back to?

                    .Chief Complaint
                    • Description of what the patient experiences or 
                    believes is wrong
                    • Specific details about the problem
                    • Nature or extent of the disability 
                    • What are the patients concerns

                    .History of Present Illness (HPI)
                        • Date of onset (duration)
                        • Manner of onset (traumatic, post-surgical, gradual)
                        • Whether the problem has remained the same over time or has changed for the better or worse
                        • Whether any activities or factors worsen or improve the problem

                    .Past Medical History (PMH)
                    • Previous injuries or illness
                    • Previous hospitalization
                    • Surgical procedures
                    o Dates, interventions and outcomes

                    .Pertinent Health Information
                    • Allergies
                    • Medications
                    • Tests specific to diagnosis
                    • Precautions

                    .Prior Level of Function
                    • Use of assistive devices
                    • Driving status
                    • Need assistance for ADLS or IADLs
                    • Activities
                    • Work
                    • Social roles

                    .Home Environment
                    • Live alone or with others
                    • Caregiver
                    • Steps
                    • Bathroom/bedroom set-up
                    • Width of halls
                    • Size of rooms
                    o Wheelchair maneuverability 

                    .Client goals – sample questions from text
                        2. Interview questions designed to engage the patient in 
                        treatment planning:

                            What specific concerns or fears do you have? What is your 
                            greatest concern?

                            What are your goals?

                            What are your expectations about what might happen with 
                            your illness or condition?

                            What would make you feel that you are making progress in 
                            dealing with your chief concern?

                            What do you hope this treatment can do for you?

                            What would be important to include in your plan of care?

                            What questions do you have?

                        3. Interview questions designed to identify desired outcomes in terms of 
                        essential functional activities:

                            How has this illness/condition affected your daily life?

                            What activities or experiences are important to you?

                            What activities do you normally do at home/work/school?

                            What activities do you have difficulty with?

                            How is this different than before your illness or condition (i.e., extra time, 
                            extra effort, different strategy)?

                            What activities have you had to give up because of your illness or 
                            condition?

                            What activities do you need help to perform that you would rather do 
                            yourself?

                            How can I help you be more independent?

                    .Observation
                        • Positioning/posture
                        • Verbal communication
                        • Non-verbal communication
                        o Facial expressions
                        o Emotional response
                        o Eye contact
                        • Movement
                        o Gait
                        o Transfers 


                    .Review of Systems (ROS)
                    • Cardiovascular/pulmonary system
                    • Integumentary system
                    • Musculoskeletal system 
                    • Neuromuscular system
                    • Gastrointestinal
                    • Genitourinary/reproductive
                    • Hematologic/lymphatic
                    • Psychological
                    • Endocrine
                    • Cognition, communication, affect, language, learning styles/preferences


                    .International Classification of Functioning, Disability, and Health ('')
                        Γ See in other sections where we have an outline.

                    .Summary
                        • The first step in the neurologic PT exam is to take a history, perform a review of 
                        systems, and observe the client
                        • The information gathered from this component of the neurologic PT exam can 
                        provide detailed information about the health condition, impairments in 
                        function, activity limitations, participation restrictions, environmental barriers, 
                        and personal factors (ICF)
                        • The information gathered from the history and review of systems allows for 
                        the formation of a patient-identified problems list, initial hypotheses regarding 
                        examination strategy and treatment approaches (HOAC II)
