                    .Neuro Exam Part 3 - Mental status examination

                    .Objectives
                    • Provide rationale for assessing mental status, including arousal, attention, 
                    cognition, perception, and communication
                    • Describe the components and procedures for a comprehensive mental status 
                    exam
                    • Explain how the findings from the mental status exam may impact the neurologic 
                    PT exam and treatment


                    .Physical Therapy Evaluation Framework
                        ### Examination Strategy
                        - Observation and History Review of Systems (ROS)

                        ### Review of Systems
                        - Tests and Measures
                        Γ We are here → - Mental Status  
                        - Cranial Nerve Examination  
                        - Sensory Assessment  
                        - Motor/Reflexes Evaluation  
                        - Coordination and Balance Testing  

                        ### Functional Assessment
                        - Observations of Movement and Task Analysis


                    .FRAMEWORK to guide care (Dr. Josbeno)


                    .Step 2 of the Framework
                        4. Mental Status Exam  
                           Γ We are here → - Basic Mental Functions, Complex Mental Functions, and Meta-cognitive Functions 

                    .Rationale for assessing mental status first
                        • Determine extent of cognitive impairment
                        • TBI, stroke
                        • Identify disease processes
                        • Cognitive impairment, Alzheimer disease
                        • Stroke, brain tumor
                        • Determine the client’s ability to participate in exam and treatment
                        • Ability to follow commands
                        • Safety considerations
                        • Assist in plan of care development (goal-setting)
                        • Home exercise program
                        • Aids in discharge planning
                        • Development of strategies to promote motor learning
                        • Determination of feedback and practice schedules
                        • Referral to other services


                    .Terminology related to mental status
                    • Alertness
                    • Arousal/Level of Consciousness
                    • Awareness
                    • Attention
                    • Executive function
                    • Memory
                    • Reasoning


                    .Mental Status  
                        1. Continuum of Mental Functions  
                           - Basic Functions  
                             - Level of Consciousness  
                             - Awareness  
                             - Alertness  
                           - Complex Functions  
                             - Language  
                             - Memory  
                             - Sequencing  
                           - Meta-Cognition  
                             - Executive Functions  
                             - Self-Awareness  
                             - Mood/Motivation  

                        This outline preserves accuracy while ensuring clarity and structure. Let me know if you need any refinements!


                    .Mental Status Exam
                    • Examination is a cascade of events
                    • Begins with observation
                    • Includes listening and watching the patient during the history part of the 
                    examination
                    • Progressing to assessing more complex mental functions and meta-cognitive 
                    functions
                    • Organization and prioritization of components will depend on setting, 
                    diagnosis, and impairments present


                    .Sequencing of tests
                    • Arousal
                    • Attention
                    • Cognition and Executive Function


                    .Arousal/Level of Consciousness
                    • Alert
                    • Lethargic
                    • Delirium
                    • Obtunded
                    • Stupor
                    • Coma

                    • Outcomes for patients with coma: Glasgow Coma Scale, Rancho Los Amigos 
                    Levels of Cognitive Function, Coma Recovery Scale-Revised


                    .Orientation – from text
                    • Person
                    • What is your name?
                    • Do you have a middle name?
                    • How old are you?
                    • When were you born?
                    • Place
                    • Do you know where you are right now?
                    • What kind of a place is this?
                    • Do you know what city and state we are in?
                    • What city or town do you live in?
                    • What is your address at home?
                    • Time
                    • What is today’s date?
                    • What day of the week is it?
                    • What time is it?
                    • Is it morning or afternoon?
                    • What season is it?
                    • What year is it?
                    • How long have you been here?


                    .Attention
                    • May observe the following during history/observation:
                        • Ability to follow a command
                        • Ability to sustain motor activity
                        • Ability to do two things at once (walk and talk)
                        • Ability to resist distractions
                    • Common tests used to assess attention
                        • Spell a word backward
                        • Count backward
                        • Digit Repetition Test (should be able to repeat 5-9 digits)
                        • Moss Attention Rating Scale (specific to brain injury)


                    .Mental Status
                        Γ Repeated slide; see previous


                    .Cognition
                    • May observe the following during history/observation
                    • Signs of agitation: restlessness, decreased visual contact, increased 
                    distractibility
                    • Difficulty with word finding
                    • Difficulty remembering past events or details of illness
                    • Common outcome measures
                    • Mini-Mental Status Examination (MMSE) 
                    • Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) 


                    .Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) 


                    .Language and Communication
                    • Observe:
                    • Quality of speech
                    • Comprehension
                    • Ability to write, name objects, repeat words
                    • Receptive language 
                    • The patient is asked to follow commands in order to demonstrate that they understand the 
                    meaning of what they have heard or read.
                    • Expressive language 
                    • The patient is asked to perform a task that requires spontaneous speech or writing, or 
                    naming of objects, repeating phrases, note fluency and correctness of words
                    • Disorders of speech
                    • Aphasia
                    • Verbal apraxia
                    • Dysarthria


                    .Memory
                    • Temporal lobe
                    • Short term memory (recent 
                    memory)
                    • The patient is asked to perform a 
                    three-word recall
                    -immediate recall
                    -delayed recall (5 mins)

                    • Frontal Lobe
                    • Working memory
                    • Subtract by 7s
                    • Abstract reasoning
                    • The patient is asked to problem 
                    solve, verbal similarities and 
                    interpret proverbs


                    .Visual Spatial Function and Perception
                    • Assess visual spatial tasks 
                    • The patient is asked to bisect a line, draw a face, clock or geometric figures 
                    (such as a cube or cylinder)
                    • Deficits are often due to loss of function in parietal association areas but can be 
                    due to lesions in other areas as well
                    • Body image/body scheme
                    • Visual discrimination
                    • Apraxia
                    • Agnosia


                    .Other Executive Functions
                    • Problem-solving
                    • Judgement
                    • Reasoning
                    • Insight
                    • Safety Awareness


                    .Mental Status


                    .Meta-cognitive Functions and Mood
                        • Self-awareness
                            • Ability to recognize one’s own behavior, character, personality, etc.
                        • Screening for depression/mood
                            • Geriatric Depression Scale
                            • Patient Health Questionnaire
                            • Beck Depression Inventory


                    .Mental Status - Management 1 ('')
                        ### Mental Status - Management
                        #### Restorative Approaches
                        - Focus on skill-based training augmented by:
                          - Strategy training programs
                          - Cognitive exercise programs

                        #### Compensatory Approaches
                        - Focus on skill-based training augmented by:
                          - Habit training
                          - Environmental adaptation

                    .Summary
                        • Assessment of mental status occurs on a continuum ranging from basic mental 
                        functions to meta-cognition
                        • Organization of the mental status exam can vary based on patient presentation, 
                        setting, and diagnosis
                        • Assessing mental status at the beginning of the neurologic PT exam will inform 
                        the structure of the exam and potential treatment options, appropriate referrals, 
                        and screening for additional impairments

                    .Neuro Exam Part 4 — Cranial Nerves

                    Γ.For this charpter, go over: 'Q&A doc::.Cranial Nerve Exams' (!!E)

                    .Objectives
                    • Describe and perform the components of a cranial nerve exam
                    • Recall the function of each cranial nerve and identify the associated deficits that 
                    are present when the nerve is lesioned
                    • Explain rationale for prioritizing a de-prioritizing the cranial nerve exam based on 
                    patient presentation

                    .Tests of Cranial Nerve Function - from text Γ(See Mnemonics: 'Q&A doc::.Cranial Nerve Exams')
                        -Cranial nerve I: Examine olfactory acuity using non-noxious odors such as lemon oil, coffee, cloves, or peppermint
                        -Cranial nerve II: Examine visual acuity using a Snellen chart; both central and peripheral vision is tested.
                        -Cranial nerves III, IV, and VI: Determine equality and size of pupils; reaction to light; presence of strabismus (loss of ocular alignment); ability 
                        of eyes to follow a moving target without head movement; presence of ptosis of eyelid.
                        -Cranial nerve V: Sensory tests of face (sharp/dull discrimination, light touch); open and close jaw against resistance; jaw jerk reflex.
                        -Cranial nerve VII: Examine any asymmetry of face at rest and during voluntary contraction.
                        -Cranial nerve VIII: Test auditory acuity using a vibrating tuning fork (Weber test) placed on vertex of skull or forehead; patient indicates on which side the tone is louder. Rub fingers together at a distance and gradually bring toward patient; note distance when first heard. Alter volume of conversation. Rinne test (conductive hearing loss), vibrating tuning fork placed on mastoid process, then near external ear canal; note hearing acuity.
                        -Cranial nerve IX: Examine taste on posterior one-third of tongue; examine gag reflex.
                        -Cranial nerve X: Examine swallowing; observe uvula and soft palate for any asymmetry (tongue depressor).
                        -Cranial nerve XI: Examine strength of the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles.
                        -Cranial nerve XII: With tongue protruded, examine ability to move tongue rapidly from side to side.


                    .Cranial Nerve I: Olfactory Nerve
                        Not typically part of PT exam
                        • Clinical Examination
                        oTest each nostril separately
                        oHave the patient report if they can smell a non-noxious 
                        odorants
                        • Treatment Considerations?
                        oTies to memory, emotions, motivations
                        oCan affect taste, appetite

                    
                    .Cranial Nerve II: Optic Nerve
                    • Visual Acuity
                    oSnellen or LogMAR chart
                    oAssess one eye at a time
                    • Visual Fields
                    oConfrontation testing one eye at a time
                    oAssess each quadrant of visual field
                    • Pupillary Light Reflexes (sensory component)
                    oUse penlight and observe pupillary response in each eye
                    oLesion to the sensory component: would not see a response in 
                    either eye
                    • Treatment considerations


                    .CN II: Optic Nerve ('')
                        Optic nerve
                        Optic chiasm
                        Optic tract
                        Lateral geniculate body
                        Superior colliculus
                        Optic radiations
                        Primary visual cortex (medial occipital lobe)


                    .Cranial Nerves III, IV, and VI: Oculomotor, Trochlear, and Abducens
                    • Conjugate eye movements
                    • Observe resting position
                    • H-Test: Observe eye movement when the patient is asked to follow a target
                    • Convergence
                    • Ask the patient to follow a target that is moved toward nose


                    .Extraocular muscles
                    • Cranial nerve III
                    • Superior, inferior, medial rectus, inferior oblique - turns eye up, 
                    down, in 
                    • Ptosis of the eyelid
                    • Efferent limb of pupillary light reflex
                    • Cranial nerve IV
                    • Superior oblique - turns the adducted eye down
                    • Cranial nerve VI
                    • lateral rectus - turns eye out

                    
                    .Ocular Movements: How We shift our Gaze
                    • Smooth Pursuit- the ability of the eyes to smoothly follow a moving 
                    object (slowly)
                    • Saccade- quick involuntary small movements of both eyes 
                    simultaneously occurs when the eyes fix on one point after another in 
                    the visual field.
                    oWhile keeping the head still the patient looks quickly between two points
                    oTest both horizontal and vertical movements
                    oBoth eyes should accurately move together to the target


                    .Cranial Nerve V: Trigeminal 1
                    • Sensory Portion
                    oFacial Sensation--face, head, cornea, mucosa of nose, mouth, hard and soft 
                    palate, and tongue
                    ▪ V1 ophthalmic division
                    ▪ V2 maxillary division
                    ▪ V3 mandibular division
                    o Corneal reflex
                    ▪ Afferent limb


                    .Cranial Nerve V: Trigeminal 2
                    • Motor Portion
                    oMuscles of mastication
                    ▪masseter
                    ▪temporalis
                    ▪med/lat pterygoid
                    ▪digastric / mylohyoid
                    ▪tensor tympani-hearing low pitch sounds
                    oJaw jerk reflex


                    .Cranial Nerve V: Trigeminal 3
                    • Clinical Examination
                    oSensory testing to face
                    ▪Can assess light touch and sharp/dull
                    ▪Bilateral forehead
                    ▪Bilateral cheek
                    ▪Bilateral lower jaw
                    oMuscles of mastication
                    ▪Open and close jaw
                    ▪Bite down on tongue depressor and observe/palpate 
                    masseter or temporalis muscles

                    
                    .Cranial Nerve VII: Facial 1
                    • Motor Portion
                    oObserve facial symmetry
                    oShow Teeth superior levator
                    oSmile buccinatior
                    oEyes Closed Tight orbicularis, frontal belly
                    oElevating Eyebrows epicranius
                    oContract Platysma platysma
                    oCorneal reflex (efferent limb)
                    • Sensory Portion
                    oTaste Anterior 2/3 of the tongue 


                    .Cranial Nerve VII: Facial 2
                    • Clinical Examination
                    oObservation of gestures and facial movements
                    oSelf-reports of taste changes
                    • Treatment Considerations
                    oBells Palsy: damage to the peripheral nerve VII
                    oFacial weakness due to cortex lesion: lower face on 
                    contralateral side is affected
                    oFacial weakness due to CN VII nucleus lesion: 
                    upper and lower ipsilateral side of face affected


                    .Cranial Nerve VIII: Vestibulocochlear 1
                        ('') Γ Repasa esta foto


                    .Cranial Nerve VIII: Vestibulocochlear 2
                    • Cochlear Portion
                    oLesion symptoms
                    ▪ Hearing loss
                    • Clinical Examination (Screen)
                    oSnap, finger rub, whisper
                    oRinne Test: place tuning fork on mastoid process, then move the tuning fork 
                    next to the ear (bone vs air conduction)
                    oWeber Test: tuning fork placed on top of head and patient is asked if they hear 
                    ringing louder in one ear than the other
                    • Treatment considerations
                    oAny sudden hearing loss should be referred to a specialist
                    oAsymmetrical hearing loss of unknown cause should be assessed with 
                    audiogram


                    .Cranial Nerve VIII: Vestibulocochlear 3
                    • Vestibular Portion (semicircular canals, utricle, saccule)
                    oClinical Assessment
                    ▪ Observe for nystagmus
                    ▪ Head Impulse Test (HIT) for vestibulo-ocular reflex
                    ▪ Balance
                    oTreatment Considerations
                    This portion of the cranial nerve will be revisited in our next unit 


                    .Cranial Nerve VIII: Vestibulocochlear 4
                    Head Impulse Test (HIT):
                    • The examiner quickly rotates the patient’s head from 10 
                    degrees to one side back to midline while the patient 
                    focuses on a target
                    o In a normal VOR response, the patient is able to fixate 
                    on central target
                    o In an abnormal response, there is an inability to 
                    maintain fixation during rotation of the head requiring a 
                    corrective saccade once head has stopped moving


                    .Cranial Nerve IX, X: Glossopharyngeal and Vagus 1
                    • Glossopharyngeal
                    oSensory, taste to the posterior 1/3 of the tongue, pharynx and soft palate
                    oMotor to stylopharyngeus muscle
                    • Vagus
                    oMotor to the pharynx, larynx, and soft palate and parasympathetic innervation 
                    to the gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, and respiratory systems


                    .Cranial Nerve IX, X: Glossopharyngeal and Vagus 2
                    • Clinical Examination
                    oObservation/ask about swallowing
                    oUsing a penlight, ask the patient to vocalize a sustained “ahh” and observe 
                    the soft palate symmetry and movement of the uvula
                    ▪ If there is an asymmetry, the uvula will deviate to the stronger side
                    oGag reflex (not often part of PT assessment)
                    ▪ When the back of the pharynx is touched with a tongue depressor, should observe a 
                    symmetrical contraction and rise of soft palate


                    .Cranial Nerve IX, X: Glossopharyngeal and Vagus 3
                    • Lesion symptoms
                    o Loss of taste
                    o Loss of gag reflex
                    o Dysphagia
                    o Vocal quality
                    • Treatment considerations
                    oSwallowing issues should be evaluated by SLP
                    oBe aware of offering liquids to a patient with suspected swallowing issues

                    
                    .Cranial Nerve XI: Spinal Accessory
                    • Motor
                    oInnervates upper trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles
                    oCharacterized by muscle atrophy and / or shoulder droop
                    • Clinical Examination
                    oRotate head
                    oElevate scapula

                    

                    .Cranial Nerve XII: Hypoglossal
                    • Motor functions of the tongue
                    • Clinical Examination
                    oMay observe/have reported issues with eating, speech
                    oAppearance of the tongue
                    ▪The tongue will deviate to the weaker side 

                    
                    .Summary
                    • Some components of the cranial nerve exam are not part of routine physical 
                    therapy examinations
                    • Not all components of the cranial nerve exam may be prioritized and will depend 
                    on the patient presentation and history
                    • Findings of the cranial nerve exam can help determine the location of a lesion 
                    (central vs. peripheral; brainstem vs. cortex) 
                    • Findings of the cranial nerve exam can help to drive further examination 
                    procedures and/or identify potential needs for referral

                    .Neuro Exam Part 5 – Sensory Systems

                    .Objectives
                    • Describe and perform the sensory component of the 
                    neurologic PT exam
                    • Provide rationale for prioritizing vs. de-prioritizing 
                    components of the sensory exam
                    • Recall the sensory pathways being tested when assessing 
                    various sensory modalities (i.e., pain and temperature vs. 
                    joint position sense and vibration)


                    .Physical Therapy Evaluation Framework
                        ### Examination Strategy
                            - Observation and History Review of Systems (ROS)

                        ### Review of Systems
                            - Tests and Measures
                            - Mental Status  
                            - Cranial Nerve Examination  
                            Γ We are here → - Sensory Assessment  
                            - Motor/Reflexes Evaluation  
                            - Coordination and Balance Testing

                    .Framework to guide care (Dr. Josbeno)
                        Γ We are here → .Step 2
                            -Identify those aspects of the individual's presentation which are functionally limiting, based on the PT examination findings and movement analysis.

                    .Step 2 of the Framework
                        2. Sensory Exam  
                            - Light Touch screen  
                            - S/D  
                            - Proprioception

                    .Sensory Exam 1
                        • Provide us with an awareness of the environment 
                        • Essential part of assessment due to the influence of sensation on 
                        movement control
                        • Examination of conscious sensation
                        • Two major sensory pathways that are examined (!!E)
                            Anterolateral system 
                            Dorsal column-medial lemniscus (DCML) system

                    .Sensory Exam 2 (!!E).Lv1
                    • A sensory deficit from a cerebral or brainstem lesion usually occur in a 
                    unilateral distribution
                        ¦Parlem de costats i creuaments
                    • A sensory deficit from a spinal cord injury usually occur in a paraplegic or 
                    tetraplegic distribution
                        ¦Parlem de nivells d'altura
                    • A sensory deficit from a spinal nerve lesion will be in a dermatome 
                    distribution
                        ¦Parlem d'un camí que te un origen (corda spinal; en este cas) i un final (el dermatoma); però tot a lo llarg del camí es afectat
                    • A sensory deficit from a peripheral nerve lesion will be in the distribution 
                    of that peripheral nerve.
                        ¦Només la perofèria es afectà o lo que concern a ixe nervi 
                    • A sensory deficit from a polyneuropathy will have a stocking and glove 
                    distribution because the longest axons are the most affected
                    May be referred to as the “dying back rule”


                    .Distributions of Sensory Deficits ('')


                    .Sensory Exam 3 (!!E)
                    • Anterolateral system
                    opain
                    otemperature
                    • DCML 
                    ojoint position sense
                    opressure touch
                    ovibration
                    • Light touch is represented in both the ALS and DCML system 
                    oUsed to screen the sensory system but not specific for either system


                    .Sensory Exam - Guidelines 1
                    • Observation/History
                    • Determine mental status
                    • Screen vs. formal sensory testing
                    • Environment set-up
                    • Patient preparation/demonstration
                    • Sequence of exam


                    .Sensory Exam- Guidelines 2
                    • Patient preparation
                    oProvide explanation of the testing
                    oPatient should not be fatigued
                    oTrial run to orient the patient to the sensation being testing and 
                    what type of response is required – should be on an area of the 
                    skin where sensation is intact
                    oOcclude the patient’s vision during the testing


                    .Sensory Exam- Guidelines 3
                    • Sequence of exam
                    oSuperficial, deep, combined cortical sensations
                    oOrganization of the exam may be performed differently based on patient 
                    presentation/diagnosis
                    ▪ Example: dermatomal pattern, distal to proximal, etc.
                    ▪ With noted deficit, additional testing in that area should be completed to identify region on sensory 
                    loss
                    ▪ Compare bilaterally
                    ▪ Application of stimuli is applied in a random order


                    .Terminology (!!E).Q&A
                    • Normal/intact sensation
                    • Absent sensation
                    • Hypoesthesia/impaired sensation
                    • Hyperesthesia – hypersensitivity
                    • Dysesthesia/allodynia – perceived as a painful sensation
                    • Paresthesia – abnormal sensation (pins and needles, burning, tingling, numbness)


                    .Sensory Exam : Superficial Sensations 1
                    • Light touch
                    oEquipment: cotton ball, tissue
                    oDemonstrate to patient
                    oClose eyes
                    oAsk to respond every time they feel the sensation
                    oProvide variability by asking the patient when no 
                    sensation is being applied


                    .Sensory Exam : Superficial Sensations 2
                    • Pain perception (sharp and dull)
                    oEquipment: paperclip or reflex hammer
                    oDemonstrate procedure, defining sharp and dull
                    oAsk patient to close eyes
                    oHold in place several seconds and ask if they feel sharp or dull sensation
                    • Temperature awareness
                    oEquipment: metal handle of reflex hammer, (hot/cold water)
                    oDemonstrate procedure defining cold
                    oAsk patient to close eyes
                    oHold in place several seconds and ask if the stimulus is cold


                    .Sensory Exam : Deep Sensations
                    • Vibration Perception: examines the ability to perceive a vibratory stimulus
                    oEquipment: 128 Hz tuning fork
                    oStrike the tuning fork on a surface and hold against a bony prominence
                    oEyes closed
                    oAsk the patient if they feel any vibration (introduce variation)
                    • Pressure touch
                    oNot usually assessed formally in PT examination
                    oDeep vs. light pressure
                    oSemmes-Weinstein monofilament testing
                    • Joint position sense (JPS): examines the awareness of joints at rest
                    • Kinesthesia/joint movement sense


                    .Vibration Sense ('')


                    .Joint Position Sense 1
                    • Hold the most distal aspect of the joint being tested by the sides while moving it 
                    slightly up or down and hold in a static position
                    • Slowly move the joint (10 degrees per second); hold in one place and ask the 
                    patient if the joint is positioned “up” or “down”
                    • Test variable directions and ranges 
                    • The patient should be able to detect small amounts of movement in fingers and 
                    toes
                    • If the patient can't accurately detect the distal movement, then progressively test 
                    a more proximal joint until they can identify the movement correctly


                    .Joint Position Sense 2 ('')


                    .Kinesthesia/Joint Movement Sense
                    • Similar to assessment of joint position sense
                    • The patient’s extremity is moved passively through a small range

                    Response: patient is to verbally describe the direction of movement while the 
                    extremity is being in motion


                    .Sensory Exam: Combined Cortical Sensations
                    Not often part of routine neurologic PT examination
                    • Stereognosis
                    • Graphesthesia
                    • Two-point discrimination
                    • Bilateral simultaneous stimulation- extinction phenomena
                    • Tactile localization
                    • Barognosis
                    • Recognition of texture


                    .Step 2 of the Framework ('')
                        2. Sensory Exam  
                           - Light Touch screen  
                           - S/D  
                           - Proprioception


                    .Summary
                    • Sensory impairments may be found in different patterns 
                    based on the pathology responsible for sensory deficits
                    • The sensory exam may be organized in various ways based 
                    on diagnosis and patient presentation but often is organized 
                    using dermatomes
                    • The sensory exam may be comprised of a comprehensive 
                    examination, or a screening based on the history, diagnosis, 
                    observation, and patient presentation

                    9:13

                    12:58

                    13:03

                    .Neuro Exam Part 6 — Motor

                    .Objectives
                        • Describe and perform the motor components of the neurologic PT 
                        exam
                        • Provide rationale for prioritizing or de-prioritizing components of the 
                        motor exam 
                        • Identify how impairments found in the motor exam affect function, 
                        activities, and participation

                    .Physical Therapy Evaluation Framework
                        ### Examination Strategy
                        - Observation and History Review of Systems (ROS)

                        ### Review of Systems
                        - Tests and Measures
                          - Mental Status  
                          - Cranial Nerve Examination  
                          - Sensory Assessment  
                          Γ We are here → - Motor/Reflexes Evaluation  
                          - Coordination and Balance Testing  

                        ### Functional Assessment
                        - Observations of Movement and Task Analysis

                    .Framework to guide care (Dr. Josbeno)
                        Γ We are here → .Step 2
                            -Identify those aspects of the individual's presentation which are functionally limiting, based on the PT examination findings and movement analysis.

                    .Step 2 of the Framework
                        Γ We are here → 5. Motor Exam  
                           - Muscle Mass  
                           - ROM  
                           - Tone  
                           - Muscle Capacity (Strength [force production], Endurance, Power)  
                           - Motor Control of Movement/Stability  
                           - Observation of Involuntary Movements

                    .Movement
                        Movement can be voluntary or involuntary

                        Movement may occur consciously or can take place 
                        unconsciously, even may take place as a reflex

                        Movement may be executed through hardwired set of 
                        instructions available at birth

                        Movement may be learned and refined to a skill after much 
                        practice 

                    .Motor System (!!E) mmm.Molt bon esquema de les àries d'interés
                        • Cortex
                            • Primary motor
                            • Premotor
                            • Supplemental motor area
                        • Subcortical nuclei
                            • Basal ganglia
                            • Thalamus
                            • Substantia nigra
                            • Red nucleus
                            • Vestibular nuclei
                            • Reticular nuclei
                        • Cerebellum
                        • Descending pathways
                            • Dorsolateral
                                • Lateral Corticospinal tract
                                • Rubrospinal tract
                            • Ventromedial
                                • Tectospinal
                                • Vestibulospinal
                                • Reticulospinal

                    .Lateral Corticospinal Tract (!!E)
                        Direct connections:
                        • Signals travel from the motor cortex to the alpha motor 
                        neurons of the spinal cord
                        Indirect connections:
                        • Bidirectional connections with extrapyramidal motor 
                        system (basal ganglia, cerebellum, brainstem)

                    .('')

                    .Ventromedial Pathways (!!E)
                        Controlled by brainstem 
                        Innervate axial and antigravity muscles and help keep head positioned during dynamic activities
                        Motor neurons that are in the medial part of the ventral horn
                            Tectospinal tract
                            Vestibulospinal tract
                            Reticulospinal tract

                    .Motor Exam: Screen
                        • Generally performed prior to transferring the patient
                        • Abnormal findings are identified and lead to a more detailed 
                        examination
                        oROM
                        oStrength 

                    .Observation/Inspection
                        • Posture/positioning
                        • Movement 
                        • Muscle mass
                        obulk (girth)
                        ocontour
                        osymmetry
                        olook for atrophy or hypertrophy

                    .Observations of Involuntary Movements (!!E)
                        • Tremors
                        oResting tremor
                        ▪ Present when muscles are resting 
                        ▪ May go away or become less noticeable with activity of the muscles that are involved 
                        ▪ Tremor is a cardinal sign of PD – often referred to as “pill-rolling” tremor
                        oAction/Intention tremor
                        ▪ Oscillations that are exaggerated at the end of the voluntary movement.
                        ▪ The tremor will often disappear while the affected body part is at rest
                        ▪ Seen with cerebellar pathologies
                        • Fasciculation-cause by an anterior horn cell and motor unit firing without a command; big enough 
                        to see; usually not big enough to move a joint
                        • Fibrillation- small firing of a muscle fiber; seen with EMG; pathological; signs of neuropathy

                    .Active Range of Motion
                        • Observe
                        oFull ROM
                        oCan provide assistance as needed (AAROM)
                        oMovement quality
                        • If full AROM cannot be attained without assistance OR 
                        movement quality is impaired, a PROM assessment is 
                        warranted

                    .Passive Range of Motion
                        • Slow movement through full ROM
                        • Assess soft tissue limitations and end feel
                        oEmpty
                        oBony
                        oFirm
                        oSoft tissue approximation

                    .Muscle Tone (!!E).Q&A
                        • Resistance of muscle to passive stretch when the patient attempts 
                        to maintain muscle relaxation.
                        • Types of abnormal tone: 
                        oFlaccidity
                        oHypotonia
                        oSpastic hypertonia
                        oRigid hypertonia
                        oDystonia

                    .Muscle Tone Assessment
                        • Can be difficult in proximal muscles
                        • Issues with inter-rater reliability
                        • May have noticed signs of abnormal tone upon observation
                        • The muscle being tested should be passively elongated while the patient is relaxed
                        • The examiner should feel for any resistance to passive movement at varying speeds 
                        (spasticity is velocity-dependent)
                        • Documentation:
                        oBody segment involved
                        oType of abnormal tone present
                        oPresence of asymmetries
                        oFactors that modify tone

                    .Severe Injury Associated with decreased LOC and coma ('') (!!E).Lv1
                        Decorticate Rigidity
                        • Occurs from disruption of influence from 
                        the cerebral cortex
                        • Spasticity of the flexor muscles of the 
                        upper extremity (static flexion posturing) 
                        and the extensors of the lower extremity 
                        (static extension posturing
                        Decerebrate Rigidity
                        • Occurs from disruption of excitatory 
                        input to brainstem nuclei
                        • Spasticity of the antigravity (extensor) 
                        muscles of the entire body

                    .Assessment of tone in biceps ('')

                    .Spasticity (!!E).Lv1
                        • Manifestation of UMN lesion (damage to corticospinal pathways)
                        • Common clinical presentations associated with spasticity
                        oClasp-knife: initial resistance with passive stretch then sudden release
                        oScissoring gait: adductor spasticity
                        oClonus
                        oBabinski sign
                        • Spasticity: may be a little as a “catch” or a very stiff limb that cannot be moved 
                        passively
                        • The tone state is velocity dependent
                        • Modified Ashworth Scale (MAS) can be used to rate the degree of spasticity

                    .Modified Ashworth Scale – from text
                        GRADE DESCRIPTION
                        0 No increase in muscle tone (no spasticity).
                        1 Slight increase in muscle tone, manifested by a catch and release or by minimal 
                        resistance but only at the end of the ROM when the affected part(s) is moved in 
                        flexion or extension.
                        1 + Slight increase in muscle tone, manifested by a catch, followed by minimal 
                        resistance detected throughout the remainder (less than half) of the ROM.
                        2 More marked increase in muscle tone detected through most of the ROM but 
                        affected part(s) are easily moved.
                        3 Considerable increase in muscle tone, passive movement difficult.
                        4 Affected part(s) rigid in flexion and extension.
                        Adapted from Bohannon RW, Smith MB. Interrater reliability of a modified Ashworth scale 
                        of muscle spasticity. Phys Ther. 1987;67(2): 206–207. 

                    .Rigidity/Rigid Hypertonia
                        • Rigidity is “lead pipe or cogwheel” resistance to passive 
                        movement 
                        • Is seen with disorders such as Parkinson’s disease
                        • The tone state is not velocity dependent to passive stretch

                    .Flaccidity and Hypotonia
                        • Often seen with LMN lesions and damage to the cerebellum
                        • Less resistance than expected to passive elongation of the muscle
                        • May see temporary flaccidity (days-weeks) after a CVA or SCI due 
                        to cerebral or spinal shock, but then may see UMN signs

                    .Reflexes
                        • Review examination of DTRs and pathologic reflexes from 
                        MSK
                        • Assessment of DTR can help to determine UMN vs LMN 
                        signs
                        • Assess bilaterally

                    .Strength (Force Production Capacity)
                        • Clinical Examination
                        oMMT
                        ▪ Utilize standardized positions
                        ▪ Identify substitutions
                        ▪ Test unaffected extremity first, then compare to the affected side
                        oDynamometry
                        oFunction
                        ▪ Estimation of strength can be made from observation of voluntary active 
                        movements

                    .Motor Control (!!E).Lv3
                        • Muscle strength alone does not fully describe intact motor function
                        • Motor control:
                        oThe process by which the brain organizes and regulates actions of 
                        movement and postural adjustment
                        oAbility of the nervous system to regulate the motor system with appropriate 
                        activation or relaxation during all normal functional activities
                        • Motor control of movement
                        oMotor control of muscles during voluntary movement
                        • Motor control of stability
                        oAbility of the brain to regulate muscles to precisely keep joints or body 
                        segments from moving at times when they should not move
                        • Motor coordination – will discuss in next lecture

                    .Motor Control of Movement
                        • Assess for quality of movement while the patient is performing a voluntary task
                        oSmoothness
                        oInitiation
                        oCessation
                        oFractionation – ability to move through small degrees of available range
                        oVary velocities

                    .Altered Motor Control of Movement: Abnormal Synergies ('')

                    .Motor Control for Stability 1 (!!E).Lv3
                        • Important for closed chain and weight-bearing activities
                        • Common examples of impaired motor control for stability in neurologic 
                        conditions:
                        oScapulothoracic instability
                        oGlenohumeral instability
                        oTrunk instability
                        oAnkle instability

                    .Motor Control for Stability
                        Γ Same as initial slide, see above

                    .Summary
                        • Clinical decision-making should be used to determine which 
                        components of the motor exam should be prioritized
                        • Assessment of ROM and tone can provide important information prior 
                        to conducting a strength assessment within the motor exam
                        • Analysis of motor control is an important component of the motor 
                        exam to determine quality of movement

                    .Neuro Exam Part 7 — Coordination

                    .Objectives
                        • Define coordination impairments and what structures are 
                        often implicated
                        • Describe and perform components of the coordination exam
                        • Provide rationale for conducting other components of the 
                        neurologic PT exam prior to a coordination assessment 
                        (observation, mental status, cranial nerves, sensory, motor)

                    .Physical Therapy Evaluation Framework
                       ### Examination Strategy
                       - Observation and History Review of Systems (ROS)

                       ### Review of Systems
                       - Tests and Measures
                         - Mental Status  
                         - Cranial Nerve Examination  
                         - Sensory Assessment  
                         - Motor/Reflexes Evaluation  
                         Γ We are here → - Coordination
                         - Balance Testing 

                    .Framework to guide care (Dr. Josbeno)
                        Γ We are here → .Step 2
                            -Identify those aspects of the individual's presentation which are functionally limiting, based on the PT examination findings and movement analysis.

                    .Step 2 of the Framework
                        8. Coordination Exam  
                           - FTN  
                           - HTS  
                           - Alt. Movements

                    .Coordination
                        • Ability to execute smooth, accurate, controlled movement
                        • Motor control interactions and cooperation between 
                        opposing muscle groups during a movement
                        • Performance depends on integrated functioning of multiple 
                        sensory systems and intact musculoskeletal and 
                        neuromuscular systems

                    .Components of Coordination 1 (!!E)
                        Motor Cortex
                            Primary Motor Cortex            
                            Supplementary motor area
                            Premotor area
                        Somatosensory cortex
                            Internal representation of the environment to provide input that guides motor responses

                        .Components of Coordination 2 mmm.Q&A.A good comparison among elements (!!E).Q&A
                            Basal Ganglia
                                Initiation and regulation of intentional movement
                                Planning and execution of complex motor task
                                Ability to accomplish automatic movements and postural adjustments
                                Facilitating desired movements while inhibiting other movements
                                Maintenance of normal background muscle tone

                    .Cerebellum (!!E)
                        • Regulation of movement, muscle tone, postural control
                        • Provides signals for error-correction

                    .Coordination Impairments (!!E)     
                        • Cerebellar pathology:
                        • Ataxia
                        oDysdiadochokinesia
                        oDysmetria
                        oIntention Tremor

                    .Purpose of Coordination Exam ('')
                        - Purpose of Coordination Exam
                          - Synergistic action of muscles
                          - Safety, risk factors for falls
                          - Level of skill, efficiency of movement
                          - Initiation, control, termination of movement
                          - Contributing underlying pathology
                          - Timing, sequencing, accuracy of movement
                          - Effect of therapy or medication on motor function
                          - Purposes of Coordination Examination
                            - DETERMINE

                    .Coordination Exam: Quantitative Assessment 1 (!!E)
                        Coordination tests focus on movement capability in the following areas:
                        • Reciprocal motion - the ability to reverse movement between opposing muscle 
                        groups
                        • Movement composition/synergy - movement control achieved by synergistic 
                        muscle groups acting together
                        • Movement accuracy - the ability to gauge or judge distance and speed of 
                        voluntary movement
                        • Fixation/limb holding - the ability to hold the position of an individual limb or limb 
                        segment

                    .Coordination Exam: Quantitative Assessment 2
                        • Each test is explained and demonstrated to the patient
                        • Observations:
                        oAre movements precise and easily reversed
                        oAre movements performed in a timely manner
                        oDoes speed affect performance
                        oDoes occluding vision alter the quality
                        oIs the impairments greater proximally or distally
                        oGreater on one side of the body

                    .Coordination Exam: Finger to Nose
                        • Clinical Examination
                        oPatient is asked to alternately touch his/her nose and tip of the 
                        examiner’s finger
                        oThe examiner’s finger is to be held far enough in front of the patient so 
                        that the patient must fully extend the arm to reach target
                        oObserve:
                        ▪ Reciprocal movement
                        ▪ Movement composition
                        ▪ Time to perform designated amount and number of errors
                        oMay see dysmetria (overshoot/undershoot) and/or intention tremor

                    .Coordination Exam: Heel to Shin 1
                        • Clinical Examination
                        oHeel is placed on the opposite shin and run up to the knee and 
                        back down to the ankle
                        oObserve:
                        ▪ Movement is performed quickly and without interruption or side to side 
                        wavering
                        ▪ Unsteady movement and unable to maintain contact between the heel 
                        and tibia crest
                        ▪ Time to perform designated amount
                        oThe inability to perform this maneuver properly indicates 
                        dysmetria

                    .Coordination Exam: Heel to Shin 2 ('')

                    .Rapid Alternating Movements
                        • Pronation/supination
                        oPatient is asked to rapidly supinate/ pronates the forearm
                        oObserve:
                        ▪ If movement are performed rapidly and rhythmically
                        ▪ Similar performance on both sides
                        oThe inability to perform rapidly alternating movements or simple 
                        motor tasks involving the rapid contraction and relaxation of the 
                        agonist/antagonist muscles is referred as 
                        DYSDIADOCHOKINESIA

                    .Coordination Exam: Heel to Shin
                        • Foot tapping
                        oIn sitting, the patient is asked to rapidly dorsiflex and plantarflex 
                        each foot while maintaining heel contact on the floor
                        oObserve:
                        ▪ If movement are performed rapidly and rhythmically
                        ▪ Similar performance on both sides
                        oThe inability to perform rapidly alternating movements or simple 
                        motor tasks involving the rapid contraction and relaxation of the 
                        agonist/antagonist muscles is referred as 
                        DYSDIADOCHOKINESIA

                    .Framework Step 2

                    .Summary
                        • Coordinated movement is a result of the integration of multiple systems including 
                        sensory, musculoskeletal, and neuromuscular systems
                        • During the coordination exam, movements should be inspected for reciprocal 
                        motion, synergy, accuracy, and limb holding
                        • Specific abnormal findings in the coordination exam may indicate different 
                        neurologic lesions to the cerebellum vs. basal ganglia vs. somatosensory 
                        systems

                    so that the patient must fully extend their arm to reach their target.
                    7:05
                    Remember that some signs of incoordination,
                    7:09
                    such as intention tremor,
                    7:12
                    are more obvious at the end range of a movement.
                    7:14
                    The examiner will observe the reciprocal movements and the movement composition.
                    7:18
                    You can measure this more objectively by counting the number of repetitions the patient
                    7:23
                    can complete in a certain time-frame such as 10 seconds.
                    7:28
                    Both sides of the body should be tested,
                    7:33
                    and you can vary the test by moving the target so that the patient
                    7:36
                    needs to readjust to accurately obtain the target,
                    7:39
                    or ask the patient to move at
                    7:43
                    faster or slower speeds to see if they are able to adjust their speed of movement.
                    7:45
                    With this test in patients with cerebellar lesions,
                    7:50
                    you may see dysmetria or a tendency to overshoot or undershoot the target.
                    7:53
                    You also may observe intention tremor.
                    7:58
                    The heel to shin test is a coordination assessment for the lower extremity.
                    8:02
                    This test was originally described in supine,
                    8:07
                    but the patient can also be seated.
                    8:10
                    The patient should place the heel of their right leg onto the shin of
                    8:13
                    their left leg and run their heel up and
                    8:17
                    down their shin from knee to ankle back and forth.
                    8:20
                    The clinician should observe the movement for speed accuracy, and again,
                    8:23
                    can measure how many repetitions the patient can complete in a certain time-frame.
                    8:28
                    Both legs should be assessed.
                    8:33
                    The inability to perform this maneuver properly or the inability to
                    8:36
                    maintain contact of their heel to their shin indicates dysmetria.
                    8:41
                    In these images, you can see the patient completing
                    8:47
                    the heel to shin test in a seated position.
                    8:50
                    Again, you may see it evaluated in sitting or in supine.
                    8:53
                    Prior to asking the patient to complete this test,
                    8:57
                    you need to determine if they have the strength and
                    9:00
                    range of motion that are necessary to complete the test,
                    9:03
                    so you would need to have assessed the lower extremities in your motor exam first.
                    9:07
                    Also included in the coordination exam should be rapid alternating movements,
                    9:12
                    which often include more finite or precise movements of the extremities.
                    9:18
                    One of the most common assessments is rapid forearm pronation and supination.
                    9:22
                    The patient is typically in a seated position and
                    9:28
                    asked to rapidly supinate and pronate their forearms.
                    9:31
                    Some clinicians ask the patient to alternate
                    9:35
                    tapping the palms of their hands and the back of their hands on their lap.
                    9:38
                    Again, the speed and the rhythm of the movement should be observed and
                    9:42
                    both sides can be compared
                    9:46
                    as the patient is asked to move both of their upper extremities together.
                    9:49
                    The inability to perform
                    9:54
                    rapid alternating movements is referred to as dysdiadochokinesia.
                    9:56
                    For the lower extremity,
                    10:01
                    a test of rapid alternating movements is foot tapping.
                    10:03
                    In sitting the patient is asked to rapidly dorsiflex and
                    10:07
                    plantarflex both feet while maintaining heel contact on the floor.
                    10:11
                    The examiner should again observe if the movement is performed rapidly and rhythmically,
                    10:16
                    and for similar performance on both sides.
                    10:21
                    Again, an inability to perform rapidly alternating
                    10:24
                    movements is a form of ataxia called dysdiadochokinesia.
                    10:28
                    Now that we've completed our coordination exam,
                    10:33
                    we should have a full appreciation of movement abilities and control of movement.
                    10:37
                    We can now move on to assess balance and
                    10:42
                    functional skills in the remaining components of the neurologic PT exam.
                    10:46
                    In summary, coordinated movement is the result of the integration of multiple systems,
                    10:51
                    including sensory musculoskeletal and neuromuscular systems.
                    10:57
                    During the coordination exam,
                    11:01
                    movements should be inspected for reciprocal motion,
                    11:03
                    synergy, accuracy, and limb holding.
                    11:06
                    Specific abnormal findings in your observation,
                    11:10
                    motor and coordination exams indicate different neurological lesions to
                    11:14
                    the cerebellum versus the basal ganglia versus somatosensory systems.
                    11:19

                .Patient Scenarios
                    Scenario 1 Γ1
                        Acute Care in a Hospital
                        A patient diagnosed with an anterior cerebral artery infarct that occurred two days ago.
                            ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                            Scenario 1 - Acute Care Setting
                                -You are a physical therapist in an acute care setting in a hospital. The next patient on your schedule has been diagnosed with an anterior cerebral artery infarct that occurred two days ago.
                                -As you plan your neurologic PT exam, what is your first step?
                                    ✓Response 1
                                        -Review the medical record for past medical history, history of present illness, related tests and measures, activity orders, lab values, and medical interventions.
                                            ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                            Correct!
                                            You should always review the medical record to collect
                                            pertinent information prior to examining the patient.
                                    ✗(Incorrect)Response 2
                                        Enter the patient's room and start to conduct a cranial
                                        nerve examination.
                    Scenario 1 Γ2
                        Acute Care Setting
                        Now that you have collected the information from the medical
                        record including past medical history, history of present illness, and
                        tests and measures related to the diagnosis, you are ready to
                        examine the patient.
                        What will you do first upon entering the patient's room?
                            ✗(Incorrect)Response 1
                                Enter the room and tell the patient who you are and why you are
                                there. Begin your neurologic PT exam by manual muscle testing
                                the patient's lower extremities because that is where you think
                                the patient will exhibit weakness.
                            ✓Response 2
                                Observe the patient as you enter the room and tell the patient
                                who you are and why you are there. You are taking inventory of
                                the following: are they lying in bed or sitting in the chair? Do
                                they look up when you enter the room?
                                    ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                    CORRECT!
                                    In this case, the best initial assessment should begin with
                                    observation. This can give you a hint about the patient's level of
                                    alertness and mental status.
                    Scenario 1 Γ3
                        Acute Care Setting
                        As you enter the room, the patient looks up when you tell them who
                        you are and why you are there. They respond to you when you ask
                        them how they are feeling.
                        What is your next step in conducting the neurologic PT exam?
                            ✗(Incorrect)Response 1
                                Now that you know they can attend to you and respond,
                                you would like to observe their function by asking them
                                to stand up and walk.
                            ✓Response 2
                                Further assess mental status by asking the patient
                                additional questions regarding orientation, attention,
                                language, and short-term memory.
                                    ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                    Correct!
                                    Given the patient history and your observations, it is
                                    appropriate to continue to assess mental function by making
                                    sure the patient is oriented to person, place, and time as well
                                    as conducting a brief assessment of attention and short-term
                                    memory so you can gauge their ability to follow commands
                                    and participate in the rest of your exam and treatment.

                    Scenario 2 Γ4
                        Outpatient Setting
                            A patient diagnosed with imbalance and peripheralneuropathy.

                            You are a physical therapist working in an outpatient clinic. The next patient on your
                            schedule has the diagnosis of imbalance and peripheral neuropathy. They walk back to the
                            gym to your treatment area using a cane and say "hello" as they sit down in a chair.
                            The patient does not have any information included in their electronic medical record, and
                            only comes in with a referral for PT to address balance issues and their intake form, which
                            states that they have difficulty with balance, numbness, and tingling in their feet and lower
                            legs.
                            What component of the neurologic exam will you assess first?
                                ✗(Incorrect)Response 1
                                    To assess mental status, you make sure the patient is alert and oriented by
                                    asking them to tell you their name, where they are, and what day it is today.
                                ✓Response 2
                                    Observe the patient's gait and transfers as they walk back to your treatment
                                    area and sit in a chair. You note that they are using an assistive device. You also
                                    observe that they are able to start a conversation with you while they are
                                    walking/sitting down.
                                        ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                        Correct!
                                        Because the patient is walking back to your treatment area,
                                        you can use this time as part of your functional screening to
                                        start to observe any gait deviations, use of assistive device,
                                        and ability to dual-task while they are walking. The patient
                                        also sits down in a chair giving you a chance to observe
                                        transfers as well.

                    Scenario 2 Γ5
                        Outpatient Setting
                            You note that the patient sometimes catches their toe on the carpet as they are walking but does not lose their balance. After the patient says
                            "hello" you start a conversation with the patient about their day so far while you take their vitals.
                            They tell you that they drove to the appointment, and they are planning to go shopping after your appointment. The patient has stable vital signs
                            and you go on to ask about the history of present illness and past medical history. You note that they are communicating with you well and
                            responding to your questions appropriately.
                            What would you prioritize as your next step in the neurologic PT exam?
                                ✓Response 1
                                    Perform a comprehensive sensory examination starting with superficial sensations such as pain and temperature and moving
                                    on to deep sensation such as joint position sense and vibration sense. Your rationale for performing a sensory exam is because
                                    you used their history and your observation as a screening of mental status and cranial nerves.
                                        ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                        Correct!
                                        In this case, the patient has good communication skills, can
                                        drive, ambulate and go shopping without assistance from
                                        another person, indicating that further assessment of
                                        mental status does not need to be a priority. In addition, the
                                        patient's diagnosis is peripheral neuropathy and, in this
                                        case, you do not suspect cranial nerves are involved.
                                        Further, you observe that they have no outward signs of
                                        visual impairment, ocular misalignment, facial asymmetry,
                                        or difficulty with swallowing and speech. For that reason,
                                        you chose to prioritize the sensory exam as this is likely to
                                        be a large contributor to their reports of imbalance in this
                                        scenario.
                                ✗(Incorrect)Response 2
                                    Thoroughly assess mental status and cognition by asking the patient to remember three words for immediate and delayed recall,
                                    to draw a clock, and to count backwards by 7's from 100. Your rationale for performing a comprehensive mental status exam is
                                    that this is the first step in the neurologic PT exam before assessing cranial nerves, sensation, and motor systems.

            //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
            //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
            3.7. Module 3 Summary
            //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
            //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

                Well done! You have completed the third of five modules for Unit 1. Before moving on to the next module, remember to review these three key learnings: 
                    -The organization of the neurologic PT exam may vary depending on patient presentation, diagnosis, preferences, and practice setting. 
                    -Organizing the neurologic PT exam (observation, mental status, cranial nerves, sensation, motor) can help you to identify specific impairments resulting in functional limitations. 
                    -Movement dysfunction can arise from a variety of neurologic diagnoses and can be the result of cognitive, sensory, motor, and/or coordination impairments. 
                  
                Learning Outcomes
                    After completing this module, you can now: 
                        -Demonstrate the ability to perform a neurologic PT examination, establish a prognosis and plan of care using evidence-based therapeutic interventions for clients with a neurologic diagnosis. 
                        -Recognize what patient/client problems are beyond the scope of physical therapist practice and know when to make an appropriate referral to another health practitioner.   
                        -Evaluate data from the PT examination to drive clinical decision making for the plan of care that is patient -centered, evidence-based and personalized to the client’s capabilities.

            4.0. Module 4 Introduction

            //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

                Introduction
                    Welcome to Module 4 of Unit 1. This week, you will learn more about the components of the neurologic physical therapy (PT) exam including assessment of balance and function. We will also review the core set of outcome measures recommended for persons with neurologic disorders. The neurologic PT exam will be used throughout the Neuromuscular Course series and serves as the foundation for examination and evaluation of individuals with neurologic disorders. 

                Learning Objectives
                    By the end of this week, you will be able to: 
                        -Demonstrate the ability to perform an assessment of balance and function for clients with a neurologic diagnosis.  
                        -Describe the variety of movement disorders and appreciate how these disorders interfere with function, activities, and participation. 
                        -Apply a core set of outcome measures in clinical settings to assess gait, balance and function for persons with neurologic diagnoses.
