                        Diagnosis: Sensory Selection and Weighting Deﬁcit
                        The primary movement system problem is the inability to screen for and attend to appropriate sensory inputs in
                        order to maintain postural orientation. Patients may have postural instability. Patients are likely to complain of
                        dizziness or visual motion sensitivity.
                        Key Tests and Signs Associated Signs Differential
                        Movement
                        Diagnosis

                        Expected Outcome Associated
                        Medical
                        Diagnosis

                        Dizziness:
                        e Dizziness associated with
                        head turning
                        Motion Sensitivity:
                        e Symptoms with smooth
                        pursuit or saccadic eye
                        movements or in situations
                        with visual motion cues such
                        as people moving in the
                        room, movement on
                        television, computer screen
                        savers, and so on
                        Task Analysis:
                        Gait:
                        e Deviation in line of
                        progression to one or both
                        sides
                        e Difﬁculty with transitions
                        from one sensory
                        environment to another;
                        instability with head turning
                        Turning around:
                        e Loss of balance or increased
                        ankle or hip sway at
                        termination
                        e Worse with faster movement
                        e Dizzy
                        Postural Control:
                        e Able to stand unsupported,
                        but may require practice
                        e Increased sway with eyes
                        closed
                        e May demonstrate hip strategy
                        during static standing tasks
                        e Postural responses may be
                        exaggerated and delayed;
                        exaggerated response leads to
                        instability
                        e Improvement with practice,
                        instruction, and
                        encouragement

                        Movement:
                        e Fractionated
                        Nonequilibrium
                        Coordination:
                        e Intact
                        Sensation:
                        e Intact
                        Head Thrust Test:
                        e May be positive
                        Dynamic Visual Acuity:
                        e May be positive

                        e Movement pattern
                        coordination deﬁcit
                        e Perceptual deﬁcit
                        e Sensory detection
                        deﬁcit

                        e Ambulation with straight
                        line of progression and
                        no loss of balance in all
                        regular sensory
                        environments
                        e May have decreased
                        tolerance to prolonged
                        exposure to highly
                        visually stimulating
                        environments
                        e May have symptoms with
                        head and body turning
                        tasks but mild to no
                        instability

                        e Stroke
                        e Brain injury
                        e Unilateral
                        vestibular loss
                        e Bilateral
                        vestibular loss
                        e Benign
                        paroxysmal
                        positional
                        vertigo with
                        postural
                        instability

                        Diagnosis: Perceptual Deﬁcit
                        The primary movement system problem is the tendency to resist correction of center-of-mass alignment related
                        to an inaccurate perception of vertical orientation, resulting in postural control deﬁcits. The condition may be in
                        the medial/lateral or anterior/posterior direction.
                        Key Tests and Signs Associated Signs Differential
                        Movement
                        Diagnosis

                        Expected Outcome Associated Medical
                        Diagnosis

                        Perception:
                        e Sensation of “falling” when
                        shifted toward correct
                        vertical alignment
                        e May have disregard or neglect
                        of involved extremities
                        Postural Control:
                        e Shifts center of mass beyond
                        limits of stability to side or
                        backward without weight
                        bearing
                        e Resists correction of center-
                        of-mass alignment
                        e Deﬁcits may be present in
                        sitting, standing, or with
                        walking, depending on
                        severity

                        Movement:
                        e Presentation is
                        variable, although
                        movement in at least
                        60% of muscle groups
                        in the LE is expected
                        e Movement may not
                        be fractionated
                        Motor Planning:
                        e May have difﬁculty
                        planning or
                        organizing movement
                        patterns into
                        purposeful actions
                        Sensation:
                        e Likely to be impaired
                        to light touch and
                        joint position sense
                        Behavior:
                        e Impulsive
                        e Poor judgment
                        e Fearful

                        e Sensory selection
                        and weighting
                        deﬁcit
                        e Sensory detection
                        deﬁcit
                        e Fractionated
                        movement deﬁcit
                        e Force production
                        deﬁcit

                        e Related to severity of
                        behavioral or cognitive
                        deﬁcits, motor function,
                        and natural recovery of
                        perceptual deﬁcit
                        e Assisted ambulation
                        with uncomplicated
                        devices such as wheeled
                        walker or along a wall
                        e Many are
                        nonambulatory and
                        require signiﬁcant
                        assistance with transfers

                        e Stroke
                        (medial/lateral)
                        e Brain injury
                        (medial/lateral)
                        e Generalized
                        debilitation
                        (anterior/posterior)
                        e Dementia (anterior/
                        posterior)?

                        (Continued)

                        Diagnosis: Fractionated Movement Deﬁcit
                        The primary movement system problem is the inability to fractionate movement associated with moderate or
                        greater hyperexcitability. May describe the UE or LE, or both. Always associated with central neurological deﬁcit.
                        Key Tests and Signs Associated Signs Differential
                        Movement
                        Diagnosis

                        Expected Outcome Associated
                        Medical
                        Diagnosis

                        Movement:
                        e Unable to fractionate
                        movement
                        e Variability in ability to move
                        against gravity
                        e Slow; unable to make rapid
                        reversals in movement
                        e Unable to generate force
                        rapidly
                        Muscle Tone:
                        e Moderate or greater
                        hyperexcitability

                        Task Analysis:
                        Sit-to-stand and transfers:
                        e Stiffness of involved
                        limbs; slow
                        e No dissociation of
                        movement at one joint
                        from movement at
                        another joint
                        e May see associated
                        reactions with
                        increased effort
                        e In forms with less
                        antigravity movement,
                        unable to stand
                        Gait:
                        e Compensatory
                        movement strategy of
                        hip hiking, vaulting, or
                        circumduction to
                        initiate swing of
                        involved extremities
                        e Stiffness of hip or knee
                        ﬂexion during swing
                        e Hip and knee often
                        ﬂexed during stance of
                        involved extremities
                        e May require AFO
                        e Likely to require
                        assistive device at least
                        early in course
                        e In forms with less
                        antigravity movement,
                        unable to stand
                        Reach and grasp:
                        e Able to reach in very
                        limited range (60°–
                        90°)
                        e Hand closure with
                        minimal relaxation or
                        minimal opening
                        Postural Control:
                        e In forms with more
                        antigravity movement,
                        able to sit unsupported
                        early in course but
                        asymmetrically
                        e Stability may improve
                        with practice, but
                        symmetry will not
                        improve with practice

                        e Force production
                        deﬁcit

                        e Related to degree of
                        antigravity movement
                        e In forms with more
                        antigravity movement,
                        ambulation in home and
                        community with
                        signiﬁcant deviations and
                        signiﬁcant reduction in
                        speed with or without a
                        cane; ascend and descend
                        stairs foot over foot with
                        or without a railing
                        e In forms with 4-limb
                        involvement, wheelchair
                        for locomotion (probably
                        electric)
                        e In all but forms with 4-
                        limb involvement, stable
                        with sitting and reaching
                        tasks
                        e Able to use UE as “assist”
                        with ADL

                        e Stroke
                        e Brain injury
                        e Spinal cord injury
                        e Multiple sclerosis
                        e Cerebral palsy

                        (Continued)

                        Diagnosis: Hypermetria
                        The primary movement system problem is related to the inability to grade forces appropriately for the distance
                        and speed aspects of a task. Movements are generally too large for their intended purpose. May describe UE or
                        LE, or both. Generally associated with cerebellar dysfunction.
                        Key Tests and Signs Associated Signs Differential
                        Movement
                        Diagnosis

                        Expected Outcome Associated
                        Medical
                        Diagnosis

                        Nonequilibrium Coordination:
                        e Difﬁculty directing
                        movement toward a target,
                        resulting in undershooting or
                        overshooting
                        e Abnormal rhythm and
                        uncoordinated during rapidly
                        alternating movements
                        e No change with practice
                        Movement:
                        e Able to move against gravity
                        e Lack of ﬂuidity

                        Postural Control:
                        e Generally able to sit
                        with UE support; may
                        be able to sit
                        unsupported
                        e Unable to stand
                        unsupported or stands
                        with wide base of
                        support and high
                        guard
                        Task Analysis:
                        Gait:
                        e Variable foot
                        placement in step
                        length and step width
                        e Generally requires
                        assistance
                        Reach and grasp:
                        e Unable to reach to
                        targets
                        e Difﬁculty grasping
                        small or light objects

                        e Movement pattern
                        coordination
                        deﬁcit

                        e Ambulation in home with
                        assistive device and
                        perhaps bracing
                        e May require wheelchair in
                        community
                        e Independent with
                        minimal UE ADL tasks
                        with adaptive equipment

                        e Stroke
                        e Cerebellar
                        degeneration
                        e Multiple sclerosis
                        e Cerebral palsy

                        (Continued)

                        Deficit in Steady State Postural Control: Postural Movement Strategies
                        Key Movement Observations from Core Task Analysis   Key Findings from Tests and Measures
                        SITTING
                        Stability:
                        •   Unable to maintain position/falls
                        •   Maintains position only with UE support
                        •   Maintains position only with atypical base of support
                        •   Maintains position with atypical postural sway
                        Alignment:
                        •   Impaired orientation of axial body segments with respect to plumbline or each other  
                        •   UE’s held close to side of body 
                        •   High guard, reaching, counter balancing with UE(s)
                         
                        STANDING
                        Stability:
                        •   Unable to maintain position/falls
                        •   Maintains position only with UE(s) support
                        •   Maintains position only with atypical base of support
                        •   Maintains position with atypical postural sway
                        Alignment:
                        •   impaired orientation of axial body segments with respect to plumbline or each other
                        •    UE’s held close to side of body 
                        •   High guard, reaching, counter balancing with UE(s)  Body Structure Function (BSF):
                        •   Insufficient muscle performance of trunk and LE’s to support body weight against gravity
                        •   Impaired reflex integrity (muscle tone); hypotonia or hypertonia in trunk or extremities
                        •   Impaired ability to isolate body segment or limb movements through available range of motion 
                        •   May demonstrate impaired interlimb or intralimb coordination deficits

                        Activity: Impaired or atypical performance on the following tests/items: 
                        •   Movement Assessment Scale1, 2 (item: Balance Sitting)
                        •   Berg Balance Scale3-6 (items #2, 6, 7, 13, 14)
                        •   Function in Sitting Test7, 8 (item: static sitting)
                        •   Postural Assessment Scale for Stroke9, 10 (items #1- 4)
                        •   BESTest11, 12 (items #11, 19A)
                        •   Mini-BESTest11-14 (items #3, 7)

                        Participation: None




                        Deficit in Steady State Postural Control: Sensory Processing
                        Key Movement Observations from Core Task Analysis   Key Findings from Tests and Measures
                        Task/environmental variations (e.g., task performance with eyes closed or on compliant surfaces) are required across all tasks to reveal deficits in steady state postural control related to sensory processing. The following observations are for those variations.

                        SITTING
                        Stability: Maintains position with atypical postural sway
                        Alignment: Impaired orientation of axial body segments with respect to plumbline or each other

                        STANDING
                        Stability: Maintains position with atypical postural sway
                        Alignment: Impaired orientation of axial body segments with respect to plumbline or each other

                            BSF: 
                        •   Impaired performance on Modified Clinical Test for Sensory Interaction in Balance15, 16 (inability to maintain each position for 30 sec)
                        •   Impaired sensory integrity – light touch, vibration, or proprioception in lower extremity
                        •   Impaired visual acuity
                        •   Impaired gaze stability (Head Impulse Test,17 Dynamic Visual Acuity18)

                        ACTIVITY: Impaired or atypical performance on the following tests/items:
                        •   Function in Sitting Test7, 8 (item: Sitting Eyes Closed)
                        •   BESTest11, 12 (items #19B-D)
                        •   Mini-BESTest11-14 (item #8)
                         
                        PARTICIPATION: None




                        Deficit in Steady State Postural Control: Verticality
                        Key Movement Observations from Core Task Analysis   Key Findings from Tests and Measures
                        SITTING
                        Verticality:
                        •   Lateral, posterior or anterior trunk lean away from midline
                        •   Pushes lateral, posterior or anterior from midline with an extremity and resists return to midline position

                        STANDING
                        Verticality:
                        •   Lateral, posterior or anterior trunk lean away from midline 
                        •   Pushes lateral, posterior or anterior from midline with and extremity and resists return to midline position

                            BSF: Impaired or atypical performance on the following tests/items: 
                        •   Scale for Contraversive Pushing Scale19, 20
                        •   Burke Lateropulsion Scale21
                        •   BESTest11, 12 (item #20)
                        •   Mini-BESTest11-14 (item #9)

                        ACTIVITY: None

                        PARTICIPATION: None






                        Deficit in Steady State Postural Control: Balance Confidence
                        Key Movement Observations from Core Task Analysis   Key Findings from Tests and Measures
                        SITTING
                        Stability: Performance may vary depending on availability of nearby support surfaces
                        Symptom Provocation: Attempts to complete task evoke symptoms such as pain, anxiety, fatigue, fear, lightheadedness, dizziness

                        STANDING
                        Stability: Performance may vary depending on availability of nearby support surfaces
                        Symptom Provocation: Attempts to complete task evoke symptoms such as pain, anxiety, fatigue, fear, lightheadedness, dizziness
                            BSF:
                        •   Vital signs: increase in respiratory rate, heart rate and/or blood pressure

                         ACTIVITY: 
                        •   Reduction of fearfulness or anxiety in more supportive environment (physical support)
                        •   Worsening of fearfulness or anxiety in more open environment

                        PARTICIPATION: None



                        Deficit in Anticipatory Postural Control: Postural Movement Strategies
                        Key Movement Observations from Core Task Analysis   Key Findings from Tests and Measures
                         SITTING
                        Task/environmental variations are required in sitting to reveal deficits in anticipatory postural control related to postural movement strategies. The following observations are for those variations.

                        Stability:
                        •   Loss of balance with ability to restore equilibrium
                        •   Maintains position only with UE(s) support
                        •   Maintains position only with atypical base of support
                        •   Maintains position with atypical postural sway
                        Alignment: High guard, reaching, counter balancing with UE(s)

                        SIT TO STAND
                        INITIATION
                        Timing: Delayed
                        Sequencing:
                        •   Altered initial direction of movement
                        •   No shift of feet posterior to knees 

                        EXECUTION
                        Amplitude:
                        •   Inadequate forward flexion of trunk over LE’s
                        •   Inadequate tibial translation over feet
                        Sequencing: Knee extension before hip extension
                         
                        TERMINATION
                        Stability:
                        •   Maintains position only with UE(s) support
                        •   Maintains position only with atypical base of support
                        •   Maintains position with atypical postural sway

                        WHOLE TASK 
                        Stability:
                        •   LOB with ability to restore equilibrium
                        •   High guard, reaching, counter balancing with UE’s  

                        STANDING
                        Task/environmental variations are required in standing to reveal deficits in APC postural movement strategies. The following observations are for those variations.

                        Stability:
                        •   Loss of balance with ability to restore equilibrium
                        •   Maintains position only with UE(s) support
                        •   Maintains position only with atypical base of support
                        •   Maintains position with atypical postural sway
                        Alignment: High guard, reaching, counter balancing with UE(s)


                        STEP UP/STEP DOWN
                        INITIATION
                        Timing: Delayed 
                        Sequencing: 
                        •   Multiple starts/stops
                        •   LE lift prior to weight shift

                        EXECUTION
                        Amplitude:
                        •   Atypical amplitude of weight shift
                        •   Decreased height of leg lift
                        Sequencing: Impaired sequencing of weight shift and leg lift
                        Timing: Impaired timing of weight shift and leg lift
                        Smoothness: Non-continuous trajectory
                        Accuracy: Impaired foot placement
                         
                        TERMINATION
                        Stability:
                        •   Maintains position only with UE(s) support
                        •   Maintains position only with atypical base of support
                        •   Maintains position with atypical postural sway

                        WHOLE TASK
                        Stability:
                        •   LOB with ability to restore equilibrium
                        •   High guard, reaching, counter balancing with UE(s)  
                         

                        WALK AND TURN
                        INITIATION
                        Timing: Delayed 
                        Sequencing:
                        •   Multiple starts/stops
                        •   LE lift prior to weight shift

                        EXECUTION
                        Speed: Marked decreased speed during turn
                        Smoothness:  
                        •   Atypical or variable foot placement 
                        •   Non-continuous trajectory of swing limb
                        Amplitude: Atypical step height
                        Timing: Hesitation or stop at turn 
                        Stability: 
                        •   Atypically wide turns
                        •   Multiple steps to turn 

                        TERMINATION
                        Stability:
                        •   Maintains position only with UE(s) support
                        •   Maintains position only with atypical base of support
                        •   Maintains position with atypical postural sway

                        WHOLE TASK
                        Stability:
                        •   Loss of balance with ability to restore equilibrium
                        •   High guard, reaching, counter balancing with UE(s)


                        REACH AND GRASP
                        INITIATION
                        Timing: Delayed 
                        Sequencing:
                        •   Multiple starts/stops
                        •   UE lift prior to weight shift

                        EXECUTION
                        Amplitude: Inadequate forward translation of trunk and reaching UE
                        Speed: Atypically slow or fast movement

                        TERMINATION
                        Stability: Moving arm used for support

                        WHOLE TASK
                        Stability:
                        •   Loss of balance with ability to restore equilibrium
                        •   High guard, reaching, counter balancing with UE(s)
                        •   Completes task only with UE(s) support  BSF: 
                        •   No deficits in muscle performance of trunk and LE’s that limit the ability to support body weight against gravity
                        •   May demonstrate interlimb or intralimb coordination deficits
                        •   Impaired ability to isolate body segment or limb movements through available range of motion

                        ACTIVITY: Impaired or atypical performance on the following tests and items:
                        •   Functional Gait Assessment22-24 (all items)
                        •   Dynamic Gait Index25, 26 (all items)
                        •   Berg Balance Scale3-6 (items #1, 4, 5, 8-14)
                        •   BESTest11, 12 (items #9-13, 21-25)
                        •   Mini-BESTest11-14 (items #1-3, 10-13)
                        •   Five Times Sit to Stand Test27, 28
                        •   Functional Reach Test29

                        PARTICIPATION: None






                        Deficit in Anticipatory Postural Control: Sensory Processing
                        Key Movement Observations from Core Task Analysis   Key Findings from Tests and Measures
                        SITTING
                        Task/environmental variations are required in sitting to reveal deficits in anticipatory control related to sensory processing. The following observations are for those variations.

                        Stability:
                        •   Loss of balance with ability to restore equilibrium when selection /use of various sensory systems is required
                        •   Maintains position only with atypical base of support 
                         
                        SIT TO STAND
                        INITIATION
                        Alignment: Widens base of support

                        EXECUTION
                        Speed: Atypically slow or fast

                        TERMINATION
                        Stability:
                        •   Atypical postural sway
                        •   Atypical base of support

                        WHOLE TASK 
                        Stability: Completes task only with use of UE support


                        STANDING
                        Task/environmental variations are required in standing to reveal deficits in anticipatory control related to sensory processing. The following observations are for those variations.

                        Stability:
                        •   Loss of balance with ability to restore equilibrium when selection /use of various sensory systems is required
                        Alignment: High guard, reaching, counter balancing with UE’s
                         

                        STEP UP/STEP DOWN
                        INITIATION
                        Timing: Delayed

                        EXECUTION
                        Speed: Atypically slow or fast speed of stepping limb

                        TERMINATION
                        Stability:
                        •   Atypical postural sway
                        •   Atypical base of support
                        Alignment: Knee hyperextension

                        WHOLE TASK
                        Stability:
                        •   Loss of balance with ability to restore equilibrium
                        •   High guard, reaching, counter balancing with UE’s
                        •   Completes task only with UE support
                        Alignment: Impaired orientation of axial body segments with respect to plumbline or each other

                        WALK AND TURN
                        INITIATION
                        Timing: Delayed     

                        EXECUTION  
                        Stability: 
                        •   Atypical base of support
                        •   Multiple steps to turn
                        •   Atypically wide turn
                        Amplitude: Atypical step length
                        Speed:
                        •   Slow or variable speed of walking
                        •   Marked decreased speed during turn
                        Timing: Hesitation or stop at turn 
                        Accuracy: Impaired precision of foot placement

                        TERMINATION
                        Stability:
                        •   Atypical postural sway
                        •   Atypical base of support

                        WHOLE TASK
                        Stability: Completes task only with use of UE support

                        REACH AND GRASP  
                        INITIATION
                        Stability: Widens BOS
                        Timing: Delayed  
                        Sequencing:
                        •   Multiple starts/stops
                        •   UE lift prior to weight shift

                        EXECUTION/TERMINATION/WHOLE TASK
                        Stability:
                        •   Loss of balance with ability to restore equilibrium
                        •   High guard, reaching, counter balancing with UE’s
                        •   Completes task only with UE support BSF: 
                        •   Impaired visual acuity
                        •   Impaired cranial/peripheral nerve integrity (oculomotor function, Dynamic Visual Acuity,17 VOR, or Head Impulse Test18)
                        •   Impaired sensory integrity in LE including light touch, proprioception, deep pressure
                        •   May demonstrate dizziness with head turning/tilting or in environments with significant visual flow information
                        •   May demonstrate positional induced vertigo and nystagmus during Dix-Hallpike Test or Roll Test
                         
                        ACTIVITY: Impaired or atypical performance on the following tests/items:
                        •   Dynamic Gait Index 25, 26(items #3, 4)
                        •   Functional Gait Assessment22-24 (items: #3, 4, 7, 8)
                        •   Berg Balance Scale3-6 (items #6-8)
                        •   BESTest11, 12 (items #19A-D)
                        •   Mini-BESTest11-14 (items #7-9)
                         
                        PARTICIPATION: None





                        Deficit in Anticipatory Postural Control: Executive Function/Multitask Ability
                        Key Movement Observations from Core Task Analysis   Key Findings from Tests and Measures
                        Task/environmental variations are required across all tasks to reveal deficits in anticipatory related to postural movement strategies. The following observations are for those variations in any task.

                        Variability of task performance with regards to 
                        timing, sequencing, smoothness, speed, and stability  

                        Difficulty maintaining attention during task performance with
                        Need for verbal or tactile cueing to complete task  BSF: Impaired cognitive/mental function as noted by performance on the following tests/items:
                        •   Mini Mental Status Exam 30, 31
                        •   Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MOCA) 32, 33 
                        •   Saint Louis University Mental Status (SLUMS) Examination 34-36
                         
                        ACTIVITY: Impaired or atypical performance on the following tests/items:
                        •   Timed Up and Go Test - Cognitive37, 38
                        •   Timed Up and Go Test - Manual37, 38
                         
                        PARTICIPATION: None









                        Deficit in Anticipatory Postural Control: Balance Confidence
                        Key Movement Observations from Core Task Analysis   Key Findings from Tests and Measures
                        Availability of nearby support surface(s) may influence performance on all tasks.
                        SITTING
                        Task/environmental variations are required to reveal deficits in anticipatory postural sway related to balance confidence. The following observations may be noted:
                        Stability:
                        •   Grasping for/clutching external supports
                        •   Completes task only with wide BOS

                        SIT TO STAND
                        INITIATION
                        Timing: Delayed
                        Stability: Widens base of support

                        EXECUTION
                        Amplitude:
                        •   Inadequate forward flexion of trunk
                        •   Inadequate tibial translation over feet
                        Speed: atypically slow speed

                        TERMINATION
                        Stability: Grasping for/clutching external supports

                        WHOLE BODY:
                        Stability:
                        •   Completes task only with UE support
                        •   Completes task only with wide BOS

                        STANDING
                        Task/environmental variations are required to reveal deficits in anticipatory postural control related to balance confidence. The following observations may be noted:
                        Stability:
                        •   Grasping for/clutching external supports
                        •   Completes task only with wide BOS

                        STEP UP/STEP DOWN
                        INITIATION
                        Timing: Delayed

                        EXECUTION
                        Speed: Atypically slow movement of moving limb

                        TERMINATION
                        Stability: Atypically wide BOS

                        WHOLE TASK
                        Stability:
                        •   High guard, reaching, counter balancing with UE’s
                        •   Completes task only with UE support

                        WALK AND TURN
                        INITIATION
                        Timing: Delayed

                        EXECUTION
                        Speed: Atypically slow walking and/or turning
                        Timing: Hesitation or stop at turn
                        Stability:
                        •   Multiple steps to turn
                        •   Atypically wide turn

                        TERMINATION
                        Stability: Atypical BOS

                        WHOLE TASK
                        Stability: Grasps for/clutches external supports

                        REACH AND GRASP
                        Task/environmental variations (next column) are required to reveal deficits in anticipatory postural control related to balance confidence. The following observations may be noted:

                        INITIATION
                        Timing: Delayed initiation

                        EXECUTION
                        Speed: Slow movement
                        Amplitude: Minimization of limb and or body excursion

                        TERMINATION/WHOLE TASK
                        Stability: 
                        •   Completes task only with external support
                        •   Completes task only with wide BOS

                        Symptom Provocation with any Task: 
                        ●   Performance may vary based on availability of nearby support surfaces
                        ●   Attempts to complete task evoke symptoms such as pain, anxiety, fatigue, fear, lightheadedness, dizziness
                            BSF:  
                        •   Vital signs: increase in respiratory rate, heart rate and/or blood pressure
                         
                        ACTIVITY:  Scores on the following tests are lower than expected as compared to the patient’s actual performance on the core tasks and performance-based outcome measures:
                        •   Activities Balance Confidence Scale39, 40 
                        •   Falls Efficacy Scale41
                         
                        Availability of nearby support surface/s may improve performance and decrease anxiety and fear on the following performance-based outcome measures: 
                        •   Dynamic Gait Index25, 26 (all items)
                        •   Functional Gait Assessment22-24 (all items)
                        •   Berg Balance Scale3-6 (items #1, 4-5, 8-14)
                        •   BESTest11, 12 (items #9-12, 21-27)
                        •   Mini-BESTest11-14 (items #1-3, 11-14)
                        •   Timed Up and Go Test37, 38
                        •   Functional Reach Test29

                         PARTICIPATION: None





                        Deficit in Reactive Postural Control: Postural Movement Strategies
                        Key Movement Observations from Core Task Analysis   Key Findings from Tests and Measures
                        ALL CORE TASKS:
                        Stability:
                        LOB with ineffective, atypical, or absent trunk and/or extremity response to stabilize or prevent a fall. Ineffective responses may be delayed (timing), slow (speed), and/or too small (amplitude) to prevent a fall.
                         
                         
                         
                         
                         
                            BSF:
                        •   Impaired ability to isolate body segment or limb movements through available range of motion
                        •   Presence of dysmetria, slowed movement, or dysdiadokokinesia during non-equilibrium tests of coordination

                        ACTIVITY: Impaired or atypical performance on the following tests/items:
                        •   Push and Release Test42, 43
                        •   Lean and Release Test12, 44 
                        •   BESTest11, 12 (items #14-18) 
                        •   Mini-BESTest11-14 (items #4-6)
                         
                        PARTICIPATION: None




                        Deficit in Reactive Postural Control: Sensory Processing
                        Key Movement Observations from Core Task Analysis   Key Findings from Tests and Measures
                        ALL CORE TASKS:
                        Stability:
                        LOB with ineffective, atypical, or absent trunk and/or extremity response to stabilize or prevent a fall. Ineffective responses may be delayed (timing), slow (speed), and/or too small (amplitude) to prevent a fall.

                         

                         
                         
                         
                          
                         
                         

                            BSF: 
                        •   Impaired sensory integrity in UE/LE including touch, pressure, proprioception, protestive sensation (Semmes-Weinstein monofilaments), contrast sensitivity, depth perception, or visual acuity
                        •   Impaired cranial/peripheral nerve integrity (Dynamic Visual Acuity Test,18 Head Impulse Test45)
                        •   Impaired performance on Modified Clinical Test for Sensory Interaction in Balance15, 16 (Fall on any item)
                         
                        ACTIVITY: Impaired or atypical performance on the following tests/items:
                        •   Push and Release Test42, 43
                        •   Lean and Release Test12, 44 
                        •   BESTest 11, 12(items # 14-18)
                        •   Mini-BESTest11-14 (items #4-6)
                         
                        PARTICIPATION: None


                        Abbreviations: BSF = Body structure/function; UE = upper extremity; LE = lower extremity; LOB = loss of balance; VOR = Vestibular-ocular reflex.

                    A Core Set of Outcome Measures for 
                    Adults With Neurologic Conditions 
                    Undergoing Rehabilitation
                    A CLINICAL PRACTICE GUIDELINE

                    CLINICAL PRACTICE GUIDELINES

                    Jennifer L. Moore, PT, DHS, NCS, 
                    Kirsten Potter, PT, DPT, MS,  
                    Kathleen Blankshain, PT, DPT,  
                    Sandra L. Kaplan, PT, DPT, PhD,  
                    Linda C. O’Dwyer, MA, MSLIS, and 
                    Jane E. Sullivan, PT, DHS, MS
                    South Eastern Norway Regional 
                    Knowledge Translation Center, Sun-
                    naas Rehabilitation Hospital, Oslo, 
                    Norway, and Institute for Knowl-
                    edge Translation, Carmel, Indiana 
                    (J.L.M); Department of Physical 
                    Therapy Education, Rockhurst Uni-
                    versity, Kansas City, Missouri (K.P.); 
                    Department of Physical Therapy and 
                    Human Movement Sciences (K.B, 
                    J.E.S) and Galter Health Sciences Li-
                    brary and Learning Center (L.C.O), 
                    Feinberg School of Medicine, North-
                    western University, Chicago, Illinois; 
                    and Department of Rehabilitation 
                    and Movement Sciences, Rutgers 
                    School of Health Professions, New-
                    ark, New Jersey (S.L.K).

                    Background: Use of outcome measures (OMs) in adult neurologic 
                    physical therapy is essential for monitoring changes in a patient’s status 
                    over time, quantifying observations and patient-reported function, en-
                    hancing communication, and increasing the efficiency of patient care. 
                    OMs also provide a mechanism to compare patient and organizational 
                    outcomes, examine intervention effectiveness, and generate new knowl-
                    edge. This clinical practice guideline (CPG) examined the literature 
                    related to OMs of balance, gait, transfers, and patient-stated goals to 
                    identify a core set of OMs for use across adults with neurologic condi-
                    tions and practice settings.
                    Methods: To determine the scope of this CPG, surveys were conducted 
                    to assess the needs and priorities of consumers and physical therapists. 
                    OMs were identified through recommendations of the Academy of 
                    Neurologic Physical Therapy’s Evidence Database to Guide Effective-
                    ness task forces. A systematic review of the literature on the OMs was 
                    conducted and additional OMs were identified; the literature search 
                    was repeated on these measures. Articles meeting the inclusion criteria 
                    were critically appraised by 2 reviewers using a modified version of the  
                    COnsensus-based Standards for the selection of health Measurement 
                    INstruments. (COSMIN) checklist. Methodological quality and the 
                    strength of statistical results were determined. To be recommended for 
                    the core set, the OMs needed to demonstrate excellent psychometric 
                    properties in high-quality studies across neurologic conditions.
                    Results/Discussion: Based on survey results, the CPG focuses on OMs 
                    that have acceptable clinical utility and can be used to assess change 
                    over time in a patient’s balance, gait, transfers, and patient-stated goals. 
                    Strong, level I evidence supports the use of the Berg Balance Scale to 
                    assess changes in static and dynamic sitting and standing balance and 
                    the Activities-specific Balance Confidence Scale to assess changes in 
                    balance confidence. Strong to moderate evidence supports the use of 
                    the Functional Gait Assessment to assess changes in dynamic balance 
                    while walking, the 10 meter Walk Test to assess changes in gait speed, 

                    ABSTRACT

                    DOI: 10.1097/NPT.0000000000000229


                    ©2018 The Authors. Published by Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. on behalf of Academy of Neurologic Physical Therapy, APTA 175

                    JNPT • Volume 42, July 2018 A Core Set of OMs for Adults With Neurologic Conditions Undergoing Rehabilitation

                    and the 6-Minute Walk Test to assess changes in walking distance. Best 
                    practice evidence supports the use of the 5 Times Sit-to-Stand to assess 
                    sit to standing transfers. Evidence was insufﬁcient to support use of a 
                    speciﬁc OM to assess patient-stated goals across adult neurologic condi-
                    tions. Physical therapists should discuss the OM results with patients and 
                    collaboratively decide how the results should inform the plan of care.

                    inﬂuence from the APTA or the ANPT. The authors declare no compet-
                    ing interest.

                    LEVELS OF EVIDENCE AND GRADE OF RECOMMENDATIONS

                    This clinical practice guideline (CPG) is intended to be a 
                    guide for rehabilitation management of adults with neu-
                    rologic conditions and to inform outcome measurement 
                    research. The CPG applies to all adult patients with neuro-
                    logic conditions, including those with acute (ie, <6 months 
                    since onset/diagnosis), chronic stable (ie, >6 months since 
                    onset/diagnosis, but not expected to worsen with time), and 
                    chronic progressive (ie, > 6 months since onset/diagnosis, 
                    but with the potential to experience additional symptoms or 
                    functional changes). Clinicians and organizations should in-
                    terpret these recommendations in the context of the patient’s 
                    situation, clinical practice, and potential for harm. The meth-
                    odology used in this CPG, including the critical appraisal 
                    and assignment of levels of evidence and strength of the 
                    recommendations, was derived from the COnsensus-based 
                    Standards for the selection of health Measurement INstru-
                    ments (COSMIN) checklist,1-5 recommendations from the 
                    APTA, and is in accordance with internationally accepted 
                    methodologies for evidence-based practice. This CPG is or-
                    ganized to present the level of evidence definitions and the 
                    grades of recommendations (Tables 1 and 2, respectively), 
                    clear and implementable recommendations in the form of 
                    9 action statements, an introduction and description of the 
                    need for this CPG, and a standardized profile for each action 

                    statement that meets the Institute of Medicine’s criteria for 
                    transparency of the CPG.6 The 9 action statements include 
                    recommendations for the core set of measures, use of the 
                    core set, and collaborative decision-making. Research rec-
                    ommendations are included in the action statement profiles 
                    and summarized at the end of the CPG.
                    Each article included in this CPG was appraised by 2 
                    reviewers, and assigned a level of evidence by the guideline 
                    development group (GDG). The grading criteria to deter-
                    mine the level of evidence that supports the recommenda-
                    tions are described in Table 1. These criteria, recommended 
                    by the Academy of Neurologic Physical Therapy (ANPT), 
                    were modified to accommodate descriptions of studies of 
                    psychometric properties. Levels I and II differentiate stron-
                    ger from weaker studies by integrating the quality of the 
                    research design and/or reporting of the study,7 as well as 
                    the strength of the psychometric data.8,9 The criteria for the 
                    grades of recommendation assigned to each action state-
                    ment are provided in Table 2. The grade reflects the over-
                    all strength of the evidence available to support the action 
                    statement. Throughout the CPG, each action statement is 
                    preceded by a letter grade indicating the strength of the rec-
                    ommendation, followed by the statement and summary of 
                    the supporting evidence.

                    TABLE 1. Levels of Evidence
                    I Level of evidence rating I: Evidence obtained from at 
                    least one high-quality (>50% critical appraisal score) 
                    study of psychometric properties
                    II Level of evidence rating II: Evidence obtained from 
                    multiple, lesser quality (<50% critical appraisal 
                    score) studies of psychometric properties
                    III Level of evidence rating III: Evidence obtained from 
                    one lesser quality (<50% critical appraisal score) 
                    study of psychometric properties
                    IV Not applicable to studies of psychometric properties 
                    V Expert opinion (or best practice)

                    TABLE 2. Grades of Recommendations
                    GRADE RECOMMENDATION STRENGTH OF RECOMMENDATION
                    A Strong evidence A preponderance of level I studies, but least 1 level I study directly on the topic supports 
                    the recommendation
                    B Moderate evidence A preponderance of level II studies, but at least 1 level II study directly on the topic 
                    supports the recommendation
                    C Weak evidence A preponderance of level III studies, but at least 1 level III study directly on the topic 
                    supports the recommendation
                    P Practice Best practice based on expert opinion (review papers, white papers, consensus documents) 
                    developed by various methodologies (e.g., Delphi and RAND) and the clinical experience 
                    of the guideline development group
                    R Research An absence of research on the topic, or conclusions from existing studies on the topic are 
                    in disagreement

                    SUMMARY OF ACTION STATEMENTS

                    A. Action Statement 1: STATIC AND DYNAMIC SIT-
                    TING AND STANDING BALANCE ASSESSMENT. 
                    Clinicians should use the Berg Balance Scale (BBS) for 
                    adults with neurologic conditions who have goals to im-
                    prove static and dynamic sitting and standing balance and 
                    have the capacity to change in this area. The BBS should be 
                    administered under the same test conditions using the proto-
                    col recommended by the CPG Knowledge Translation (KT) 
                    Committee at admission, and discharge, and when feasible, 
                    between these periods for patients with:
                        •   Acute   conditions: Evidence    quality:    I;  recommenda-
                    tion strength: strong
                        •   Chronic stable  conditions: Evidence    quality:    I;  recom-
                    mendation strength: strong
                        •   Chronic progressive conditions: Evidence    quality:    I;  
                    recommendation strength: strong
                    B. Action Statement 2: WALKING BALANCE ASSESS-
                    MENT. Clinicians should use the Functional Gait Assess-
                    ment (FGA) for adults with neurologic conditions who have 
                    goals to improve balance while walking and have the capacity 
                    to change in this area. The FGA should be administered un-
                    der the same test conditions using the protocol recommended 
                    by the CPG KT Committee at admission, and discharge, and 
                    when feasible, between these periods for patients with:
                        •   Acute   conditions: Evidence    quality:    I;  recommenda-
                    tion strength: strong
                        •   Chronic stable  conditions: Evidence    quality:    I;  recom-
                    mendation strength: strong
                        •   Chronic progressive conditions: Evidence    quality:    I;  
                    recommendation strength: moderate
                    A. Action Statement 3: BALANCE CONFIDENCE AS-
                    SESSMENT. Clinicians should use the Activities-specific 
                    Balance Confidence (ABC) Scale to assess self-reported 
                    changes in balance confidence in adults with neurologic 
                    conditions who have goals and the capacity to change in this 
                    area. The ABC should be administered under the same test 
                    conditions using the protocol recommended by the CPG KT 
                    Committee at admission, discharge, and, when feasible, be-
                    tween these periods for patients with:
                        •   Acute   conditions: Evidence    quality:    I;  recommenda-
                    tion strength: strong
                        •   Chronic stable  conditions: Evidence    quality:    I;  recom-
                    mendation strength: strong
                        •   Chronic progressive conditions: Evidence    quality:    I;  
                    recommendation strength: strong
                    B. Action Statement 4: WALKING SPEED ASSESS-
                    MENT. Clinicians should use the 10 meter Walk Test (10mWT) 
                    for adults with neurologic conditions who have goals to im-
                    prove walking speed and have the capacity to change in this 
                    area. The 10mWT should be administered (per the protocol by 
                    Steffen and Seney,10 as adapted by the CPG KT Committee) 
                    under the same test conditions at admission, and discharge, 
                    and when feasible, between these periods for patients with:

                        •   Acute   conditions: Evidence    quality:    V;  recommenda-
                    tion strength: best practice
                        •   Chronic stable  conditions: Evidence    quality:    I;  recom-
                    mendation strength: strong
                        •   Chronic progressive conditions: Evidence    quality:    I;  
                    recommendation strength: strong
                    B. Action Statement 5: WALKING DISTANCE AS-
                    SESSMENT. Clinicians should use the 6-Minute Walk Test 
                    (6MWT) for adults with neurologic conditions who have 
                    goals to improve walking distance and the capacity to change 
                    in this area. The 6MWT should be administered (per the 
                    Quinn et al protocol,11 as adapted by the CPG KT Committee) 
                    under the same test conditions at admission, and discharge, 
                    and when feasible, between these periods for patients with:
                        •   Acute   conditions: Evidence    quality:    V;  recommenda-
                    tion strength: best practice
                        •   Chronic stable  conditions: Evidence    quality:    I;  recom-
                    mendation strength: moderate
                        •   Chronic progressive conditions: Evidence    quality:    I;  
                    recommendation strength: strong
                    P. Action Statement 6: TRANSFER ASSESSMENT. Cli-
                    nicians should document the transfer ability of adults with 
                    neurologic conditions who have goals to improve transfers 
                    and have the capacity to change. Documentation should 
                    include the type of transfer, level of required assistance, 
                    equipment or context adaptations, and time to complete. In 
                    patients who have goals and the capacity to improve sit-to-
                    stand transfers, the 5 Times Sit-to-Stand (5TSTS) may be 
                    used. The 5TSTS and documentation of other transfers may 
                    be administered under the same test conditions using the 
                    protocol recommended by the CPG KT Committee at admis-
                    sion, and discharge, and when feasible, between these peri-
                    ods for adult patients with neurologic conditions (Evidence 
                    quality: V; recommendation strength: best practice).
                    P. Action Statement 7: DOCUMENTATION OF PA-
                    TIENT GOALS. Clinicians should document patient-stated 
                    goals and monitor changes in individuals with neurologic 
                    conditions, using an outcome measure (OM) such as the 
                    Goal Attainment Scale (GAS), reporting the task, the per-
                    formance conditions, and the time to complete or level of in-
                    dependence desired. Patient goals should be documented at 
                    least 2 times, at admission and discharge, and, when feasible, 
                    between these testing periods (Evidence quality: V; recom-
                    mendation strength: best practice).
                    B. Action Statement 8: USE OF THE CORE SET OF 
                    OUTCOME MEASURES. Clinicians should use and doc-
                    ument the OMs in the core set to assess changes over time. 
                    The core set includes the BBS, FGA, ABC, 10mWT, 6MWT, 
                    and 5TSTS, and the recommended patient goal assessment 
                    for adults who are undergoing neurologic physical therapy. 
                    The core set should be administered with patients who have 
                    goals and the capacity to improve transfers, balance, and/or 


                    JNPT • Volume 42, July 2018

                    180 ©2018 The Authors. Published by Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. on behalf of Academy of Neurologic Physical Therapy, APTA

                    gait. In cases when a patient cannot complete one or more 
                    core set OMs (eg, a patient who is unable to walk; thus, can-
                    not complete the 10mWT or the 6MWT), a score of 0 should 
                    be documented. The core set should be administered under 
                    the same test conditions at least 2 times, at admission and 
                    discharge, and when feasible between these periods (Evi-
                    dence quality: II; recommendation strength: moderate).
                    P. Action Statement 9: DISCUSS OUTCOME MEA-
                    SURE RESULTS AND USE COLLABORATIVE/
                    SHARED DECISION-MAKING WITH PATIENTS. Cli-
                    nicians should discuss the purpose of OMs, OM results, and 
                    how these results influence treatment options with patients 

                    undergoing neurologic physical therapy. Collaboratively, the 
                    clinician and the patient should decide how these data should 
                    inform the plan of care (Evidence quality: V; recommenda-
                    tion strength: best practice).
                    These guidelines were issued in 2018 based on the scientific 
                    literature published before March 2016. These guidelines 
                    will be considered for review by 2023, or sooner if new evi-
                    dence becomes available. The ANPT will oversee the pro-
                    cess and methodology for updating the CPG. The GDG will 
                    work collaboratively with the ANPT Evidence-Based Guide-
                    line Committee. Any updates to the guidelines in the interim 
                    period will be noted on the ANPT Web site.
