                        Abstract
                        The American Physical Therapy Association’s Vision Statement of 2013 asserts that physical therapists optimize movement in
                        order to improve the human experience. In accordance with this vision, physical therapists strive to be recognized as experts
                        in movement analysis. However, there continues to be no accepted method to conduct movement analysis, nor an agreement
                        of key terminology to describe movement observations. As a result, the Academy of Neurologic Physical Therapy organized
                        a task force that was charged with advancing the state of practice with respect to these issues, including the development
                        of a proposed method for movement analysis of tasks. This paper presents the work of the Task Force, which includes (1)
                        development of a method for conducting movement analysis within the context of the movement continuum during 6 core
                        tasks (sitting, sit to stand, standing, walking, step up/down, and reach/grasp/manipulate); (2) glossary of movement constructs
                        that can provide a common language for movement analysis across a range of tasks: symmetry, speed, amplitude, alignment,
                        verticality, stability, smoothness, sequencing, timing, accuracy, and symptom provocation; and (3) recommendations for task
                        and environmental variations that can be systematically applied. The expectation is that this systematic framework and
                        accompanying terminology will be easily adapted to additional patient or client-speciﬁc tasks, contribute to development of
                        movement system diagnostic labels, and ultimately improve consistency across patient/client examination, evaluation, and
                        intervention for the physical therapy profession. Next steps should include validation of this framework across patient/client
                        groups and settings.
                        Keywords: Movement Analysis, Movement System, Task Analysis

                        Downloaded from https://academic.oup.com/ptj/article/101/9/pzab154/6307338 by UNIVERSITY OF PITTSBURGH user on 12 November 2021


                        2 Framework for Movement Analysis of Tasks

                        Introduction
                        In 2013, the American Physical Therapy Association (APTA)
                        set forth a vision statement for the physical therapy pro-
                        fession,1 identifying the movement system as central to the
                        identity of physical therapy practice.2 In accordance with this
                        vision statement, physical therapists are movement system
                        experts,3 and central to this is the proposed development of
                        movement system diagnoses.4 Rather than being classified by
                        traditional health conditions or diseases, movement system
                        diagnosescategorizepatients/clientsbyimpairmentsandlimi-
                        tationsrelatedtotheirmovementabilities.Assuch,movement
                        analysis,whereintherapistsuseobservationtoexaminemove-
                        ment during tasks and activities, is a key component of the
                        evaluation process and development of diagnoses. However,
                        atpresent,ourprofessiondoesnothaveaunifyingframework
                        to conduct movement analysis across a range of tasks and
                        activities,withconsiderationoftheconceptsofmotorcontrol
                        that are essential to identification of movement dysfunction.5
                        In 2015, the Academy of Neurologic Physical Therapy
                        (ANPT) developed a Movement System Task Force, which
                        was charged with developing an evidence-based framework
                        for conducting movement analysis as well as developing
                        movementsystemdiagnoses,forindividualswithneurological
                        disorders.The Task Force published a white paper6 outlining
                        essentialelementsnecessarytodevelopasystematicapproach
                        to movement analysis to aid in the diagnostic process. In
                        2017, 2 new task forces were created: a Movement Analysis
                        Task Force and a Balance Diagnosis Task Force. The ANPT
                        Board of Directors invited physical therapists to apply for a
                        position on the Movement Analysis Task Force in October
                        2017; the authors of this paper were subsequently chosen
                        to serve. The 7 members have a mean of 24.4 years of
                        clinical experience, most in neurological rehabilitation but
                        also including musculoskeletal and general rehabilitation
                        (range= 15–37 years). They represent different geographic
                        regions of the United States (3 Midwest, 1 Mid-Atlantic, 1
                        Northeast, 2 Southwest) and varied primary roles (4 aca-
                        demician/researchers, 1 academician/clinician, 2 clinicians).
                        This paper represents the combined effort of the task force
                        members, who met for 2 face-to-face weekend meetings and
                        conductedmonthlyconferencecallsoveran18-monthperiod.
                        Thegrouppresentedtheirpreliminaryworkinaneducational
                        session at the 2019 Combined Sections Meeting of the APTA
                        and its final recommendations in an educational session at
                        the 2020 Combined Sections Meeting of the APTA.
                        This paper presents a framework for physical therapists
                        to systematically conduct movement analysis during task
                        performance.Indoingso,wehopetostrengthentheemphasis
                        on movement analysis in everyday practice, lead to more
                        consistency in examination procedures, and ultimately to
                        improve the ability of physical therapists to use movement
                        analyses as 1 component of developing movement system
                        diagnoses. Although this framework was initially designed
                        for application to clients with neurologic impairments, we
                        see this framework as applying more broadly to movement
                        system dysfunctions originating from different systems (eg,
                        musculoskeletal, cardiopulmonary, etc) or combinations
                        thereof.

                        Movement Constructs
                        The observation, analysis, and ultimately the fostering of
                        humanmovementisthefoundationofourpracticeasphysical

                        therapists.7–9 Analysis of movement during performance of
                        tasks is a key tenet of physical therapy practice, and keen
                        observation skills have been central to physical therapy since
                        the beginning of the profession. Contemporary theories of
                        motor control10,11 emphasize that movement emerges from a
                        complexinteractionbetweenthetask,theperformer,andtheir
                        environment. Individuals choose optimal movement strate-
                        gies that meet the demands of the task given their current
                        limitations and abilities. With this in mind, we propose a
                        framework for the systematic analysis of movement during
                        tasks,withsome initial taskand environmental constraints to
                        allow for consistent observation of an individual’s movement
                        patterns or strategies. Systematic observation of movement
                        allows for theorization of underlying reasons for particular
                        movement patterns and may ultimately lead to a method for
                        making movement system diagnoses that can drive evidence-
                        based treatment decisions. Although this task force has cho-
                        sen a series of core tasks for initial movement observation,
                        including static (sitting and standing) and dynamic tasks (sit
                        tostand,walking,stepup/downandreach/grasp/manipulate),
                        this framework may be applied to any goal-directed task
                        of interest (eg, lying to sit; throwing a ball) or indeed any
                        functional movement (eg,reaching,squatting).
                        To ensure consistency in our approach to movement analy-
                        sis,wemustfirstagreeonterminologytodescribemovement.
                        Furthermore, there is extensive motor control literature in a
                        range of tasks that have elucidated our understanding of the
                        complex nature of how the nervous system interacts with the
                        musculoskeletal, cardiovascular, pulmonary, integumentary,
                        and endocrine systems in order for movement to emerge.12,13
                        We have created a glossary of movement constructs (Tab.1)
                        that were chosen by expert consensus through a multi-year
                        iterative process and are grounded in contemporary motor
                        control literature. The task force members triangulated pri-
                        mary, secondary, and tertiary sources to arrive at this list.
                        Although we believe this list represents unique observations
                        that are applicable to a large range of tasks, we recognize
                        that continued evaluation and refinement of these terms is
                        warranted.
                        Motor control is defined as the ability to regulate or direct
                        the mechanisms essential to movement.12 Our constructs
                        consistofobservableaspectsofmotorcontrol;inotherwords,
                        those that can be seen or reported during movement. The
                        constructs are symmetry, speed, amplitude, alignment, ver-
                        ticality, stability, smoothness, sequencing, timing, accuracy,
                        and symptom provocation (Tab.1). We have grouped 6 of
                        these constructs within 2 broader motor control concepts of
                        postural control and coordination. Verticality and stability
                        are components of postural control, which is defined as the
                        ability to control the body’s position in space with respect
                        to gravity, the environment (eg, visual surroundings), and
                        internal references for the dual purposes of stability and
                        orientation.14 Smoothness, sequencing, timing, and accuracy
                        are components of coordination, which can be defined as
                        smooth, efficient, and accurate movement of body segments
                        associated with orderly sequencing, timing, and grading of
                        muscle activity.11

                        The Movement Continuum
                        Hedman et al7 has described a movement continuum that
                        serves as a useful framework for movement observations
                        across a range of tasks. The stages of the movement

                        continuum consider movement from its initial conditions to
                        outcome of the task goal and environment.
                        As seen in the Figure, movement analysis begins with eval-
                        uation of the initial conditions, which includes evaluation of
                        the environment and observing starting posture.As discussed
                        above, we believe it is important to apply some constraints
                        on both the environment (eg, initial condition for walking
                        would be a smooth surface in a quiet location) and initial
                        posture (eg, initial condition for sit to stand would be sitting
                        upright with feet flat on floor) and then to systematically
                        alter the environmental conditions to observe changes in
                        movement strategies. Movement preparation, although an
                        important component of motor planning and execution, is
                        generally not observable; however, assessment of whether an
                        individualunderstandstheinstructionsortherequirementsof
                        a task can reflect the construct of movement preparation. In
                        addition, various observations at subsequent stages can also
                        provide a window into the preparation stage. For dynamic
                        tasks (eg, sit to stand, walking, stepping up and down, and
                        reach/grasp/manipulate),wefocusonobservablestagesofthe
                        movementcontinuum(initiation,execution,andtermination).
                        Initiationofmovementistheinstantwhenthedisplacementof
                        thesegmentsbegins,executionistheperiodofactualsegment
                        movement,and termination is the instant when motion stops.
                        Thus, within a given task, we recommend consideration of
                        each of these 3 phases of movement, which can provide dif-
                        ferent information pertaining to the key constructs discussed
                        above. The final component of the movement continuum
                        defined by Hedman et al7 is outcome, referring to whether
                        the goal of the movement was reached successfully.Similar to
                        the initial conditions, the outcome of the task is pre-defined
                        bytheinstructionsgiventotheindividualperformingthetask

                        (eg,standfor30seconds)andcanbesystematicallyalteredto
                        make the task goal easier or harder to achieve.

                        Core Tasks
                        We chose 6 core tasks—sitting, sit to stand, standing, walk-
                        ing, step up/down, and reach/grasp/manipulate—following a
                        consensusprocedureamongtheoriginaltaskforcegroup(see
                        Hedman et al6) (Tab.2). Examining movement constructs
                        across these tasks allows consideration of a range of task
                        requirements: the ability to maintain positions (siting, stand-
                        ing),moving within a position (reach,grasp and manipulate),
                        moving between positions (sit to stand),and moving through
                        theenvironment(stepup/down,walkandturn).Werecognize
                        that core tasks may differ based on patient/client groups and
                        settings, and the tasks presented here may be limited for
                        individuals who are non-ambulatory and also for individuals
                        at high performance levels such as athletes. However, we
                        believe that these core tasks can be a starting point in a wide
                        range of clinical situations,and additional tasks can be added
                        to this framework as needed using the same structure and
                        format.

                        Principles for Movement Analysis
                        Movement analysis should be conducted in a structured and
                        environmentally controlled manner to facilitate consistent
                        observation of an individual’s movement patterns and strate-
                        gies. Although we recognize the importance of ecologically
                        valid assessments, it is also important to have consistency in
                        assessment procedures and to take into account the impact of
                        the environment and the task requirements. We also suggest

                        return the cup to the table surface.”

                        thatmovementanalysisbeconductedearlyintheexamination
                        process to help inform appropriate tests and measures within
                        varioussystems(eg,musculoskeletal,neuromotor,integumen-
                        tary, etc). As a therapist observes movement, they should
                        be generating hypotheses about the contributing factors to
                        any movement dysfunction.This may include specific impair-
                        ments (eg, impaired sensation), which would warrant further
                        testing. (The worksheets provided in the Suppl. Appendix,
                        include examples of suggested systems evaluations.)
                        Here we propose recommendations for testing efficiency,
                        instructions and environmental set up, repetitions, use of
                        physical support, and systematic modifications to the task
                        and environment to change the challenge of the task and
                        adapt to an individual’s performance. Importantly, we make
                        recommendations for ways to systematically alter tasks and
                        theenvironmenttomorecomprehensivelyevaluatemovement
                        constructs.

                        Testing Efﬁciency
                        Astructuredmovementanalysisoftasksshouldbeconducted
                        in a set order, followed as closely as possible between indi-
                        viduals and for subsequent testing if feasible within clinical
                        settings. This standardization helps to ensure consistency
                        betweentestingandmaximizeefficiency.Werecommendeval-
                        uatingperformanceonall6tasksinthesuggestedorderwhen
                        possible, which allows the therapist to observe consistent
                        issues that may be common across tasks.

                        Instructions and Environmental Setup
                        (Standardizing Initial Conditions)
                        The environmental setup and instructions are designed to
                        minimize constraints on the task and observe the individual’s

                        chosen strategy for performing the task. The focus of
                        movement analysis is on observing the movement patterns
                        andstrategiesusedtoperformthetask.Itisnotaboutjudging
                        level of assistance, and as such, the therapist should provide
                        the least amount of assistance to enable the individual to
                        attemptthetasksafely.Itisessential,therefore,toobservethe
                        individual performing the movement as they would naturally
                        perform it.

                        Repetitions
                        For all tasks except sitting and standing, individuals should
                        be asked to perform the task at least twice. During the first
                        repetition, the therapist determines if they understood the
                        task instructions and can perform the task without assistance
                        or support (Fig.). Additional repetitions can then be used
                        to further evaluate movement constructs, to observe how
                        movement patterns may change with practice, and to draw
                        out potential factors affecting performance (eg, endurance,
                        strength).

                        Task and Environmental Variations
                        Inadditiontomultipletaskrepetitions,taskandenvironmen-
                        tal variations can be used to evaluate movement capabilities
                        and observe changes in strategies or performance with differ-
                        ent constraints,supports,or verbal instructions.If an individ-
                        ual is unable to complete a task as instructed,we suggest first
                        alteringthetaskorenvironmentalconditionstopromotesuc-
                        cess.Weadvocateforasystematicframeworktoalterenviron-
                        mentalandtaskconstraints15,16 (Tab.3)andfurtherclassified
                        these changes into either regressions or progressions.17
                        Task and environmental regressions are variations that
                        are generally designed to simplify or make the task less

                        Figure. The movement continuum framework of Hedman et al7 provides the foundation for movement analysis of tasks proposed in this paper. The

                        pre-determined for the ﬁrst performance of a task but can be systematically varied in subsequent repetitions. Movement preparation, deﬁned as the

                        challengingtoperform.Simplifyingataskallowsthetherapist
                        to observe independent movement in someone who could not
                        otherwise perform a task. Examples of task regressions may
                        include increasing the base of support or changing the task
                        speed (either faster or slower). Examples of environmental
                        regressionsincludealteringthesurfacetypeorheight;provid-
                        ingcueing,physicalassistance,orexternalsupport;oraltering
                        environmental inputs. The choice of assistance or cueing
                        depends on many factors, including the individual’s physical
                        and cognitive abilities; however, we generally recommend
                        providingassistanceinthefollowingorder:(1)verbalcue,(2)
                        tactile cue, and (3) physical assistance. Of course, therapists
                        will need to make a judgement for the safety of the individual
                        performing the task or themselves about whether to attempt
                        tasks without assistance or cueing.
                        Conversely, if the task is not sufficiently challenging for
                        an individual, we recommend adding task progressions. Task
                        progressions are task variations that are generally designed
                        to increase complexity or make the task more challenging to
                        perform. Adding complexity to the task may enable the ther-
                        apist to better understand capacity of the movement system
                        that is not elucidated by the baseline task. Examples of task
                        progressions include narrowing base of support, changing
                        taskspeed,addinginternalperturbations(eg,headturns),and
                        adding dual tasks. Examples of environmental progressions
                        includealteringsurfaceheightortype,oralteringenvironmen-
                        tal inputs (eg, adding motion to the environment or adding
                        external perturbations). We recommend the addition of at
                        least 1 task regression for individuals who are unable or have
                        difficultytoperformatask,and1taskprogressiontoprovide
                        challenges when there is no identifiable problem during task
                        performance.

                        Movement Analysis Worksheets
                        Wehavedevelopedaccompanyingworksheetstoillustratethe
                        application of this framework for movement analysis of tasks
                        in clinical practice (see Suppl. Appendix). We recognize that
                        the worksheets are detailed and there may be challenges to
                        their use in practice settings. However, these may have utility
                        as a teaching tool or to provide novice clinicians with a struc-
                        tured format for conducting movement analysis.Importantly,
                        although these worksheets have undergone extensive review
                        and revisions by expert clinicians, they have not undergone
                        reliability and validity testing. We recommend that they be
                        used as a guide to direct the novice clinician to conduct
                        movement analysis in a systematic manner as well as for
                        experienced clinicians who can use them to assess and re-
                        assess their own skills in movement analysis.
                        The worksheets include questions designed to prompt
                        therapists to key observations for each task. These questions
                        were developed based on review of the corresponding
                        literature in each of the tasks: sitting,18–25 sit to stand,26–32
                        standing,14,33–37 walking,38–40 step up/down,41–46 and
                        reach/grasp/manipulate.47,48 Importantly, these questions do
                        not focus on detailed biomechanical analysis but rather on
                        observations thought to be key to task success. In addition,
                        the worksheets provide suggestions for additional tests
                        and measures within various systems (eg, musculoskeletal,
                        neuromotor,integumentary,etc).

                        Quantifying Movement Analysis
                        Movement analysis in clinical practice is typically based on
                        visual observations, and the worksheets (Suppl. Appendix)
                        can be used as a guide to facilitate systematic observation.

                        quantifymovementconstructs,eithertobetterunderstandthe
                        natureofthemovementdysfunctionorforuseasanoutcome
                        measure(seemeasurementexamplesinTab.1).Astechnology
                        becomes ubiquitous in clinical settings, with apps used to
                        evaluate gait speed,49 mobility,50 and spatiotemporal gait
                        analysis,49,51 we encourage therapists to incorporate these
                        into their clinical practice. Although use of technology may
                        not always be feasible or warranted, it can provide a method
                        formovementanalysistoevaluatemovementconstructsmore
                        reliably and accurately than the naked eye. Wearable and
                        mobiletechnologiesareadvancingrapidly,andasaprofession
                        we should be open to incorporating more accurate ways
                        of conducting movement analyses and evaluating outcomes.
                        Importantly, this should not diminish the value of our visual
                        observations and the skill involved in conducting accurate
                        movementanalysis.Aswithmanytechnologies,clinicaljudge-
                        ment is required to determine which technology to use and
                        how to use it, and therapists’ initial observations may be
                        important screens for technology selection.

                        Discussion and Summary
                        The 2013 APTA vision statement established the movement
                        system as the cornerstone of physical therapist practice, thus
                        identifying physical therapists as movement system experts.
                        As such, physical therapists work to improve the human
                        experience by optimizing movement. To do this, physical

                        therapists must make sound decisions regarding treatment
                        based on movement system diagnoses that should stem from
                        a systematic assessment of movement as part of a physi-
                        cal therapy examination. This paper proposes a framework
                        for observation of movement constructs during tasks that
                        representcommondailyactivities.Thesystematicapproachto
                        movement observation and environmental control promotes
                        consistency in movement analysis of tasks.
                        Previous papers have identified similar movement con-
                        structs and “observational targets,” including a recent paper
                        by McClure et al.9 McClure’s model focuses on fewer
                        dimensions of movement than the framework presented here,
                        although there is considerable overlap with our constructs.
                        Both models include symmetry, amount (amplitude), speed,
                        and symptoms. Additionally, McClure et al9 include “con-
                        trol” to refer to smoothness, coordination, and timing of
                        movement. Rather than combining together these features
                        into 1 construct, our model delineates these into 2 important
                        features of motor control: postural control (verticality
                        and stability) and coordination (smoothness, sequencing,
                        timing, and accuracy). We further include the construct of
                        alignment, which is distinct from symmetry. We believe that
                        particularly for individuals with more complex movement
                        dysfunctions, the distinction between these constructs is
                        necessary to accurately identify contributing factors to
                        movement dysfunction.
                        This paper is a first step in providing a structured method
                        for conducting movement analysis of tasks and placing it at

                        Downloaded from https://academic.oup.com/ptj/article/101/9/pzab154/6307338 by UNIVERSITY OF PITTSBURGH user on 12 November 2021


                        Quinn et al 7

                        the center of the physical therapy examination. We believe
                        this framework aligns well with the work of APTA and other
                        groupstodefinemovementdiagnoses,andweultimatelyhope
                        asaprofessionwecanalignourselvesacrossareasofpractice.
                        Our next steps will be to validate this framework and
                        accompanying terminology across patient/client groups and
                        settings. It is our ultimate goal that the adoption of this
                        frameworkintoclinicalpracticewillimproveawarenessofthe
                        movement system and further strengthen physical therapists’
                        identity as movement system experts.

                    Abstract
                    The movement system was identiﬁed as the focus of our expertise as physical therapists in the revised vision statement for
                    the profession adopted by the American Physical Therapy Association in 2013. Attaining success with the profession’s vision
                    requires the development of movement system diagnoses that will be useful in clinical practice, research, and education. To
                    date, only a few movement system diagnoses have been identiﬁed and described, and none of these speciﬁcally address
                    balance dysfunction. Over the past 2 years, a Balance Diagnosis Task Force, a subgroup of the Movement System Task Force
                    of the Academy of Neurologic Physical Therapy, focused on developing diagnostic labels (or diagnoses) for individuals with
                    balance problems. This paper presents the work of the task force that followed a systematic process to review available
                    diagnostic frameworks related to balance, identify 10 distinct movement system diagnoses that reﬂect balance dysfunction,
                    and develop complete descriptions of examination ﬁndings associated with each balance diagnosis. A standardized approach
                    to movement analysis of core tasks, the Framework for Movement Analysis developed by the Academy of Neurologic Physical
                    Therapy Movement Analysis Task Force, was integrated into the examination and diagnostic processes. The aims of this
                    perspective paper are to (1) summarize the process followed by the Balance Diagnosis Task Force to develop an initial set
                    of movement system (balance) diagnoses; (2) report the recommended diagnostic labels and associated descriptions; (3)
                    demonstrate the clinical decision-making process used to determine a balance diagnosis and develop a plan of care; and (4)
                    identify next steps to validate and implement the diagnoses into physical therapist practice, education, and research.
                    Impact. The development and use of diagnostic labels to classify distinct movement system problems is needed in physical
                    therapy. The 10 balance diagnosis proposed can aid in clinical decision making regarding intervention.
                    Keywords: Balance, Decision Making, Clinical Diagnosis, Movement System

                    Downloaded from https://academic.oup.com/ptj/article/101/9/pzab153/6307337 by UNIVERSITY OF PITTSBURGH user on 12 November 2021


                    2 Movement System Diagnoses for Balance Dysfunction

                    Introduction
                    The 2013 revised vision statement of the American Physical
                    Therapy Association (APTA)1 states that adoption of the
                    movement system as the focus of physical therapist expertise
                    is key to our professional identity. Development of movement
                    system diagnoses that are useful in clinical practice, research,
                    and education will facilitate realization of this vision. In
                    2015, the APTA endorsed “the development of diagnostic
                    labels and/or classification systems that reflect and contribute
                    to the physical therapist’s ability to properly and effectively
                    manage disorders of the movement system.”1 Accordingly, the
                    Academy of Neurologic Physical Therapy (ANPT) appointed
                    a Movement System Task Force in 2015 to explore this
                    issue for individuals with primary neurologic dysfunction. The
                    task force identified 4 characteristics necessary for the clin-
                    ically meaningful movement system diagnostic labels: (1) be
                    based on a sound, evidence-based theoretical framework(s);
                    (2) emphasize systematic movement observation and analysis
                    of core standardized tasks as central to the clinical exam-
                    ination and evaluation; (3) represent a unique cluster of
                    movement observations and associated examination findings
                    that can impact a variety of tasks; and (4) provide unique and
                    non-ambiguous labels for each movement system diagnosis.2
                    Subsequently, ANPT formed 2 new subgroups of the Move-
                    ment System Task Force in 2018 to develop (1) a standardized
                    approach to movement analysis of tasks, and (2) develop
                    diagnostic labels (or diagnoses) for individuals with balance
                    problems. This paper represents the work of the members who
                    comprised the Balance Diagnosis Task Force. The aims of this
                    perspective paper are to (1) summarize the process that the
                    Balance Diagnosis Task Force followed to develop an initial
                    set of movement system-related balance diagnoses for physical
                    therapists, (2) report the recommended diagnoses (diagnos-
                    tic labels and associated descriptions), (3) demonstrate the
                    clinical decision-making process used to determine a balance
                    diagnosis and develop a plan of care, and (4) identify critical
                    next steps to validate and implement balance diagnoses into
                    physical therapist practice, education, and research.

                    ANPT Balance Diagnosis Task Force Process
                    The ANPT Board of Directors invited ANPT members to
                    apply for a position on the Balance Diagnosis Task Force in
                    October 2017; the authors of this paper were subsequently
                    chosen to serve. The 9 members have a mean of 25.5 years
                    of experience working with individuals with neurologic dis-
                    orders (range = 10–42 years). They represent different geo-

                    graphic regions of the United States (4 Midwest, 4 Northeast,
                    1 Southwest) and varied primary roles (1 academician/re-
                    searchers, 2 academician/clinicians, 2 academicians, 2 clini-
                    cian/administrators, 1 academician/clinician/researcher, and 1
                    administrator). Of the 9 task force members, 5 are American
                    Board of Physical Therapy Specialties–certified neurologic
                    clinical specialists, and 1 is dual certified by the American
                    Board of Physical Therapy Specialties as a clinical specialist
                    in both geriatric and neurologic physical therapy.
                    The Balance Diagnosis Task Force was convened in January
                    2018 and was charged to develop an initial set of move-
                    ment system diagnoses that were applicable to individuals
                    with balance deficits and met the criteria developed by the
                    initial ANPT Movement System Task Force.2 The group was
                    also charged with developing a description (or diagnostic

                    template) for each diagnostic label that identified the specific
                    movement observations and associated examination findings
                    unique to the individuals with each proposed movement sys-
                    tem (balance) diagnosis. The development of clear and specific
                    diagnostic templates has been suggested because they can aid
                    in the differential diagnostic process.3 The group conducted
                    monthly virtual conferences and met on 2 occasions for 2-
                    day face-to-face meetings over an 18-month period. The group
                    presented their preliminary work in an educational session at
                    the 2019 Combined Sections Meeting of the APTA and its
                    final recommendations in an educational session at the 2020
                    Combined Sections Meeting of the APTA.

                    Synthesis of Theoretical Frameworks of Balance
                    Figure 1 summarizes the process that the group used to
                    develop and describe the recommended balance diagnoses.
                    First, the group identified and reviewed the existing relevant
                    literature regarding theoretical frameworks4–17 related to
                    balance to analyze their conceptual elements and determine if
                    it was possible to adopt an existing framework to underpin the
                    balance diagnosis work. We decided that the terms “balance”
                    and “postural control” would be used interchangeably for
                    the purposes of this work and the following definition was
                    adopted: Postural control (balance) is “the ability to control
                    the body’s position in space with respect to gravity, support
                    surfaces, visual surround and internal references for the dual
                    purposes of stability and orientation. Stability is defined as
                    the ability to control the body’s center of mass in relation to
                    the base of support under quasi-static (minimal accelerations
                    are occurring) and dynamic conditions. Orientation is the
                    relationship between the body’s segments, and between the
                    body and environment.”18,19
                    The group determined that there was no single existing
                    framework that included all the relevant and current concep-
                    tual elements related to balance. None of the frameworks suf-
                    ficiently covered perceptually based problems (eg, backward
                    disequilibrium, contraversive pushing), nor were behaviorally
                    based factors (eg, balance confidence, falls self-efficacy, fear of
                    falling, past experience with falls) adequately represented in
                    the frameworks. The group arrived at the consensus that the
                    conceptual elements from a combination of the frameworks
                    described by Horak and colleagues,8–10 Shumway-Cook and
                    colleagues,18 Huxham,11 Gentile,5,6 Sibley,20,21 and biobe-
                    havioral models11,13,18,22,23 would be useful for developing
                    diagnoses related to balance.
                    The group organized the conceptual elements into 2 dis-
                    tinct categories to help develop balance diagnoses. The first
                    category relates to control strategies for balance; these are
                    identified by Shumway-Cook and Woolacott18 as well as oth-
                    ers11,13 and are partly defined by Horak and colleagues.8–10
                    The described control strategies for balance include steady
                    state postural control, anticipatory postural control, and reac-
                    tive postural control (definitions provided in Tab. 1).
                    The second category relates to the underlying determinants
                    of balance, which are defined as those elements or body
                    systems that contribute to producing and maintaining body
                    orientation and stability during tasks and activities.24 Under-
                    lying determinants of balance are associated primarily with
                    the following:

                    Musculoskeletal system (eg, range of motion, flexibility,
                    muscle performance, alignment/posture)

                    Downloaded from https://academic.oup.com/ptj/article/101/9/pzab153/6307337 by UNIVERSITY OF PITTSBURGH user on 12 November 2021


                    Gill-Body et al 3

                    Figure 1. Steps used in the process to identify balance diagnoses and develop diagnostic templates. Steps used in the process of developing and
                    reﬁning movement system diagnoses for balance dysfunction are identiﬁed in this ﬁgure. Each step is explained in detail in the manuscript.

                    Neuromuscular system (eg, coordination, postural move-
                    ment strategies, sensory integrity, sensory processing,
                    perceptual function including verticality)
                    • Cognitive/mental function (eg, arousal, attention,

                    executive function, multi-task ability)
                    • Behavioral factors (eg, balance confidence, falls self-

                    efficacy, fear of falling, past experience with falls)

                    The group developed operational definitions for all these
                    relevant terms using the available literature (Tab. 1). When
                    faced with more than 1 current definition, the group used
                    consensus to finalize the operational definition.

                    Classiﬁcation of Balance Dysfunction
                    Based on our work and as a first step in developing balance
                    diagnoses, the group classified balance dysfunction based
                    on the control strategies for balance: deficit in steady state
                    postural control, deficit in anticipatory postural control, and
                    deficit in reactive postural control. At this point in the process,
                    the group was considering these classifications as potential
                    balance diagnoses. Therefore, it was important that the labels
                    meet the criteria developed by ANPT as described above2
                    as well as those developed by the APTA.25 The APTA crite-
                    ria state that diagnostic classification systems/labels should
                    (1) use recognized movement-related terms to describe the

                    condition or syndrome of the movement system; (2) be as
                    succinct and direct as possible to improve clinical usefulness;
                    and (3) strive for movement system diagnoses that span all
                    populations, health conditions, and the lifespan.

                    Identiﬁcation of Key Movement Observations for
                    Each Classiﬁcation of Balance Dysfunction
                    The group next used the Framework for Movement Analysis
                    and checklists developed by the ANPT Movement Analysis
                    Task Force,2 the available literature, and our clinical experi-
                    ence to identify the key movement observations that would
                    likely be demonstrated by individuals with each balance
                    dysfunction classification. “Key movement observations” are
                    defined as deviations from typical movement performance
                    that guide detection of deficits in balance dysfunction. To
                    accomplish this, the group used the observable movement con-
                    structs described in the Framework for Movement Analysis.26
                    These observable movement constructs include alignment,
                    verticality, stability, symmetry, speed, amplitude, smoothness,
                    sequencing, timing, accuracy, and symptom provocation.
                    Examining these observable movement constructs across the
                    6 core tasks recommended by the ANPT Movement Analysis
                    Task Force allows consideration of the following elements of
                    balance control: maintenance of positions (siting, standing),
                    movement within positions (reach, grasp and manipulate),

                    Table 1. Conceptual Elements Related to Balance
                    Conceptual Elements Related to Balance Operational Definition
                    Control strategies for balance
                    Steady state postural control Ability to control the location of the body’s center of mass within the area defined by the base of
                    support under predictable, quasi-static conditions. This includes the ability to adapt motor
                    behavior to meet the demands of different task and environmental conditions.12,16,18
                    Anticipatory postural control Ability to generate postural adjustments prior to the onset of and during voluntary movement
                    for the purpose of either countering an upcoming postural disturbance due to voluntary
                    movement or realigning the body’s center of mass prior to changing the base of support. This
                    includes the ability to adapt motor behavior to meet the demands of different task and
                    environmental conditions.12,18
                    Reactive postural control Ability to respond to sensory input that signals a need for a response to ensure successful
                    maintenance of postural control. The need for a response is unanticipated but may be
                    generated externally (perturbation originating external to body) or secondarily to an internally
                    generated movement. This includes the ability to adapt motor behavior to meet the demands
                    of different task and environmental conditions.13,14
                    Underlying determinants of balance
                    Musculoskeletal system
                    Range of motion Arc through which active and passive movement occurs at a joint or a series of joints and the
                    angle(s) created during movement
                    Flexibility (muscle length, joint mobility) Maximum extensibility available at the muscle-tendon unit in conjunction with joint
                    extensibility and soft tissue extensibility19
                    Muscle performance (includes strength,
                    power, and endurance)

                    Muscle performance: capacity of a muscle or a group of muscles to generate forces to produce,
                    sustain, and modify posture and movement prerequisite to functional activity19
                    Strength: muscle force exerted to overcome resistance under a specific set of circumstances
                    Power: work produced per unit of time or the product of strength and speed
                    Endurance: ability of muscle to sustain forces repeatedly and over a period of time19
                    Alignment (posture) Biomechanical relationship of body segments to one another as well as to the base of support18
                    Neuromuscular system
                    Postural movement strategies Coupling of muscles, segments, and joints of the body to maintain posture and balance during
                    voluntary movement and in response to an external perturbation. Postural movement
                    strategies include anticipatory postural adjustments, fixed support (corrective) responses, and
                    change-in-support (protective) responses.39–41
                    Coordination Smooth, efficient, and accurate movement of body segments associated with orderly sequencing,
                    timing, and grading of muscle activity within a movement or task42
                    Sensory integrity The soundness of the body’s sensory systems, including vision, somatosensation, hearing, taste,
                    and vestibular inputs (modified from Guide to PT Practice)19
                    Sensory processing Ability of the central nervous system to select, weight, and integrate sensory information to
                    develop accurate and meaningful perceptions of the body and environment that allow for
                    maintenance of postural control as task and environmental conditions change43,44
                    Perceptual function: verticality Ability to orient the body in relation to the line of gravity10,21,45
                    Cognitive/mental function
                    Executive function A set of complex cognitive skills, including insight, judgement, memory, problem solving, and
                    attention, that are responsible for the planning, initiation, sequencing, and monitoring of
                    goal-directed behavior46–48
                    Multi-task capacity Ability to successfully participate in multiple tasks and/or reconcile concurrent sources of
                    sensory input during goal-directed behavior48,49
                    Arousal and alertness Arousal: responsiveness to stimuli1
                    Alertness is a basic arousal process that allows the individual to respond to external stimuli.18
                    Behavioral factors
                    Balance confidence Degree of certainty that an individual has in their ability to maintain balance and remain stable
                    while performing tasks36,50
                    Falls self-efficacy A person’s perception about their abilities to deal with a fall23
                    Fear of falling A lasting concern or worry about falling regardless of history of fall(s)51,52
                    Activity avoidance The limiting of an activity that an individual is capable of performing that can result in an
                    increased risk of falling and deterioration in physical and mental health and quality of life51,52

                    movement between positions (sit-to-stand), and movement
                    through the environment (step up/step down, walk and turn).

                    Development of 10 Diagnoses of Balance
                    Dysfunction
                    In considering the clinical utility of the 3 balance dysfunction
                    classifications, the task force identified the need for more
                    specificity to guide the plan of care. The group agreed that
                    a balance diagnosis that reflects the key underlying determi-
                    nants contributing to a deficit in steady state, anticipatory,
                    or reactive postural control would make the balance diag-
                    nostic labels more informative and useful in formulating the
                    plan of care. After revisiting the literature and reflecting on
                    clinical experience, the group expanded the 3 classifications
                    of balance dysfunction to 10 balance diagnoses (Fig. 2). The
                    group used an iterative process of review and editing until
                    consensus was reached on the key movement observations

                    associated with each of the 10 balance diagnoses (Suppl.
                    Appendix).
                    Identiﬁcation of Underlying Determinants Using
                    Key Tests/Measures (Examination Results)
                    Finally, the group proceeded to identify the likely findings of
                    key tests/measures that help to identify the primary underlying
                    determinants of each balance diagnosis (Suppl. Appendix). In
                    determining the relevant tests/measures to include for each
                    diagnosis, we used the framework of the International Classi-
                    fication of Functioning, Disability and Health27 and consid-
                    ered tests/measures at the levels of body structure/function,
                    activity, and participation. We used the work of Pardasaney22
                    and Sibley20,21 to classify the individual items from stan-
                    dardized measures of balance (eg, BESTest,28,29 Berg Bal-
                    ance Scale)30–33 as they relate to steady state, anticipatory,
                    and reactive postural control. Groups of 2 or 3 task force
                    members worked separately and then collaboratively to reach

                    6 Movement System Diagnoses for Balance Dysfunction

                    consensus on this step; drafts were then reviewed and edited
                    until consensus was reached. Any overlapping key tests/mea-
                    sures (and likely findings) initially identified were prioritized
                    by considering tests/measures recommended by the various
                    ANPT EDGE groups34 and in the Core Set of Outcome
                    Measures for Adults with Neurologic Conditions.35

                    Outcomes: Diagnostic Templates
                    The group organized the movement observations for the 6
                    core tasks and key examination findings for each balance diag-
                    nosis into 10 unique diagnostic templates that are presented
                    in the Supplementary Appendix. Each diagnostic template
                    specifies the unique cluster of movement observations and
                    associated examination findings that best describe how a
                    patient would likely present with each of these movement
                    system diagnoses for balance dysfunction. We recognize that
                    the diagnostic templates contain many details and propose
                    that they are best used as a reference for clinicians as they
                    classify an individual’s balance dysfunction. They may also
                    have utility as a teaching tool or to provide novice clinicians
                    with a structured process for determining movement system
                    diagnoses.

                    Clinical Application of Diagnostic
                    Framework for Balance Dysfunction
                    Historically, physical therapy management and research has
                    often been organized by medical diagnoses. An underlying
                    assumption of the value of movement system diagnoses is
                    that a movement diagnosis can better inform the plan of care
                    than a medical diagnosis because it is based on identifying
                    and understanding each individual’s movement deficits.3 For
                    example, an individual with deficits in steady state postural
                    control, regardless of the medical diagnosis, may benefit from
                    training that is directed at steady state control deficits. This
                    assumption needs validation in future work across movement
                    system diagnoses.
                    In this paper, we illustrate the link between balance diag-
                    noses and intervention in 2 ways. First, we include a table
                    that summarizes possible connections between the 10 balance
                    diagnoses and task-specific interventions described in the
                    literature. To develop the summary table, the group reviewed
                    current evidence to identify examples of interventions that
                    illustrate ways that task-specific training may be implemented
                    to preferentially focus on specific types of balance deficits (as
                    reflected by the 10 balance diagnoses). Table 3 summarizes
                    the group’s results by identifying the primary intervention goal
                    for task-specific training for individuals with each balance
                    diagnosis (Column 2) and then citing examples of different
                    approaches to task-specific training that have been suggested
                    in the literature that aligns with each primary intervention
                    goal (Column 3). These proposed connections between the
                    10 balance diagnoses and interventions are illustrative only
                    at this point in the development and application of movement
                    system diagnoses; further work is needed to validate and test
                    these ideas. However, we believe taking such an approach
                    to align interventions with movement system diagnoses may
                    ultimately serve to enhance clinical decision making and
                    reduce unwarranted variability in care. It is also worth noting
                    that the interventions and suggested examples identified in
                    Table 3 focus on task-specific training only and do not address

                    additional impairment-based interventions that may also be
                    useful to include in the plan of care.
                    Second, a case example is included below to demonstrate
                    the clinical application of the concepts presented in this paper
                    to an individual with balance dysfunction. The purpose of
                    the case example is to demonstrate the differential diagnosis
                    process used by a clinician to determine a movement system
                    balance diagnosis and to plan and implement a plan of care.

                    Case Example
                    Background and Systems Review
                    Mr. G is a 73-year-old-man with advanced Parkinson disease
                    (functional capacity fluctuated between Hoehn and Yahr
                    Stages 3 and 4) who fell and sustained a subdural hematoma.
                    He received care in an acute hospital followed by rehabili-
                    tation in a skilled nursing facility for 3 months. Mr. G has
                    a medical history of unrepaired left rotator cuff tear, right
                    shoulder dislocation with brachial plexus injury, chronic bilat-
                    eral shoulder osteoarthritis, right ankle fusion, cervical spine
                    fusion, and recurrent benign paroxysmal positional vertigo.
                    Notably, he had a deep brain stimulator implanted 15 years
                    ago and recently had a PEG tube placed for continuous
                    infusion of carbidopa/levodopa (Duopa). Prior to his hospi-
                    talization, Mr. G had several episodes of outpatient physical
                    therapy to address problems with balance and recurrent falls
                    while walking in his home (3–5 times per day). He had
                    poor safety awareness and low adherence to physical therapy
                    recommendations, including trial of an assistive device to
                    decrease falling frequency.
                    At the time of this outpatient physical therapy evaluation,
                    it had been approximately 6 months since Mr. G’s subdural
                    hematoma. He lived at home with 24/7 home health aide
                    support. A mechanical lift was used to get out of bed on most
                    days. Throughout the day, he required moderate assistance for
                    bed mobility and stand-pivot transfers and his performance
                    fluctuated. His ability to transfer from sitting and walking (4–
                    6 steps) varied from minimum to maximum assistance. Prior
                    to his injury, Mr. G, a retired attorney, was active in his church
                    and community; he frequently attended lectures, composed
                    music, and participated in wellness exercise programs (dance
                    and yoga). His personal goal was to walk independently and
                    resume his prior activities.

                    Examination: Movement Observation of
                    6 Core Tasks
                    A systematic assessment of Mr. G’s ability to perform the 6
                    core tasks was performed to develop differential diagnoses to
                    explain his difficulty with mobility and balance dysfunction.
                    Using the ANPT’s Framework for Movement Analysis,26 Mr.
                    G’s movements were observed and analyzed under a variety
                    of task and environmental variations to include a range of
                    postural control demands to help detect possible underlying
                    determinants of his balance dysfunction.

                    Sitting
                    Because Mr. G demonstrated adequate ability to maintain
                    the sitting position in midline (steady state control), task
                    variations of sitting with feet unsupported, trunk leaning,
                    dual task ability, and external perturbations were selected
                    to reveal possible deficits in anticipatory postural control,
                    reactive postural control, and the ability to adapt steady state
