                    control. Mr. G was able to maintain sitting with his eyes closed
                    without foot support with minimal sway. He was unable to
                    elevate either buttock during attempts to weight shift. He was
                    unable to reach with either upper extremity but could lean
                    his trunk 3 inches to each side, 1 inch backwards, and 5
                    inches forward before needing assist to return to midline or
                    maintain balance, suggesting possible deficits in anticipatory
                    postural control. Mr. G was able to perform dual tasks in
                    sitting (counting backwards by 3s while performing paced leg
                    exercises) without an observable change in movement ability
                    or stability. With feet unsupported, external perturbations
                    in all directions were attempted to assess reactive postural
                    control, but Mr. G adopted a stiff/rigid position, thereby
                    self-limiting his movements and not allowing for accurate
                    assessment of reactive postural control.
                    Sit-to-Stand
                    To initiate the task, Mr. G adopted a wide base of support
                    and used a strategy of large range posterior to anterior trunk
                    rocking (altered initial direction of movement). His move-
                    ments were slow throughout the task, and he demonstrated
                    multiple starts/stops with decreased amplitude of forward
                    trunk lean. During execution of the task, Mr. G demonstrated
                    impaired sequencing (by extending his hips prior to knee
                    extension after lift-off) and difficulty timing his anterior trunk
                    movement with lift-off. These findings are consistent with
                    inadequate anticipatory postural control (Suppl. Appendix).
                    Mr. G demonstrated a posterior loss of balance on several
                    attempts to rise to stand/return to sit with ineffective ability
                    to restore equilibrium suggesting a deficit in reactive postural
                    control.
                    Standing
                    Mr. G demonstrated a self-selected wide base of support in
                    standing and could maintain the position for 30 seconds
                    independently with minimal sway. With feet together, he
                    demonstrated mild increased sway and required supervision,
                    suggesting difficulty adapting to steady state postural

                    conditions. The therapist did not conduct further testing of his
                    ability to adapt steady state control because the therapist did
                    not think that this was a major contributor to his recurrent
                    falls. Given his loss of balance during sit-to-stand, the task
                    variation of Modified Lean and Release Test10 was selected.
                    Under these conditions, Mr. G demonstrated excessive trunk
                    sway and did not effectively restore his center of mass,
                    resulting in a consistent loss of balance in posterior and lateral
                    directions (no loss of balance in anterior direction) consistent
                    with a deficit in reactive postural control. Specifically, he did
                    not step quickly enough with either lower extremity or use
                    his upper extremities to reach and stabilize his posture.

                    Walk and Turn
                    Mr. G was observed walking for 10 feet under 2 task varia-
                    tions: (1) walking with minimum assistance with no assistive
                    device, and (2) walking with supervision and verbal cues using
                    a U-Step rolling walker (In-Step Mobility Products Corp.,
                    Skokie, IL, USA). Throughout both task variations, Mr. G
                    demonstrated a forward flexed trunk, absent axial trunk
                    rotation, external rotation of right hip/lower extremity (align-
                    ment), and reduced gait speed (speed of movement). Mr. G also
                    walked with decreased bilateral step length and prolonged
                    double limb stance time. He did not demonstrate hip extension
                    beyond 0 degrees/neutral and did not achieve the trail limb
                    position in terminal stance (impaired sequencing). At each
                    change in direction, Mr. G demonstrated brief freezing of gait.
                    These findings are consistent with a deficit in anticipatory
                    postural control. While turning to return to the chair, Mr.
                    G experienced a loss of balance with ineffective ability to
                    recover stability (required maximum assistance) consistent
                    with a deficit in reactive postural control.

                    Step Up/Step Down
                    Mr. G was unable to perform this task under the typical con-
                    ditions of no upper extremity support (he repeatedly demon-
                    strated loss of balance to the stance side). As a result, the

                    Downloaded from https://academic.oup.com/ptj/article/101/9/pzab153/6307337 by UNIVERSITY OF PITTSBURGH user on 12 November 2021


                    Gill-Body et al 9

                    task was modified to allow for use of right-hand support
                    on a railing. At initiation, Mr. G demonstrated flexion at
                    the trunk, hips, knees, and ankles. While stepping up, Mr.
                    G relied heavily on his right upper extremity for support
                    and appeared to pull up on the railing. He demonstrated
                    delayed timing of unweighting the stepping leg. He remained
                    flexed at the trunk and lower extremities throughout the
                    task. Impairments in timing and sequencing of stepping as
                    well as reduced amplitude of movement were observed in
                    the lower extremities, reinforcing the hypothesis of impaired
                    anticipatory postural control. Mr. G experienced a loss of
                    balance during step down, requiring moderate assistance to
                    prevent a fall. Mr. G made no attempts to correct his loss of
                    balance consistent with deficits in reactive postural control.
                    Reach, Grasp, and Manipulate
                    Due to chronic deficits in shoulder function, Mr. G was unable
                    to reach for an object on a table in the sitting position and was
                    therefore unable to perform this task.
                    Examination: Tests and Measures
                    Based on the movement analysis of the core tasks, the therapist
                    hypothesized that Mr. G had deficits in both anticipatory
                    and reactive postural control systems contributing to his
                    imbalance across functional movements. The therapist
                    further hypothesized that Mr. G may have inadequate
                    coordination, postural movement strategies, muscle strength,
                    flexibility, and sensation as possible underlying determinants
                    of his postural control deficits. A thorough examination
                    focused on the hypothesized underlying determinants was
                    completed to rule in and rule out possible deficits as part
                    of the differential diagnosis process to arrive at a balance
                    diagnosis. Both performance-based outcome measures and
                    tests/measures at the body function/structure level were
                    included. Outcome measures included the Activities-Specific
                    Balance Confidence Scale36 (score = 30%) and the Berg
                    Balance Scale30 (score = 23/56; impaired performance

                    on items #1, 4, 5, and 8–14). The Timed Up and Go
                    Test37 (TUG) was not performed initially because Mr. G
                    consistently required assistance during turns to avoid a loss of
                    balance.
                    At the body function/structure level, extra-ocular move-
                    ments were intact, visual acuity was 20/30 (no corrective
                    lenses used), and the Montreal Cognitive Assessment38 score
                    was 27/30. Mr. G denied dizziness and pain, and he had
                    intact proprioception and detection of light touch in both
                    lower extremities. He demonstrated bilateral lower extrem-
                    ity hypometria, bradykinesia, and intra-limb coordination
                    deficits. At rest, he demonstrated right upper extremity dyski-
                    nesia. Further examination findings revealed insufficient mus-
                    cle performance of trunk muscles and proximal lower extrem-
                    ities required to support body weight against gravity. Manual
                    muscle testing revealed weakness throughout trunk and prox-
                    imal lower extremities (grossly 3+/5 to −4/5 across bilateral

                    lower extremities, grossly 3/5 for trunk flexors and extensors).
                    He was unable to elevate either shoulder against gravity due to
                    chronic shoulder injuries. Flexibility was reduced throughout
                    the spine, bilateral shoulders, and right ankle. Considering all
                    the examination findings, deficits in sensory processing and
                    multi-task ability were ruled out whereas impairments in pos-
                    tural movement strategies, muscle strength, and coordination
                    were ruled in as likely contributing underling determinates of
                    his balance dysfunction.

                    Movement System Diagnosis for Balance
                    Dysfunction
                    Throughout the evaluation, the therapist was developing a
                    differential diagnosis of balance dysfunction using the Bal-
                    ance Diagnoses Templates (Suppl. Appendix). These templates
                    served as a guide to interpret the examination findings and
                    arrive at the balance diagnosis(es). This case example demon-
                    strates the complexity of factors and underlying determi-
                    nants that contribute to impaired mobility due to balance
                    dysfunction. Because Mr. G demonstrated deficits in pos-
                    tural control both prior to initiating and during voluntary
                    movement (anticipatory postural control) as well as after
                    perturbations (reactive postural control), 1 balance diagnosis
                    was not sufficient to identify his balance dysfunction across
                    functional tasks. Based on the movement observation of core
                    tasks and the examination findings, the therapist determined
                    that Mr. G had balance diagnoses of (1) Deficit in Anticipatory
                    Postural Control: Postural Movement Strategy; and (2) Deficit
                    in Reactive Postural Control: Postural Movement Strategy.
                    Competing alternative diagnoses related to sensory processing
                    and executing function/multi-task ability were ruled out by
                    the therapist based on the key movement observations and
                    examination findings described above. Low balance confi-
                    dence was ruled out as a possible underlying determinant
                    of Mr. G’s balance dysfunction because his Activities-Specific
                    Balance Confidence Scale score (30%) was aligned with his
                    actual balance ability.

                    Linking Balance Diagnosis to Initial Plan of Care
                    The primary focus of physical therapist intervention was to
                    address Mr. G’s deficits in the postural movement strategies
                    required for anticipatory and reactive postural control to
                    reduce his risk for falling and improve his independence
                    with functional mobility. Evidence-based, task-specific train-
                    ing (see Tab. 3) for improving postural movement strategies
                    was selected for Mr. G to specifically address his deficits. Addi-
                    tional interventions were also prescribed to address decreased
                    muscle performance, reduced flexibility, and endurance.

                    Interventions for Deﬁcits in Anticipatory Postural
                    Control-Postural Movement Strategies
                    Initial interventions focused on standing while repeatedly
                    performing tasks that required predictable dynamic control
                    of the center of mass through small ranges of movement
                    (modified reaching, weight shifting, head and upper-body
                    turns to the side), allowing Mr. G to maintain balance without
                    needing to change his base of support or activate his reactive
                    postural control system. Base of support in standing as well
                    as movement speed and amplitude were progressed over
                    time as stability improved. In addition, interventions included
                    stepping in various directions, sit-to-stand training using var-
                    ious height surfaces, transfer training, gait training using an
                    overhead harness support system, and dynamic tasks with 2-
                    person close guarding to avoid a fall. As Mr. G progressed, he
                    was able to complete more challenging standing activities such
                    as simulated boxing as well as turning in place and walking
                    household distances using a U-Step walker.

                    Interventions for Deﬁcits in Reactive Postural
                    Control-Postural Movement Strategies
                    Initial interventions focused on performing standing activities
                    with no upper extremity support using an overhead harness

                    Downloaded from https://academic.oup.com/ptj/article/101/9/pzab153/6307337 by UNIVERSITY OF PITTSBURGH user on 12 November 2021


                    10 Movement System Diagnoses for Balance Dysfunction

                    system for safety. Repeated practice of tasks that require
                    recovery of balance after unexpected self-initiated or external
                    perturbations were performed (sideways steps to widen or
                    narrow the base of support, manual perturbations with feet
                    in various positions). Tasks were slowly progressed to include
                    forward/backward stepping and turning while Mr. G was
                    supported with the harness and contact guarding. In addition,
                    repeated sit-to-stand at various speeds and foot positions
                    (wide to narrower base of support, right and left semi-tandem
                    positions) was performed with 2-person close guard to enable
                    Mr. G to practice balance recovery strategies during this task.

                    Outcomes
                    Over the course of 6 months, Mr. G progressed to perform-
                    ing all bed mobility and transfers with minimal assistance
                    and without the need for a mechanical lift. He improved
                    to walking with contact guard and verbal cuing within his
                    apartment 10 to 20 feet several times per day. He discontinued
                    use of the U-Step walker because of his inability to keep
                    his right hand on the walker due to dyskinesia. His reactive
                    postural control remained quite impaired and contributed to
                    his ongoing high risk for falls. Objectively, Mr. G’s balance
                    and balance confidence improved (Berg Balance Scale 37/56,
                    Activities of Balance Confidence Scale 50%, TUG using no
                    device with close contact guard = 21.3 seconds; initial TUG

                    was not scored due to assistance required to walk and turn).
                    Mr. G’s anticipatory postural control improved as evidenced
                    by increased independence with transfers, improved safety
                    and speed while walking, and improvement on items 1, 4,
                    5, and 8 to 14 of the Berg Balance Scale. His fall frequency
                    reduced to 1 per month, and he has sustained no further
                    injuries from falls. Mr. G resumed community activities at a
                    manual wheelchair level and continues to require assistance
                    for propulsion due to chronic shoulder impairments. Mr.
                    G continues with chair exercises and cycling in his home.
                    His safety awareness improved, but he still has a goal to
                    walk independently in the community. Future decisions must
                    consider his potential for further recovery in postural control
                    as his Parkinson disease progresses with an increased focus on
                    compensatory gait strategies and possible power wheelchair
                    prescription.

                    Summary
                    This paper describes a systematic process for developing and
                    describing movement system diagnoses for various types of
                    balance dysfunction based on current theoretical frameworks
                    and knowledge. Ten distinct balance diagnoses are identified
                    and described based on systematic movement observation
                    of core tasks and key examination findings. The iterative
                    diagnostic process a clinician can use to develop hypotheses
                    to explain the underlying causes of movement dysfunction
                    and then determine a definitive balance diagnosis(es) is illus-
                    trated in a case example. Determining a movement system
                    diagnosis related to balance dysfunction may allow clinicians
                    to make specific informed choices regarding the most appro-
                    priate interventions to include in the plan of care and guide
                    prioritization and progression of interventions in response to
                    intervention over time. We illustrate examples of interventions
                    associated with different balance diagnoses to demonstrate
                    the critical link between diagnosis and intervention planning.
                    Although our focus was on developing movement system
                    diagnoses related to balance dysfunction, we expect that our

                    process is applicable to other movement system problems and
                    all patient populations.
                    The 10 balance diagnoses described in this paper repre-
                    sent an initial effort to identify diagnostic labels for bal-
                    ance dysfunction; future work is needed to determine both
                    their mutual exclusivity and clinical utility. It is possible that
                    although the differential diagnosis of balance dysfunction is
                    a complex process that physical therapists must engage in
                    routinely, the application of 10 different balance diagnoses
                    may be cumbersome. Therefore, it is important to conduct
                    both validation and implementation studies to refine the
                    balance diagnoses and diagnostic templates to ensure that they
                    are independent of each other and clinically useful. It would be
                    also useful to create decision making algorithms that can be
                    used to guide clinicians and students through the diagnostic
                    process of interpreting clinical data to arrive at a balance
                    diagnosis and to determine when it is indicated to have mul-
                    tiple balance diagnoses. To help translate this foundational
                    work into practice, future research needs to be designed and
                    conducted to examine which interventions are most effective
                    for each balance diagnosis. Finally, continued work is needed
                    to arrive at consensus for the use and integration of movement
                    system diagnoses across the profession.

                        ▪Motor systems- execution of motor responses (involuntary and 
                        voluntary) to meet the demand of the task
                        ▪CNS integration and action plan
                    
                    .Sensory Systems in Balance 1
                        • Visual System
                        oDetects orientation of the body in reference to the environment
                        oLocalizes features within our environment

                    .Sensory Systems in Balance 2
                        • Somatosensation (Proprioception)
                        oMuscle and joint proprioception provide bodyawareness
                        oCutaneous and pressure sensation of support surface

                    .Sensory Systems in Balance 3
                        • Vestibular System
                        oDetects angular and linear acceleration/deceleration forces of the 
                        head with reference to gravity
                        oStabilizes gaze during head movement (VOR)
                        oAssists in regulation of postural tone via vestibulo-spinal reflexes

                    .Definitions - Postural Control (!!E)
                        • Ability to maintain center of mass (COM) within the base of support (BOS) under 
                        given sensorimotor demands and environmental conditions 
                        • Reactive postural control: a response to an external force acting on the body 
                        displacing the COM or BOS
                        • Anticipatory postural control: occurs in anticipation of internally generated 
                        destabilizing forces due to body movement (i.e., throwing, catching)
                        • Adaptive postural control: allows for modification of postural responses with 
                        changing environmental and task demands

                     
                    .Sitting and Standing Balance
                        Perturbed stance/Dynamic balance
                        • Sitting or standing with an unstable 
                        support surface or displacement of 
                        COM over BOS (moving surface or 
                        perturbation)

                        Quiet stance/static balance
                        • Sitting or standing on a stable 
                        support surface with stable 
                        surroundings

                    .Strategies to Maintain or Restore Balance ('') (!!E)
                        Ankle strategy
                        Hip strategy
                        Stepping strategy

                    .Standing Balance Therapeutic Intervention
                        Static 
                        • Treatment may include but is not 
                        limited to interventions that have 
                        a focus in improving stability 
                        during static sitting or standing 
                        tasks
                        oNarrow BOS
                        oVary sensory condition such 
                        as EO/EC 
                        oVary surface

                        Dynamic 
                        • Treatment may include but 
                        is not limited to 
                        interventions that have a 
                        focus in improving stability 
                        during dynamic standing 
                        tasks
                        oWeight shifting
                        oStepping activities
                        oFunctional training

                
                    .Walking Balance/Dynamic Gait
                        • Ability to generate postural adjustments to counter postural 
                        disturbances due to realigning the COM over a changing BOS 
                        oPostural control is adaptive, able to modify in response to a changing task 
                        and environmental demands 


                    .Walking Balance Therapeutic Interventions
                        • Level surface situations
                        oFloor 
                        oTreadmill
                        • Complex - variable walking situation 
                        oBackward
                        oWalk with turns 
                        oWalking a figure-eight
                        oWalk with head movements
                        oDual-task activities (cognitive and motor)
                        oWalk on uneven surfaces

                    
                    .Balance Exam
                    • Observation of postural alignment in standing, when moving
                    • Clinical outcome measures


                        .Core Set of Outcome Measures for Adults with Neurologic Conditions 1
                            • The guidelines establish the minimum measures needed 
                            to quantify function in the constructs of balance, walking 
                            speed, walking endurance/distance and transfer ability
                            • These measures should be performed on all patients with 
                            neurologic diagnoses who have goals and the capacity to 
                            improve in the areas of standing balance (the Berg Balance 
                            Scale), walking balance (Functional Gait 
                            Assessment), walking speed (10mWT), walking distance 
                            (6MWT) transfers (5 times sit to stand) and Balance 
                            Confidence (Activities-Specific Balance Confidence Scale).


                    .Core Set of Outcome Measures for Adults with Neurologic Conditions 2
                        • Berg Balance Scale (BBS) 
                        • Functional Gait Assessment (FGA) 
                        • Activities-specific Balance Confidence (ABC) Scale
                        oThe ABC is a patient-reported outcome measure (PROM), it is not 
                        performance based but it provides valuable information on 
                        confidence


                        .Additional Outcome Measures
                            • Function in Sitting Test (FIST)
                            • Modified Clinical Test of Sensory Interaction in Balance (mCTSIB)
                            • Mini Balance Evaluation Systems Test (Mini-BESTest)
                            • Timed Up and Go Test (TUG)
                    
                    .The Balance Evaluation Systems Test (BESTest) (!!E).Lv3
                        Differentiate balance into six underlying systems that may constrain balance: (36 items)
                            Biomechanical
                            Stability Limits
                            Postural Responses
                            Anticipatory Postural 
                            Adjustments
                            Sensory Orientation
                            Dynamic Balance during Gait
                            Cognitive Effects
                        The Mini-BESTest - a short version of the BESTest

                    .Mini-BESTest: Anticipatory postural control
                        Balance Evaluation Systems Test
                        ANTICIPATORY SUB SCORE: /6
                        1. SIT TO STAND
                        Instruction: "Cross your arms across your chest. Try not to use your hands unless you must. Do not let your legs lean 
                        against the back of the chair when you stand. Please stand up now"
                        (2) Normal: Comes to stand without use of hands and stabilizes independently.
                        (1) Moderate: Comes to stand WITH use of hands on first attempt.
                        (0) Severe: Unable to stand up from chair without assistance OR needs several attempts with use of hands.
                        2. RISE TO TOES
                        Instruction: "Place your feet shoulder width apart. Place your hands on your hips. Try to rise as high as you can onto 
                        your toes. I will count out loud to 3 seconds. Try to hold this pose at least 3 seconds. Look straight ahead. Rise now."
                        (2) Normal: Stable for 3 seconds with maximum height.
                        (1) Moderate: Heels up, but not full range (smaller than when holding hands), OR noticeable instability for 3 seconds.
                        (0) Severe: < 3 seconds.


                    .Mini-BESTest: Anticipatory postural control continued
                        Balance Evaluation Systems Test
                        ANTICIPATORY (continued)
                        3. STAND ON ONE LEG
                        Instruction: "Look straight ahead. Keep your hands on your hips. Lift your leg off of the ground 
                        behind you without touching or resting your raised leg upon your other standing leg. Stay standing 
                        on one leg as long as you can. Look straight ahead. Lift now."
                        LEFT: Time in seconds Trial 1:____Trial 2:____
                        RIGHT: Time in seconds Trial 1:____Trial 2:____
                        (2) Normal: 20 seconds
                        (1) Moderate: < 20 seconds
                        (0) Severe: Unable
                        To score each side separately use the trial with the longest time.
                        To calculate the sub-score and total score use the side [left or right] with the lowest 
                        numerical score [i.e., the worse side].


                    .Mini-BESTest: Reactive postural control
                        REACTIVE POSTURAL CONTROL SUB SCORE: /6
                        4. COMPENSATORY STEPPING CORRECTION – FORWARD
                        Instruction: "Stand with your feet shoulder width apart, arms at your sides. Lean forward against my hands beyond 
                        your forward limits. When I let go, do whatever is necessary, including taking a step, to avoid a fall."
                        (2) Normal: Recovers independently with a single, large step (second realignment step is allowed).
                        (1) Moderate: More than one step used to cover equilibrium.
                        (0) Severe: No step, OR would fall if not caught, OR falls spontaneously.
                        5. COMPENSATORY STEPPING CORRECTION – BACKWARD
                        Instruction: "Stand with your feet shoulder width apart, arms at your sides. Lean backward against my hands beyond 
                        your backward limits. When I let go, do whatever is necessary, including taking a step, to avoid a fall."
                        (2) Normal: Recovers independently with a single, large step.
                        (1) Moderate: More than one step used to recover equilibrium.
                        (0) Severe: No step, OR would fall if not caught, OR falls spontaneously.


                    .Mini-BESTest: Reactive postural control continued
                        REACTIVE POSTURAL CONTROL (continued)
                        6. COMPENSATORY STEPPING CORRECTION – LATERAL
                        Instruction: "Stand with your feet shoulder width apart, arms at your sides. 
                        Lean into my hand beyond your sideways limit. When I let go, do whatever is 
                        necessary, including taking a step, to avoid a fall."
                        LEFT RIGHT
                        (2) Normal: Recovers independently with one step (crossover or lateral okay)
                        (1) Moderate: Several steps to recover equilibrium
                        (0) Severe: Falls or cannot step.
                        Use the side with the lowest score to calculate sub-score and total 
                        score.


                    .Mini-BESTest: Sensory orientation
                        SENSORY ORIENTATION SUB SCORE: /6
                        7. STANCE (FEET TOGETHER); EYES OPEN, FIRM SURFACE
                        Instruction: "Place your hands on your hips. Place your feet together until almost touching. Be as stable and still as 
                        possible, until I stay stop."
                        Time in seconds:
                        (2) Normal: 30 seconds
                        (1) Moderate: < 30 seconds
                        (0) Severe: Unable
                        8. STANCE (FEET TOGETHER); EYES CLOSED, FOAM SURFACE
                        Instruction: "Step onto the foam. Place your hands on your hips. Place your feet together until almost touching. Be as 
                        stable and still as possible, until I stay stop. I will start timing when you close your eyes."
                        Time in seconds:
                        (2) Normal: 30 seconds
                        (1) Moderate: < 30 seconds
                        (0) Severe: Unable


                    .Mini-BESTest: Sensory orientation continued
                        SENSORY ORIENTATION (continued)
                        9. INCLINE – EYES CLOSED
                        Instruction: "Step onto the incline ramp. Please stand on the incline ramp with your 
                        toes toward the top. Place your feet shoulder width apart and have your arms 
                        down at your sides. I will start timing when you close your eyes"
                        Time in seconds:
                        (2) Normal: Stands independently 30 seconds and aligns with gravity
                        (1) Moderate: Stands independently < 30 seconds OR aligns with surface
                        (0) Severe: Unable


                    .Mini-BESTest: Dynamic gait
                        DYNAMIC GAIT SUB SCORE: /10
                        10. CHANGE IN GAIT SPEED
                        Instruction: "Begin walking at your normal speed, when I tell you 'fast,' walk as fast as you can. When I 
                        say 'slow,' walk very slowly."
                        (2) Normal: Significantly changes walking speed without imbalance.
                        (1) Moderate: Unable to change walking speed or signs of imbalance.
                        (0) Severe: Unable to achieve significant change in walking speed AND signs of imbalance.
                        11. WALK WITH HEAD TURNS – HORIZONTAL
                        Instruction: "Begin walking at your normal speed, when I say 'right,' turn your head and look to the right. 
                        When I say 'left,' turn your head and look to the left. Try to keep yourself walking in a straight line."
                        (2) Normal: performs head turns with no change in gait speed and good balance.
                        (1) Moderate: performs head turns with reduction in gait speed.
                        (0) Severe: performs head turns with imbalance.


                    .Mini-BESTest: Dynamic gait continued 1
                        DYNAMIC GAIT (continued)
                        12. WALK WITH PIVOT TURNS
                        Instruction: "Begin walking at your normal speed. When I tell you to 'turn and stop,' turn as quickly 
                        as you can, face the opposite direction, and stop. After the turn, your feet should be close together."
                        (2) Normal: Turns with feet close FAST (< 3 steps) with good balance.
                        (1) Moderate: Turns with feet close SLOW (> 4 steps) with good balance.
                        (0) Severe: Cannot turn with feet close at any speed without imbalance.
                        13. STEP OVER OBSTACLES
                        Instruction: "Begin walking at your normal speed. When you get to the box, step over it, not around 
                        it and keep walking."
                        (2) Normal: Able to step over box with minimal change of gait speed and with good balance.
                        (1) Moderate: Steps over box but touches box OR displays cautious behavior by slowing gait.
                        (0) Severe: Unable to step over box OR steps around box.


                    .Mini-BESTest: Dynamic gait continued 2
                        DYNAMIC GAIT (continued)
                        14. TIMED UP & GO WITH DUAL TASK (3 METER WALK)
                        Instruction TUG: "When I say 'Go,' stand up from chair, walk at your normal speed across the tape on the floor, turn 
                        around and come back and sit in the chair."
                        Instruction TUG with Dual Task: "Count backward by threes starting at . When I say 'Go,' walk at your normal 
                        speed across the tape on the floor, turn around, and come back to sit in the chair. Continue counting backwards the 
                        entire time."

                        TUG: seconds; Dual Task TUG: seconds
                        (2) Normal: No noticeable change in sitting, standing or walking while backward counting when compared to TUG 
                        without Dual task.
                        (1) Moderate: Dual Task affects either counting OR walking (> 10%) when compared to the TUG without Dual Task.
                        (0) Severe: Stops counting while walking OR stops walking while counting.
                        When scoring item 14, if subject's gait speed slows more than 10% between the TUG without and with a Dual 
                        Task the score should be decreased by a point.
                        TOTAL SCORE: /28


                    .Movement System Diagnoses for Balance
                        ### Deficit in Steady State Postural Control (SSPC)
                        - Deficit in SSPC - Postural Movement Strategies: primarily related to abnormal postural movement strategies.
                        - Deficit in SSPC - Sensory Processing: primarily related to abnormal sensory integrity/processing.
                        - Deficit in SSPC - Balance Confidence: primarily related to fear of falling/reduced self-efficacy.
                        - Deficit in SSPC - Verticality: primarily related to impaired orientation with respect to gravity.

                        ### Deficit in Anticipatory Postural Control (APC)
                        - Deficit in APC - Postural Movement Strategies: primarily related to abnormal postural movement strategies.
                        - Deficit in APC - Sensory Processing: primarily related to abnormal sensory integrity/processing.
                        - Deficit in APC - Balance Confidence: primarily related to fear of falling/reduced self-efficacy.
                        - Deficit in APC - Executive Function/Multitask Ability: primarily related to impaired dual-task ability.

                        ### Deficit in Reactive Postural Control (RPC)
                        - Deficit in RPC - Postural Movement Strategies: primarily related to abnormal postural movement strategies.
                        - Deficit in RPC - Sensory Processing: primarily related to abnormal sensory integrity/processing.

                    .Balance Exam overview 1 (!!E).Q&A
                        • Be aware of the benefits and limitations of the test chosen
                        • Determine the outcome measure that is most appropriate for the patient in front 
                        of you
                        oUsually based on prior information obtained from the history, mental status, sensory, motor 
                        and coordination exam
                        • Use the best information from the examination to drive the treatment
                        • No single test can give a complete picture of the patient’s balance abilities
                        • Also need a description of the situation that causes the patient to lose their 
                        balance and/or fall

                    .Balance Exam Overview 2 (!!E).Lv3
                        The balance exam is conducted after the sensory and motor assessment because balance may be affected by:
                            Diminished or absent proprioception
                            Soft tissue tightness (heel cords)
                            Impaired strength in the quads and gluteal muscles motor coordination deficits

                    .Step 2 of the Framework

                    .Summary
                        • The balance exam may include an assessment of sitting balance, static standing 
                        balance, and/or dynamic standing or walking balance, depending on the patient 
                        presentation
                        • The visual, somatosensory, and vestibular systems are all involved in the 
                        maintenance of postural control/upright posture
                        • It is important to conduct sensory, motor, and coordination exams prior to the 
                        balance exam because balance can be affected by sensory deficits, ROM and 
                        strength limitations, and coordination deficits

                    .References
                        • Horak, FB, et al: The Balance Evaluation Systems Test (BESTest) to 
                        differentiate balance deficits. PhysTher 89(5):484, 2009.
                        • Franchignoni, F, et al: Using psychometric techniques to improve the 
                        Balance Evaluation System’s Test: The mini-BESTest. J Rehabil Med 42(4):323, 
                        2010.

                    The balance evaluation systems test,
                    12:32
                    or BES test, was developed by Dr. Fay Hornbeck.
                    12:35
                    The goal of this measure is to differentiate balance into
                    12:38
                    six underlying systems that may constrain balance,
                    12:42
                    including biomechanical stability limits, postural responses,
                    12:45
                    anticipatory postural adjustments,
                    12:50
                    sensory orientation and dynamic balance during gait with cognitive effects.
                    12:52
                    The best test was 36 items and is lengthily and time-consuming to perform in the clinic.
                    12:57
                    Therefore, the mini best was developed and includes only 14 items.
                    13:03
                    This test is comprehensive because it assesses
                    13:08
                    the many various domains of balance and can
                    13:11
                    assist with providing specific interventions
                    13:14
                    for balanced deficits in these various domains.
                    13:17
                    The first component of the mini best test includes
                    13:21
                    assessment of anticipatory postural control.
                    13:24
                    The patient is asked to complete a sit to stand,
                    13:27
                    and to rise onto their toes.
                    13:31
                    The patient is then scored on a scale from 0-2 for each item.
                    13:33
                    The last component of the anticipatory postural control examination
                    13:38
                    is standing on one leg.
                    13:43
                    Both legs are assessed and the patient is given two trials.
                    13:44
                    The next section of the test assesses reactive postural control.
                    13:49
                    In this section, you will ask the patient to lean into your hands in forward,
                    13:54
                    backward, and lateral directions.
                    13:59
                    This part of the test can be challenging
                    14:01
                    for the clinician because you need to be ready to
                    14:03
                    catch the patient if they are unable to recover their balance after you let go of them.
                    14:05
                    The next part of the test assesses sensory orientation or integration.
                    14:13
                    For the first item,
                    14:19
                    the patient is asked to stand with feet together with
                    14:20
                    eyes open on a firm surface for 30 seconds.
                    14:23
                    Then they are asked to stand with their eyes closed on a foam surface for 30 seconds.
                    14:26
                    Lastly, the patient is asked to stand with their eyes
                    14:32
                    closed on an inclined surface for 30 seconds.
                    14:36
                    The last part of the mini best test is an assessment of Dynamic Gait.
                    14:40
                    These items are adapted from the functional gait assessment,
                    14:44
                    so there is some overlap with some of the other outcome measures
                    14:48
                    included in the core outcomes clinical practice guideline.
                    14:51
                    The first item is assessing a change in gait speed,
                    14:55
                    then assessing walking while turning the head in a horizontal direction.
                    14:59
                    Then assessment of walking while making a pivot turn,
                    15:05
                    as well as walking over obstacles.
                    15:10
                    The last item is
                    15:13
                    the timed up and go test and the timed up and go test with a cognitive dual task.
                    15:15
                    Again, each of the items on this scale are scored from
                    15:21
                    0-2 and the total score is out of 28 points.
                    15:24
                    As I mentioned, the mini best tests can be helpful in identifying
                    15:29
                    specific areas of balance that are impaired in your patient.
                    15:33
                    The Academy of neurological physical therapy has
                    15:37
                    developed a movement systems task force,
                    15:41
                    and their project was to define movement system diagnosis for balance.
                    15:44
                    They came up with 10 specific movement system diagnosis for balance.
                    15:49
                    You can see the three main diagnoses are
                    15:54
                    deficit in steady-state postural control or static balance.
                    15:57
                    Deficit in anticipatory postural control,
                    16:02
                    and deficit in reactive postural control.
                    16:05
                    Then they further subdivided these based on what is the underlying issue.
                    16:09
                    For example, is there an issue with sensory processing?
                    16:14
                    Or is there an issue with balanced confidence that is driving the impairment?
                    16:18
                    I would encourage you to review the article by Gill Buddy and colleagues.
                    16:23
                    They provide a nice description of
                    16:28
                    these diagnoses using a clinical case and also identify
                    16:30
                    potential treatment ideas for patients with
                    16:34
                    each of these movements system diagnosis for balance.
                    16:37
                    While it is not imperative that you memorize all of these specific diagnosis,
                    16:40
                    it is important for when you are evaluating
                    16:45
                    your patient to identify the specific impairment and
                    16:48
                    potential reasons for what is driving the balance deficit so
                    16:51
                    that you can provide targeted treatment to best serve the patient in front of you.
                    16:56
                    In conclusion, a balance exam may include a variety of different observations,
                    17:01
                    tests, and clinical measures.
                    17:07
                    It is up to you to determine the best outcome measures to use
                    17:09
                    for your specific patient based on the best available evidence.
                    17:13
                    The core set of outcome measures is a great place to start
                    17:17
                    because you know that these measures are supported by the highest levels of evidence.
                    17:20
                    However, there may be a more appropriate test based on the information that you have
                    17:24
                    collected as part of
                    17:28
                    your neurologic PT exam and your observations of the individual patient.
                    17:29
                    There is no single test that provides a complete picture of
                    17:34
                    the patient's balance abilities so usually we are using a combination of assessments.
                    17:37
                    For example, we may use the modified CTSIB
                    17:43
                    to assess static balance and sensory integration.
                    17:46
                    We may use the functional gait assessment to assess dynamic gait and the activities
                    17:49
                    specific balanced confidence scale to capture
                    17:54
                    the patient's confidence in their own balance abilities.
                    17:57
                    As we talked about,
                    18:00
                    it is important to determine and document
                    18:01
                    the specific deficits that you see in regards to the components of postural control.
                    18:04
                    We typically conduct the balanced exam after our assessment of sensory and motor,
                    18:10
                    because we know that balance can be affected by deficits in sensory and motor systems.
                    18:16
                    For example, we would expect to see
                    18:22
                    significant balance difficulties if the patient has impaired proprioception.
                    18:24
                    We would expect this to be even more pronounced in eyes closed conditions.
                    18:29
                    We may have found that the patient has
                    18:34
                    tight heel cords which may impair standing balance.
                    18:37
                    Maybe they would be unable to assume the position of standing on an incline in
                    18:40
                    the mini best test without bending their knees
                    18:45
                    or to compensate for the soft tissue tightness.
                    18:48
                    Or maybe they have impaired strength in their quads or
                    18:51
                    gluteal muscles that would affect motor coordination during gait.
                    18:53
                    It is important that we have already conducted these components of
                    18:57
                    the neurologic PT exam prior to our balance exam.
                    19:00
                    Now that we have completed our balance examination,
                    19:05
                    we will move on to functional skills next.
                    19:08
                    In summary, the balance exam may include an assessment of sitting balance,
                    19:11
                    static standing balance, and/or
                    19:16
                    dynamic standing or walking balance depending on your patient presentation.
                    19:18
                    The visual somatosensory and vestibular systems
                    19:23
                    are all involved in the maintenance of postural control.
                    19:26
                    It is important to conduct sensory,
                    19:30
                    motor and coordination exams prior to
                    19:32
                    the balanced exam because balance can be affected by sensory deficits,
                    19:34
                    range of motion and strength limitations and coordination deficits.
                    19:39

                        I. Body functions and structures

                    .Conceptual Basis for Outcome Measurement 
                        #### ICF (2001) - International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health  

                        1. Health Conditions  
                           - Underlying diagnosis or pathology  
                             - Tissue level  
                               - Stroke  

                        2. Body Function Body Structures  
                           - Impairments  
                             - Loss or abnormality in structure/Function  
                               - Organ level  
                                 - Paralysis  
                                 - Aphasia  
                                 - Spasticity

                             - Functional limitations in daily life  
                               - Person level  
                                 - Assistance needed for  
                                   - Ambulation  
                                   - Self Care

                             - Involvement or restriction in Life Situations  
                               - Societal level  
                                 - Changes in  
                                   - Work roles  
                                   - Social roles

                    .Function Exam 1
                        • Provides baseline information for setting functional goals
                        • Serve as an indicator of a patient’s initial abilities and progression toward more 
                        complex functional levels
                        • Assist with placement decisions (e.g., inpatient rehabilitation, extended care, or 
                        community services)
                        • Identification of safety in performing a particular task and the risk of injury 
                        • Determine effectiveness of a specific intervention on function
                        • Assist with documentation to support payer requirements of change in functional 
                        status during an episode of care

                    .Function Exam 2
                        • Observation
                        • Clinical assessments/Performance-
                        based tests
                        • Patient-reported outcome measures

                        • Bed mobility
                        • Transfers
                        • Gait
                        • Level surfaces
                        • Varied surfaces
                        • Reaching/grasping

                    .Skillful Movement
                        • Successfully achieve a motor task safely with purposeful and well-coordinated 
                        movements
                        • The movements are smooth, efficient, continuous and accurate to meet the 
                        demands of task and environment

                    .Temporal Model for Task analysis
                        ('')
                            - Initial conditions
                              - Posture
                              - Ability to interact with the environment
                              - Environmental context
                            - Preparation
                              - Stimulus identification
                              - Response selection
                              - Response programming
                            - Initiation
                              - Timing
                              - Direction
                              - Smoothness
                            - Execution
                              - Amplitude
                              - Direction
                              - Speed
                              - Smoothness
                            - Termination
                              - Timing
                              - Stability
                              - Accuracy
                            - Outcome
                              - Outcome achieved?

                            Comments on Interactions:
                            Each stage logically progresses to the next, reflecting the natural flow of movement or task performance. The Initial Conditions provide the foundation for Preparation, where responses are identified and selected. Initiation marks the beginning of movement, which smoothly transitions into Execution. The Termination phase evaluates control and precision, ultimately determining whether the desired Outcome has been achieved.

                    .Movement Continuum Framework (Quinn et al., PTJ 2021)
                        Here’s the precise transcription of the slide, formatted as an outline:

                        # Movement Continuum Framework  
                        _(Quinn et al., PTJ 2021)_

                        ## Core Tasks  
                        - Sitting  
                        - Sit to Stand  
                        - Standing  
                        - Walking  
                        - Step Up & Down  
                        - Reach/Grasp/Manipulate  

                        ## Movement Continuum  
                        ### Initial Conditions  
                        - Set the initial conditions for the first task performance.  
                        - Initial conditions can be systematically varied in subsequent repetitions.  

                        ### Preparation  
                        - Evaluate if the performer understood the instructions and task requirements.  

                        ### Initiation  
                        - Evaluate movement patterns and strategies using observable movement constructs.  

                        ### Execution  

                        ### Termination  

                        ## Repeat  
                        - At least once with progression as needed  
                        - With task regression  

                        ## Expected Outcome Achieved?  
                        - Yes  
                        - No  

                        Would you like me to highlight any specific interactions among these elements? I can add comments where the relationships may need clarification.

                    .Sit to Stand Transfer Movement Analysis
                        • Initiates movement
                        oAppropriate timing
                        oAppropriate direction
                        • Executes standing
                        oBody segment alignment
                        oAppropriate amplitude of forward weight shift, adequate hip and knee 
                        flexion, ankle DF, throughout flexion and early lift phases
                        oAppropriate trunk, hip, knee extension during extension phase
                        • Termination of task maintain COM over BOS without excessive sway
                        • Overall, note speed, smoothness, continuity, efficiency, symptoms, 
                        consistency

                    .Walking on Level Surface Movement Analysis
                        • Initiation movement
                        oAppropriate timing
                        oAppropriate direction
                        • Execution
                        oDo the body segments achieve and maintain an adequate position during 
                        single limb support
                        oAppropriate base of support maintained during double limb support
                        oSwing limb advanced past stance limb
                        oLimbs move in symmetrical, alternating pattern
                        oBody progression forward to achieve adequate trailing limb position
                        oSwing limb achieves clearance
                        • Termination of walking – maintenance of COM over BOS without excessive sway
                        • Overall, note speed, smoothness, continuity, efficiency, symptoms, consistency

                    .Progressions or Regressions
                        Progressions
                        • Narrow BOS
                        • Vary speed
                        • Add dual task
                        • Add perturbation
                        • Lower height
                        • Alter surface
                        • Add environmental challenge (auditory, 
                        visual)

                        Regressions
                        • Widen BOS
                        • Vary speed
                        • Add cueing
                        • Add physical assistance
                        • Raise height
                        • Add external support
                        • Quieter environment

                    .Core Set of Outcome Measures for Adults with Neurologic Conditions
                        • The guidelines establish the minimum measures needed to quantify function 
                        in the constructs of balance, walking speed, walking endurance/distance 
                        and transfer ability
                        • These measures should be performed on all patients with neurologic 
                        diagnoses who have goals and the capacity to improve in the areas  of 
                        standing balance (the Berg Balance Scale-BBS), walking balance 
                        (Functional Gait Assessment- FGA), walking speed (10mWT), walking 
                        distance (6MWT)  transfers (5 times sit to stand) and Balance Confidence 
                        (Activities-Specific Balance Confidence Scale- ABC scale).

                    .Activity (Limitations) Assessment
                        • 5 times sit to stand (5TSTS)
                        • 10-meter walk test (10MWT)
                        • Six-minute walk test (6MWT)

                    .Summary
                        • Components of the function exam may be conducted in the initial observation, 
                        during the motor, coordination, and/or balance exams
                        • Functional exam allows the clinician to identify limitations in functional activities 
                        that are important to the patient
                        • The six core tasks for movement analysis include sitting, sitting to standing, 
                        standing, walking, stepping up/down, and reaching

                    11:27
                    any assistance that is needed and the surface that was used.
                    11:32
                    To assess walking speed,
                    11:36

                    11:38
                    or the time it takes the patient to walk ten meters.
                    11:41
                    To assess walking distance,
                    11:45

                    11:46

                    11:49

                    11:52

                    .CARE Set

                    .Objectives
                        • Explain CARE set origin and how CMS uses data 
                        • Understand how CARE Set scores are used for payment
                        • Explore functional areas of CARE set Physical Therapy is responsible for 

                    .CARE Set
                        • Continuous Assessment Record and Evaluation (CARE)
                        • Standardized assessment tool developed as part of the Medicare Post Acute 
                        Care Payment Reform Demonstration (PAC-PRD)
                        • “Designed to standardize assessment of patients’ medical, functional, cognitive, 
                        and social support status across acute and post-acute settings, including long-
                        term care hospitals (LTCHs), inpatient rehabilitation facilities (IRFs), skilled 
                        nursing facilities (SNFs), and home health agencies (HHAs)”

                        https://www.cms.gov/Medicare/Quality-Initiatives-Patient-Assessment-Instruments/Post-Acute-Care-Quality-Initiatives/CARE-Item-Set-and-
                        B-CARE.html

                    .('')
                        1. Current reason for services  
                           - Example: CVA, SCI, TKA  

                        2. History of present illness  

                        3. Functional status  
                           - Current functional status across several domains  

                        4. Social history  
                           - Home setup, prior level of function, social support  

                        5. Medical comorbidities  
                           - Added complexity for diagnosis such as HTN, DM, COPD  

                        Each section is interconnected, forming a comprehensive approach to patient assessment. The relationships between these elements are clear through their structure, showing how different domains of health influence one another.

                    .But why do we care?

                    .How we get reimbursed
                        ## Admission Score
                        - Compared to the nation of similar scores

                        ### Breakdown (Pie chart with four sections)
                        - History of Present Illness
                        - Functional Status
                        - Social History
                        - Medical Comorbidities

                        ## Discharge Score
                        - Compared to the nation of similar scores

                        ### Breakdown (Pie chart with four sections)
                        - History of Present Illness
                        - Functional Status
                        - Social History
                        - Medical Comorbidities

                        ## Relationship Between Admission Score & Discharge Score
                        - Arrow connecting the two scores
                        - Key consideration: "How long to get here?" (Measured in either days or visits)

                    .CARE Set functional section scoring
                        • Allow patient to perform activity as independently as possible while keeping 
                        him/her safe

                        o Patient report
                        o Direct care staff report

                        .CARE Set
                            Patient Assistance Levels Scoring System
                            1. Score 6: Independent
                               - Patient completes the activity without any help.

                            2. Score 5: Set Up or Clean Up Assistance
                               - Helper prepares or tidies up, but patient completes the activity on their own.

                            3. Score 4: Supervision or Touching Assistance
                               - Helper provides verbal cues or physical support throughout or intermittently.

                            4. Score 3: Partial or Moderate Assistance
                               - Helper does less than half of the effort.

                            5. Score 2: Substantial/Maximal Assistance
                               - Helper does more than half of the effort.

                            6. Score 1: Dependent
                               - Helper completes all the effort, or the patient requires two-person assistance.

                            ------------------------------------------------------------------------------

                            1. Score: 7  
                               - Description: Patient refused  
                               - Definition:  
                                 - Patient refuses to complete and refuses to allow helper to complete  
                                 - Should be rare  
                                 - If refusal is due to medical reasons, choose 88  

                            2. Score: 9  
                               - Description: Activity is not applicable  
                               - Definition:  
                                 - Did not complete at the time of assessment  
                                 - Did not complete prior to the current illness, injury, or exacerbation  
                                 - Will not complete at discharge  

                            3. Score: 10  
                               - Description: Not attempted due to environmental limitations  
                               - Definition:  
                                 - Lack of equipment  
                                 - Weather constraints  

                            4. Score: 88  
                               - Description: Not attempted due to medical or safety concerns  
                               - Definition:  
                                 - Unable to complete activity due to medical or safety reasons  
                                 - Fatigue, pain, wound, etc.

                    .What CARE Set is not …
                        • CARE Set is an outcome measure but doesn't necessarily provide the most 
                        pertinent information
                        o For example: If a patient in a moderate assistance slide board transfer and 
                        requires the assistance of a second person to manage an IV pole and oxygen 
                        tank- what would their CARE set score be?
                        o If in the chart for this person you read they were dependent for bed<>chair 
                        transfer because of needing two people, are you preparing for your treatment 
                        differently?

                    .Take home points
                        • CARE set is an essential part of the functional component of PT evaluation in 
                        SNF, IPR, HH, and LTAH
                        o Coming soon to outpatient 
                        • Vital to score appropriately as it affects reimbursement 
                        • Scores must be assessed on admission and discharge 
                        • Take home - CARE Set does not replace accurate documentation!
