                .('20 Module 4 UMN and LMN signs.pdf') (!!E).UMNvsLMN.Capítul molt importat. Casi tot es prioritat.
                    .Upper motor neuron and lower motor neuron signs

                    .Objectives
                        • Compare and contrast signs of an upper motor neuron and lower motor neuron 
                        lesion
                        • Identify diagnoses and/or lesions that may lead to upper motor neuron or lower 
                        motor neuron signs

                    .Upper Motor Neuron (UMN) Syndrome
                        UMN syndrome is characterized  by a 
                        lesion found in descending motor 
                        tracts:
                        • Cerebral cortex
                        • Internal capsule
                        • Brainstem
                        • Spinal cord

                        Descending pyramidal tracts Γ(carrie morotor commands)
                            Corticospinal tracts
                            Corticobulbartracts

                    .Examples of diagnoses that result in UMN lesions
                        Stroke
                        TBI
                        Multiple Sclerosis (MS)
                        Cerebral Palsy (CP)
                        Spinal Cord Injury (SCI)
                        Amyotrophic lateral Sclerosis (ALS)

                    .Positive and Negative Features of Upper Motor Neuron Syndrome (Table 5.2)
                        Negative Features
                        • Paresis and paralysis 
                        • Loss of dexterity 
                        • Fatigue 

                        Positive Features
                        • Spasticity
                        • Stereotyped movement synergies; spastic 
                        dystonia
                        • Spasms (flexor, extensor/adductor)
                        • Spastic co-contraction
                        • Extensor plantar response (Babinski sign)
                        • Clonus
                        • Exaggerated deep tendon reflexes (DTR)
                        • Associated reactions
                        • Disturbances in movement efficiency and 
                        speed; mass movements

                    .UMN Syndrome: Paralysis and paresis
                        • Muscle weakness:
                        • Common finding
                        • Varies considerably
                        • A selective distribution of muscle weakness commonly seen with 
                        UMN lesions:
                        • Results in an imbalance of activity

                    .Spasticity
                        • Spasticity is increased, involuntary, 
                        resistance to movement during 
                        passive movement 
                        • Velocity-dependent increase in 
                        muscle tone with resistance to 
                        stretch
                        • This movement disorder occurs 
                        secondary to an UMN lesion 
                     
                    .Table 5.3 Typical Patterns of Spasticity in Upper Motor Neuron Syndrome
                        #### 1. Upper Limbs
                        - Scapula
                          - Actions: Retraction, downward rotation
                          - Muscles Affected: Rhomboids
                        - Shoulder
                          - Actions: Adduction, internal rotation, depression
                          - Muscles Affected: Pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, teres major, subscapularis
                        - Elbow
                          - Actions: Flexion
                          - Muscles Affected: Biceps, brachialis, brachioradialis
                        - Forearm
                          - Actions: Pronation
                          - Muscles Affected: Pronator teres, pronator quadratus
                        - Wrist
                          - Actions: Flexion, adduction
                          - Muscles Affected: Flexor carpi radialis
                        - Hand
                          - Actions: Finger flexion, clenched fist, thumb adducted in palm
                          - Muscles Affected: Flexor digitorum profundus/sublimis, adductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis

                        #### 2. Lower Limbs
                        - Pelvis
                          - Actions: Retraction (hip hiking)
                          - Muscles Affected: Quadratus lumborum
                        - Hip
                          - Actions: Adduction (scissoring), internal rotation, extension
                          - Muscles Affected: Adductor longus/brevis, adductor magnus, gracilis, gluteus maximus
                        - Knee
                          - Actions: Extension
                          - Muscles Affected: Quadriceps
                        - Foot and Ankle
                          - Actions: Plantarflexion, inversion, equinovarus, toe clawing (tarsometatarsal extension, metatarsophalangeal flexion), toe curling (tarso- and metatarsophalangeal flexion)
                          - Muscles Affected: Gastrocnemius/soleus, tibialis posterior, long toe flexors, extensor hallucis longus, peroneus longus

                        #### 3. Hip   and Knee (Prolonged Sitting Posture)
                        - Actions: Flexion, sacral sitting
                        - Muscles Affected: Iliopsoas, rectus femoris, pectineus, hamstrings

                        #### 4. Trunk
                        - Actions: Lateral flexion with concavity, rotation
                        - Muscles Affected: Rotators, internal/external obliques

                        #### 5. Posture (Prolonged Sitting)
                        - Actions: Excessive forward flexion, forward head
                        - Muscles Affected: Rectus abdominis, external obliques, psoas minor

                    .Treatment of Spasticity - Medical Management
                        • Surgical
                        • Tendon lengthening
                        • Selective dorsal rhizotomy
                        • Inject the nerve with phenol
                        • Pharmaceutical interventions
                        • Baclofen
                        • Benzodiazepines
                        • Calcium Channel Blockers
                        • Botox 

                        • Rehabilitative
                        • Sustained positioning/PROM
                        • Serial casting
                        • Orthotic devices
                        • Deep pressure
                        • Thermal applications (hot/cold)
                        • NMES
                        • Motor re-education and task-
                        specific activity

                    .UMN Syndrome: Altered Reflexes
                        • Hyper-reflexive
                        • Hypo-reflexive initially in some conditions
                        • Primitive reflexes may re-emerge
                        • Babinski, ATNR, STNR
                        • Associated reactions may be present, which are non-
                        purposeful movement that accompanies another 
                        movement

                    .Lower Motor Neuron (LMN) Syndrome
                        • Lesions to cranial nerve nuclei or 
                        nerve fibers (peripheral)
                        • Lesions to alpha motor neurons 
                        (cell bodies or peripheral nerve 
                        fibers)

                        Descending pyramidal tracts
                            Corticospinal tracts
                            Corticobulbar tracts

                    .Examples of LMN lesions that result in LMN Weakness
                        • Demyelinating polyneuropathies (Guillain–Barré syndrome)
                        • Spinal muscular atrophy
                        • Muscular dystrophy
                        • Poliomyelitis
                        • Cauda equina syndrome
                        • Amyotrophic lateral Sclerosis (ALS)

                    .LMN Syndrome
                        • Signs (Motor deficits) 
                        • Paralysis or paresis is limited to segmental or focal pattern, root innervated 
                        pattern
                        • Flaccid paralysis – paralysis accompanied by muscle loss
                        • Decreased muscle tone that is not velocity dependent (hypotonia)
                        • Hypoactive or areflexia deep tendon reflexes
                        • The presence of fasciculations and fibrillations (!!E)

                    .LMN signs (!!E)
                        • Fasciculation
                        • Caused by an anterior horn cell and motor unit firing without a command
                        • Visible spontaneous contractions involving small groups of muscle fibers 
                        • Does not always denote pathology
                        • Usually not large enough to move a joint
                        • Fibrillation
                        • Involuntary, spontaneous contraction of a single muscle fiber
                        • Caused by instability of muscle fiber membrane
                        • Seen with EMG
                        • Pathological; signs of neuropathy

                    .UMN vs. LMN Signs
                        - Atrophy
                          - UMN: Due to disuse
                          - LMN: Severe

                        - Fasciculations & Fibrillations
                          - UMN: None
                          - LMN: Common

                        - Tone
                          - UMN: Heightened
                          - LMN: Decreased

                        - Distribution of Weakness
                          - UMN: Reflects decreased activity of neuronal circuitry, resulting in loss of selective control of movement
                          - LMN: Distal/segmental

                        - Tendon Reflexes
                          - UMN: Hyperactive
                          - LMN: Hypoactive (absent)

                        - Abnormal Reflexes (Babinski’s Sign)
                          - UMN: Present
                          - LMN: Absent

                    .Table 5.9 Differential Diagnosis: Comparison of Upper Motor Neuron (UMN) and Lower Motor Neuron (LMN) Syndromes (!!E).Lv3.Immersion3A
                        1. Location of Lesion & Structures Involved  
                           - UMN Lesion: Cortex, brain stem, corticospinal tracts, spinal cord  
                           - LMN Lesion: Cranial nerve nuclei/nerves, anterior horn cell, spinal roots, peripheral nerve  

                        2. Diagnosis & Pathology  
                           - UMN Lesion: Stroke, traumatic brain injury, spinal cord injury  
                           - LMN Lesion: Polio, Guillain-Barré, peripheral nerve injury, peripheral neuropathy, radiculopathy  

                        3. Tone
                           - UMN Lesion: Increased (hypertonia), velocity dependent  
                           - LMN Lesion: Decreased/absent (hypotonia, flaccidity), not velocity dependent  

                        4. Reflexes  
                           - UMN Lesion: Increased (hyperreflexia, clonus, exaggerated cutaneous/autonomic reflexes, +Babinski)  
                           - LMN Lesion: Decreased/absent (hyporeflexia, reduced cutaneous reflexes)  

                        5. Involuntary Movements  
                           - UMN Lesion: Muscle spasms (flexor or extensor)  
                           - LMN Lesion: Fasciculations (with denervation)  

                        6. Strength  
                           - UMN Lesion: Weakness/paralysis, ipsilateral (stroke) or bilateral (SCI), contralateral if above decussation, ipsilateral if below, distribution never focal  
                           - LMN Lesion: Ipsilateral weakness/paralysis, segmental or focal distribution  

                        7. Muscle Bulk  
                           - UMN Lesion: Disuse atrophy (variable, widespread, especially antigravity muscles)
                           - LMN Lesion: Neurogenic atrophy (rapid, focal, severe wasting)  

                        8. Voluntary Movements  
                           - UMN Lesion: Impaired/absent (dyssynergic patterns, obligatory mass synergies)  
                           - LMN Lesion: Weak/absent if nerve interrupted  

                    .Summary
                        • Weakness due to UMN and LMN lesions presents differently with different 
                        patterns and observations
                        • UMN lesions typically affect corticospinal tract, whereas LMN lesions affect alpha 
                        motor neurons, cranial nerve nuclei, or peripheral nerves

                    .Movement System Diagnoses for Patients with Neuromuscular Conditions

                    .Objectives
                        • Describe the movement system diagnoses for individuals with neuromuscular 
                        conditions
                        • Identify common findings on the neurologic PT exam that are associated with 
                        movement system diagnoses

                    .Academy of Neurologic Physical Therapy (ANPT) Movement Systems Task Force actions: 
                        • Proposed need for diagnostic classifications of movement system problems 
                        (need to be developed, tested, and validated) in neurologic PT 
                        • Identified 4 essential elements necessary to develop and implement movement 
                        system diagnoses with primarily neurologic involvement from existing movement 
                        system classifications (next slide)
                        • Recognized the impact of movement system diagnoses in neurologic PT: 
                        • Clinical practice
                        • Education
                        • Research 

                        White Paper: Movement System Diagnoses in Neurologic Physical Therapy. JNPT, 42(2):110-117, April 2018. 

                    .Neurologic PT clinical practice uses movement system diagnosis within:
                        • Examination
                        • MOVEMENT OBSERVATION AND ANALYSIS
                        • Movement Construct Terminology; The Movement Continuum
                        • CORE TASKS FOR MOVEMENT OBSERVATION
                        • Principles for Movement Analysis; Testing Efficiency; Environmental Setup; Repetitions; 
                        Task and Environmental Variations
                        • Evaluation
                        • Diagnosis

                        • Intervention
                        • Diagnostic label should guide PT plan of care and specific intervention(s). 

                        Synthesis & interpretation of movement observations and 
                        standardized tasks lead to hypotheses of how motor control 
                        affected à iterative process resulting in an assigned 
                        diagnostic label or movement system diagnosis
                    
                    .Movement System Diagnoses
                        • A set of human movement system 
                        diagnoses for neuromuscular 
                        conditions
                        • Based on clinical observation and the 
                        results of diagnostic tests administered 
                        during a standardized clinical 
                        assessment (neuro PT exam)
                        • Patient can have more than one 
                        movement system diagnosis

                        • Movement Pattern Coordination Deficit
                        • Force Production Deficit
                        • Sensory Detection Deficit
                        • Sensory Selection and Weighting Deficit
                        • Perceptual Deficit
                        • Fractionated Movement Deficit
                        • Hypermetria
                        • Hypokinesia
                        • Cognitive Deficit
                        Scheets PL , Sahrmann SA, Norton BJ. Diagnosis for physical therapy for patients with neuromuscular conditions. Neurol Rep. 1999;23:158–169.
                        
                    .Movement Pattern Coordination Deficit
                        • Difficulty with timing and sequencing of 
                        one body segment in relation to 
                        another
                        • May be observed in the LE during 
                        postural control tasks
                        • May be observed in UE during 
                        manipulation of objects, grasp and 
                        release, reaching

                        • Examples of associated medical 
                        diagnoses
                        • Stroke
                        • Multiple Sclerosis (MS)
                        • Parkinson Disease (PD)
                        • Generalized debilitation
                        • Multisensory gait and balance 
                        disturbance
                        • Post-surgery

                    .Movement Pattern Coordination Deficit, continued
                        • Examples of key signs and findings
                        • Altered sequencing during sit to stand
                        • Variable foot placement or slow, cautious gait
                        • May need some assistance for balance/gait
                        • Slowed or awkward reaching
                        • Difficulty adjusting grip
                        • Inappropriate amplitude of postural adjustments or responses
                        • Increased sway during stance activities

                    .Force Production Deficit
                        • Primary problem is weakness
                        • Origin of weakness may be muscular, 
                        neuromuscular junction, peripheral 
                        nerve, or central nervous system 
                        dysfunction
                        • May be limited to one joint/muscle 
                        group or may be present in a body 
                        segment (extremity, hemibody)
                        • Could be related to fatigue

                        • Examples of associated medical 
                        diagnoses
                        • Generalized debilitation
                        • Disuse atrophy
                        • Stroke
                        • Brain injury
                        • MS
                        • Myopathy
                        • Muscular dystrophy
                        • Spinal cord injury (SCI)

                    .Force Production Deficit, continued
                        • Examples of key signs and findings
                        • MMT < 5/5
                        • Deterioration in range of motion or speed of movement with repetition
                        • Failure during initiation of sit to stand
                        • May need manual assistance or assistive devices to maintain upright posture
                        • Significant gait deviations or inability to ambulate
                        • Difficulty or failure to reach
                        • Unable to maintain appropriate force to grip objects

                    .Sensory Detection Deficit
                        • Inability to execute movement due to 
                        lack of joint position sense or 
                        multisensory failure
                        • May affect JPS, vision, or the 
                        vestibular system
                        • May be present in UE, LE, or both

                        • Examples of associated medical 
                        diagnoses
                        • Stroke
                        • Brain injury
                        • Peripheral neuropathy
                        • Multisystem failure
                        • Bilateral vestibular loss

                    .Sensory Detection Deficit, continued
                        • Examples of key signs and findings
                        • Impaired joint position sense and/or protective sensation
                        • Visual field deficit
                        • Variable foot placement with gait, need of assistance
                        • Slow and/or uncoordinated reaching/grasping
                        • Loss of balance or increased sway with eyes closed
                        • Improved movement with visual guidance
                        • VOR dysfunction/oscillopsia

                    .Sensory Selection and Weighting Deficit
                        • Inability to utilize or attend to 
                        appropriate sensory inputs to maintain 
                        postural control
                        • May have postural instability, 
                        dizziness, and/or visual motion 
                        sensitivity

                        • Examples of associated medical 
                        diagnoses
                        • Stroke
                        • Brain injury
                        • Vestibular loss (unilateral or 
                        bilateral)
                        • Generalized debility

                    .Sensory Selection and Weighting Deficit, continued
                        • Examples of key signs and findings
                        • Dizziness associated with head turns
                        • VOR dysfunction (abnormal HIT, DVA)
                        • Dizziness with eye movements or in visually stimulating environments
                        • Deviation outside of path with gait
                        • Difficulty/increased symptoms with turns
                        • Increased sway, particularly with eyes closed
                        • Difficulty transitioning to different environments

                        This Photo by Unknown Author is licensed 
                        under CC BY-NC-ND

                    .Perceptual Deficit
                        • Tendency to resist correction of center 
                        of mass alignment 
                        • Due to inaccurate perception of 
                        vertical orientation
                        • Result is postural control deficits
                        • Can be in anterior/posterior or 
                        medial/lateral directions

                        • Examples of associated medical 
                        diagnoses
                        • Stroke
                        • Brain injury
                        • Generalized debilitation
                        • Dementia

                    .Perceptual Deficit, continued
                        • Examples of key signs and findings
                        • Sense of falling when shifted toward vertical
                        • Disregard or neglect for involved extremities
                        • Resists correction of center of mass alignment
                        • May be present in sitting, standing, or with walking
                        • May have loss of fractionated movement and/or sensory loss as well
                        • May have difficulty with motor planning
                        • May have poor judgement, impulsive or fearful behavior

                    .Examples: Perceptual Deficit
                        Unilateral neglect: lack of awareness of aspects 
                        of the body and/or the environment

                        Pusher syndrome: active pushing with the onger extremities toward the hemiparetic side

                    .Fractionated Movement Deficit
                        • Inability to fractionate movement 
                        • May be present in UE, LE, or both
                        • Always associated with a central 
                        neurologic deficit (lateral CST)

                        • Examples of associated medical 
                        diagnoses
                        • Stroke
                        • Brain injury
                        • SCI
                        • MS
                        • Cerebral palsy (CP)

                    .Fractionated Movement Deficit, continued
                        • Examples of key signs and findings
                        • Unable to fractionate movement
                        • Variability in ability to move against gravity
                        • Slow movement
                        • Increased tone
                        • Hip hiking, vaulting, circumduction with gait
                        • Likely to require an assistive device and/or orthotics
                        • Reaching may only occur in limited range
                        • Hand closure with minimal opening
                        • Asymmetrical postural control

                    .Example: hemiplegic abnormal synergy patterns ('')

                    .Synergy Patterns
                        Table 15.10 Obligatory Synergy Patterns Following Stroke

                        I. Upper Extremity
                           A. Flexion Synergy Components
                              1. Scapular retraction/elevation or hyperextension
                              2. Shoulder abduction, external rotation
                              3. Elbow flexion
                              4. Forearm supination
                              5. Wrist and finger flexion

                           B. Extension Synergy Components
                              1. Scapular protraction
                              2. Shoulder adduction, internal rotation
                              3. Elbow extension
                              4. Forearm pronation
                              5. Wrist and finger flexion

                        II. Lower Extremity
                           A. Flexion Synergy Components
                              1. Hip flexion, abduction, external rotation
                              2. Knee flexion
                              3. Ankle dorsiflexion, inversion
                              4. Toe dorsiflexion

                           B. Extension Synergy Components
                              1. Hip extension, adduction, internal rotation
                              2. Knee extension
                              3. Ankle plantarflexion, inversion
                              4. Toe plantarflexion

                    .Hypermetria
                        • Inability to grade forces appropriately 
                        for the distance and/or speed aspects 
                        of a task
                        • Movements are generally too large for 
                        the intended purpose
                        • May be present in UE, LE, or both
                        • Generally associated with cerebellar 
                        dysfunction

                        • Examples of associated medical 
                        diagnoses
                        • Stroke
                        • Cerebellar degeneration
                        • MS
                        • CP

                    .Ataxia
                        • Unsteadiness, incoordination of volitional movement, difficulty regulating force, 
                        range, direction and timing of movement
                        • Signs and symptoms
                        • Dysmetria
                        • Dysdiadochokinesia
                        • Intention (action tremor)
                        • Overshooting/undershooting a target
                        • Gait ataxia
                        • Characterized by wide base of support
                        • Arms may be held in high guard position due to instability
                        • Stepping patterns are irregular in distance and direction

                    .Chorea
                        • Movements are rapid, involuntary, 
                        irregular
                        • Involve multiple joints
                        • Dance like
                        • More distally involved and more 
                        apparent in UEs
                        • Cannot be voluntarily inhibited
                        • Characteristic of Huntington’s disease

                    .Hemiballismus
                        • Large-amplitude sudden and 
                        involuntary flailing motions of 
                        the arm and leg of one side of 
                        the body
                        • Primarily involves axial and 
                        proximal limb musculature
                        • Lesion to the contralateral 
                        subthalamic nucleus

                    .Hypokinesia
                        • Slowness in initiating and executing 
                        movements
                        • May be associated with stoppage of 
                        an ongoing movement

                        • Examples of associated medical 
                        diagnoses
                        • PD
                        • Extra-pyramidal syndromes
                        • Stroke

                    .Rigidity
                        • Stiffness and resistance to movement that is 
                        independent of velocity of movement
                        • Excess supraspinal drive (UMN Facilitation) 
                        acting on the alpha motor neurons
                        • Spinal reflex - typically normal
                        • Involves both antagonist and agonist
                        • Lead Pipe rigidity
                        • Constant hypertonia felt throughout the range of 
                        movement with passive movement 
                        • Cogwheel rigidity
                        • Refers to the ratchet-like jerk responses of the 
                        muscles when force is applied while bending a 
                        limb

                    .Bradykinesia
                        • Decreased amplitude and velocity of voluntary movement
                        • Dysfunction in the extrapyramidal motor system
                        • Associated with Parkinson’s disease

                    .Cognitive Deficit
                        • Deficit in movement is related to lack 
                        of cognitive ability
                        • Examples of key signs and findings:
                        • Difficulty following commands
                        • Difficulty remembering instructions 
                        and/or movement patterns
                        • Difficulty staying on task, 
                        particularly in complex 
                        environments or in dual task 
                        conditions
                        • Lack of safety awareness, insight 
                        into deficits

                        • Examples of associated medical 
                        diagnoses
                        • Brain injury
                        • Dementia

                    .Table 5.10 Differential Diagnosis: Comparison of Major Types of Central Nervous System Disorders
                        1. Location of Lesion
                           - Cerebral Cortex & Corticospinal Tracts → Stroke
                           - Basal Ganglia → Parkinson’s disease

                        2. Key Characteristics
                           - Sensation
                             - Stroke: Impaired/absent, contralateral sensory loss
                             - Parkinson’s: Not affected
                           - Tone
                             - Stroke: Hypertonia/spasticity (velocity-dependent), initial flaccidity (cerebral shock)
                             - Parkinson’s: Lead-pipe rigidity (uniform resistance) & Cogwheel rigidity (ratchet-like resistance)
                           - Reflexes
                             - Stroke: Hyperreflexia
                             - Parkinson’s: Normal or may be decreased
                           - Strength
                             - Stroke: Contralateral weakness/paralysis (hemiplegia or hemiparesis); disuse weakness in chronic stage
                             - Parkinson’s: Disuse weakness in chronic stage
                           - Muscle Bulk
                             - Stroke: Normal in acute stage, disuse atrophy in chronic stage
                             - Parkinson’s: Normal or disuse atrophy
                           - Involuntary Movements
                             - Stroke: Spasms
                             - Parkinson’s: Resting tremor
                           - Voluntary Movements
                             - Stroke: Dyssynergic (abnormal timing, co-activation, fatigability)
                             - Parkinson’s: Bradykinesia (slowness), Akinesia (absence of movement)
                           - Postural Control
                             - Stroke: Impaired or absent (depends on lesion location), impaired balance
                             - Parkinson’s: Stooped posture, impaired balance
                           - Gait
                             - Stroke: Impaired due to weakness, abnormal synergies, spasticity, timing deficits
                             - Parkinson’s: Shuffling, festinating gait

                    .Table 5.10 Differential Diagnosis: Comparison of Major Types of Central Nervous System Disorders
                        1. Location of Lesion
                           - Cerebellum
                           - Spinal Cord

                        2. Diagnosis / Pathology
                           - Cerebellum: Tumor, stroke
                           - Spinal Cord: Trauma, tumor, vascular insult (complete/incomplete spinal cord injury)

                        3. Sensation
                           - Cerebellum: Not affected
                           - Spinal Cord: Impaired or absent below the level of lesion

                        4. Tone
                           - Cerebellum: Normal or may be decreased
                           - Spinal Cord: Hypertonia/spasticity below the lesion, initial flaccidity (spinal shock)

                        5. Reflexes
                           - Cerebellum: Normal or may be decreased
                           - Spinal Cord: Hyperreflexia

                        6. Strength
                           - Cerebellum: Normal or weak (asthenia)
                           - Spinal Cord: Impaired or absent below the lesion (paraplegia, paraparesis, tetraplegia, tetraparesis)

                        7. Muscle Bulk
                           - Cerebellum: Normal
                           - Spinal Cord: Disuse atrophy

                        8. Involuntary Movements
                           - Cerebellum: None
                           - Spinal Cord: Spasms

                        9. Voluntary Movements
                           - Cerebellum: Ataxia (intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, dysmetria, dyssynergia, nystagmus)
                           - Spinal Cord: Above lesion—normal; Below lesion—impaired or absent

                        10. Postural Control
                           - Cerebellum: Impaired (truncal ataxia, balance deficits)
                           - Spinal Cord: Impaired below lesion (balance deficits)

                        11. Gait
                           - Cerebellum: Impaired (ataxic gait, wide-based, unsteady)
                           - Spinal Cord: Impaired or absent (depends on lesion level)

                    .Summary
                        • Movement system diagnoses for individuals with neuromuscular conditions can 
                        be used as a framework to organize or classify findings on the neurologic PT 
                        exam
                        • These categories of movement deficits can be used to identify appropriate 
                        treatment interventions

                    ('Patient With Spinocerebellar Ataxia Types 2 and 10.mp4')
                        The spinocerebellar ataxias (SCAs) are a heterogeneous group of autosomal dominant neurodegenerative diseases characterized by progressive cerebellar ataxia and different genetic mutations. The presence of more than 1 SCA mutation within a single individual is rare. SCA8 mutations coexisting with SCA1, SCA3, or SCA6 mutations have been described in several individuals.1-3SCA3 and SCA17 mutations co-occurred in 2 individuals from the same kindred4; these individuals, however, were asymptomatic and had intermediate-range CAG/CAA expansions in the SCA17 TATA-binding protein gene. Herein, we report a symptomatic patient who carries mutations in both the SCA2 and SCA10 genes, a combination, to our knowledge, that has not been previously reported.

                        Report of a case

                        Play Video
                        His history was significant for ataxia in multiple family members including his sister, mother, and maternal grandmother (Figure 1). His maternal ancestry was of Mexican, American Indian (Yaqui tribe), and French descent. His sister reported a 20-year history of slowly progressive gait and limb ataxia (onset age, 34 years), along with dysarthria and mild cognitive impairment. His mother developed gait and limb ataxia at about age 60 years and required a wheelchair after about 10 years of disease. Both affected family members reported muscle spasms, dysphagia, and urinary incontinence; neither has had documented seizures, although his sister has been treated with carbamazepine for episodes of bilateral leg stiffening. The patient's paternal ancestry was also of Mexican and French descent; however, there is no known history of ataxia or neurologic disease in his father or paternal relatives. All of these relatives lived far from the patient and were unavailable for direct examination.

                        Figure 1. Family pedigree. Squares indicate men; circles, women; diagonal lines, deceased. An arrow indicates the index case. Symptoms include ataxia (cases II.4, III.6, IV.2, and IV.3); dysarthria, dysphagia, and muscle cramps (cases III.6, IV.2, and IV.3); paresthesias and possible seizures (case IV.2); and cognitive impairment (case IV.3).
                        Figure 1. Family pedigree. Squares indicate men; circles, women; diagonal lines, deceased. An arrow indicates the index case. Symptoms include ataxia (cases II.4, III.6, IV.2, and IV.3); dysarthria, dysphagia, and muscle cramps (cases III.6, IV.2, and IV.3); paresthesias and possible seizures (case IV.2); and cognitive impairment (case IV.3).

                        Play Video
                        Figure 2. Brain magnetic resonance imaging. T1-weighted sagittal image demonstrating cerebellar and brainstem atrophy in our patient.
                        Figure 2. Brain magnetic resonance imaging. T1-weighted sagittal image demonstrating cerebellar and brainstem atrophy in our patient.

                        Comment

                        Both SCA2 and SCA10 are dominantly inherited SCAs but result from different genetic mutations. The SCA2 mutation is due to an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat in the gene coding for the cytoplasmic protein ataxin-2 on chromosome 12q24.6 Affected SCA2 individuals have 32 or more CAG repeats, with 37 to 39 repeats representing the most frequent pathologic expansion.6,7 Normal alleles range from 15 to 31 CAG repeats (most commonly 22 repeats) and may have CAA interruptions.6-9 Anticipation may occur, particularly with paternal transmission; those affected individuals generally have longer CAG repeat lengths and earlier symptom onset age.7,9,10 Mean age at onset is typically in the fourth decade. SCA2 has been reported in various ethnicities including Cuban, Indian, Italian, Mexican, South African, and Spanish.11 Besides ataxia, SCA2 features may include slowed saccades (which may progress to ophthalmoparesis), brisk deep tendon reflexes (which may progress to areflexia), peripheral neuropathy, dementia, myoclonus, dystonia, chorea, and levodopa-responsive parkinsonism. Milder phenotypes with less prominent ataxia, neuropathy, dystonia, and myoclonus but greater parkinsonian features have been associated with shorter CAG repeat expansions.8,12

                        SCA10 maps to chromosome 22q13 and is caused by an unstable pentanucleotide repeat expansion ATTCT in intron 9 of the SCA10 gene, ataxin-10.13,14 Affected SCA10 individuals have 800 to 4500 ATTCT repeats; normal alleles range from 10 to 29 repeats.15 Penetrance is usually complete, although reduced penetrance has been reported in individuals with 360 to 370 repeats.16 Greater instability of repeat expansion occurs with paternal transmission; in SCA10, however, unstable repeat lengths may lead to either intergenerational expansion or contraction.17,18 Anticipation has been observed with contraction of ATTCT repeats,17 thereby suggesting a more complex genotype-phenotype relationship between repeat length and onset age. Symptoms typically begin around ages 10 to 40 years. Besides ataxia, epilepsy (generalized or complex partial seizures), mild cognitive impairment, and abnormal eye movements (eg, ocular dysmetria, fragmented pursuit, and gaze-evoked nystagmus) may occur.15,18-20SCA10 has been described predominantly in Mexican and Brazilian kindreds15,19,20 but also in Argentinean and Venezuelan families.21,22 Common American Indian ancestry has been hypothesized to play a role in the origins of SCA10 in Mexican and South American families.23 Interestingly, our patient has both Mexican and American Indian heritage. The SCA10 phenotype, however, differs in Mexican and South American populations.15,19,21,22 Epilepsy is notable in Mexican kindreds, and some patients have hematologic or hepatic dysfunction. Brazilian patients, however, do not have seizures and lack prominent extracerebellar involvement (ie, neuropathy, cognitive dysfunction, or systemic disease); epilepsy was found in only 3.75% of the Brazilian SCA10 cases, in contrast to up to 60% of SCA10 patients from other geographic regions.24 Dystonia and parkinsonism were reported in the Argentinean family, and peripheral neuropathy has been noted primarily in Mexican patients.24

                        Our patient has a combination of genetic mutations for 2 different SCAs, types 2 and 10, a combination that, to our knowledge, has not been previously reported. His phenotype includes features common to both SCAs, namely cerebellar ataxia, dysarthria, sensory polyneuropathy, and mild cognitive dysfunction, but also elements specifically associated with the 2 distinct SCA syndromes. His muscle spasms, cramps, and hyporeflexia are more typical for SCA2, whereas his Mexican heritage and possible seizures are more frequently associated with SCA10. While his repeat expansions for both SCAs fall within the pathological ranges, the expansions are mild, a feature that may explain some aspects of his presentation. Whereas prominent slow saccades, highly characteristic of SCA2, were not evident in our patient, prior studies demonstrate that saccadic velocity deficits correlate with repeat length.8,25 As such, his very mildly slowed saccades may reflect the smaller SCA2 repeat expansions (ie, 38 alleles). Alternatively, his SCA10 mutation may have influenced the phenotypic expression of the saccadic deficits. Overall, our patient exhibits a unique clinical phenotype not explained by either SCA2 or SCA10 alone.

                        By using distinct clinical features (eg, cerebellar syndromes with or without parkinsonism, retinopathy, or dementia), the clinician may consider testing for specific SCAs, although in many cases, there is phenotypic overlap. In our case, we tested for both SCA types because of his overlapping clinical features and ancestral background. Our patient, along with the few other combined SCA case reports,1-4 demonstrates that patients who harbor shared SCA phenotypes could actually carry 2 different SCA mutations. With the growing availability of commercial genetic testing panels, it is important to raise the clinician's awareness of this possibility and not to stop the evaluation with 1 positive test result in cases of atypical presentation.

                        This patient and his family also may provide unique opportunities to study the interactions of 2 genetic mutations and their effect on clinical expression of disease. Though the clinical and genetic effects of combined SCA mutations are unknown, it has been postulated that SCA8 may modify the effect of polyglutamine transcripts in SCA6 patients.1 Whether SCA10 similarly modifies SCA2, or vice versa, remains to be seen. Furthermore, finding 2 genetic mutations in a patient may have important implications regarding counseling on genetic risk, genetic testing, and disease prognosis.

                For these assignments, you will video record yourself performing the selected skills on a subject of your choosing. 
                    Please take note of the following considerations when selecting a subject: 
                        -Make certain that the individual does not have any injury, condition, pain or other problems that might be worsened by performing this particular skill. 
                        -Never assume this is the case and always ask specifically if the person is aware of “any problems in the body region that could potentially be aggravated”. If you live in close proximity to a classmate, this is an ideal choice of subject. 
                        -The subject should be dressed appropriately to allow proper performance of the skill and full viewing of the target area. 
                        -It is strongly recommended that you practice the skill several times before recording and to view your performance for quality prior to submitting. You may re-record the skill as many times as you like but once you submit the product is final.

                 Please take note of the following considerations before recording: 
                    1.First state the name of the skill and the specific structure or body region that is being assessed.
                        For example: “This video will show a manual muscle test for the quadriceps muscles” or “I will now demonstrate a range of motion assessment on the hip.”

(In other words, speak to the subject as if they were your actual patient you are seeing in the clinic.)

While performing the skill, briefly describe what you are doing to the camera as if you were teaching someone to do this skill for the first time. Include a description of specific aspects of the skill that you have learned in this course are essential for effective performance.
                        -While you may have learned other approaches during your observational experiences, it is important that you demonstrate as you were taught in this program so that instructors can adequately assess your ability to internalize the information presented.
                        -Please assume that the patient requires close supervision so that we can appropriately grade your guarding and patient safety.
                    4.At the end of the video, please provide a brief description of an abnormal or significant test finding and how this might impact patient function per the rubric.
                    5.Keep each video as short as possible while including all needed elements. You should be able to do everything you need in 5 minutes or less.

            //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
            4.8. Module 4 Summary
            //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
            //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

                Well done! You have completed the fourth of five modules for Unit 1. Before moving on to the next module, remember to review these three key learnings: 

                Neurologic conditions can impact movement in a variety of ways resulting in less movement (weakness, spasticity, bradykinesia), too much movement (tremor, chorea, hemiballismus), and/or impaired movement patterns. 
                A comprehensive balance exam may include assessment of static and dynamic sitting and/or standing balance, and an assessment of gait (walking balance). 
                Functional skills may be observed as part of your initial observation, during the motor, balance, or functional components of the neurologic exam. 
                  

                Learning Outcomes
                After completing this module, you can now: 

                Demonstrate the ability to perform an assessment of balance and function for clients with a neurologic diagnosis.
                Describe the variety of movement disorders and appreciate how these disorders interfere with function, activities, and participation.
                Apply to core set of outcome measures in clinical settings to assess gait, balance, and function for persons with neurologic diagnoses.

            5.0. Immersion Module 5 Introduction
            ////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

                Introduction
                    In this module you will come to campus for on site Lab Immersion 5. During the immersion lab, you will practice the skills you learned during Unit 1 including the Neurologic PT Examination, assessing the Core Outcome Measures, task analysis, and development of effective practice to promote skill acquisition. 

                Learning Outcomes
                    By the end of this week, you will be able to: 
                        -Perform a PT examination, establish a prognosis and plan of care using evidence-based therapeutic interventions for clients with a neurologic diagnosis. 
                        -Evaluate data from the PT examination to drive clinical decision making for the plan of care that is patient–centered, evidence-based and individualized to the client’s capabilities.  
                        -Apply the core set of outcome measures in clinical settings to assess gait, balance, and function for persons with neurologic diagnoses. 
                        -Apply motor learning strategies to drive skill acquisition and recovery of function.

            ////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
            5.1. Background Readings and Materials
            ////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
            ////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

                Review the following resources before your first lab. 

                    .Laboratory Safety ('https://www.safety.pitt.edu/ehs/laboratory-safety')
                        Check out the latest resources from CSHEMA regarding: 
                            Chemical storage (PDF)
                                Best Practices for Chemical  
                                Storage are critical to ensure the  
                                safety of the research community.  
                                Maintain the safe and responsible use of  
                                chemicals in an academic research setting.                           
                                Properly dispose of chemical wastes according to                
                                University guidelines.  
                                • Always consult the safety data sheet (SDS) from the specific chemical vendor for storage 
                                and segregation requirements for chemicals and chemical wastes.  
                                • Review the chemical SDS of all new chemicals to ensure researchers are utilizing the 
                                necessary engineering controls (ex. chemical fume hood) and have the proper personal 
                                protective equipment (PPE).  
                                • Store chemicals in compatible groups. Do not store your chemicals in 
                                alphabetical order, except within each compatible class of chemicals. Consult the University 
                                Guideline on Compatible Chemical Storage Groups (EH&S Guideline # 04-025). 
                                • Store your flammable chemicals in UL/FM approved flammable cabinets that are specifically 
                                designed for that storage purpose. Store flammables separate from acids, bases & oxidizers.  
                                • Label ALL chemicals with the common chemical name. All chemical waste containers must 
                                have a completed ‘Waste Chemical’ label affixed to the container upon initial collection of 
                                waste.  
                            Greenhouse safety (PDF)
                                Greenhouses are integral to research and  
                                educational activities, yet safety concerns  
                                are frequently overlooked.  
                                Follow the safety guidelines: 
                                1. Always Maintain Closed Doors 
                                Greenhouse doors should be kept closed to ensure proper  
                                temperature regulation. Open doors not only disrupt climate  
                                control systems but also facilitate the entry of pests. 
                                2. Monitor for Structural Damage 
                                Rust on structural elements is a significant safety concern. Corroded  
                                metal surfaces can weaken over time, posing potential risks to individuals. 
                                3. Ensure Clear Walkways 
                                All walkways and floor surfaces within the greenhouse should be level and  
                                free from trip hazards. Gravel areas should be routinely maintained to eliminate  
                                weeds and ensure a smooth, even surface to prevent accidents. 
                                4. Inspect for Cracked or Broken Panels 
                                Cracked or broken glass or plastic panels can present significant hazards, as the  
                                damage may progress into sharp, jagged edges. Regularly check for any signs of panel 
                                damage and replace any compromised panels immediately to mitigate the risk of injury. 
                                5. Conduct Regular Maintenance and Inspections 
                                Due to their constant exposure to environmental factors, greenhouses require periodic 
                                maintenance. Routine inspections should be scheduled to identify any potential issues,  
                                such as weather-related wear or structural deterioration, and necessary repairs should  
                                be promptly addressed. 
                            Hazard identification and risk assessment (PDF)
                                Risk assessments are crucial for  
                                conducting research projects safely. 
                                The process of identifying hazards,  
                                determining the severity of potential risks  
                                and establishing that suitable/proper control  
                                measures are in place is a key component to  
                                keep the academic community safe. 
                                • Risk assessments of planned research should be undertaken 
                                before proceeding with research activities. Consult your research 
                                advisor prior to any scale-up operations to review potentially 
                                hazardous conditions.  
                                • Reviewing Safety Data Sheets (SDS), scheduling consultation with 
                                the EHS staff and discussing the work projects are important steps 
                                in determining the risks and how to address and control them. 
                                • Risk assessments (RAs) should be revised periodically. Review RAs 
                                with any changes to the research experiment, like introducing new 
                                chemicals, adding steps to the process, using new equipment, or 
                                changes in the concentration of already assessed chemicals. 
                                • To minimize risks, the hierarchy of controls is used, done by 
                                elimination, substitution, engineering controls, administrative 
                                controls and personal protective equipment (PPE).   
                            Lab housekeeping (PDF)
                                Good lab housekeeping reduces  
                                the number of accidents, minimize risks  
                                & consequences of slips, trips, falls,  
                                unplanned reactions and fire.   
                                Space is always at a premium. Don’t be a hoarder! 
                                ● Good housekeeping provides more space for research materials, 
                                making it safer to move around the lab without tripping or 
                                potentially being exposed to chemical/biological materials. 
                                ● Limiting or reducing flammable solvents and combustible 
                                materials like paper or cardboard reduces the risk of fire. 
                                ● Never block emergency exits, fire extinguishers, safety showers, 
                                eyewashes, or electrical panels. 
                                ● Consider scheduling frequent lab clean-out days (at least quarterly). 
                                Inspections help keep the lab space clean. Establishing an internal 
                                inspections program improves the lab safety culture. 
                                ● Periodically thaw freezers to minimize ice build-up. 
                                ● Make arrangements to service and maintain lab equipment; do 
                                not use damaged or broken equipment. 
                            Makerspaces (PDF)
                                Makerspace safety is best achieved via a  
                                collaborative relationship between the  
                                responsible person and Environmental Health  
                                and Safety. Elements of safety-by-design, user  
                                training, and strategies for monitoring and access  
                                control are essential for makerspace safety.  
                                • Makerspace supervisors and EHS should work collaboratively to 
                                implement safety-by-design. Examples include: Selection of  
                                fabrication equipment to meet guarding and safety requirements;  
                                Effective general ventilation and local exhaust ventilation in areas of  
                                subtractive and additive manufacturing; Work area design and layout;  
                                Mechanical lifting device selection and equipment.  
                                • Makerspace users and employees should have documented training. This 
                                training should be tied to authorization to use equipment or makerspace  
                                areas. Training matrices and tracking systems can be used. Color coding on  
                                badges can be used. Advanced facilities should consider card-swipe-access to  
                                machines or areas that is tied to training.  
                                • Makerspaces used by the public and students should have accessible standard 
                                operating procedures for equipment. These SOPs should not be generic but be  
                                created from the user manual of the specific equipment. SOPs should call attention  
                                to primary hazards, controls, safe sequence of use for common operations, and 
                                operations that require assistance from a qualified person.  
                                • Makerspaces should have some level of access control and monitoring. Consider locking 
                                and securing high risk equipment when qualified employees are not present. Consider 
                                preventing access to certain areas when qualified employees are not directly monitoring 
                                users. Implement protocols that prohibit individuals from working alone.  
                                • Makerspaces should capture and properly process hazardous waste operations such as: 
                                Resin 3D printers and related cleaning solvents; Metalworking lubrication; Coating and 
                                paint residue.   
                            Personal protective equipment (PPE) and general lab safety (PDF)
                                Personal protective equipment (PPE)  
                                helps to minimize exposure to hazards  
                                that cause serious workplace injuries and  
                                illnesses.  

                                These injuries and illnesses may result from  
                                contact with chemical, radiological, physical,  
                                electrical, mechanical, or other workplace hazards.  
                                • Basic protection for most laboratories includes safety glasses, shoes and 
                                proper shirts/pants.  
                                • Closed-toed shoes are essential in a laboratory to protect yourself from 
                                chemical splashes or broken glass.  
                                • Chemical splash goggles or face shields should be worn when there is a 
                                risk of splashing hazardous materials or flying particles.  
                                • If respirators are to be used for protection against airborne 
                                contaminants, equipment listed and approved by the National Institute 
                                for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) may be used if properly 
                                selected and fit-tested as part of a complete respiratory protection 
                                program. Contact EH&S with questions about respirators.  
                                • Any laboratory operation that exposes lab personnel to a significant 
                                noise source of 85 decibels or greater for an 8-hour average duration 
                                should utilize hearing protection in the form of ear plugs or muffs.  
                            Safety Equipment in the lab (PDF)
                                Lab safety starts with a safe attitude.  
                                Training with and keeping safety equipment  
                                in good working condition is critical in               
                                protecting the safety and health of individuals.  
                                • Emergency showers, eyewash units, fire extinguishers, 
                                spill kits and other safety equipment keep the community safe  
                                and ready for emergency response.  
                                • Regularly check if appropriate safety equipment and supplies are 
                                present and in good condition. Replenish immediately if used. 
                                • Having a regular training and maintenance program for safety 
                                equipment is imperative. Do not use broken or damaged 
                                equipment – notify and schedule repair service immediately.  
                                • Know the location of the nearest emergency eyewash and 
                                safety shower before starting any work in the laboratory. 
                                • Access to the eyewash, safety shower, fire extinguishers, 
                                and spill kits must be unobstructed. 
                            We're all in this together (PDF)
                                Safety is everyone’s responsibility.  
                                When each person in the lab does their 
                                part, the lab is a safer place to work.   
                                ● Avoid working alone in the lab. Notify others if 
                                solitary work cannot be avoided and follow           
                                established procedures for working alone in a lab. 
                                ● Review standard operating procedures and follow 
                                them carefully.  
                                ● Review chemical Safety Data Sheets (SDS) and be 
                                knowledgeable about the hazards of the chemical being 
                                handled and proper method of waste disposal.  
                                ● Frequently check hazardous waste accumulation storage 
                                areas and arrange for disposal as needed.  Avoid 
                                accumulating large amounts of hazardous waste.  
                                ● A clean lab is a safe lab! Keep areas tidy and organized. 
                                ● Include safety topics in your lab, school, and departmental 
                                meetings.  
                                ● EHS is here to support the academic community in safely 
                                achieving their research goals.

                        5.0
                            Answers questions and/or performs techniques correctly with minimal delay in response. All element(s) are well performed with appropriate positioning, stabilization, precision, direction, and amplitude of force
                        4.0 Answers questions and/or performs techniques correctly but requires some extra time and/or slight redirection. All element(s) are adequately performed but may lack slightly in regard to positioning, stabilization, precision, direction or amplitude of force
                        3.0 Answers questions and/or performs techniques only after cueing or prompting is received. Minimal re-direction is required to produce an adequate performance of the required element or technique
                        2.0  Answers questions and/or performs techniques only after cueing or prompting is received. Moderate re-direction is required to produce an adequate performance of the required element or technique
                        1.0 Provides a partially correct/incomplete response in the presence of cueing or prompting. Moderate redirection is required to produce a partially adequate performance of the required element or technique. 
                        0.0 Provides a completely incorrect response or performs technique incorrectly. Unable to demonstrate an acceptable level of performance, despite the presence of cueing or prompting.

                        ``.Case vignettes
                            Discuss and demonstrate specific tests and measures that you would use to assess your patient’s chief complaints and functional limitations.  Make sure you thoroughly examine your patient (i.e., assess both sides of the body and/or body segment [LE/UE]). 
                                Case 1: Your patient is reporting stiffness in his or her calf when trying to move fast- such as when he/she is “hustling” to open the front door when the doorbell rings.

                                Case 2: Your patient is reporting decreased “feeling” in the right hand and reports dropping items when not looking at his/her hand.

                                Case 3: Your patient is c/o double vision.

                                Case 4: Your patient reports difficulty remembering recent events.

                                Case 5: Your patient c/o difficulty maintaining balance in the dark or dimly lit areas.

                                Case 6: Your patient demonstrates irregular and inaccurate upper limb movements during activities such as bringing a cup to his/her mouth.

                                Case 7: Your patient presents with an inability to smile symmetrically.

                                Case 8: Your patient demonstrates an inability to reach out for a “protective response” when perturbation in sitting.

                                Case 9: Your patient tells you that he has fallen last week while walking outdoors, no injuries, and has an extensive past medical history with multiple co-morbidities.

                                Case 10: Your patient had a sudden loss of hearing on the left side and experienced acute dizziness. They are now having difficulty with their balance when they turn their head while standing and walking.

                                Specific comments   Example Outcome measures    Clinical relevance
                            Observation 
                            History Information gathered from chart review or patient interview
                            present complaint, HPI, PMH, pertinent health information, social support (home environment)
                                    Allows you to gather data, clarify information, establish baseline, make appropriate referrals


                            Review of Systems 


                                Series of brief tests that provide an overview of the specific system of interest.      Used to determine the need for a further detailed examination.

                            Rule out or differentiate specific system involvement.

                            Identify system related impairments that contribute to activity limitations and participation.  

                            Determine if there are RED flags and if
                            referral is warranted.

                            Mental Status: Basic mental functions
                            Level of Consciousness (LOC):
                            Alertness

                                Be specific in documenting level of alertness: 
                            -able to follow commands such as 
                            1) eye movements/responses 
                            2) motor responses 
                            3) verbal responses
                                Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)    LOC is the most sensitive indicator of change in neurological status.
                             
                            Common terms to describe assessment of LOC:
                            Alert, drowsy, obtunded, comatose
                            Orientation 
                                Ask for patient’s 
                            1) full name, age, birthplace 
                            2) where they are now, type of place, city they are in
                             3) the date, day of week, what time it is, season  The Mini-Mental State Exam (MMSE)
                            Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA)
                                Disorientation to time appears before disorientation to place then self.
                            Mental Status:  Complex mental functions
                            Language
                                Assess both receptive and expressive language











                                MMSE
                            MoCA

                            •   Global
                            Memory

                                Assess immediate recall and STM by naming 3 objects, having the patient repeat the 3 objects immediately and then sometime later. Provide distracters during the delay to prevent the patient from rehearsing.

                            Clock drawing   MMSE
                            MoCA    Impaired visuospatial function is more severe with damage to the right (parietal lobe) hemisphere
