                                in a higher position than the rest of the canal [22,
                                41, 122]. Gravity allows otoconia either ﬂoating in
                                the canal or attached to the cupula to deﬂect the
                                cupula and produce horizontal nystagmus, the direc-
                                tion of which depends on the side and location of
                                the otoconia and thus the direction of deﬂection of
                                the cupula. Pseudo-spontaneous nystagmus is there-
                                fore a form of positional nystagmus that happens to
                                occur with the head in the neutral position and the
                                eyes straight ahead, making it appear similar to hor-
                                izontal spontaneous peripheral vestibular nystagmus


                                78 S.D.Z. Eggers et al. / Classiﬁcation of nystagmus and nystagmus-like movements

                                (2.1.1.). It will generally beat toward the affected ear
                                in the apogeotropic type but toward either ear in the
                                geotropic type [106]. Pseudo-spontaneous nystagmus
                                should disappear by pitching the head forward 30◦
                                to place the horizontal canal in the horizontal plane
                                with respect to gravity and should reverse directions
                                by pitching forward even further.
                                2.3.1.1.3. Anterior semicircular canal BPPN:
                                Positional nystagmus, attributed to BPPV, elicited
                                immediately or after a latency of one or few sec-
                                onds by the Dix-Hallpike maneuver or in the supine
                                straight head-hanging position. The nystagmus beats
                                predominantly downward but with a small torsional
                                component in which the upper pole of the eye beats
                                toward the affected ear [10, 156].
                                Comment: Canalolithiasis affecting the anterior
                                canal is a rare variant of BPPV that must be distin-
                                guished from central positional nystagmus (2.3.1.3.)
                                and should have a duration of less than 1 minute
                                during positional testing. It is sometimes the apo-
                                geotropic variant of posterior semicircular canal
                                BPPV [154].
                                2.3.1.2. Other forms of peripheral vestibular
                                positional nystagmus: Positional nystagmus due to
                                a peripheral vestibular disorder other than BPPV.
                                Comment: Ingestion of alcohol (or other sub-
                                stances with a speciﬁc gravity different from
                                endolymph) can produce horizontal positional nys-
                                tagmus. According to the buoyancy hypothesis,
                                compounds of different speciﬁc gravity diffuse into
                                and out of the cupula and endolymph at different
                                rates, causing a transient density gradient and gravity-
                                dependent deﬂection of the cupula. During initial
                                alcohol intoxication, the cupula becomes relatively
                                lighter than the surrounding endolymph, producing
                                geotropic horizontal positional alcohol nystagmus.
                                While sobering up, the cupula becomes relatively
                                heavy, resulting in apogeotropic nystagmus [24].
                                Other peripheral vestibular disorders have been
                                reported to occasionally cause positional nystagmus
                                that must be differentiated from BPPV based on
                                additional symptoms and signs, including vestibular
                                paroxysmia (neurovascular cross-compression of the
                                vestibulocochlear nerve) [25, 74], vestibular schwan-
                                noma [147], Meni

                                `

                                ere’s disease [101], and vestibular

                                atelectasis [162].
                                2.3.1.3. Central positional nystagmus: Positional
                                nystagmus attributed to disease affecting the central
                                nervous system.
                                Comment: Positional nystagmus can be caused by
                                neurological diseases affecting the central vestibulo-
                                cerebellar pathways, such as cerebellar degeneration,

                                multiple sclerosis, posterior fossa neoplasm, Chiari
                                malformation, stroke, vestibular migraine, or a para-
                                neoplastic syndrome. Additional neurological or
                                ocular motor symptoms or signs are typically present
                                to suggest a diagnosis other than BPPV [19, 31,
                                32]. In their absence, several clues suggest a cen-
                                tral cause. The nystagmus may have any trajectory,
                                but pure downbeat and pure horizontal forms are far
                                more common than upbeat, torsional, or mixed forms
                                [120]. Positional nystagmus whose trajectory does
                                not align with a semicircular canal in head-referenced
                                coordinates, such as purely vertical or purely tor-
                                sional positional nystagmus (provided visual ﬁxation
                                is blocked), suggests central nervous system disease
                                [18, 19, 28, 29, 48, 100, 157]. Failure to fatigue after
                                repeated positional testing or resolve after appro-
                                priate canalith repositioning procedures suggests a
                                central cause [20, 55]. Intense positional nystagmus
                                with little to no vertiginous sensation may also sug-
                                gest a central cause.
                                Positional downbeat nystagmus is particularly
                                likely to have a central cause [18, 19], though a small
                                torsional component with the upper pole of the eye
                                beating toward the affected ear may suggest anterior
                                canal BPPN (2.3.1.1.3.) [10].
                                Central horizontal positional nystagmus (particu-
                                larly apogeotropic) is sometimes indistinguishable
                                from the nystagmus of horizontal canal BPPV at the
                                bedside [19, 31, 83, 91], though in central positional
                                nystagmus the intensity is typically at its peak ini-
                                tially and decreases exponentially over time [32],
                                rather than gradually building up over 10–20 seconds
                                and then decreasing slowly over time as in hori-
                                zontal cupulolithiasis [15]. With ﬁxation removed,
                                patients with apogeotropic central positional nystag-
                                mus usually also have low-intensity horizontal central
                                vestibular nystagmus that is similar in both the sitting
                                and supine positions. With respect to the nystagmus
                                direction while supine, the apogeotropic nystagmus
                                evoked in the ear-down position with the supine roll
                                test may be called “ipsiversive” if it continues to beat
                                in the same direction or “contraversive” if it beats
                                in the opposite direction. Unlike in apogeotropic
                                horizontal canal BPPN (2.3.1.1.2.), the nystagmus
                                intensity of apogeotropic central positional nystag-
                                mus is usually similar in the right- and left-ear down
                                positions [31].
                                2.3.2. Headshaking-induced nystagmus: Nys-
                                tagmus triggered by and occurring after repetitive
                                headshaking.
                                Comment: Headshaking-induced nystagmus is
                                typically elicited by shaking the upright subject’s


                                S.D.Z. Eggers et al. / Classiﬁcation of nystagmus and nystagmus-like movements 79

                                head vigorously at about 2 Hz horizontally (prefer-
                                ably with the head pitched forward 30◦ to align
                                the horizontal semicircular canals with the plane of
                                head rotation) for about 20 cycles and then stop-
                                ping abruptly to look for jerk nystagmus [30]. Note
                                that if the examiner moves the head in a circular or
                                elliptical fashion instead of back and forth, this will
                                induce post-rotational nystagmus (1.3.) rather than
                                headshaking-induced nystagmus [72]. Headshaking-
                                induced nystagmus may be monophasic and in a
                                unilateral inhibitory vestibular lesion usually beats
                                toward the better ear. Sometimes the ﬁrst phase is fol-
                                lowed by a weaker second phase beating toward the
                                hypofunctioning side that decays more slowly [67,
                                88]. Vertical headshaking may produce nystagmus
                                beating toward the paretic ear due to activation of the
                                posterior canal, which produces a horizontal com-
                                ponent. Headshaking-induced nystagmus may also
                                occur in central vestibular disorders, in which it may
                                beat toward the side of the lesion, quickly reverse
                                direction, or show a cross-coupled nystagmus (2.3.3.)
                                [75].
                                Terms not recommended: Post-headshaking nys-
                                tagmus; headshaking nystagmus
                                2.3.3. Cross-coupled nystagmus: Nystagmus
                                developing in a plane different from the plane stimu-
                                lated by caloric irrigation, head rotation, or following
                                headshaking.
                                Comment: Cross-coupled nystagmus most com-
                                monly occurs as vertical (usually downbeat)
                                nystagmus following horizontal canal stimulation in
                                the setting of central vestibular lesions [75, 93, 158].
                                Previous term: Perverted nystagmus
                                2.3.4. Sound-induced nystagmus: Nystagmus
                                triggered by an auditory stimulus.
                                Comment: Sound-induced nystagmus occurs most
                                commonly in superior canal dehiscence syndrome
                                [116], in which case the nystagmus trajectory aligns
                                with the affected semicircular canal plane [39]. The
                                frequency and amplitude of the sound stimulus and
                                the ear(s) to which the stimulus was applied should be
                                speciﬁed. Sound-induced nystagmus may be elicited
                                by external sound sources or by the patient’s own
                                voice, e.g. during singing or humming. For the latter
                                clinical sign, the term “fremitus nystagmus” has been
                                proposed [65].
                                Previous term: Tullio phenomenon
                                2.3.5. Valsalva-induced nystagmus: Nystagmus
                                triggered by any bodily maneuver that increases
                                intracranial or middle ear pressure.
                                Comment: Valsalva-induced nystagmus occurs
                                most commonly in superior canal dehiscence syn-

                                drome [116]. Actions that reduce venous return
                                from the intracranial space by raising intrathoracic
                                pressure against a closed glottis (glottic Valsalva)
                                include coughing, sneezing, straining, or lifting heavy
                                objects. By contrast, nose-pinched Valsalva forces
                                air directly into the middle ear cavity without a
                                signiﬁcant change in intrathoracic pressure. Note
                                should be made whether nystagmus is triggered
                                by glottic Valsalva, nose-pinched Valsalva, or both,
                                and the nystagmus direction with each. Nystag-
                                mus induced by pneumatic otoscopy/insufﬂation and
                                other “extrinsic” pressure changes should be classi-
                                ﬁed as pressure-induced nystagmus (2.3.6.).
                                2.3.6. Pressure-induced nystagmus: Nystagmus
                                triggered by extrinsic pressure changes such as
                                insufﬂation with pneumatic otoscopy or tragal com-
                                pression.
                                Comment: Nystagmus occurs in conditions where
                                external ear pressure changes can be transmitted
                                across the tympanic membrane to the middle and
                                inner ear (e.g. in superior canal dehiscence syndrome,
                                in which the nystagmus occurs in the plane of the
                                affected canal). Note should be made whether nys-
                                tagmus is triggered by positive or negative pressure
                                in the external ear canal. Nystagmus triggered by
                                bodily maneuvers that increase intracranial or middle
                                ear pressure should be classiﬁed as Valsalva-induced
                                nystagmus (2.3.5.).
                                Previous term: Hennebert’s sign
                                Term not recommended: Fistula test
                                2.3.7. Vibration-induced nystagmus: Nystagmus
                                triggered by vibration applied to the head or neck.
                                Comment: Typically, a hand-held vibrator is ﬁrmly
                                applied to the head (generally the mastoid processes
                                and the vertex) or neck (generally the sternoclei-
                                domastoid muscle) for 10 seconds, observing for
                                nystagmus with visual ﬁxation blocked. Vibration-
                                induced nystagmus most commonly occurs with
                                unilateral vestibular loss [30, 46]. The location of
                                vibrator application and direction of nystagmus with
                                each stimulus should be recorded.
                                2.3.8. Hyperventilation-induced nystagmus:
                                Nystagmus triggered by hyperventilation.
                                Comment: Hyperventilation may induce nystag-
                                mus in some central or peripheral vestibular disorders
                                [30, 34, 115, 159]. Hyperventilation-induced nystag-
                                mus that beats toward the side of reduced hearing or
                                vestibular dysfunction may alert one to the presence
                                of a cerebellopontine angle tumor [34]. Subjects are
                                typically instructed to rapidly take many large breaths
                                through the mouth for 30 to 90 seconds and observed
                                with visual ﬁxation blocked.


                                80 S.D.Z. Eggers et al. / Classiﬁcation of nystagmus and nystagmus-like movements

                                2.3.9. Pursuit-induced nystagmus: Nystagmus
                                triggered by and occurring during smooth pursuit of
                                a moving target in which the nystagmus occurs in a
                                different plane than the pursuit.
                                Comment: Torsional nystagmus has been reported
                                to develop during vertical pursuit in the setting of a
                                cavernous angioma of the middle cerebellar peduncle
                                [60]. Such nystagmus has been attributed to asym-
                                metric damage to vertical pursuit pathways that are
                                purportedly encoded in a labyrinthine (vertical semi-
                                circular canal) coordinate system. Pursuit-induced
                                nystagmus differs from the saccadic breakdown of
                                impaired smooth pursuit in which saccades occur in
                                the same plane and direction as the moving target
                                stimulus.
                                3. Nystagmus-like movements: Some oscillatory
                                eye movements may resemble nystagmus but instead
                                represent saccadic intrusions or remain ambiguous.
                                3.1. Saccadic intrusions and oscillations: Inap-
                                propriate saccades that disrupt foveal vision by taking
                                the eye away from a target during intended ﬁxation.
                                Comment: Saccades are normally suppressed dur-
                                ing steady visual ﬁxation. Saccadic intrusions should
                                be distinguished from excessive distractibility, in
                                which case novel but behaviorally irrelevant visual
                                stimuli evoke inappropriate reﬂexive saccades. The
                                spectrum of saccadic intrusions ranges from small
                                square wave jerks in normal subjects to the large
                                pathologic saccadic oscillations of ocular ﬂutter and
                                opsoclonus [110]. Ocular ﬂutter and opsoclonus are
                                of particular clinical relevance to distinguish from
                                nystagmus and other oscillations because of their
                                strong association with paraneoplastic or parainfec-
                                tious encephalitis [59, 97].
                                3.1.1. Square-wave jerks: Pairs of small hori-
                                zontal conjugate saccades (typically < 2 degrees) that
                                take the eyes away from the ﬁxation position and then
                                return them after an interval of about 200 to 400 ms.
                                Comment: Square wave jerks often occur in
                                series and are common in normal subjects, though
                                may be more frequent or larger in elderly subjects.
                                They may become almost continuous, though still
                                <2 Hz, in certain cerebellar, brainstem, and cerebral
                                hemispheric diseases, in which case they have been
                                called square-wave oscillations. Macrosquare-wave
                                jerks refer to large (typically >5 degrees) 2-3 Hz
                                saccadic oscillations with an intersaccadic interval
                                of about 70–150 ms that often occur in bursts of
                                varying amplitude.
                                3.1.2. Macrosaccadic oscillations: Oscillations
                                around a ﬁxation point due to saccadic hypermetria,
                                typically consisting of runs of (usually horizontal)

                                saccades that build up and then decrease in amplitude,
                                with intersaccadic intervals of about 200 ms.
                                Comment: Macrosaccadic oscillations reﬂect sac-
                                cadic dysmetria in which primary and corrective
                                saccades are so hypermetric that they continue over-
                                shooting the target and oscillate around the intended
                                ﬁxation point. They are most commonly associated
                                with lesions affecting the cerebellar fastigial nucleus
                                or its output pathways in the superior cerebellar
                                peduncle.
                                3.1.3. Saccadic Pulses: Saccadic pulses are brief
                                intrusions upon steady ﬁxation caused by an unin-
                                tended saccade away from the ﬁxation position,
                                sometimes followed by an immediate drift back.
                                Comment: Single saccadic pulses are followed by a
                                drift back to the original position, suggesting absence
                                of a step signal (pulse-step mismatch) [102]. Dou-
                                ble saccadic pulses consist of an initial saccade away
                                from ﬁxation followed immediately by a return sac-
                                cade back to ﬁxation [7, 94]. Saccadic pulses may
                                sometimes occur in a series or alternate directions.
                                3.1.4. Ocular ﬂutter: Intermittent bursts of con-
                                jugate horizontal saccades without an intersaccadic
                                interval, often beginning after a voluntary saccade.
                                Comment: The oscillation frequency is typically
                                10–25 Hz, higher with small-sized movements. If
                                very small (microﬂutter), they might be only seen
                                with an ophthalmoscope or recording device.
                                3.1.5. Opsoclonus: Combined conjugate multidi-
                                rectional (horizontal, vertical, and torsional) saccadic
                                oscillations without an intersaccadic interval that
                                interfere with steady ﬁxation.
                                Comment: The saccadic oscillations of opsoclonus
                                are typically large and are present during pursuit,
                                convergence, blinks, eyelid closure, and sleep.
                                3.1.6. Voluntary saccadic oscillations: Also
                                referred to as voluntary ﬂutter or voluntary nystag-
                                mus, some normal subjects can voluntarily induce
                                conjugate high-frequency saccadic oscillations that
                                are usually conﬁned to the horizontal plane.
                                Comment: The same saccadic oscillations some-
                                times occur “involuntarily” as a functional disorder
                                and may be superimposed upon smooth pursuit
                                movements. Such oscillations can generally be dis-
                                tinguished from pathologic ocular ﬂutter since they
                                are usually not sustained and are often accompanied
                                by convergence (and pupillary constriction), facial
                                grimacing, or eyelid ﬂutter.
                                Terms not recommended: Voluntary nystagmus
                                (since the oscillations occur without a slow phase
                                movement and so are technically not a form of nys-
                                tagmus); psychogenic ﬂutter


                                S.D.Z. Eggers et al. / Classiﬁcation of nystagmus and nystagmus-like movements 81

                                3.2. Other nystagmus-like movements: Some
                                oscillatory eye movements do not solely represent
                                saccadic movements but also do not ﬁt the strict def-
                                inition of jerk or pendular nystagmus.
                                3.2.1. Convergence-retraction nystagmus: A
                                condition in which upward saccades or fast phases
                                are replaced by rapid convergent or retractory (pulling
                                the globes into the orbit) eye movements, or both.
                                Comment: Convergence-retraction nystagmus is
                                almost invariably caused by lesions of the dorsal mid-
                                brain in the region of the posterior commissure and
                                is associated with impaired upgaze. Convergence-
                                retraction nystagmus is typically elicited by having
                                the patient attempt to make a voluntary upward
                                saccade or track a downwardly moving optokinetic
                                tape or drum, thus inducing rapid upward conver-
                                gent or retractory eye movements. The retraction can
                                best be seen by watching the globe while observ-
                                ing the patient from the side. It remains unsettled
                                scientiﬁcally whether the convergent movements are
                                abnormal opposed adducting saccades or a disor-
                                der of the vergence system or both [125, 131]. It
                                resembles but is not truly a jerk nystagmus. Pretectal
                                pseudobobbing, which may be a form of convergence
                                nystagmus seen in acute obstructive hydrocephalus,
                                consists of non-rhythmic, rapid movements that carry
                                the eyes downward and medially with a frequency of
                                about 0.3 to 2 Hz, followed by a slow return to central
                                position [90].
                                3.2.2. Ocular oscillations in spasmus nutans:
                                Intermittent, small amplitude, high frequency, pre-
                                dominantly horizontal pendular oscillations that vary
                                in their amplitude and phase relationship between the
                                two eyes attributed to spasmus nutans.
                                Comment: These “shimmering oscillations” usu-
                                ally develop in the ﬁrst year of life as part of an
                                early-life syndromic triad including irregular head
                                nodding and anomalous head positions, then remit
                                after a few years. Spasmus nutans can be distin-
                                guished from infantile or latent nystagmus by its
                                intermittency, vertical component, high frequency,
                                and dissociated features.
                                3.2.3. Ocular bobbing and its variants: Several
                                related types of spontaneous eye movements may
                                be encountered in patients with decreased levels of
                                consciousness (Fig. 4). Though their pathophysiol-
                                ogy may differ from other forms of spontaneous jerk
                                nystagmus, their waveforms have both slow and fast
                                components and have similar frequencies and ampli-
                                tudes to each other.
                                Comments: Classic ocular bobbing consists of
                                intermittent, usually conjugate, rapid downward eye

                                Fig. 4. Schematic summary of the waveforms of ocular bobbing
                                and its variants. Adapted from Leigh and Zee [109].

                                movements followed by a slower return to the
                                straight-ahead position. Reﬂex horizontal eye move-
                                ments are usually absent. Classic ocular bobbing is
                                usually a sign of intrinsic pontine lesions such as
                                hemorrhage or extrinsic compression. Ocular dip-
                                ping consists of intermittent, usually conjugate, slow
                                downward eye movements followed by a rapid return
                                to the straight-ahead position. Reverse ocular bob-
                                bing consists of intermittent, usually conjugate, rapid
                                upward eye movements followed by a slower return
                                to the straight-ahead position. Reverse ocular dip-
                                ping consists of intermittent, usually conjugate, slow
                                upward eye movements followed by a rapid return
                                to the straight-ahead position. Ocular bobbing and
                                reverse ocular bobbing may be forms of single sac-
                                cadic pulses [140].
                                Previous term for ocular dipping: Inverse ocular
                                bobbing
                                Previous term for reverse ocular dipping: Con-
                                verse bobbing
                                3.2.4. Superior oblique myokymia: Bursts of
                                small, irregular, high-frequency monocular oscil-
                                lations attributed to abnormal discharges of the
                                trochlear nerve.
                                Comment: Eye movement recordings have demon-
                                strated initial intorsion and depression followed by
                                irregular small oscillations [108]. These tiny oscil-
                                lations may only be visible with ophthalmoscopy or
                                close inspection of the conjunctival vessels during
                                attacks.


                                82 S.D.Z. Eggers et al. / Classiﬁcation of nystagmus and nystagmus-like movements

                                3.2.5. Ping-pong gaze: Slow continuous horizon-
                                tal conjugate deviation of the eyes, alternating every
                                few seconds [58, 79].
                                Comment: Ping-pong gaze is typically seen in
                                obtunded patients with severe bilateral cerebral hemi-
                                spheric dysfunction but has also been described in
                                collicular infarction [117]. It may be smooth in deeply
                                obtunded patients or comprised of many small sac-
                                cades in patients whose level of consciousness is
                                higher [84, 142]. The frequency of approximately
                                0.25 Hz is too low to be considered pendular nystag-
                                mus. Ping-pong gaze should be distinguished from
                                periodic alternating gaze deviation (2.1.2.1.2.), con-
                                sisting of horizontal conjugate deviation of the eyes
                                alternating right and left approximately every 2 min-
                                utes [136].
                                Term not recommended: Ocular clonus, a term that
                                has been used in criteria for serotonin toxicity [47]
                                but is likely referring to ping-pong gaze [51, 77, 128].
                                3.2.6. Pendular pseudonystagmus: Pendular
                                ocular oscillations due to the combination of head
                                tremor and vestibular hypofunction.
                                Comment: Pendular pseudonystagmus is due to
                                an inadequate vestibulo-ocular reﬂex that is unable
                                to stabilize gaze during the oscillating movements
                                of head tremor. Patients may experience oscillopsia,
                                and though no nystagmus is present on examination,
                                the examiner may mistakenly diagnose pendular nys-
                                tagmus due to oscillation of the optic disc during
                                ophthalmoscopy. It is “pseudo” nystagmus because
                                it disappears once the head is stabilized. It can occur
                                with central vestibular disorders such as multiple
                                sclerosis or in those with bilateral peripheral vestibu-
                                lopathy [27, 137].

                    .Objectives  
                    • Describe the peripheral and central components of the vestibular system  
                    • Describe the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) and adaptation of the VOR after a vestibular insult  

                    .Peripheral Vestibular Anatomy  
                    • 3 Semicircular canals  
                    • Horizontal  
                    • Anterior (superior)  
                    • Posterior (inferior)  
                    • Sense angular velocity  
                    • 2 Otolith organs  
                    • Utricle  
                    • Saccule  
                    • Linear acceleration  

                    Created with BioRender.com  

                    .Motion Detection  
                    • Semicircular canals  
                    • Hair cells in cupula respond to deflection of the cupula and produce signal to the vestibular nerve that the head is rotating  
                    • Otolith organs  
                    • Otoconia on gelatinous membrane deflect hair cells with linear acceleration  

                    .Cupula  
                    Example of what an actual cupula looks like within a semicircular canal

                    • See how the labyrinths lie on the temporal bone  
                    • The cochlea faces towards the nose

                    .Orientation of Semicircular Canals  
                    Figure 21.7 O’Sullivan text  

                    .Vestibular Projections
                    • Ocular – Eye movements  
                    • Vestibulo-Ocular Reflex (VOR)  
                    • Spinal – Postural Balance and Head Position  
                    • Vestibulospinal Reflex (VSR)  
                    • Medial vestibulospinal pathway  
                    • Lateral vestibulospinal pathway  
                    • Vestibulocollic Reflex  
                    • Cerebral – spatial orientation  
                    • Autonomic  

                    .Vestibular Ocular Reflex 1
                    • The ratio of eye velocity to head velocity is referred to as the gain of the VOR  
                    • The ideal gain in a normal subject equals 1 (eye velocity/head velocity = -1)  
                    • VOR gain is reduced in persons with a unilateral vestibular dysfunction  
                    • A window into the labyrinth  
                    • Best way to assess the integrity of the peripheral vestibular system is to look at the outputs of the system  
                    • VOR  
                    • VSR  

                    .Vestibulo-ocular Reflex 2 (!!E)
                    • Responsible for maintaining the stability of an image on the fovea of the retina during head movements  
                    • The VOR generates a rapid compensatory eye movement in the opposite direction of head rotation  

                    .Vestibulospinal Reflex  
                    • VSR is elicited by head tilt that activates the otolith organs  
                    • VSR pathway  
                    • Vestibular afferents synapse with lateral vestibulospinal tract neurons  
                    • The lateral vestibulospinal tract neurons signal lower motor neurons innervating antigravity muscles that stabilize posture  
                    • If the head and body are tilted to the right, the vestibulospinal reflex laterally flexes the left side of the trunk to return the body to upright (B)  

                    .Vestibular Connections to Cerebellum  
                    • Cerebellum plays critical role in:  
                    • Vestibular plasticity  
                    • Motor control  
                    • Response to injury  

                    .What Happens When There is Vestibular System Dysfunction? (!!E.f).Lv1.Q&A (!!T)
                        • Peripheral  
                            • Acute unilateral vestibulopathy  
                            • Bilateral vestibulopathy  
                            • Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)  
                        • Central  
                            • Cardiovascular accident (PICA or AICA)  
                            • Traumatic brain injury  
                            • Cerebellar disorders  
                            • Multiple sclerosis  

                    Lundy Ekman Chapter 21; Figure 21-17  

                    .Peripheral Vestibulopathy (!!E) (See [xxx_] 00:00sec) ← Açò està molt ben explicat en un OnLive video xo no m'enrocorde quin

                    .Vestibular Plasticity (!!E)
                    • Habituation: decreased response with repeated stimulation  
                    • Adaptation: per-stimulus response decline (sometimes used interchangeably with habituation)  
                    • Compensation: changes in vestibular responses following a peripheral vestibular abnormality

                    .VOR Compensation
                    • Unilateral peripheral vestibular injury  
                    • Cerebellum ‘turns off’ the system due to the significant asymmetry in vestibular nuclei  
                    • Vestibular nuclei on the lesion side increases activity (from other sources)  
                    • Static compensation occurs  
                    • Resolution of spontaneous nystagmus in room light and symptoms at rest occurs within days  

                    .Dynamic Vestibular Compensation of the VOR
                    • Retinal slip or “image motion” on the retina, when associated with head movement in room light is likely what drives VOR compensation  
                    • The retinal slip is probably the error signal that the brain tries to minimize  
                    • Necessary to have a healthy vestibulocerebellum for full compensation  
                    • Over time, there is a rebalancing of firing rate in the vestibular nuclei (reducing right-left difference)  
                    • Individuals who are well-compensated for a unilateral peripheral vestibular loss will be asymptomatic with most activities   

                    .Central Vestibular Disorders (!!E).Q&A
                    • Traumatic brain injury  
                    • Multiple sclerosis  
                    • Cerebellar disorders  
                    • Cardiovascular accident (PICA or AICA)  

                    .Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)  
                    • Most common cause of vestibular dysfunction  
                    • Mechanical dysfunction of the peripheral vestibular system  
                    • Otoconia are misplaced from the otolith organs into the semicircular canals  
                    • When the head is moved relative to gravity, the otoconia move in the canal and cause the endolymph to move, deflecting the cupula  
                    • This causes excitation to the vestibular nuclei resulting in dizziness, nausea, and vomiting (often associated with position change)  

                    .Summary  
                    • The peripheral vestibular organs include the 3 semi-circular canals and 2 otolith organs (utricle and saccule)  
                    • Peripheral vestibular dysfunction often results in reduced gain of the VOR which affects dynamic visual acuity (visual acuity during head/body motion)  
                    • Adaptation of the VOR is driven by retinal slip and can be promoted with vestibular rehabilitation exercises to improve gaze stabilization

                .('23 Signs and Symptoms.pdf')
                    Faculty

                    Neuromuscular PT1

                    Department of Physical Therapy

                    Pam Dunlap, DPT, PhD

                    .Signs and Symptoms of Vestibular Disorders


                    • Identify common signs and symptoms caused by vestibular 
                    dysfunction
                    • Describe how nystagmus is named 
                    • Identify physiologic causes of normal and pathologic nystagmus
                    • Describe how to examine a patient for nystagmus

                    .Objectives 


                    .Common Symptoms
                    • Dizziness
                    • Vertigo
                    • Lightheadedness
                    • Disequilibrium
                    • Oscillopsia

                    • Duration, timing, and circumstances of 
                    symptoms
                    • Constant vs. Episodic
                    • Associated with movements, 
                    positions, or at rest
                    • Associated with other symptoms 
                    (headache, nausea, diplopia)

                    Symptom Possible Causes
                    Vertigo BPPV, unilateral peripheral or central lesion, migraine
                    Light-headedness Orthostatic hypotension, hypoglycemia, anxiety, panic disorder, 
                    PPPD
                    Disequilibrium Bilateral peripheral lesions, chronic unilateral lesions, 
                    somatosensory loss, central lesions
                    Adapted from Table 21.2 O’Sullivan 


                    .Patient-Reported Outcome Measures
                    Measures of body functions (ICF)
                    • Dizziness Visual Analogue Scale
                    • 0-10
                    • Severity of dizziness symptoms
                    • Visual Vertigo Analogue Scale
                    • 0-100 
                    • Severity of dizziness in visually 
                    challenging environments

                    Measures of Activity and 
                    Participation
                    • Dizziness Handicap Inventory (DHI)
                    • 25 questions
                    • Total score: 0-100
                    • Higher score = greater disability due 
                    to dizziness
                    • MCID=18
                    • Activity-Specific Balance Confidence 
                    Scale (ABC)
                    • 0-100%
                    • Higher score = greater confidence 
                    in balance
                    • Scores <67% associated with falls 
                    risk

                    .Observation
                        • Cranial nerve signs
                            • Ocular misalignment
                            • Facial asymmetry
                            • Nystagmus
                        • Head tilt
                        • Postural control
                        • Gait

                    .Observation of Nystagmus
                    • One can have physiologic nystagmus (normal) or pathologic 
                    nystagmus
                    • Has slow and fast phases
                    • Slow phase reflects function of VOR
                    • Beating direction named after fast phase
                    oE.g., left beating nystagmus, fast phase to left

                    .Components of Nystagmus

                    .Examination of Nystagmus 
                        • Observe the position of the eye in the orbit
                        • Check with fixation
                        • Observe the direction of the nystagmus
                        • Observe the head position
                            Any of the above can affect what eye movements you see and will help you to determine what is the PT diagnosis

                    .Physiologic (Normal) Nystagmus
                        • Vestibular induced (caloric, rotational)
                        • Visually induced (optokinetic)
                        • End-gaze

                    .Vestibular Induced Nystagmus
                    Caloric Testing
                    Rotational Chair testing

                    .Visually Induced (Optokinetic) Nystagmus

                    .End-Gaze Nystagmus

                    .Abnormal Nystagmus (!!E)
                        • Congenital Nystagmus
                            • No fast or slow phase
                        • Acquired Nystagmus
                            • Spontaneous: nystagmus seen in primary position in room light
                            • Positional: nystagmus that is provoked with certain positions (BPPV)
                            • Gaze evoked: nystagmus which changes direction with gaze

                    • The slow component of the nystagmus reflects the VOR 
                    response to the underlying pathology
                    • The direction of the fast component defines the repositioning of 
                    the eye driven by the parapontine reticular formation
                    • Therefore, the direction of the fast phase is opposite the side of 
                    the lesion
                    • REMEMBER: NYSTAGMUS WILL BEAT TOWARD THE MORE 
                    NEURALLY ACTIVE SIDE

                    .Peripheral Vestibular Nystagmus, continued ('') ← Diagram.(!!E).Lv1
                    • Follows Alexander’s Law
                    • Looking in the direction of the fast 
                    component of the nystagmus increases 
                    the amplitude and frequency of the 
                    nystagmus
                    • Looking in the opposite direction of the 
                    fast component decreases the amplitude 
                    and frequency of the nystagmus
                    • Visual fixation will decrease the intensity of 
                    peripheral nystagmus

                    Hotson JR, Baloh RW. N Engl J Med 1998;339:680-685.

                    .Spontaneous Nystagmus
                    Without visual fixation With fixation
                    From: Luxon L.  Textbook of Audiological Medicine, 2003

                    Right beating 
                    nystagmus

                    Nystagmus stops 
                    with fixation

                    .Peripheral Nystagmus, Continued (!!E)
                    • First degree nystagmus: seen only 
                    when looking toward the fast phase of 
                    the nystagmus
                    • Second degree nystagmus: seen in 
                    primary gaze position AND when 
                    looking toward the fast phase of the 
                    nystagmus
                    • Third degree nystagmus: present 
                    when looking away from the fast 
                    phase, in primary gaze, AND when 
                    looking toward the fast phase of the 
                    nystagmus

                    .Positional Nystagmus (!!E)
                    • Persistent positional nystagmus can be an indication of a central disorder (but 
                    can be peripheral)
                    • Transient positional nystagmus is characteristic of BPPV (but can also be central)

                    .Gaze-Evoked Nystagmus (and Downbeat)

                    .Downbeat Nystagmus

                    .Summary
                    • Nystagmus has a fast and slow phase and is named for the fast 
                    phase
                    • When assessing for nystagmus, observe the eyes, the position of the 
                    eyes and head, and the direction of the fast phase
                    • Nystagmus that does not change direction and decreases or stops 
                    with visual fixation is indicative of peripheral nystagmus
                    • Gaze evoked, downbeat, or nystagmus that increases or stays the 
                    same with visual fixation is indicative of central nervous system 
                    involvement

                    Faculty

                    Neuromuscular PT1

                    .Neurologic Exam in Persons with Vestibular Disorders Part 1

                    Department of Physical Therapy

                    Pam Dunlap, DPT, PhD

                    .Objectives
                    • Describe the components of the neurologic PT exam for persons with 
                    vestibular disorders
                    • Describe specific tests for oculomotor function

                    .Neurologic PT Exam for Persons with Vestibular Disorders (!!E).Q&A doc
                    Priorities
                    • Cranial nerve exam
                    • Vestibular-specific tests and 
                    measures
                    • Balance Exam
                    • Functional Exam

                    .History (!!E).Q&A doc
                        • HPI, PMH, Medications
                        • Onset, duration, frequency, intensity, and timing of signs and symptoms can help guide differential diagnosis
                        • Precipitating factors, co-occurring symptoms
                        • Identification of red flags
                        • Identification of comorbidities
                        • Self-reported activity limitations and participation restrictions
                        • Fall history
                        • Patient goals

                    .History of Present Illness and Past Medical History (!!E).Lv1.Q&A doc
                        History of Present Illness
                            • Symptoms
                                • Balance loss
                                • Dizziness/vertigo
                                • Nausea
                                • Headache
                                • Blurry Vision
                                • Space and motion discomfort
                            • Onset
                                • Gradual
                                • Sudden
                                • Traumatic

                        Past Medical History
                            • Migraine
                            • Anxiety
                            • Depression
                            • Strabismus/ocular misalignment
                            • Previous eye surgery
                            • Impaired cognition
                            • Impaired vision
                            • Impaired hearing, tinnitus, fullness
                            • Diabetes mellitus

                    .Review of Systems
                        • Cardiovascular/pulmonary
                            • Vital signs
                        • Musculoskeletal
                            • Gross symmetry, ROM, strength with functional movements
                            • Cervical range of motion: prior to VOR assessments and positional tests
                        • Communication and cognitive abilities, psychological state and affect

                    .Mental status, cognitive function 
                        • Screening or detailed assessment, depending on patient presentation
                        • Should not be impacted directly by peripheral vestibular disorders
                        • May be impacted with central vestibular disorders (depending on diagnosis)
                        • Cognitive impairment may be a comorbidity

                    .Cranial Nerve Exam
                        • Cranial nerve assessment is a priority for persons with vestibular disorders
                        • We can use the eyes to assess vestibular function via the VOR but first need to 
                        make sure the eyes are functioning normally
                        • Priorities:
                            • Cranial nerve 2: visual acuity, visual fields, pupillary light reflex
                            • Cranial nerve 3, 4, and 6: oculomotor alignment and function
                                • Ocular ROM
                                • Smooth pursuits
                                • Saccades
                            • Cranial nerve 8: hearing screen, head impulse test/VOR assessment
                        • May also include a screen of other cranial nerves

                    .Ocular range of motion
                        • Observe the eyes at rest 
                        • Ask your patient to look in all 9 quadrants
                            • Observe for range of movement
                            • Observe for alignment
                            • Observe for any nystagmus
                            • Observe for a drift back to the center position (impaired gaze holding)
                                • The patient will need to hold in eccentric gaze for up to 30 seconds

                        This Photo by Unknown Author is licensed under CC BY-SA

                    .Smooth Pursuits
                        • Smooth pursuit eye movements are not affected by peripheral vestibular loss 
                        • Smooth pursuit movement is at <60°/s
                        • Pursuit eye movements enable the individual to visually pursue a moving object across the visual field without making compensatory head movements
                        • Damage to the smooth pursuit system is often caused by cerebellar lesions


                    .Assessment of smooth pursuits
                        • Examiner should present a specific target (e.g., fingertip, point of a pen)
                        • The target should be about 3 feet from the patient
                        • The examiner should ask the patient to follow the target without moving their head
                        • The examiner should slowly move the target from side to side
                        • Important to note the smoothness and conjugacy of the eye movement
                            • Do the eyes move together?
                            • Do the eyes move smoothly?
                        • Repeat moving the target up and down
                        • Smooth pursuit dysfunction may appear saccadic or “choppy” and would indicate central (brain) involvement

                    .Saccades
                        • Saccadic eye movements are rapid voluntary movements that allow re-foveation of stationary targets 
                        • Move at 350-600°/sec
                        • Series of saccadic eye movements are used when we read
                        • Impaired function may be indicative of a central nervous system lesion


                    .Assessment of saccades
                        • Examiner should use 2 specific targets (e.g., fingertips, pen tips)
                        • Targets should be about 3 feet from the target and oriented about 1.5 feet from midline to each side
                        • The examiner instructs the patient to move their eyes as quickly as possible from one target to the other (side to side) without moving their head
                        • Re-orient the targets vertically and repeat asking the patient to look up and down
                        • Examiner should note speed, conjugacy, latency, accuracy
                        • Abnormal findings include slow saccades, hypermetric (overshooting), or hypometric (undershooting), and/or restricted amplitude


                    .Abnormal saccades often indicate central nervous system involvement
                        • Parkinson’s disease
                        • Progressive supranuclear palsy
                        • Intranuclear ophthalmoplegia
                        • Drug intoxication
                        • Olivopontocerebellar atrophy
                        • Huntington’s disease
                        • Cranial nerve 3, 4, 6 palsy

                    .Vergence
                        • Convergence
                            • Adduction of both eyes together allowing for binocular fixation on a target
                        • Divergence
                            • Symmetrical abduction of both eyes as a visual target moves away from the face

                    .Assessment of Vergence
                        • Examiner asks the patient to focus on a target (14-point font) held at arms length
                        • The patient should focus on the target as it is moved toward their nose
                        • Measure near point of convergence
                            • Point at which the image doubles or eyes diverge
                            • Repeat at least 3 times and average
                        • >5 cm is abnormal indicating convergence insufficiency
                        • Convergence insufficiency is present in 35-55% of individuals after mild traumatic brain injury

                    .Ocular alignment
                        • Strabismus: A general term for misalignment
                        • Amblyopia: decreased acuity from disuse due to strabismus 
                        • Tropia: misalignment or deviation of the visual axes, visible in room light with both eyes open
                        • Phoria: misalignment without binocular fixation on an object
                        • Abnormal alignment of the eye
                            oEso: deviation medially
                            oExo: deviation laterally
                            oHyper: deviation upward
                            oHypo: deviation downward

                    .Cover/Uncover Test 
                        • Cover test: assessing for tropias
                        • Ask the patient to focus on a far target (approximately 10 feet)
                        • Cover one eye with an occluder
                        • Look for any movement in the opposite eye
                            • Movement in = exotropia
                            • Movement out = esotropia
                            • Movement up = hypotropia
                            • Movement down = hypertropia
                        • Repeat in opposite eye
                        • Normal alignment: no movement of either eye 

                    .Cross Cover Test 1
                        • Cross cover test: assessing for phorias (if cover test was normal)
                            • Ask the patient to focus on a far target (approximately 10 feet)
                            • Cover one eye with an occulder 
                            • Hold for a few seconds then quickly move to cover the opposite eye and repeat
                            • Look for movement in the eye that is being uncovered (look at the occlude as you uncover the eye)
                                • Movement in = exophoria
                                • Movement out = esophoria
                                • Movement up/down = hyper/hypo-phoria

                    .Cover Uncover Test 2 ¿?.Com quedem?! Les imatges confundixen!

                    .Cross Cover Test: Exophoria

                    .Why assess ocular alignment
                        • Provides a baseline prior to an assessment of VOR and vestibular-specific tests
                        • Rule out red flags
                        • Better estimate prognosis
                        • Determine treatment strategies, specific interventions
                        • Identify appropriate referrals or need for concurrent treatments

                    .Skew Deviation 1
                        • Vertical misalignment of the eye due to a central nervous system lesion
                        • Can be obvious with observation
                        • Identified with cross cover test
                            • Will see one eye move up and one eye move down

                    .Skew Deviation 2

                    .Cranial nerve 8 auditory screening 1
                    • Can screen hearing by rubbing the fingers next to the 
                    patient’s ears and asking if they hear both sides equally
                    • Weber test
                    • Use a 512-Hz or 256-Hz tuning fork
                    • Place the base of the tuning fork on top of the 
                    patient’s head in midline
                    • The patient is asked if they hear ringing louder in 
                    one ear than the other

                    .Cranial nerve 8 auditory screening 2
                    • Rinne Test
                    • Ask the patient to close their eyes
                    • Place tuning fork on mastoid process and ask 
                    them to tell you when the sound is no longer 
                    heard
                    • Then move the tuning fork next to the ear and 
                    ask the patient if the vibration is heard again
                    • The patient should be able to hear the sound 
                    through the air after bone conduction has 
                    ceased (air conduction > bone conduction)

                    .Summary
                    • The clinical oculomotor exam for persons with vestibular disorders 
                    includes tests for gaze holding, smooth pursuit and saccadic eye 
                    movement, convergence, and ocular alignment
                    • Oculomotor findings may guide treatment, determine prognosis, and 
                    identify needs for referral and/or red flags

                .('25 Vestibular Exam Part 2.pdf')
                    .Neurologic Exam in Persons with Vestibular Disorders Part 2

                    .Neurologic PT Exam for Persons with Vestibular Disorders
                        Priorities
                        →• Cranial nerve exam
                        • Vestibular-specific tests and 
                        measures
                        • Balance Exam
                        • Functional Exam

                    .Vestibular-specific tests
                        • VOR
                        • Head impulse test (HIT)
                        • Head shake test (head shaking nystagmus)
                        • Dynamic visual acuity test (DVA)
                        • Vibration-induced nystagmus
                        • VORx1
                        • VOR cancellation
                        • Positional testing for BPPV

                    .Head Impulse Test
                        • Assessment of semicircular canal function (angular VOR)
                        • Ask the patient to look at a target in midline (usually examiner’s nose)
                        • The patient’s neck should be flexed about 30 degrees 
                        • Grasp the head and rotate it slowly 15-20 degrees to the right or left and 
                        then briskly return the head to the center
                        • Head ‘impulse’ should be:
                        • Small amplitude (5-15 degrees)
                        • Moderate velocity (approximately 200 deg/sec)
                        • High acceleration (3,000-4,000 deg/sec2)
                        • Head impulse should be delivered with unpredictable timing and direction 
                        for optimal sensitivity

                    .Head Impulse Test considerations
                        • Normal response: The patient should be able to focus on the central target 
                        (eyes will move in the opposite direction of the head movement)
                        • Vestibular loss: the VOR will not move the eyes as quickly as the head 
                        rotation, causing a “corrective” saccade to re-fixate on the target
                        • Unilateral vestibular hypofunction: corrective saccade will be present when 
                        the head is rotated toward the side of the lesion
                        • Bilateral vestibular hypofunction: corrective saccade will be present in both 
                        directions
                        • Sensitivity of the HIT for identifying vestibular hypofunction was 71% for 
                        UVH and 84% for BVH
                        (Schubert MC et al., 2004)

                    .('')

                    .Normal Impulse Test ('')

                    .Abnormal Head Impulse Test ('')

                    .Head Impulse Nystagmus Test of Skew (HINTS)
                        • Cluster of tests to help identify central causes from peripheral causes of acute 
                        dizziness
                        • Often used in ED settings among individuals with acute dizziness/vertigo with 
                        spontaneous nystagmus
                        ``• Among individuals with acute dizziness and spontaneous nystagmus, findings that indicate a central pathology include any of the following: (!!E)
                               • Presence of NORMAL head impulse test (HIT)
                               • Direction-changing nystagmus with gaze (gaze evoked nystagmus)
                               • Skew deviation with cover test
                        • Sensitivity 100%; Specificity 96% (more specific than early MRI)
                        Kattah et al., 2009

                    .Head Shake Test 1
                        • Can aid in diagnosis of a unilateral peripheral vestibular disorder
                        • Vision should be occluded
                        • The patient is instructed to close their eyes 
                        • The examiner flexes the head by about 30 degrees and then 
                        oscillates the head horizontally for 20 cycles at the frequency of 2 
                        repetitions per second (2 Hz)
                        • The patient is then asked to open their eyes
                        • The examiner should observe for nystagmus

                    .Head Shake Test 2
                        • Normal response: no nystagmus present
                        • Unilateral vestibular hypofunction: horizontal nystagmus with the 
                        quick phase beating toward the healthy ear (slow phase toward the 
                        lesioned ear)
                        • Presence of vertical nystagmus post-head shaking could indicate a 
                        central lesion
                        • The nystagmus occurs because of the asymmetry of vestbulo-ocular 
                        reflex (VOR) 
                        • Positive findings have been related to the degree of caloric weakness

                        (Zee, in Herdman SJ, 2000; Perez P et al, 2004)

                    .Head shaking nystagmus ('')

                    .Dynamic Visual Acuity Test
                        • A measure of visual acuity during horizontal motion of the head
                        • Clinical version and instrumented (computerized) versions
                        • First, the examiner should determine static visual acuity for the patient by 
                        asking them to read an eye chart (identify the lowest complete line)
                        • Then, the examiner rotates the patient’s head to the right and left at 2 
                        cycles per second (2 Hz) while the patient reads the eye chart again
                        • Identify the difference between static and visual acuity (how many lines 
                        were lost with dynamic visual acuity)
                        • Normal response: loss of 2 lines or less
                        • A loss of greater than 2 lines is indicative of vestibular hypofunction

                    .Dynamic Visual Acuity ('')

                    .Vibration Induced Nystagmus (Iwasa H et al., 1983)
                        • Vibration is applied over the mastoid 
                        (60 Hz) 
                        • It was never seen in people without 
                        disease, seldom with central disease, 
                        and only rarely in people with BPPV
                        • 92% of people with peripheral vestibular 
                        disorders had a positive response
                        • With unilateral vestibular loss, persons 
                        had horizontal nystagmus with slight 
                        torsion with the fast phase beating 
                        towards the strong ear

                        (Hamann and Schuster, 1999)

                    .Vibration Induced Nystagmus ('')

                    .VOR Cancellation
                        • We need to suppress the VOR sometimes during eye-head movement so that the image 
                        can stay on the fovea
                        • To assess, the patient should sit and focus on a target or thumb held at arm’s length
                        • The head and body/arm should rotate together approximately 80 degrees to each side at 
                        a comfortable speed 
                        • The patient should maintain gaze on the target
                        • Normal response: the eyes will maintain focus on the target
                        • Abnormal response: presence of corrective saccades or inability to focus on the target 
                        (indicates a central lesion)
                        • Peripheral vestibular lesions will not lead to impaired VOR cancellation
                        • However, patients with peripheral vestibular lesions may become symptomatic with this 
                        test


                    .Other vestibular-specific tests and measures
                        • Positional testing for BPPV (reviewed in detail in another module)

                    .Sensory, Motor, and Coordination Assessment
                        • May also prioritize in the assessment of persons with vestibular disorders depending on:
                           • Diagnosis (central versus peripheral)
                           • PMH, comorbidities
                           • Patient presentation
                           • Exam findings

                    .Balance Exam
                        • Modified Clinical Test for Sensory Interaction in Balance (mCTSIB)
                        • Computerized Dynamic Posturography
                        • Functional Gait Assessment (FGA)
                        • Dynamic Gait Index (DGI)
                        • Berg Balance Scale

                        Eyes open Eyes closed Eyes open Eyes closed

                        mCTSIB

                    .Functional Exam
                        • 5xSTS
                        • Timed up and go (TUG)
                        • Gait speed
                        • Assessment of positioning that brings on symptoms

                    .Summary
                        • Clinical tests for VOR function and gaze stability include the head impulse test, 
                        the head shaking test, and the dynamic visual acuity test
                        • Positive findings in clinical tests of VOR function and gaze stability are often 
                        indications of peripheral vestibular hypofunction
                        • Often, the aspects of the neurologic exam that are prioritized for persons with 
                        vestibular disorders are the cranial nerve exam, vestibular-specific tests and 
                        measures, balance, and function assessments
                        • Other aspects of the neurologic exam should be included as appropriate

                        • Subtests

                            oCalorics

                    .Positional Testing
                        • Purpose: test effect of different head positions within the gravitational field
                        • Slow movement into stationary position
                            oSitting
                                ▪ Head left & right
                            oSupine
                                ▪ Head straight, left, & right
                            oRight decubitus (side lying)
                            oLeft decubitus
                            oPre-caloric position
                                ▪ Head & shoulders elevated 30° from supine

                    .Positional Nystagmus
                        • Criteria for clinical significance 
                            oSlow Component Velocity (SCV) > 5 deg/s in any position
                            oSCV < 6 deg/s – persistent in 4+ positions
                            oSCV < 6 deg/s – sporadic in all positions
                        • Interpretation
                            oSomething wrong with vestibular system – hard to localize
                            oDirection fixed all positions – probably peripheral
                            oDirection changing - central until proven otherwise
                            oNystagmus with visual fixation – probably central

                    • Subtests
                        oOculomotor evaluation
                        oPositional tests
                        oBPPV tests (Dix – Hallpike, Roll)
                            ▪Been There, Done That
                        oCalorics
                        oRotational Chair
                        oHead Impulse Test (HIT)
                        oVestibular Evoked Myogenic Potentials

                    .Vestibular Lab Test Battery
                        • Know innervation for end-organs
                        • Oculomotor tests 
                        oSince vestibular tests measure eye movements 
                        (mostly), need to make sure eyes are working
                        • Positional tests 
                        oStatic – not BPPV
                        oTell you if something is wrong, but not where

                    • Purpose: Test sensitivity of horizontal 
                    canal to thermally-induced endolymph 
                    movement
                    • Thermal gradient using water or air
                    • Position: horizontal canal in the 
                    vertical plane
                    • Warm (44° C) and cool (30° C) water 
                    or air into external auditory canal 
                    • Each ear tested alone
                    • Normal response is nystagmus and

                    .Semicircular Canal Testing- Comparing - Frequency Ranges ('')
                    • Nystagmus:
                    o Cold
                    o Opposite
                    o Warm
                    o Same

                    measuring the velocity of the 
                    slow component, which reflects 
                    the intensity of the vestibular 
                    response
