                    .Central Vestibular Disorders

                    Department of Physical Therapy®py

                    Pam Dunlap, DPT, PhD


                    .Objectives
                    • Describe common findings associated with central 
                    vestibular disorders
                    • Identify appropriate management and referral sources 
                    for central vestibular disorders

                    .Central Causes of Dizziness
                        • Degenerative conditions
                            • Cerebellar degeneration
                            • Multiple sclerosis
                        • Acquired conditions
                            • Traumatic brain injury (concussion reviewed in another module)
                            • CVA, TIA
                        • Other
                            • Vestibular migraine
                            • Functional disorders (persistent postural perceptual dizziness)
                            • Psychiatric diagnoses
                            • Arnold-Chiari malformation
                            • Tumor

                    .Typical Central Signs and Symptoms
                        Γ Same as '.('32...::Central Signs and Symptoms — Red Flags'
                        • Cranial nerve signs
                            • Changes in pupillary size
                            • Ptosis
                            • Difficulty with swallowing
                        • Other neurologic signs
                            • Downbeat nystagmus
                            • Cerebellar signs and symptoms
                            • Headaches 
                            • Associated head injuries/cervical dysfunction
                            • A sense of tilting by the patient
                            • Changes in sensation
                            • A positive Babinski, increased DTR’s, or clonus
                            • Impaired gait/ataxia

                    .Vestibular Migraine
                        • The most common central vestibular disorder (1-2.7% of general population)
                        • Characterized by episodic dizziness (minutes to hours)
                            • Internal vertigo (sensation of self-motion)
                            • External vertigo (sensation that visual surround is spinning)
                            • Positional vertigo, occurring with change in head position
                            • Visually-induced vertigo triggered by complex visual scene/stimulus
                            • Head motion-induced vertigo occurring during head motion
                            • Head motion-induced dizziness with nausea
                        • Other symptoms
                            • Nausea/vomiting
                            • Transient auditory symptoms
                            • Unsteadiness

                    .Vestibular Migraine: Diagnostic Criteria
                        • At least 5 episodes with vestibular symptoms of moderate or severe intensity lasting 5 minutes to 72 hours
                        • Current or previous history of migraine with or without aura according to the International Classification of Headache Disorders (ICHD)
                        • One or more migraine features with at least 50% of vestibular episodes
                            • Headache with at least 2 of the following:
                                • One sided location
                                • Pulsating quality
                                • Moderate or severe pain
                                • Aggravation by routine physical activity
                            • Photophobia or phonophobia
                            • Visual aura
                        • Not better accounted for by another vestibular or ICHD diagnosis
                        Lempert et al, 2021

                    .Provoking Factors for Vestibular Migraine
                        • Lack of sleep
                        • Stress
                        • Menstruation
                        • Dehydration
                        • Food triggers
                            • Caffeine
                            • Additives/preservatives

                    .Vestibular Migraine vs. BPPV
                        • Vestibular migraine may present with positional vertigo, which mimics BPPV
                        • The positional nystagmus is usually persistent with a slower velocity than is consistent with the what one typically sees with classic BPPV
                        • Episodes of dizziness or vertigo due to vestibular migraine are usually more frequent than BPPV recurrences
                        • Complicating factor: BPPV is more common in patients with migraine
                            • Therefore, may be co-existing with vestibular migraine

                    .Migraine and Meniere's Disease
                        • The overlap between the two conditions in some people makes 
                        diagnosis difficult
                        • Migraine is more common in persons with Meniere's Disease (MD) 
                        compared to healthy controls
                        • Pathophysiologic relationship between migraine and MD is uncertain
                        • Fluctuating hearing loss, aural pressure, tinnitus, photophobia and 
                        migraine auras can occur in both conditions 
                        • For diagnosis of both, the patient would need to meet the criteria for 
                        each condition separately

                        (Johnson GD, 1998; Radke T et al., 2002; Radtke A et al., 2011; 
                        Brantberg K and Baloh RW, 2011; Lempert T et al, 2012)

                    .Management for Vestibular Migraine
                        • Lifestyle modification
                            • Avoidance of triggers, balanced diet
                            • Staying hydrated
                            • Regular activity
                            • Sleep hygiene 
                            • Address medication overuse
                        • Pharmacological management
                            • Medications for acute headache events (abortive)
                            • Preventative medications
                        • Vestibular rehabilitation

                         B. Amitriptyline

                    .Vestibular Migraine of Childhood
                        • Episodic syndrome in children associated with migraine
                        • Five episodes of vestibular symptoms of moderate or severe intensity lasting between 5 minutes to 72 hours
                        • A current or past history of migraine with or without aura
                        • One or more migraine features with at least 50% of vestibular episodes
                            • Headache with at least 2 of the following:
                                • One sided location
                                • Pulsating quality
                                • Moderate or severe pain
                                • Aggravation by routine physical activity
                            • Photophobia or phonophobia
                            • Visual aura
                        • Age < 18 years
                        • Not better accounted for by another headache disorder, vestibular disorder, or other condition
                        Van de Berg et al, 2021

                    .Vascular Vertigo
                        Etiology
                            • Stroke or transient ischemic attack
                                • PICA
                                • AICA
                                • Labyrinthine infarct
                            • Vertebral artery 
                            insufficiency/compression
                        Presentation
                            • Can present similar to AUVP (acute vestibular syndrome)
                                • Dizziness
                                • Nausea or vomiting
                                • Head motion intolerance
                                • Unsteadiness 
                            • Can be prolonged (symptoms lasting 24 hours or more) or transient (lasting <24 hours)

                    .PICA infarct (Haines atlas)
                        • Results in damage to the dorsolateral medulla (PICA syndrome, Wallenberg syndrome, lateral medullary syndrome) 
                        • In some cases, the lateral medullary syndrome may result from occlusion of the vertebral artery at the origin of the PICA with consequent loss of flow into PICA
                        • Structural Damage
                            • Anterolateral system fibers
                            • Spinal trigeminal tract and nucleus
                            • Nucleus ambiguus, roots of 9th and 10th nerves
                            • Descending hypothalamospinal fibers
                            • Vestibular nuclei (mainly inferior and medial)
                            • Restiform body and spinocerebellar fibers
                        • Deficits:
                            • Contralateral loss of pain and thermal sense on body
                            • Ipsilateral loss of pain and thermal sense on face and in the oral cavity
                            • Dysphagia, soft palate paralysis, hoarseness, diminished gag reflex
                            • Ipsilateral Horner syndrome (miosis, ptosis, anhidrosis, flushing of face)
                            • Nausea, diplopia, tendency to fall to ipsilateral side, nystagmus, vertigo
                            • Ataxia to the ipsilateral side

                    .AICA infarct
                        • Supplies the middle cerebellar peduncle, lower lateral pons, anteroinferior surface of the cerebellum, flocculus and the choroid plexus of the lateral ventricle.
                        • The labyrinthine artery (branch of AICA) supplies labyrinth and cochlea of the inner ear along with CN VII and CN VIII
                        • Signs and symptoms:
                            • sudden onset of severe vertigo, nausea, vomiting, nystagmus (vestibular nuclei)
                            • ipsilateral hemiataxia (middle cerebellar peduncle)
                            • ipsilateral, lower motor neuron facial weakness, ipsilateral loss of lacrimation and salivation, ipsilateral loss of taste from anterior 2/3rd of tongue and loss of corneal reflex (CN VII nucleus and nerve)
                            • ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature from the face (spinal trigeminal nucleus) 
                            • ipsilateral hearing loss and tinnitus (cochlear nuclei)
                            • ipsilateral Horner's syndrome (descending sympathetic tracts)
                            • contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation from the body (lateral spinothalamic tract). 

                    .Vascular Vertigo Diagnostic Criteria
                        Acute prolonged vascular vertigo 
                            • Acute vertigo, dizziness, or unsteadiness lasting for 24 hours or more
                            • Imaging evidence of ischemia or hemorrhage in the brain or inner ear, which corresponds to signs, symptoms, and findings
                            • Not better accounted for by another disease or disorder
                        Transient vascular vertigo or acute vascular vertigo in evolution
                            • Acute vertigo, dizziness, or unsteadiness lasting < 24 hours
                            • Imaging evidence of ischemia or hemorrhage in the brain or inner ear, which corresponds to signs, symptoms, and findings
                            • Not better accounted for by another disease or disorder
                        Kim et al, 2022

                    .Probable Vascular Vertigo Diagnostic Criteria
                        Prolonged
                            • Acute vertigo, dizziness, or unsteadiness lasting for 24 hours or more
                            • At least one of the following:
                                • Focal central neurologic signs and symptoms (hemiparesis, sensory loss, dysarthria, dysphagia, ataxia)
                                • At least one component of the HINTS exam
                                • Other central oculomotor abnormalities (central nystagmus, impaired smooth pursuit or saccades)
                                • Increased risk for vascular events (atrial fibrillation, ABCD2 score of 4 or more)
                            • Not better accounted for by another disease or disorder
                        Transient
                            • Acute vertigo, dizziness, or unsteadiness lasting for more than 3 hours but not yet 24 hours
                            • At least one of the following:
                                • Focal central neurologic signs and symptoms or severe ataxia
                                • At least one component of the HINTS exam
                                • Other central oculomotor abnormalities (central nystagmus, impaired smooth pursuit or saccades)
                                • New onset of moderate to severe craniocervical pain
                                • Increased risk for vascular events (atrial fibrillation, ABCD2 score of 4 or more)
                            • Not better accounted for by another disease or disorder
                            Kim et al, 2022

                    .Functional and Psychiatric Disorders
                        • Persistent postural perceptual dizziness (PPPD)
                            • Chronic vestibular condition
                            • Functional disorders: A change in the mode of action of an organ without structural change
                            • May be precipitated by structural vestibular and/or psychological disorders
                            • Generalized anxiety disorder
                            • Panic disorder
                            • Phobias
                            • Fear of falling
                            • Acrophobia

                    .Common features of psychophysiological dizziness 1 
                        (Baloh, 1998)
                        • Describe floating, swimming in head, spinning in head
                        • Complain of tension headaches, palpitations, gastric disorders
                        • Symptoms may be constant but are increased with stress, certain 
                        situations, hyperventilation, or cardiac arrhythmias
                        • May see syncope and/or paresthesia

                    .Common features of psychophysiological dizziness 2
                        (Baloh, 1998)
                        • Features of panic attacks:
                            • Shortness of breath
                            • Choking
                            • Chest pain
                            • Nausea
                            • Shaking
                            • Fear of dying
                            • Loss of control
                            • Sweating
                            • Palpitations

                    .PPPD: Diagnostic Criteria
                        • One or more symptoms of dizziness, unsteadiness, or non-spinning vertigo are present on most days for 3 months or more
                            • Symptoms last for prolonged periods of time but may fluctuate in severity
                            • Symptoms need not be continuous throughout the day
                        • Persistent symptoms occur without specific provocation but are exacerbated by three factors:
                            • Upright posture
                            • Active or passive motion without regard to direction or position
                            • Exposure to moving visual stimuli or complex visual patterns
                        • The disorder is precipitated by conditions that cause vertigo, unsteadiness, or problems with balance (acute, episodic, or chronic vestibular syndromes, neurologic or medical illnesses, or psychological distress
                        • Symptoms cause significant distress or functional impairment
                        • Symptoms are not better accounted for by another disease or disorder

                    .('')
                        Persons with PPPD showed gray matter volume decreases in the temporal cortex, precentral 
                        gyrus, hippocampus, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, caudate nucleus, cingulate cortex, and 
                        cerebellum compared to control subjects

                    .Chiari Malformation Signs and Symptoms
                        • Headache
                        • Neck pain
                        • Vertigo
                        • Balance problem
                        • Weakness
                        • Dysphagia
                        • Downbeat nystagmus
                        • Vertigo with neck extension

                        This Photo by Unknown Author is licensed under CC BY-NC

                    .Multiple Sclerosis
                        • Focal neurologic signs
                            • Oculomotor impairments
                            • UMN signs
                            • Ataxia, gait disturbances
                        • Recurrent spontaneous attacks of vertigo (due to lesions in brainstem, cerebellum, vestibular and/or visual pathways)
                        • Vertical nystagmus that is non fatiguing
                        • If person is 20-40 years old with the above symptoms, suspect MS

                    .Post-Traumatic Dizziness
                        • Temporal bone fracture
                        • Concussion (mTBI)
                        • Moderate to severe TBI
                        • Whiplash injuries
                            • Cervical vertigo

                    .Summary
                        • Disorders of the CNS that cause dizziness can include vascular disorders, 
                        degenerative disorders, psychiatric disorders, functional disorders, among 
                        others
                        • It is important to recognize the signs and symptoms of central vestibular 
                        disorders so that the patient can be managed appropriately
                        • Some signs and symptoms of central vestibular disorders can mimic peripheral 
                        disorders, so it is important to conduct a thorough neurologic PT exam

                    ``.(Γ)I need a clear way to differentiate between "Vestibular Migraine", "Meniere's Disease", "Vascular Vertigo" (in general), "PICA infarct", "AICA infarct", "psychophysiological dizziness", "PPPD", "Chiari Malformation", "Multiple Sclerosis", and "Post-Traumatic Dizziness" when a patient comes to the clinic. Make up challenging cases and quiz me as usual.

                    .Peripheral Vestibular Disorders

                    .Objectives
                        • Describe common signs and symptoms associated with peripheral 
                        vestibular disorders
                        • Describe and demonstrate tests and measures used in a PT 
                        examination for persons with peripheral vestibular disorders
                        • Describe typical medical management for persons with peripheral 
                        vestibular disorders

                    .Peripheral Vestibular Disorders (!!E)
                        • Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (covered elsewhere)
                        • Acute Unilateral Vestibulopathy
                        • Chronic Unilateral Vestibulopathy
                        • Bilateral Vestibulopathy
                        • Other peripheral vestibular disorders
                            • Labyrinthitis
                            • Meniere’s Disease
                            • Ramsay Hunt Syndrome
                            • Superior Canal Dehiscence
                            • Acoustic neuroma/vestibular schwannoma (may be mixed central/peripheral)

                    .Acute Unilateral Vestibulopathy (AUVP) ('')
                        • Synonymous with vestibular neuritis (!!E).Lv1
                        • Pathophysiology
                            • Inflammation of the vestibular nerve
                        • Likely etiology (!!E)
                            • Viral
                            • Autoimmune
                            • Vascular

                    .Diagnostic Criteria for AUVP
                        • Acute or subacute onset or sustained spinning or non-spinning vertigo of moderate to severe intensity lasting at least 24 hours
                        • Spontaneous peripheral vestibular nystagmus
                            • Generally horizontal-torsional
                            • Direction-fixed (unidirectional)
                            • Enhanced by removal of visual fixation
                        • Unambiguous evidence of reduced VOR function on the side opposite the direction of the fast phase of the nystagmus
                            • HIT (preferred vHIT), caloric test
                        • No evidence of acute central neurological or audiological symptoms 
                        • No acute central neurological or audiological signs (skew deviation, gaze-evoked nystagmus)
                        • Not better accounted for by another disease process or disorder
                        Strupp et al, 2022

                    .AUVP: Typical Symptom Report
                        • Dizziness
                            • Spinning (vertigo), oscillopsia
                            • Initially constant then decreasing in severity/frequency
                            • May be worse with head motion/position changes
                        • Poor balance but usually can ambulate
                        • Nausea/vomiting initially
                        • Onset may be associated with an upper respiratory/viral illness

                    .AUVP: Atypical Symptom Report
                        • Hearing loss, tinnitus, fullness may indicate other peripheral or central disorders
                        • Headache (more frequently seen in persons with central disorders)
                        • Inability to walk/ataxic gait
                        • Diplopia (double vision)
                        • Lightheadedness

                    .AUVP: Typical Signs
                        • Acutely, spontaneous nystagmus will be seen in room light
                            • Direction-fixed (unidirectional)
                            • More intense without visual fixation
                            • Typically, horizontal-torsional
                        • Within days, the static VOR should compensate
                        • After static compensation of the VOR, may still see nystagmus but not as severe as that seen acute phase
                            • May only see with fixation blocked
                            • May only see first or second-degree nystagmus compared to third degree

                    .AUVP: Medical Management
                        Medication Management
                            • Treatment with methylprednisolone tapering dose schedule
                                • Research is mixed regarding the effectiveness of steroid management for long-term outcomes
                            • Medications for symptom management
                                • Antiemetics for nausea
                                • Anticholinergics, antihistamines
                        Tests and Measures
                            • Vestibular function testing
                                • Caloric test
                                • Rotational chair
                                • VEMPs
                                • vHIT
                            • May have had MRI to rule out central diagnoses
                        Early Vestibular Rehabilitation = better outcomes for AUVP!

                    .What PT Tests and Measures Should be Used?
                        • Screen for central neurologic signs and auditory symptoms
                            • Hearing screen
                            • HINTS
                            • Neurologic exam (cranial nerve, UMN, cerebellar signs)
                        • Oculomotor assessment
                        • VOR assessment
                        • Positional testing (BPPV present in 15-20% of individuals with peripheral vestibular disorders)
                        • Balance, gait, functional exam 

                    .AUVP: PT Exam Findings
                        • No central vestibular or neurologic signs
                            • No UMN, cerebellar signs
                            • Normal oculomotor exam
                        • No hearing loss
                        • Positional testing
                            • May or may not have co-occurring BPPV
                        • VOR assessments
                            • Positive HIT
                            • Positive head shake test
                            • Positive DVA
                            • Positive vibration-induced nystagmus
                        • Balance, gait, functional exam
                            • Difficulty standing on foam with eyes closed (condition 4 mCTSIB)
                            • Difficulty walking with head turns
                            • Difficulty with turns, quick head movements, position changes

                    .When to Refer Out
                        • They have new headaches with the onset of the vertigo
                        • If you note neurologic signs and symptoms
                        • If the vertigo has not improved at all within 48 hours
                        • New onset hearing loss with the onset of vertigo
                        • HINTS exam positive

                    .Chronic Unilateral Vestibulopathy
                        • Typically refers to those who have had symptoms for > 3 months
                        • Dynamic VOR may be uncompensated or only partially compensated
                        • Potential factors that may impact recovery:
                            • Comorbidities
                                • Number of comorbid conditions
                                • Binocular vision abnormalities
                                • Cognitive impairment
                                • Anxiety
                                • Depression
                                • CNS diagnoses
                            • Long-term vestibular suppressant medication use
                            • Avoidance of movement, activity
                        • Individuals with Chronic Unilateral Vestibulopathy still benefit from vestibular rehabilitation
                        Hall et al, 2021

                    .Chronic Unilateral Vestibulopathy Findings
                        • Spontaneous nystagmus should not be present
                        • May see nystagmus with fixation blocked, although may only be first degree
                        • VOR assessments
                            • Clinical HIT may or may not be positive
                            • vHIT would likely be positive
                            • Head shake, DVA, vibration-induced nystagmus may or may not be positive
                        • Balance, gait, and functional assessments
                            • Likely difficulty on condition 4 of mCTSIB
                            • Difficulty with higher level gait involving head turns, turning, etc. 

                    .Bilateral Vestibulopathy
                        • Bilateral impairment or loss of peripheral vestibular input
                        • Results in deficits such as:
                            • Impaired VOR
                            • Impaired VSR
                            • Difficulty with spatial orientation, navigation, and memory
                        • Likely etiology
                            • Result of ototoxic drugs (antibiotics, chemotherapy, loop diuretics)
                            • Bilateral Meniere’s disease
                            • Meningitis/Inflammation
                            • Tumors
                            • Autoimmune disease
                            • Genetic factors

                    .Bilateral Vestibulopathy: Diagnostic Criteria
                        • Chronic vestibular syndrome with unsteadiness when walking or standing and at least 1 of the following:
                            • Movement-induced blurred vision or oscillopsia during walking or quick body movements
                            • Worsening of unsteadiness in darkness or on uneven ground
                        • No symptoms when sitting or lying down (static conditions)
                        • Bilaterally reduced or absent angular VOR 
                            • vHIT
                            • Caloric response
                            • Rotational chair
                        • Not better accounted for by another disease 
                        Strupp et al, 2017

                    .Bilateral Vestibulopathy: Typical Signs and Symptoms
                        • Oscillopsia: visual jumping of the environment with movement
                        • Postural instability
                        • Gait impairments (wide based)
                        • History of falls
                        • Vertigo not usually described

                    .Bilateral Vestibulopathy: PT Exam Findings
                        • VOR assessment
                            • HIT: positive bilaterally
                            • DVA: usually significant loss of visual acuity with head movement (>2 lines)
                        • Balance assessment
                            • Loss of balance eyes closed
                            • Difficulty with conditions 2, 4, and sometimes 3 of mCTSIB
                        • Gait assessment
                            • Gait deviations (wide based gait, gait may appear ataxic)
                            • Difficulty on uneven surfaces, low light conditions
                        • Should guard the patient closely when assessing balance and gait!

                    .Bilateral Vestibulopathy: Patient Example ('')

                    .Labyrinthitis
                        • Inflammation of the entire labyrinth (blue in figure)
                        • Symptoms are similar to AUVP
                        • Typically, also experience:
                            • Hearing loss
                            • Ear pain
                            • Tinnitus (ringing)
                        • Management similar to AUVP
                        • Important to refer out if you find hearing loss and/or ear symptoms

                    .Pattern of Symptoms
                        ### 📋 Table Transcription

                        | Disorder                        | Tempo                            | Symptoms                              | Circumstance                                     |
                        |------------------------------------|--------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|
                        | Reduced Vestibular Function        |                                      |                                           |                                                      |
                        | Acute Unilateral Vestibulopathy    | Sudden onset; acute dizziness        | Vertigo, imbalance, N/V, oscillopsia      | Spontaneous, exacerbated by head movement            |
                        | Labyrinthitis                      | Sudden onset; acute dizziness        | As above; hearing loss; tinnitus          | Spontaneous, exacerbated by head movement            |
                        | Chronic Unilateral Vestibulopathy  | Chronic dizziness                    | Dizziness, imbalance                      | Induced by head movement; complex environment        |
                        | Bilateral Vestibulopathy           | Post-treatment with ototoxic medications | Imbalance, oscillopsia                | Imbalance and/or oscillopsia with movement           |

                        ### 🗂️ Outline Transcription

                        1. Reduced Vestibular Function
                           - Acute Unilateral Vestibulopathy
                             - Tempo: Sudden onset; acute dizziness
                             - Symptoms: Vertigo, imbalance, N/V, oscillopsia
                             - Circumstance: Spontaneous, exacerbated by head movement
                           - Labyrinthitis
                             - Tempo: Sudden onset; acute dizziness
                             - Symptoms: As above; hearing loss; tinnitus
                             - Circumstance: Spontaneous, exacerbated by head movement
                           - Chronic Unilateral Vestibulopathy
                             - Tempo: Chronic dizziness
                             - Symptoms: Dizziness, imbalance
                             - Circumstance: Induced by head movement; complex environment
                           - Bilateral Vestibulopathy
                             - Tempo: Post-treatment with ototoxic medications
                             - Symptoms: Imbalance, oscillopsia
                             - Circumstance: Imbalance and/or oscillopsia with movement

                    .Meniere’s Disease
                        • Synonymous with endolymphatic hydrops
                        • Accumulation of endolymph in the cochlear duct and the vestibular organs
                        • Etiology: likely combination of genetic and environmental factors
                        • Prevalence increases with age
                        • Associated with comorbid conditions such as:
                            • Arthritis
                            • Psoriasis
                            • Gastroesophageal reflux disease
                            • Irritable bowel syndrome
                            • Migraine 
                        Lopez-Escamez et al, 2015

                        Image from: https://thehearingdoctor.com/hearing-resources/menieres-disease/ 

                    .Meniere’s Disease Diagnostic Criteria
                        • Two or more spontaneous episodes of vertigo lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours
                        • Audiometric findings: low to medium frequency sensorineural hearing loss in one ear during or after one of the vertigo episodes
                        • Fluctuation aural symptoms
                            • Hearing
                            • Tinnitus
                            • Fullness
                        • Not better accounted for by another vestibular diagnosis
                        Lopez-Escamez et al, 2015

                    .Meniere’s Disease Typical Signs and Symptoms
                        • Acute dizziness/vertigo lasting hours
                        • Nausea/vomiting
                        • Aural symptoms: hearing loss, tinnitus, fullness on the affected side
                        • Drop attacks

                    .Meniere's Disease: Medical Management
                        • Dietary recommendations: limit sodium and caffeine
                        • Vestibular rehabilitation between attacks
                        • Pharmacological management
                            • Diuretic medication
                            • Vasodilators, immunotherapy?
                            • Intratympanic steroids
                        • Vestibular ablation
                            • Intratympanic gentamycin
                            • Surgical
                            • Vestibular neurectomy
                            • Labyrinthectomy
                        • Endolymphatic sac surgery
                            Nevoux et al, 2018

                    .Ramsay Hunt Syndrome
                        • Herpes zoster (shingles) infection of CN VII/VIII
                        • Clinical presentation:
                            • Initially burning ear pain and blisters, vertigo, hearing disorders and facial paresis
                            • The symptoms can begin before the skin rash or even without a skin rash
                        • Treatment
                            • Corticosteroids
                            • Antiviral therapy
                            • Pain management
                            • Vestibular rehabilitation for vertigo and balance issues
                            • Facial nerve therapy

                    .Superior Canal Dehiscence 
                        • Sound and/or pressure-induced vertigo due to bone dehiscence of the superior semicircular canal
                        • Abnormality identified on CT temporal bones as dehiscence of the SCC
                        • Signs and symptoms
                            • Loud sounds caused objects in visual surround to move
                            • Dizziness induced by sneezing, laughing, coughing, heavy lifting (Valsalva)
                            • Conductive hearing loss (low frequency)
                            • Hear their voice, heartbeat or even their eyes movements in the affected ear
                            • Tulio phenomenon: Recorded eye movements in response to sounds 
                            • Hennebert sign: eye movements induced by pressure in the external auditory canal

                    .Tulio’s Phenomenon ('')

                    .Superior Semicircular Canal Dehiscence: Treatment
                        • Conservative management
                            • Ear plugs
                            • Minimize Valsalva, scuba diving, popping ears
                        • Surgical
                            • For those with debilitating auditory or vestibular symptoms and positive clinical findings and CT findings
                        • Vestibular rehab may be helpful pre and/or post surgery
                        Image from: https://scds.info/ 

                    .Cochlear Implants & Vestibular Implants
                        Cochlear implants
                            • For profound hearing loss
                            • Children with cochlear implants may have poorer balance compared to children of similar age without cochlear implant
                        Vestibular implants
                            • Ongoing research
                            • For those with profound bilateral vestibular loss

                    .Summary
                        • Patients with acute unilateral vestibular hypofunction often present 
                        with vertigo, imbalance, nausea, and spontaneous nystagmus
                        • Patients with unilateral vestibular hypofunction often display positive 
                        findings on the following clinical tests: head impulse test, head 
                        shaking test, clinical DVA
                        • Medical management for acute peripheral vestibular hypofunction 
                        often includes oral corticosteroids

                    .Visual or Verbal Analogue Scale
                        • Scales of 0-10 for dizziness are helpful to determine if persons with vestibular disorders become symptomatic during their exercises
                            00 - no symptoms
                            010 - worst symptoms that they have ever experienced (need to go to the emergency room)

                            1. 0 - No symptoms
                            2. 1–3 - Mild
                            3. 4–6 - Moderate
                            4. 7–9 - Severe
                            5. 10 - Worst symptoms that they have ever experienced (need to go to the emergency room)

                    .('')
                        1. Please choose from 0 to 10 corresponding to your perceived difficulty of each exercise:
                            - 0: Extremely easy
                            - 1: Easy
                            - 2: Easy
                            - 3: Somewhat easy
                            - 4: Somewhat easy
                            - 5: Somewhat hard
                            - 6: Somewhat hard
                            - 7: Hard
                            - 8: Hard
                            - 9: Extremely hard
                            - 10: Extremely hard

                        2. Please choose from A to E corresponding to your perceived difficulty of each exercise:
                            - A: I feel completely steady
                            - B: I feel a little unsteady or off-balance
                            - C: I feel somewhat unsteady or like I may lose my balance
                            - D: I feel very unsteady or like I definitely will lose my balance
                            - E: I lost my balance

                    .Vestibular Adaptation
                        • Induced by retinal slip, i.e., movement of visual images across the retina
                        • Retinal slip results in an error signal that the brain attempts to minimize 
                        • Over time, there is a rebalancing of the firing rate in the vestibular nuclei
                            • Reducing the asymmetry
                            • Increasing the VOR gain

                    .Principles of the Adaption Approach
                        • CNS response to exercise takes time
                        • Adaptation is context specific - exercises should stress the system in different ways (frequency, position, direction)
                        • Encourage mental effort to improve response
                        • Patients should always work at their limit of ability 

                    .Adaption Exercises: Gaze Stability Exercises
                        • X1 viewing exercises (VORx1):
                            • Head moving while visually fixating on a stationary target
                        • VORx1 with vergence:
                            • Head moving while visually fixating on a target moving toward the nose
                        • X2 viewing exercises (VORx2):
                            • Head moving while visually fixating on a moving target

                    .Adaption Exercises: X1 viewing
                        • Hold or place a business card with a letter (i.e., hold an “X” at arms length or tape to the wall)
                        • Turn head side to side or up and down 20 – 300 in either direction
                        • Maintain clear and stable target

                    .Increasing the VOR gain
                        • Do VORx1 with vergence 

                    .Adaption Exercises: X2 viewing
                        • Hold a business card with a letter (i.e., an “X” at arms length)
                        • Turn head side to side or up and down 10-15 degrees in either direction while moving the target in the opposite direction
                        • Maintain clarity of target 

                    .Guidelines for Performing Adaptation Exercises
                        • Target must be clear when doing the exercise
                        • Head movement:
                            • ~20- 30°
                            • Must be smooth
                            • Should be practiced horizontally & vertically
                        • Observe eye movements to make sure they are focused on the target
                        • Push upper limits of patient ability – find the “just right” challenge!
                        • Can use a metronome so that you have an idea of how fast they are moving
                        • Goal: 1-2 minute of continuous gaze stability exercise 4-6 times/day

                    .Progression of Adaptation Exercises
                              I. Duration  
                               A. 1 ➔ 2 minutes per exercise  

                              II. Frequency  
                               A. 2 ➔ 5 times per day  

                              III. Velocity  
                               A. Increase head speed while keeping target in focus  

                              IV. Target Size  
                               A. Large ➔ Small  

                              V. Target Distance  
                               A. Near ➔ Far  

                              VI. Background  
                               A. Simple ➔ Complex  

                              VII. Position of Patient  
                               A. Supported Sitting ➔ Walking  

                              VIII. Support Surface  
                               A. Firm ➔ Compliant  

                              IX. Stance  
                               A. Wide ➔ Narrow BOS
                        
                    .X1 Viewing Exercise: Complex Background ('')

                    .Substitution Exercises for dizziness/oscillopsia
                        • Purpose: To foster the use of alternative strategies to replace the lost or compromised vestibular function (often bilateral loss)
                        • Goals:
                            Improve gaze stabilization
                            Maximize postural stability
                            Central preprogramming
                            Use of other strategies:
                                Corrective eye saccades
                                Slowed head movements
                                Increase use of smooth pursuit

                    .Substitution Exercises
                        • Eye-Head Saccade Exercise
                            Facilitates use of saccadic or smooth pursuit strategies and central pre-programming
                        • Remembered/Imaginary Targets
                            Improve voluntary control and central pre-programming

                    .Eye-Head Saccade Exercise
                        • Hold two targets at eye level 25-30 cm apart, head in midline
                        • Move eyes to one target
                        • Maintain eyes on target and turn head to same target
                        • Shift eyes to second target
                        • Move head to second target
                        • Repeat in opposite direction

                    .Remembered/Imaginary Targets
                        • Place target directly in front of you (patient should not hold the target)
                        • While looking at the target, close eyes
                        • Slowly turn head away while imagining the target 
                        • Open eyes and verify still focused on the target adjust gaze if necessary 
                        • Repeat in multiple directions and at variable speeds

                    .General Progression of Substitution Exercises
                        I. Duration  
                         A. 1 ➔ 2 minutes per exercise  

                        II. Frequency  
                         A. 2 ➔ 5 times per day  

                        III. Velocity  
                         A. Increase head speed while keeping target in focus  

                        IV. Target Size  
                         A. Large ➔ Small  

                        V. Target Distance  
                         A. Near ➔ Far  

                        VI. Background  
                         A. Simple ➔ Complex  

                        VII. Position of Patient  
                         A. Supported sitting ➔ Walking  

                        VIII. Support Surface  
                         A. Firm ➔ Compliant  
                         B. Wide ➔ Narrow BOS

                    .Habituation Exercises ('')
                        • Reduction of symptoms after repeated stimulation
                        • VOR cancellation can be used for habituation
                        • Virtual reality scenes and YouTube videos

                    .Binocular vision abnormalities
                        • Office-based therapy with home exercise program
                            • Pencil push-ups
                            • Brock string
                        • If not responding to treatment – refer out

                        This Photo by Unknown Author is licensed under CC BY-SA

                    .Adjunct treatments and patient education
                        • Diagnosis
                        • Lifestyle recommendations
                        • Treatment plan
                        • HEP
                        • Prognosis
                        • Transition toward independence/back to regular activity and participation
                        • Medications
                        • Psychologically-informed techniques
                        • Vision therapy
                        • Incorporate other team members as appropriate

                    .Summary
                    • Vestibular rehabilitation exercises include adaptation, substitution, 
                    and habituation training
                    • Adaptation training is prescribed to promote VOR adaptation and 
                    improve gaze stability
                    • Substitution training is often utilized in persons with bilateral 
                    vestibular loss to substitute other mechanisms (such as COR) for the 
                    VOR
                    • Habituation training is used to desensitize individuals to movements 
                    or visual scenes by providing graded exposure

                    3:36

                    3:39

                    3:43

                    3:48

                    3:53

                    3:57

                    5:16

                    11:01

                    11:08

                    11:11

                    11:17

                    11:35

                    11:55

                    11:59

                    12:07

                    15:13

                    15:18

                    PT2261 Neuromuscular PT1

                    .CPG for Peripheral Vestibular Hypofunction

                    .Vestibular Rehabilitation for Peripheral Vestibular Hypofunction: Updated Clinical Practice Guideline Guideline Development Group 
                    Courtney D. Hall, PT, PhD (team lead)
                    Susan J. Herdman, PT, PhD, FAPTA 
                    Susan L. Whitney, PT, PhD, NCS, ATC, 
                    FAPTA
                    Eric R. Anson, PT, PhD
                    Wendy J. Carender, PT, MPT, NCS
                    Carrie W. Hoppes, PT, PhD, NCS, OCS, 
                    ATC

                    2021, JNPT

                    .What’s New?
                    • Current evidence supports that vestibular physical therapy (VPT) provides clear and 
                    substantial benefit to individuals with UVH and BVH 
                    oNEW: 18 RCTs, 9 prospective and 8 retrospective cohort studies
                    • Support for a variety of balance training modalities 
                    oLow technology, virtual reality, optokinetic stimulation, platform perturbations, 
                    and vibrotactile feedback.
                    • Earlier initiation of VPT (<2 weeks of acute onset of UVH) may optimize 
                    rehabilitation outcomes
                    • Dosage recommendations for balance and gaze stability exercises
                    • Expanded recommendations on factors that may impact outcomes 
                    oMedications and mild cognitive impairment

                    .Earlier initiation of VPT

                    (Lacour et al., 2019)


                    (Lacour et al., 2019)

                    .Mechanisms underlying change may differ


                    .Is there a critical time to intervene with UVL?

                    (Lacour et al, 
                    2020)


                    .Action Statement 1: Effectiveness of Vestibular Rehabilitation in 
                    adults with acute and subacute unilateral vestibular hypofunction
                    • Clinicians should offer vestibular rehabilitation to patients with acute 
                    or subacute unilateral vestibular hypofunction. (Evidence quality: I; 
                    Recommendation Strength: Strong) 
                    • Level I. Based on 5 Level I randomized controlled trials and 4 Level II 
                    randomized controlled trials

                    .('')


                    .Action Statement 2: Effectiveness of Vestibular Rehabilitation in 
                    adults with chronic unilateral vestibular hypofunction. 
                    • Clinicians should offer vestibular rehabilitation to patients with chronic 
                    unilateral vestibular hypofunction. (Evidence quality: I; 
                    Recommendation Strength: Strong)
                    • Level I. Based on 3 Level I and 1 Level II randomized controlled trials 


                    .Action Statement 3: Effectiveness of Vestibular Rehabilitation in 
                    adults with bilateral vestibular hypofunction.
                    • Clinicians should offer vestibular rehabilitation to patients with 
                    bilateral vestibular hypofunction.  (Evidence quality: I; 
                    Recommendation Strength: Strong)
                    • Level I. Based on 4 Level I randomized controlled trials.


                    .Action Statement 4: (!!E) Effectiveness of saccadic or smooth pursuit 
                    exercises in persons with peripheral vestibular hypofunction (unilateral 
                    or bilateral). 
                    • Clinicians should not offer saccadic or smooth-pursuit eye exercises 
                    in isolation (i.e., without head movement) as specific exercises for 
                    gaze stability to patients with unilateral or bilateral vestibular 
                    hypofunction. (Evidence quality: I; Recommendation Strength: 
                    Strong) 
                    • Level I. Based on 3 Level I randomized controlled trials. 
                    • Poorer outcomes in patients performing only saccadic or smooth-
                    pursuit eye movements without head movement when compared to 
                    vestibular rehabilitation.


                    .Action Statement 5: Comparative Effectiveness of Different Vestibular 
                    rehabilitation modalities in individuals with vestibular hypofunction
                    • Clinicians may provide targeted exercise techniques to accomplish 
                    specific goals appropriate to address identified impairments and 
                    functional limitations. (Evidence quality: II; Recommendation 
                    strength: Moderate)
                    • Support for a variety of balance training modalities 
                    oLow technology, virtual reality, optokinetic stimulation, platform 
                    perturbations, and vibrotactile feedback


                    .('')
                    Balance training with 
                    vibrotactile belt improved 
                    balance in adults who had 
                    not achieved good outcomes 
                    with VPT (Brugnera et al., 
                    2015).

                    Coupling immersive virtual reality with head movement 
                    may provide additional benefit, including reduced 
                    symptoms and improved balance (Micarelli et al., 2017).

                    Balance exercises may be more 
                    enjoyable and less tiring using virtual 
                    reality (Meldrum et al., 2015).

                    .Action Statement 6
                        -Action statement 6a: optimal balance exercise dose in the treatment of individuals with peripheral vestibular hypofunction (unilateral and bilateral)
                            -Clinicians may prescribe static and dynamic exercises for a minimum of:
                                • No specific dosage recommendations for individuals with acute/subacute unilateral hypofunction at this time
                                • 20 minutes daily for at least 4-6 weeks for individuals with chronic unilateral hypofunction
                                • 20 minutes daily for 6-9 weeks for individuals with bilateral vestibular hypofunction
                                • Evidence quality: II; Recommendation strength: weak/expert opinion

                        -Action statement 6B: optimal gaze stabilization exercise dosage of treatment in persons with peripheral vestibular hypofunction (unilateral or bilateral)
                            -Clinicians may prescribe weekly clinic visits plus a home exercise program of gaze 
                            stability exercises consisting of a minimum of:
                                • 3 times per day for a total of at least 12 minutes per day for patients with acute/subacute vestibular hypofunction
                                • 3-5 times per day for a total of at least 20 minutes per day for patients with chronic vestibular hypofunction
                                • 3-5 times per day for a total of 20-40 minutes per day for approximately 5-7 weeks for individuals with bilateral vestibular hypofunction 
                                • Evidence Quality: II; Recommendation Strength: weak

                    .Action Statement 7: Effectiveness of supervised vestibular rehabilitation
                        • Clinicians should offer supervised vestibular physical therapy in individuals with unilateral or bilateral peripheral vestibular hypofunction. (Evidence Quality: I; Recommendation Strength: Strong)
                        • Evidence suggests that: 
                            oIndividuals drop out at higher rates when unsupervised 
                            oIndividuals older than 50 years of age may benefit more from supervision 
                            oIndividuals who are fearful of falling may not do well in an unsupervised program
                        • Regular in-person monitoring may be more beneficial than a remotely monitored HEP for individuals with UVH/BVH plus cognitive impairment (Varriano et al., 2019)

                    .Action Statement 8: Decision rules for stopping vestibular rehabilitation in individuals with peripheral vestibular hypofunction (unilateral and bilateral)
                        • Clinicians may use achievement of primary goals, resolution of symptoms, normalized balance and vestibular function, or plateau in progress as reasons for stopping therapy (Evidence Quality: II; Recommendation strength: Moderate)
                        • Ultimately, the individual decides whether to participate and when to stop
                        • Individuals with moderate to severe cognitive or mobility impairments may need additional treatment sessions.  
                            oThese individuals are often excluded in research, so stopping rules may not be appropriate for them  

                    .Action Statement 9: factors that modify rehabilitation outcomes
                        • Clinicians may evaluate factors that could modify rehabilitation outcomes.
                            (Age: Evidence quality: I; Recommendation strength: Strong; Other Factors: Evidence quality: II; Recommendation strength: Moderate)
                                oAge and gender do not affect rehabilitation potential for improvement
                                oParticipation in vestibular exercises results in improved outcomes regardless 
                                of time from onset in individuals with chronic UVH
                                    § Potential harm of delaying intervention warrants initiating rehabilitation as soon as possible
                                oCertain co-morbidities (anxiety, depression, peripheral neuropathy, migraine, abnormal binocular vision, and abnormal cognition) may negatively impact rehabilitation outcomes. 
                                    § Consider co-morbidities when setting goals and refer to other healthcare professionals as appropriate

                    .FACTORS THAT MODIFY REHABILITATION OUTCOMES
                        -Long-term use of vestibular suppressant medication may negatively impact an individual’s recovery
                        -Short-term use of low-dose antihistamines in individuals with chronic vestibular disorders may help control symptoms during VPT without negative impact on outcomes
                        -Exercise approaches should be designed to take these factors into account 

                    .Action Statement 10: the harm/benefit ratio for vestibular rehabilitation in terms of quality of life
                        • Clinicians should offer vestibular physical therapy to persons with peripheral vestibular hypofunction with the intention of improving quality of life. (Evidence quality: Level I; Recommendation strength: Strong)
                            oImproved quality of life and psychological outcomes of individuals undergoing VPT compared to controls
                        • Nearly half of individuals with BVH changed their driving habits, reported reduced participation in social activities and difficulties of daily living: 
                            oClinical Pearl: PT evaluation, treatment, and education should include these common activities to help address quality of life

                    .Additional Clinical Pearls
                        -Risk of fall-related injury may last up to one year after acute UVH 
                        -Fall prevention education is imperative for this population!
                        -Use of a balance rating scale to measure perceived intensity of balance exercises may assist in appropriate modifications to balance exercises (Alsubaie et al., 2019)
                        -Use of a balance rating scale to measure perceived intensity of balance exercises may assist in appropriate modifications to balance exercises (Alsubaie et al., 2019)

                    1:57
                    These types of exercises are indicated for individuals who report
                    2:01

            7.8. Module 7 Summary
            //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
            //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

                Well done! You have completed the second of six modules for Unit 2. Before moving on to the next module, remember to review these three key learnings: 

                It is important to be able to identify peripheral from central signs in persons with dizziness so that the appropriate treatment decision (and potential referral) can be made. 
                Clinical practice guideline supports the treatment of peripheral vestibular hypofunction with an individualized vestibular rehabilitation program. 
                Vestibular rehabilitation exercises fall into three main categories: adaptation, substitution, and habituation/optokinetic exercises and should be selected based on the functional impairments identified in the PT examination. 
                Learning Outcomes
                After completing this module, you can now: 

                Perform appropriate treatment interventions for clients with central and peripheral vestibular disorders. 
                Monitor clients progress and adjust treatment plan accordingly and determine need for additional referral for persons with vestibular disorders. 
                Provide appropriate patient education and follow up recommendations for persons with vestibular disorders. 
                Evaluate data from the PT examination for persons with vestibular disorders to make clinical judgements regarding the care of clients that is patient–centered, evidence-based, and individualized.

        Module 8: Diagnosis and Management of Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)
        //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
        //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////


            //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
            //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
            8.0. Module 8 Introduction
            //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
            //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

                Welcome to Module 8 of Unit 2. This week, you will learn about specific tests and measures used to diagnose persons with benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV). You will also learn evidence-based interventions for individuals with BPPV including canalith repositioning maneuvers as well as the importance of patient education. 

                Learning Objectives
                By the end of this week, you will be able to: 

                Perform appropriate treatment interventions for clients with benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV). 
                Perform appropriate patient education and follow up recommendations for persons with benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV).


            //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
            //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
            8.1. Background Readings and Materials
            //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
            //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

                Read the following resources before engaging with the rest of the module. 
                    Bhattacharyya N, et al. (2017) Clinical Practice Guideline: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (Update).
                        .('Clinical Practice Guideline - Benign.pdf')
                            https://doi.org/10.1177/0194599816689667

                            Otolaryngology–
                            Head and Neck Surgery
                            2017, Vol. 156(3S) S1–S47
                            © American Academy of 
                            Otolaryngology—Head and Neck 
                            Surgery Foundation 2017
                            Reprints and permission:  
                            sagepub.com/journalsPermissions.nav
                            DOI: 10.1177/0194599816689667
                            http://otojournal.org

                            Sponsorships or competing interests that may be relevant to content are 
                            disclosed at the end of this article.

                            Abstract
                            Objective. This update of a 2008 guideline from the American 
                            Academy of Otolaryngology—Head and Neck Surgery Foun-
                            dation provides evidence-based recommendations to benign 
                            paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), defined as a disorder of 
                            the inner ear characterized by repeated episodes of position-
                            al vertigo. Changes from the prior guideline include a consum-
                            er advocate added to the update group; new evidence from 
                            2 clinical practice guidelines, 20 systematic reviews, and 27 
                            randomized controlled trials; enhanced emphasis on patient 
                            education and shared decision making; a new algorithm to 
                            clarify action statement relationships; and new and expanded 
                            recommendations for the diagnosis and management of BPPV.
                            Purpose. The primary purposes of this guideline are to improve 
                            the quality of care and outcomes for BPPV by improving the 
                            accurate and efficient diagnosis of BPPV, reducing the inappro-
                            priate use of vestibular suppressant medications, decreasing 
                            the inappropriate use of ancillary testing such as radiographic 
                            imaging, and increasing the use of appropriate therapeutic re-
                            positioning maneuvers. The guideline is intended for all clini-
                            cians who are likely to diagnose and manage patients with 
                            BPPV, and it applies to any setting in which BPPV would be 
                            identified, monitored, or managed. The target patient for the 
                            guideline is aged ≥18 years with a suspected or potential 
                            diagnosis of BPPV. The primary outcome considered in this 
                            guideline is the resolution of the symptoms associated with 
                            BPPV. Secondary outcomes considered include an increased 
                            rate of accurate diagnoses of BPPV, a more efficient return 
                            to regular activities and work, decreased use of inappropri-
                            ate medications and unnecessary diagnostic tests, reduction  
                            in recurrence of BPPV, and reduction in adverse events 

                            associated with undiagnosed or untreated BPPV. Other out-
                            comes considered include minimizing costs in the diagnosis 
                            and treatment of BPPV, minimizing potentially unnecessary re-
                            turn physician visits, and maximizing the health-related quality 
                            of life of individuals afflicted with BPPV.
                            Action Statements. The update group made strong recommenda-
                            tions that clinicians should (1) diagnose posterior semicircular 
                            canal BPPV when vertigo associated with torsional, upbeating 
                            nystagmus is provoked by the Dix-Hallpike maneuver, per-
                            formed by bringing the patient from an upright to supine posi-
                            tion with the head turned 45° to one side and neck extended 
                            20° with the affected ear down, and (2) treat, or refer to a cli-
                            nician who can treat, patients with posterior canal BPPV with 
                            a canalith repositioning procedure. The update group made 
                            a strong recommendation against postprocedural postural re-
                            strictions after canalith repositioning procedure for posterior 
                            canal BPPV. The update group made recommendations that the 
                            clinician should (1) perform, or refer to a clinician who can 
                            perform, a supine roll test to assess for lateral semicircular 
                            canal BPPV if the patient has a history compatible with BPPV 
                            and the Dix-Hallpike test exhibits horizontal or no nystagmus; 
                            (2) differentiate, or refer to a clinician who can differentiate, 
                            BPPV from other causes of imbalance, dizziness, and vertigo; 
                            (3) assess patients with BPPV for factors that modify manage-
                            ment, including impaired mobility or balance, central nervous 
                            system disorders, a lack of home support, and/or increased 
                            risk for falling; (4) reassess patients within 1 month after an 
                            initial period of observation or treatment to document reso-
                            lution or persistence of symptoms; (5) evaluate, or refer to a 
                            clinician who can evaluate, patients with persistent symptoms 
                            for unresolved BPPV and/or underlying peripheral vestibular 
                            or central nervous system disorders; and (6) educate patients 
                            regarding the impact of BPPV on their safety, the potential for 
                            disease recurrence, and the importance of follow-up. The up-
                            date group made recommendations against (1) radiographic im-
                            aging for a patient who meets diagnostic criteria for BPPV in

                            Differences from Prior Guideline
                            This clinical practice guideline is as an update and replace-
                            ment for an earlier guideline published in 2008 by the 
                            American Academy of Otolaryngology—Head and Neck 
                            Surgery Foundation (AAO-HNSF).1 An update was necessi-
                            tated by new primary studies and systematic reviews that 
                            might suggest a need for modifying clinically important rec-
                            ommendations. Changes in content and methodology from 
                            the prior guideline include the following:

                            • Addition of a patient advocate to the guideline devel-
                            opment group
                            • New evidence from 2 clinical practice guidelines, 20 
                            systematic reviews, and 27 randomized controlled 
                            trials (RCTs)
                            • Emphasis on patient education and shared decision 
                            making
                            • Expanded action statement profiles to explicitly state 
                            quality improvement opportunities, confidence in the 
                            evidence, intentional vagueness, and differences of 
                            opinion
                            • Enhanced external review process to include public 
                            comment and journal peer review

                            • New algorithm to clarify decision making and action 
                            statement relationships
                            • New recommendation regarding canalith reposition-
                            ing postprocedural restrictions
                            • Expansion of the recommendations regarding radio-
                            graphic and vestibular testing
                            • Removal of the “no recommendation” for audiomet-
                            ric testing
                            • Addition of a diagnostic and treatment visual algo-
                            rithm

                            Introduction
                            A primary complaint of dizziness accounts for 5.6 million 
                            clinic visits in the United States per year, and between 17% 
                            and 42% of patients with vertigo ultimately receive a diagno-
                            sis of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV).2-4 BPPV 
                            is a form of positional vertigo.
                            • Vertigo is defined as an illusory sensation of motion 
                            of either the self or the surroundings in the absence 
                            of true motion.
                            • Positional vertigo is defined as a spinning sensa-
                            tion produced by changes in head position relative 
                            to gravity.
                            • BPPV is defined as a disorder of the inner ear char-
                            acterized by repeated episodes of positional vertigo 
                            (Table 1).
                            Traditionally, the terms “benign” and “paroxysmal” have 
                            been used to characterize this particular form of positional 
                            vertigo. In this context, the descriptor benign historically 
                            implies that BPPV was a form of positional vertigo not due 
                            to any serious central nervous system (CNS) disorder and 
                            that there was an overall favorable prognosis for recovery.5 
                            This favorable prognosis is based in part on the fact that 
                            BPPV can recover spontaneously in approximately 20% of 
                            patients by 1 month of follow-up and up to 50% at 3 
                            months.6,7 However, the clinical and quality-of-life impacts 
                            of undiagnosed and untreated BPPV may be far from 
                            “benign,” as patients with BPPV are at increased risk for 
                            falls and impairment in the performance of daily activities.8
