                            Γ Mira millor versió "Q&A doc" (es el mateix xo amb notes adicionals)
                            Γ Seguir l'estudi d'este amb les mnemotècnies en Q&A doc::Imm3B_PracticalExam_Mnemo
                            ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                           .V1.Nine Quadrant Test
                              1º.The patient looks at a 9-point grid (high/middle/low X left/center/right) as the physical therapist (PT) moves a target (index finger).
                              -May need to lift eyelid for down gaze positions.
                              -The PT observes for nystagmus in any of the directions.
                              ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                              This is ROM

                           .V2.Gaze Holding Nystagmus
                              Una creu
                              30 degrees + hold 30 seconds

                              1º.The PT asks the patient to look in eccentric gaze for up to 30 seconds while the PT observes for presence of nystagmus.
                              2º.The patient should look to the right about 30 degrees and hold that position, then switch to about 30 degrees to the left while looking at a target (such as the PT’s fingertip or a pen).
                              3º.The patient should also look up and down 30 degrees. This can be combined with eye movement range of motion testing.

                           .V3.Smooth Pursuit
                              Una creu
                              ✓30 degrees + ✗hold 30 seconds
                              2 seconds to go from right to left

                              1º.The PT holds a target (fingertip) at a distance of 3 feet from the patient.
                              2º.The PT asks the patient to follow the target as the PT slowly moves the target left to right, then up and down.
                                 -The PT does not exceed 30 degrees from the nose for each eye.
                                 -The target should be moved at a rate requiring approximately 2 seconds to go from right to left, another 2 seconds to go from left to right, and the same timing for up and down.
                              ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                              Test the ability to follow a slowly moving target. The patient and the examiner are seated. The examiner holds a fingertip at a distance of 3 ft. from the patient. The patient is instructed to maintain focus on the target as the examiner moves the target smoothly in the horizontal direction 1.5 ft. to the right and 1.5 ft. to the left of midline. One repetition is complete when the target moves back and forth to the starting position, and 2 repetitions are performed. The target should be moved at a rate requiring approximately 2 seconds to go fully from left to right and 2 seconds to go fully from right to left. The test is repeated with the examiner moving the target smoothly and slowly in the vertical direction 1.5 ft. above and 1.5 ft. below midline for 2 complete repetitions up and down. Again, the target should be moved at a rate requiring approximately 2 seconds to move the eyes fully upward and 2 seconds to move fully downward. Record: Headache, Dizziness, Nausea & Fogginess ratings after the test. (Figure 1)

                           .V4.Horizontal and Vertical Saccades
                              1º.The PT holds two single points (fingertips) horizontal at a distance of 3 feet from the patient; 1.5 feet to the right and 1.5 feet to the left of midline so that the patient must gaze 30 degrees to the left and 30 degrees to the right.
                              2º.The PT instructs the patient to move their eyes as quickly as possible from one point to the next. The same process is repeated up and down.
                              ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                              Horizontal Saccades:
                                 The examiner holds two single points (fingertips) horizontally at a distance of 3 ft. from the patient, and 1.5 ft. to the right and 1.5 ft. to the left of midline so that the patient must gaze 30 degrees to left and 30 degrees to the right. Instruct the patient to move their eyes as quickly as possible from point to point. One repetition is complete when the eyes move back and forth to the starting position, and 10 Γ(both sides are one) repetitions are performed. Record: Headache, Dizziness, Nausea & Fogginess ratings after the test.
                              Vertical Saccades:
                                 Repeat the test with 2 points held vertically at a distance of 3 ft. from the patient, and 1.5 feet above and 1.5 feet below midline so that the patient must gaze 30 degrees upward and 30 degrees downward. Instruct the patient to move their eyes as quickly as possible from point to point. One repetition is complete when the eyes move up and down to the starting position, and 10 repetitions Γ(both sides are one)are performed. Record: Headache, Dizziness, Nausea & Fogginess ratings after the test. (Figure 3)

                           .V5.Convergence
                              Scores of ≤5 cm are considered normal

                              1º.The PT holds up a stick that is marked with a 14 point font target in front of the patient.
                              2º.The PT instructs the patient to watch the target with both eyes as it comes toward the patient’s face and state when the target doubles.
                              3º.The PT records the distance from the patient’s nose to where the patient says the target doubled.

                              -Scores of ≤5 cm are considered normal.
                              ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                              Measure the ability to view a near target without double vision. The patient is seated and wearing corrective lenses (if needed). The examiner is seated front of the patient and observes their eye movement during this test. The patient focuses on a small target (approximately 14 point font size) at arm’s length and slowly brings it toward the tip of their nose. The patient is instructed to stop moving the target when they see two distinct images or when the examiner observes an outward deviation of one eye. Blurring of the image is ignored. The distance in cm. between target and the tip of nose is measured and recorded. This is repeated a total of 3 times with measures recorded each time. Record: Headache, Dizziness, Nausea & Fogginess ratings after the test. Abnormal: Near Point of convergence ≥ 6 cm from the tip of the nose.

                           .V6.Cover and Uncover Test
                              indicates tropia
                                 Inward movement = exotropia
                                 Outward movement = esotropia
                                 Downward movement = hypertropia
                                 Upward movement = hypotropia

                              COVER (indicates tropia if positive):
                              1º.The patient is seated looking straight ahead at a target approximately 10 feet away.
                              2º.The paddle (occluder) is placed over one eye and the PT observes for any eye movement of the uncovered eye.
                                 Note if the eye moves in or out, up or down.
                              3º.Then UNCOVER. Repeat for the other eye.
                                 If a corrective movement is seen, it means that a misalignment was present.
                                    Inward movement means that an exotropia was present and named for the eye that moved.
                                    Outward movement means that an esotropia was present.
                                    Downward movement means a hypertropia was present.
                                    Upward movement means a hypotropia was present.

                              A tropia can be
                                 fixed or
                                 alternating

                           .V7.Cross-Cover Test
                              indicates phoria
                              The same movement will be seen in both eyes, so phorias are not named by side.
                              The occluder is held over one eye for 3–4 seconds and it is then quickly placed over the other eye.
                                 Repeat for 3–4 cycles.

                                 Inward movement = exophoria
                                 Outward movement = esophoria
                                 Downward movement = hyperphoria
                                 Upward movement = hypophoria

                              CROSS COVER (indicates phoria, if COVER test is negative):
                              1º.The patient is seated looking straight ahead at a target approximately 10 feet away.
                              2º.The occluder is held over one eye for 3–4 seconds and it is then quickly placed over the other eye.
                                 Repeat for 3–4 cycles
                                 The PT observes the eye that that is being uncovered and notes if it moves in or out, up or down.
                                    -The same movement will be seen in both eyes, so phorias are not named by side
                                    -If a corrective movement is seen, it means that a misalignment was present.
                                       Inward movement means that an exophoria was present.
                                       Outward movement means that an esophoria was present.
                                       Downward movement means a hyperphoria was present.
                                       Upward movement means a hypophoria was present.

                           .V8.Head Impulse Test (Horizontal Canal)
                              1º.The patient is instructed to look at a target in midline.
                              2º.The PT slowly moves the patient’s head in the yaw plane about 15–20 degrees and then quickly moves the patient’s head to midline (the impulse) while the patient attempts to keep their eyes on the target.
                              3º.The head is rapidly stopped, and the PT checks to see if the patient has a “catch-up” saccade that will refixate their eyes on the target.

                              -The head can be moved away from midline for the impulse, but it is better to move toward the midline.
                              -The movement must be fully stopped before doing the next impulse.

                              -A normal VOR response to rapid passive head rotation is that the patient is able to fixate on the central target without saccades.
                              -An abnormal response occurs when head is rotated to the side of the vestibular lesion and there is an inability to maintain fixation during rotation of the head requiring a corrective saccade once the head has stopped moving.

                           .V9.HINTS Exam (V3., V6., & V8.)
                              to identify a posterior circulation stroke
                              cluster of tests
                                 V8.Horizontal head Impulse Testing
                                 Direction changing Nystagmus
                                    Γ V3.Smooth Pursuit (only)
                                 Vertical Test of Skew
                                    Γ V6.Cover and Uncover Test

                              -The HINTS exam can be used as a tool to identify a posterior circulation stroke.
                              -The cluster of tests includes
                                 Horizontal head Impulse Testing
                                 Direction changing Nystagmus
                                 Vertical Test of Skew
                              -A single central finding on any of the three components rules in a posterior circulation stroke.

                           .V10.Head Shake Test (Head Shaking Nystagmus)
                              WITH GOGGLES – PREFERRED
                              WITHOUT GOGGLES

                              head forward 20–30 degrees
                              shakes eyes closed for 20 cycles quickly
                                 post-shake nystagmus

                              1º.The PT tilts the patient’s head forward 20–30 degrees and shakes the head in the yaw plane with eyes closed for 20 cycles quickly.
                              2º.The PT has the patient open their eyes and observes for post shake nystagmus.

                           .V11.Dynamic Visual Acuity Test
                              1º.Static Visual Acuity
                              2º.shake the patient’s head 20–30 degrees in the yaw plane with head flexed 30 degrees at 2 Hz (240 beats (!!E.V) on a metronome, head is in right or left position with each beat).
                              3º.note the lowest complete line (Dynamic Visual Acuity)
                              4º.positive test = patient lost more than two lines while moving the head versus while the head is still and indicates a deficit in the functional VOR.

                              1º.The patient sits at a distance that is marked at the top of the LogMAR Eye chart.
                              2º.The PT insturcts the patient to read the LogMAR Eye chart first with the head still, and notes the lowest complete line (Static Visual Acuity).
                              3º.The PT then shakes the patient’s head 20–30 degrees in the yaw plane with head flexed 30 degrees at 2 Hz (240 beats on a metronome, head is in right or left position with each beat).
                              4º.The PT notes the lowest complete line (Dynamic Visual Acuity).

                              -A positive test occurs if the patient lost more than two lines (!!E.V) while moving the head versus while the head is still and indicates a deficit in the functional VOR.

                           .V12.Vibration Induced Nystagmus
                              vibration with a frequency of 100Hz is applied to the mastoid process
                              In someone with unilateral vestibular loss, the resulting nystagmus will beat away from the affected ear

                              1º.While the patient is sitting with goggles donned, vibration with a frequency of 100Hz is applied to the mastoid process.

                              -In someone with unilateral vestibular loss, the resulting nystagmus will beat away from the affected ear.

                           .V13.Rinne test Γ(V13. & V14. go togerther)
                              discern sound transmitted through air versus bone and helps assess for unilateral hearing loss

                              1º.strike the fork inducing vibration
                              2º.The stem of the tuning fork is placed on the mastoid process of the patient
                              3º.The patient is then asked to cover their other ear with their hand
                              4º.The patient informs the PT when the sound can no longer be heard.
                              5º.The process is then repeated with the tines of the tuning fork held near the external auditory canal and the patient again informs the examiner when the sound can no longer be heard

                              Results:
                                 Normal hearing is observed when:
                                    the vibrating tuning fork positioned near the ear is louder and lasts twice as long compared to when placed on the mastoid.
                                 Abnormal:
                                    When the sound is at least equally loud or louder when the fork is placed on the mastoid compared to when it is held next to the ear.

                              .V14.Weber test Γ(V13. & V14. go togerther)
                                 Used to assess for a unilateral hearing loss and to characterize conductive versus sensorineural loss.

                                 1º.Using a 512-Hz tuning fork, the PT strikes the fork tines to induce vibration
                                 2º.The stem of the tuning fork is then placed on the top of the patient’s head
                                 3º.The patient is asked “is the sound louder in your right ear, left ear, or the same in both?”

                                 Results:
                                    Normal hearing is confirmed when:
                                       -the sound is heard midline and equally on both sides
                                    ΓAbnormal:
                                       Unilateral sensorineural hearing loss is observed if:
                                          the patient hears the sound louder (lateralizes) in the unaffected ear
                                       Unilateral conductive hearing loss is observed if:
                                          the patient hears the sound louder (lateralizes) in the affected ear
                                       Symmertical conductive hearing loss is observed if:
                                          the patient does not exhibit lateralization

                        II.Clinical Treatment
                           .CT1.VOR x1 (x1 viewing)
                              Horizontal
                              Vertical

                              18–24 inches away from eyes
                              pt. moves head in either pitch or yaw planes while keeping the target in focus
                                 move their head as quickly as possible but to keep the target in focus
                              PT determines if the head movements increase their symptoms and at what speed
                                 They should be able to move their head at about 100–120 (!!E.V) beats per minute on a metronome without symptoms
                              ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                              Vestibular-Ocular Reflex (VOR) Test
                                 Assess the ability to stabilize vision as the head moves. The patient and the examiner are seated. The examiner holds a target of approximately 14 point font size in front of the patient in midline at a distance of 3 ft.
                                    Horizontal VOR Test:
                                       The patient is asked to rotate their head horizontally while maintaining focus on the target. The head is moved at an amplitude of 20 degrees to each side and a metronome is used to ensure the speed of rotation is maintained at 180 beats/minute (one beat in each direction). One repetition is complete when the head moves back and forth to the starting position, and 10 repetitions are performed. Record: Headache, Dizziness, Nausea and Fogginess ratings 10 sec after the test is completed.
                                    Vertical VOR Test:
                                       The test is repeated with the patient moving their head vertically. The head is moved in an amplitude of 20 degrees up and 20 degrees down and a metronome is used to ensure the speed of movement is maintained at 180 beats/minute (one beat in each direction). One repetition is complete when the head moves up and down to the starting position, and 10 repetitions are performed. Record: Headache, Dizziness, Nausea and Fogginess ratings after the test. (Figure

                           .CT2.VOR Cancellation (Visual Motion Sensitivity)
                              Horizontal
                              Vertical

                              1º.pt. extends their arm directly in front of their body or clasps their hands together
                              2º.pt. instructed to visually fixate on the target and maintain fixation.
                                 -The entire body is then rotated 80 degrees (!!E.V) back and forth to each side at a comfortable speed for several cycles (use a metronome at 50 beats/minute) (!!E.V).
                                 -May use a swivel chair/stool or the patient can twist from waist using a stationary seat or stand with feet apart.
                                 -NOTE: Patient must keep the head, neck and shoulders moving together as a unit and their hands/thumbs straight out in front of their body. 
                              Normal response is when:
                                 the eyes remain stationary and motionless throughout the test
                              ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                              Visual Motion Sensitivity (VMS) Test
                                 Test visual motion sensitivity and the ability to inhibit vestibular-induced eye movements using vision. The patient stands with feet shoulder width apart, facing a busy area of the clinic. The examiner stands next to and slightly behind the patient, so that the patient is guarded but the movement can be performed freely. The patient holds arm outstretched and focuses on their thumb. Maintaining focus on their thumb, the patient rotates, together as a unit, their head, eyes and trunk at an amplitude of 80 degrees to the right and 80 degrees to the left. A metronome is used to ensure the speed of rotation is maintained at 50 beats/min (one beat in each direction). One repetition is complete when the trunk rotates back and forth to the starting position, and 5 repetitions are performed. Record: Headache, Dizziness, Nausea & Fogginess ratings after the test.

                           .CT3.VOR Plus Vergence
                              VORx1 Γ(CT1.) exercise while moving the target toward and away from their nose
                                 they are doing vergence + the VORx1 exercise simultaneously

                           .CT4.Head Impulse Exercise
                              1º.The patient is seated and focusing on a target about 3 feet from their nose
                              2º.They quickly move their head about 15–20 degrees toward the affected side and then slowly move their head back to center

                           .CT5.Eye Head Saccade Exercises
                              For pt. with:
                                 unilateral and bilateral loss
                                 but definitely for patients with bilateral loss

                              1º.There are two targets in front of them at least 18 inches away at about a 30 degree angle from their nose to the right and the left (or up and down)
                              2º.The patient is to look at one target, and then move their eyes ONLY to the second target, then move their head and repeat this in the opposite direction

                              Goal: to attempt to have the saccadic eye system help to compensate for the damage to the VOR

                           .CT6.Imaginary Targets (Remembered Targets)
                              NOTE: The patient should NOT be holding the target.

                              1º.pt. looks at a target directly in front of them
                              2º.close eyes and turn their head slightly in the yaw plane imagining that they are still looking at the target
                              3º.open eyes and see if they were able to keep their eyes on the target
                              4º.repeat the exercise in the opposite direction

                           .CT7.Brock String
                              1º.The patient holds one end of the Brock string at the tip of their nose and the other end is attached to a stationary object so that the string is taut
                              2º.Move the nearest bead to the near point of convergence or just closer
                              3º.Move the far bead to arm’s length and place the middle bead at the midpoint of the other two
                              4º.pt. starts by focusing on the far bead and holds for 5–10 seconds
                                 pt. should report seeing two lines diverging toward them like the letter "A" from the far bead
                              5º.Next, the patient changes focus to the middle bead and holds for 5–10 seconds
                                 -The patient should report seeing two lines diverging toward and away from them like the letter "X" from the middle bead
                              6º.Then the patient changes focus to the close bead and holds for 5–10 seconds
                                 -The patient should report seeing two lines diverging away from them like the letter "V" from the close bead.
                              7º.Then the patient moves focus back to the middle bead and far bead, holding each for 5–10 seconds
                              8º.This should be repeated until symptoms increase by several units or the patient needs to take a break
                              10º.Progress by changing starting point, increasing reps, or adding more beads to the string.
                        
                        III.Posterior Canal BPPV Positional Tests
                           .BPPV.1.Dix-Hallpike ('Dix Hallpike.mp4') ('Dix-Hallpike test.mp4')
                              WITHOUT GOGGLES
                              WITH GOGGLES–PREFERRED

                              1º.After checking cervical range of motion
                              2º.with the patient in long-sitting position on a mat table
                              3º.the PT places patient’s head in 45 degrees of yaw rotation
                                 Γ Towards PT - Afected side 
                              4º.The PT quickly (1–2 seconds) lowers the patient to supine position with head extended 30 degrees below the edge of the mat.
                              5º.The PT observes for nystagmus to become evident over 30 seconds and notes the direction of the nystagmus.
                                 5º.1.For posterior canal BPPV
                                    nystagmus should be upbeating and torsional toward the tested side

                              -Good body mechanics are utilized to avoid injury
                              -The PT maintains contact with the patient after bringing the patient back up to the sitting posture and is careful throughout the maneuver to avoid neck or back pain for the patient and back pain for the PT
                              ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                              The head is rotated 45 deg and extended 20-30 deg over the edge of a bed. You are expecting to see a torsional-upbeating nystagmus in BOTH eyes. The torsion is beating down towards the affected ear. It is imperative that you hold the person by the shoulders when they come back to the long sit position. You will repeat the above test to the opposite side.
                                 What does it mean?
                                    If unilateral BPPV, you will observe torsional upbeating nystagmus when the head is turned to the affected side. You would expect the nystagmus to have a latency, increase then decrease in intensity (crescendo- decrescendo), and then last under one minute and typically the person experiences vertigo. If they have bilateral BPPV, they will have torsional upbeating nystagmus on both sides.
                                 Interventions
                                    Modified Epley (first choice)
                                       The PT instructs and demonstrates for patient and explains the purpose to the patient.
                                          STEP 1:
                                             Seat the patient on the table in long sitting with head in 45 degrees rotation toward the affected ear. Quickly lower to supine (1-2 sec) so they may be taken back to the head-hanging position with the neck in slight extension (20-30 degrees of extension). The PT stabilizes the head with hands and waits for the nystagmus to stop. Observe for eye movement in the head hanging position.
                                          STEP 2:
                                             Then rotate the head 90 deg towards the uninvolved side by turning the head toward opposite side - PT observes eyes- wait for nystagmus to stop. Keep neck in extension during the turn to the opposite side and wait 30 sec.
                                          STEP 3:
                                             Log roll patient onto unaffected side so that the head is turned to face ground- hold and wait 30 sec.
                                          STEP 4:
                                             Keep chin tucked towards their shoulder and have them rise to sitting but HOLD ON TO THEM when they sit up with both hands. Then slowly turn head back to midline. HOLD ON TO THEM when as they come to sitting and up to a minute or more after completion of the maneuver.

                           .BPPV.2.Loaded Dix-Hallpike
                              Perform the same as Dix-Hallpike, except
                                 begin with head rotated 45 degrees towards the side being texted,
                                 flexed 30 degrees to chest,
                                 and while in the long sitting position (i.e., pre-loading the head).
                              Hold for 30 seconds before placing the patient in supine.
                              ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                              The person’s head is rotated 45 degrees to the affected side and flexed forward 30 degrees in the plane of the posterior canal for 30 seconds, before placing patient in supine.
                                 What does it mean?
                                    -This is a test for posterior canal BPPV but with the additional 30 degrees of flexion, it may result in longer duration of nystagmus and more intense symptoms, hopefully making the diagnosis easier for you to see.
                                 Interventions

                           .BPPV.3.Modified Dix-Hallpike Test With Head Over Pillow
                              Place the person in the middle of the bed. Turn their head 45 degrees and lie them over the pillow. The sensitivity of the test was 96% and the specificity was 88%
                                 What does it mean?
                                    It is comparable to the Dix-Hallpike test and provides another alternative for testing

                           .BPPV.4.Sidelying Test
                              1º.The patient starts in sitting with legs resting over edge of table (hips/knees at 90 degrees)
                              2º.The PT has the patient turn their head 45 degrees away from the ear being tested and brings them rapidly down sidelying to the table on the side being tested, with the nose toward the ceiling.
                              3º.The PT observes for nystagmus to become evident over 30 seconds and notes the direction of the nystagmus. 
                                 positive test: ¿? 
                              4º.The PT brings the patient back up to sitting, taking care to hold onto the patient as they return to sitting and for about 30 seconds to 1 minute after they have returned to sitting.
                              ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                              -The person is sitting on the edge of the bed.
                              To test the right posterior canal, the head is rotated 45 deg towards the left.
                              -You then bring the patient down to the bed onto their right side with their head extended while maintaining the rotation.
                              -Upon rising to sitting, hold the persons shoulders so that they do not fall back.
                              -You will repeat the above test to the opposite side to test the L posterior canal.
                              -If they have bilateral BPPV, they will become symptomatic to both sides.
                                 What does it mean?
                                    -The patient should only have vertigo or nystagmus if the right ear is involved with the test when the person lays to the right.

                        IV.Posterior Canal Canalith Repositioning Maneuvers
                           .PCCRM.1.Modified Epley ('Modified Epley Maneuver.mp4')
                              With Goggles–preferred
                              Without Goggles
                        
                              STEP 1:
                                 -The PT seats the patient on the table in long sitting with the head in 45 degrees rotation toward the affected ear.
                                 -The PT quickly lowers the patient to supine (1–2 seconds) so they may be taken back to the head-hanging position with the neck in slight extension (20–30 degrees of extension).
                                 -The PT stabilizes the head with their hands and waits for the nystagmus to stop.
                                 -The PT observes for eye movement in the head hanging position.
                              STEP 2:
                                 -The PT rotates the head 90 degrees towards the uninvolved side by turning the head toward opposite side.
                                 -The PT observes the patient’s eyes and waits for nystagmus to stop. Keep the neck in extension during the turn to the opposite side and wait 30 seconds.
                              STEP 3:
                                 Log roll patient onto unaffected side so that the head is turned to face ground.
                                 Hold and wait 30 seconds.
                              STEP 4:
                                 -The patient keeps their chin tucked towards their shoulder and rises to sitting while the PT HOLDS ON TO THE PATIENT with both hands.
                                 -The PT slowly turns the patient’s head back to midline.
                                 -The PT HOLDS ON TO THE PATIENT as they come to sitting and up to a minute or more after completion of the maneuver. 
                              ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                              The PT instructs and demonstrates for patient and explains the purpose to the patient.
                                 STEP 1:
                                    Seat the patient on the table in long sitting with head in 45 degrees rotation toward the affected ear. Quickly lower to supine (1-2 sec) so they may be taken back to the head-hanging position with the neck in slight extension (20-30 degrees of extension). The PT stabilizes the head with hands and waits for the nystagmus to stop. Observe for eye movement in the head hanging position.
                                 STEP 2:
                                    Then rotate the head 90 deg towards the uninvolved side by turning the head toward opposite side - PT observes eyes- wait for nystagmus to stop. Keep neck in extension during the turn to the opposite side and wait 30 sec.
                                 STEP 3:
                                    Log roll patient onto unaffected side so that the head is turned to face ground- hold and wait 30 sec.
                                 STEP 4:
                                    Keep chin tucked towards their shoulder and have them rise to sitting but HOLD ON TO THEM when they sit up with both hands. Then slowly turn head back to midline. HOLD ON TO THEM when as they come to sitting and up to a minute or more after completion of the maneuver.

                           .PCCRM.2.Semont ('Semont & Maneuver.mp4')
                              1º.The PT rotates the patient’s head 45 degrees away from the affected side
                              2º.and quickly moves the patient into side-lie (head now facing up, image 3).
                              3º.Stay in this position for 1–2 minutes.
                              4º.Quickly, in one motion, sit up and move the patient onto the opposite side-lie (good side) without changing head position (nose now facing the ground, image 6).
                              5º.Stay in this position for 1–2 minutes.

                              -Remember that modeling suggests the ‘flip’ needs to be completed in <1.5 seconds. The PT then returns the patient slowly to sitting.
                              -If reversal of nystagmus occurs (or unsure), repeat up to three repetitions.

                           .PCCRM.3.Semont Plus
                              1º.The patient begins sitting upright and facing forward,
                              2º.then the PT turns the patient’s head away from the affected ear.
                              3º.The PT quickly lays the patient down on the side of the involved ear, over the edge of the table about 20–30 degrees so that the patient’s dependent arm can abduct off the table and rest on the stool.
                              4º.The patient stays there until the vertigo passes.
                              5º.The PT QUICKLY sits the patient up and then lays them on their other side while KEEPING the patient’s head pointing over the shoulder the entire time (the orientation of the head should not change).
                                 -This should be completed in one movement without stopping in the middle.
                                 -The patient should be facing down toward the ground.
                              6º.Wait there until any vertigo/nystagmus passes.
                              7º.The PT then HOLDS ON TO THE PATIENT as they come to sitting, and continues holding onto them for up to a minute or more after completion of the maneuver.
                              ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                              Semont plus (from Strupp RCT)
                                 The PT explains the purpose to the patient; the patient is rapidly moved from lying on one side to lying on the other. You can move the table up to a comfortable position for you and have a stool placed at the end of the table to which you will be moving patient first. Start sitting and turn the head away from the affected ear. Then lie patient down on involved ear side quickly over the edge of the table about 20-30 degrees, so that their dependent arm can abduct off the table and rest on the stool. The patient is to stay there until the vertigo passes. The PT QUICKLY sits the patient up and then lays them on their other side but KEEPING the patient’s head pointing over the shoulder during the entire time (Do not change the orientation of the head). The patient should be facing down to the ground. Also do not stop in the middle of this movement. Wait there until any vertigo/nystagmus passes. Then patient sits up and you must HOLD ON TO THEM when as they come to sitting and up to a minute or more after completion of the maneuver.

                           .PCCRM.4.Li Maneuver ('Li Maneuver.mp4')
                              1º.Start with patient in sitting with legs hanging over edge of the table (hips/knees at 90 degrees)
                              2º.The PT moves the patient down quickly to their involved side with their nose forward while holding their head (no turning of the head is required for this maneuver)
                              3º.After 1 minute, or after resolution of the nystagmus, the PT rapidly moves the patient 180 degrees with the healthy ear down on the table and their nose facing forwards
                              4º.The patient lies there for 4 minutes and then the PT rapidly lifts them back to sitting
                              5º.The PT HOLDS ON TO THE PATIENT for up to several minutes after completion of the Li maneuver
                              ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                              -Li maneuver for the posterior canal Start in sitting with legs hanging over edge of mat (hips/knees at 90 deg).
                              -The PT moves the patient down quickly to their involved side with their nose forward while you hold their head (no turning of the head is required for this maneuver).
                              -After 1 minute or after resolution of the nystagmus, rapidly move them 180 degrees with the healthy ear down on the mat with their nose facing forwards.
                              -Lie there for 4 minutes and then rapidly lift them back to sitting. HOLD ON TO THEM for up to several minutes after completion of the Li maneuver.

                        V.Horizontal Canal BPPV Positional Tests
                           .HC-BPPV-PT.1.Long Sit to Supine
                              1º.The patient starts in long sitting
                              2º.and then moves to supine quickly, ending in approximately 30 degrees of neck flexion (on a pillow will usually work fine)
                              3º.The PT observes eye movement if there is any. 

                           .HC-BPPV-PT.2.Roll Test (Pagnini-McClure Roll Test) ('Roll test with sit to supine test.mp4')
                              WITH GOGGLES – PREFERRED
                              WITHOUT GOGGLES

                              1º.The patient starts supine with their head flexed 20–30 degrees.
                              2º.The PT quickly moves the head to the right and holds for 30 seconds.
                              3º.The PT observes for nystagmus to become evident over 30 seconds and notes the direction of the nystagmus.
                              4º.The PT moves the head back to midline and waits for 30 seconds before quickly moving the head to the left and holding for 30 seconds.
                              5º.The PT observes for nystagmus to become evident over 30 seconds and notes the direction of the nystagmus.
                                 -If positive, nystagmus should be beating towards the ground (geotropic), OR away from the ground (ageotropic), in both right and left head positions.
                              6º.The PT should note which side the patient experienced the worse symptoms and which side had the more intense nystagmus.
                              ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                              -From the supine position with head flexed to 30 deg,
                              -move head to the right and wait for 30 sec.
                              -Then return to center and wait 30 sec or until nystagmus stops.
                              -Then roll head to the left and wait for 30 sec,
                              -and return to center.
                              -Observe the nystagmus throughout to determine which direction the nystagmus is beating (towards or away from earth).

                                 What does it mean?
                                    Nystagmus beating towards earth is called “geotropic” nystagmus and if it beats away from earth it is called “ageotropic or apogeotropic” nystagmus.

                                    If geotropic, you should see greater nystagmus on the affected side during the roll test. To confirm, you should have seen the nystagmus beat TOWARDS the good side in the sit to supine test.

                                    If ageotropic, you should see greater nystagmus on the unaffected side during the roll test. To confirm, you should have seen the nystagmus beat TOWARDS the affected side in the sit to supine test.

                                 Interventions
                                    Geotropic Gufoni liberatory maneuver (GLM)
                                       Patient sits in the middle of a bed and is briskly brought down onto the unaffected ear and held for 30 sec. The head is then quickly turned down by 45 deg and held there for 2-3 minutes, then the patient is brought back into the sitting position.
                                    Li quick repositioning maneuver
                                       Start in supine in the middle of a large bed. Log roll patient 90 deg onto the affected side and wait until the symptoms resolve. The clinician then is to stand behind the patient grabs the patient’s hand on the involved side and QUICKLY log rolls them 180 deg onto their unaffected side. Stay on the unaffected left side for 2 minutes and then bring the patient to sitting. The maneuver takes approximately 3 minutes to perform.

                           .HC-BPPV-PT.3.Bow and Lean Test ('Bow and Lean test.mp4')
                              WITH GOGGLES – PREFERRED
                              WITHOUT GOGGLES
                              
                              1º.The patient begins in sitting.
                              2º.BOW: The patient flexes their head to be parallel to floor and holds for 30 seconds.
                              3º.The PT notes the direction of nystagmus.
                                 -If geotropic nystagmus is observed with the roll test, the nystagmus will beat towards the affected ear.
                                 -If ageotropic nystagmus is observed with the roll test, the nystagmus will beat towards the healthy ear.
                              4º.LEAN: The patient extends their head as if looking at ceiling for 30 seconds.
                              5º.The PT notes the direction of nystagmus, which should be opposite to what you saw in the BOW test.
                                 -If geotropic nystagmus is seen with the roll test, the nystagmus will beat towards the healthy ear.
                                 -If ageotropic nystagmus is seen with the roll test, the nystagmus will beat towards the affected ear.
                                 -(Geotropic — nystagmus beats toward Good, Ageotropic — Affected)

                              -Results from this test will be used to confirm the side of the affected ear if there is uncertainty about which ear had the greatest nystagmus/vertigo.
                              ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                              (need to integrate the information from the roll test to make sense of this)
                              -Person is sitting. With neck flexion about 60 deg (the Bow), observe the nystagmus that occurs with the change of head position.
                              -In long sitting, then extend the head about 60 deg from neutral (the Lean) and observe the nystagmus. 
                              
                              IMPORTANT:
                                 -to optimize patient comfort and efficiency of testing, it is best to perform the horizontal canal BPPV tests in the following order:
                                    1.Bow and Lean 
                                    2.Sit to supine
                                    3.Roll

                                    Make sure to write down the findings in each position. You may not see anything with the bow and lean or long sit to supine tests.

                                 What does it mean?
                                    If geotropic during the roll test,
                                       with neck flexion
                                          the nystagmus should beat TOWARDS the affected side.
                                       With neck extension,
                                          the nystagmus should beat TOWARDS the good side.
                                    If ageotropic,
                                       you should see greater nystagmus on the unaffected side during the roll test.
                                          With neck extension,
                                             the nystagmus should beat TOWARDS the affected side. Used to confirm side of affected ear if intensity of nystagmus/vertigo is uncertain during roll test.
                                 Interventions
                                    Ageotropic
                                       Kim maneuver
                                          Starting in supine, log roll the patient 135 deg towards the affected side so that their nose is almost facing the floor. Put the vibrator over their mastoid of affected side for 30 sec; wait for the nystagmus to stop. Then do a series of log rolls away from affected ear and wait for 3 minutes in each position or until vertigo/nystagmus stop. Log roll them back to side lying (90 deg from supine). Then log roll to supine nose up position. Then log roll 90 deg to unaffected side and vibrate over the mastoid again for 30 sec. Finally log roll to prone. The PT will move the patient carefully and ensure that they do not excessively pull on their cervical spine.
                                       Gufoni liberatory maneuver (GLM)
                                          Patient sits in the middle of a mat table with legs hanging over side and head in midline. The PT will have the person look straight and then bring the patient down onto their AFFECTED side. After 30 sec, they will turn their head up towards the ceiling and let them rest in this position approximately 2 minutes. At the end of the 2 minutes, they should bring the subject back to sitting holding onto them throughout. If this does not work, most of us will try the same maneuver but have the nose tilted down towards the floor.

                        VI.Horizontal Canal Canalith Repositioning Maneuvers
                           .HC-CCRM.1.Barbecue Maneuver for Canalithiasis
                              1º.The patient begins in a supine position with their head flexed 30 degrees.
                              2º.The PT then rotates the patient’s head 90 degrees towards the affected side; this position is held for 30 seconds after the nystagmus stops.
                              3º.From here the PT rotates the patient’s head back to neutral.
                              4º.Next, the patient’s head is rotated 90 degrees towards the unaffected side.
                                 -Again, this position is held for 30 seconds after the nystagmus stops.
                              5º.The patient then rolls prone
                              6º.after 30 seconds from when the nystagmus stops, the patient can either get up from the prone position or complete the roll and return to sitting from the sidelying position.

                           .HC-CCRM.2.Gufoni Maneuver for Canalithiasis ('Gufoni Maneuver Geotropic.mp4')
                              1º.The patient sits in the middle of a mat table with legs hanging over the side and the head in midline.
                              2º.The PT briskly moves the patient down onto the UNAFFECTED side and holds for 30 seconds.
                              3º.The head is then quickly turned down by 45 degrees and held there for 2–3 minutes,
                              4º.then the patient is brought back into the sitting position.

                           .HC-CCRM.3.Li Quick Maneuver for Canalithiasis ('Li for canalithiasis.mp4')
                              1º.The patient starts in supine in the middle of a large bed.
                              2º.The PT log rolls the patient 90 degrees onto the affected side and waits until the symptoms resolve.
                              3º.The PT then stands behind the patient and grabs the patient’s hand on the involved side and QUICKLY log rolls them 180 degrees onto their unaffected side.
                              4º.The patient stays on the unaffected left side for 2 minutes and then the PT brings the patient to sitting.

                              -The maneuver takes approximately 3 minutes to perform.

                           .HC-CCRM.4.Gufoni Maneuver for Cupulolithiasis ('Gufoni Maneuver Apogeotropic.mp4')
                              1º.The patient sits in the middle of the table with legs hanging over the side and head in midline.
                              2º.The PT instructs the patient to look straight ahead, then brings the patient down onto their AFFECTED side for 30 seconds.
                              3º.Then the PT turns the patient’s head up towards the ceiling and lets them rest in this position approximately 2 minutes.
                              4º.At the end of the 2 minutes, the PT brings the patient back to sitting, holding onto the patient throughout.
                                 -If this does not work, it is common to try the same maneuver but with the patient’s nose tilted down towards the floor.

                           .HC-CCRM.5.Kim Maneuver for Cupulolithiasis ('Kim for cupulolithiasis.mp4')
                              1º.Starting with the patient in supine, the PT log rolls the patient onto the affected side
                              2º.then turns the patient’s head 135 degrees towards the floor.
                              3º.The PT places the vibrator over the mastoid of the affected side for 30 seconds and waits for the nystagmus to stop.
                              4º.The PT log rolls the patient back to side lying (90 degrees from supine),
                              5º.then log rolls the patient to supine nose up position.
                              6º.Next the PT logs rolls the patient 90 degrees to the unaffected side and vibrates over the mastoid again for 30 seconds.
                              7º.Finally log roll the patient to prone.

                              -The PT will move the patient carefully and ensure that they do not excessively pull on the cervical spine.

            8.2. Video Series: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)

                .('37 Intro to BPPV.pdf')
                    .Introduction to Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo

                    .Objectives
                        • Describe the pathophysiology of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo 
                        (BPPV)
                        • Describe factors that are associated with the diagnosis of BPPV
                        • Identify key questions and components of the history that are 
                        suggestive of a diagnosis of BPPV

                    .What is BPPV?
                        • It is a mechanical problem within the peripheral 
                        vestibular system
                        • Otoconia are displaced from the otolith organs into one 
                        of the semicircular canals
                        • When the head is moved relative to gravity, the 
                        otoconia move in the canal and cause the endolymph to 
                        move, deflecting the cupula
                        • This causes excitation to the vestibular nuclei resulting 
                        in dizziness, nausea, and vomiting (often associated 
                        with position change)
                        • Caused by free floating otoconia – called canalithiasis
                        • Otoconia can also get “stuck” in the canal (likely at the 
                        cupula) and is called cupulolithiasis

                    .What causes BPPV?
                        • Idiopathic
                        • Traumatic event

                    .Where does BPPV come from? ('')

                    .Otoconia 1 ('')

                    .Otoconia 2 ('')

                    .Prevalence of BPPV
                        • Most common vestibular disorder
                        • Lifetime prevalence of BPPV is 2.4%
                        • In adults over 60 years old, 1-year prevalence is 3.4% (compared to 
                        0.5% among those ages 18-39)
                        • Twice as prevalent in women compared to men
                        • Only 8% of individuals diagnosed with BPPV receive effective 
                        treatment

                        Von Brevern et al, 2007

                    .What factors are associated with BPPV?
                        • Ageing
                        • Associated with peripheral vestibular dysfunction 
                            • Meniere's disease 
                            • Peripheral vestibular hypofunction
                        • TBI 
                            • Estimates up to 58% with BPPV
                        • Migraines
                        • Osteoporosis
                        • Post-surgical? (positioning in OR)

                        (Pollak L et al, 2002; Katasrkas et al, 1999; Gordon C et al, 2004; Hughes and Proctor, 1997; Marcus et al, 2019; Harrell et al, 2023)

                   .BPPV Related to Osteoporosis and Vitamin D
                    • Chan et al. (2017) studied 6,649 persons with osteoporosis and 
                    26,596 matched controls
                    • Persons with osteoporosis had a 1.8 greater chance of having 
                    BPPV compared to the control group
                    • Han et al. (2017) in a retrospective study of 85 women with new 
                    onset BPPV and 80 age matched controls compared their serum 
                    Vitamin D levels (serum 25-hydroxyl vitamin D)
                    • The odds ratio was 2.1 associated with having BPPV with low 
                    Vitamin D levels

                    .Seasonality of Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo ('')
                        Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV) Visit Volume in March, April, and May Compared With Other Months The mean of 5-
                        year pooled BPPV visit values for early spring months was significantly greater than that for non–early spring months (P = .01). Error 
                        bars indicate standard deviation.

                        Figure Legend: 

                        Whitman GT and Baloh, 2015

                        • Whitman GT and Baloh RW (2015) 
                        suggest that the season of the year 
                        may affect BPPV
                        • Less exposure to the sun may affect 
                        onset of BPPV

                    .Key questions to ask during the patient interview (!!E)
                        Γ(See also: [NM1 06.mp4] 44:36sec)
                        • Do you get dizzy (spin) when you roll over in bed?
                        • Do you get dizzy (spin) when you sit up in the morning or lie down at night?
                        • Do you get dizzy (spin) when you look up or bend over?
                        • Can you lie flat without a pillow?
                        • How long do your symptoms last?
                            • Response should be seconds to a minute (not all patients can reliably tell you this though)

                    .A Good Clinical Rule (!!P)
                        An inability to walk usually indicates a central disorder
                        People who can not walk do not just have BPPV

                    .Provoking Positions
                        • Getting out of bed
                        • Lying down from sit to supine
                        • Bending over
                        • Looking up or reaching overhead
                        • Rolling in bed
                        • Going from supine to sit
                        • An inability to sleep without several pillows

                    .Other provoking positions
                        Washing hair
                        Dental chairs
                        Painting overhead
                        Changing a light bulb
                        Working under the car/plumbing
                        Getting clothes out of the dryer

                    .BPPV by canal type (!!E).Lv1
                        ### 📋 Table Transcription

                        | BPPV by canal type     | Posterior                | Horizontal                                  | Anterior               |
                        |----------------------------|------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------|----------------------------|
                        | Estimated frequency        | 81–89%                       | 8–17%                                            | 1–3%                       |
                        | Provocative maneuver       | Dix Hallpike                 | Supine Roll Test (Pagnini-McClure)              | Dix Hallpike               |
                        | Nystagmus                  | Upbeat, torsional            | Horizontal Direction Changing                   | Downbeat, torsional        |

                        ---

                        ### 🧾 Outline Transcription

                        1. BPPV by canal type
                           - Posterior
                             - Estimated frequency: 81–89%
                             - Provocative maneuver: Dix Hallpike
                             - Nystagmus: Upbeat, torsional
                           - Horizontal
                             - Estimated frequency: 8–17%
                             - Provocative maneuver: Supine Roll Test (Pagnini-McClure)
                             - Nystagmus: Horizontal Direction Changing
                           - Anterior
                             - Estimated frequency: 1–3%
                             - Provocative maneuver: Dix Hallpike
                             - Nystagmus: Downbeat, torsional

                    .Summary
                    • BPPV is a mechanical problem where otoconia are displaced from 
                    the otolith organs into the semicircular canals
                    • BPPV is more prevalent in certain populations including older adults, 
                    persons with other peripheral vestibular disorders, migraine, and/or 
                    osteoporosis
                    • A thorough history should include questions about positions that 
                    provoke dizziness and how long symptoms last

                .('38 Posterior Canal BPPV.pdf')
                    .Examination and Treatment of Posterior Canal BPPV

                    .Objectives
                        • Describe evidence-based tests used to assess for the presence of 
                        posterior canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)
                        • Describe evidence-based canalith repositioning maneuvers 
                        recommended for treatment of posterior canal BPPV


                    .Dix-Hallpike Test (Dix & Hallpike,1952)
                    • Was developed in the 1950’s and is considered the “gold standard” for the 
                    diagnosis of posterior canal BPPV 
                    • Clinicians should diagnose posterior canal BPPV when vertigo associated with 
                    torsional upbeating nystagmus is provoked by Dix-Hallpike maneuver 
                    • Strong recommendation by clinical practice guideline
                    • Lopez-Escamez reported a sensitivity of 82% and specificity of 71% for the Dix-
                    Hallpike
                    • Hanley and O’Dowd reported a positive predictive value of 83% and a negative 
                    predictive value of 52% for the Dix-Hallpike 
                    • In other words, a negative test does not necessarily rule out posterior canal BPPV (!!E)
                    • Therefore, the Dix-Hallpike may be repeated, particularly if BPPV is strongly suspected (Bhattacharyya et al, 2017; Nunez et al, 2000; Viirre et al, 2005) (!!E)


                    .The Dix-Hallpike Test
                        • Turn the head 45 degrees toward the side being assessed
                        • Bring the patient into a supine position with 20- 30 degrees extension over the edge of the bed

                    Γ('semicircular canals Positions 2.jpg')
                    Γ('semicircular canals Positions.jpg')
                    Γ('semicircular canals Positions - Mirror.jpg')

                    .Dix-Hallpike ('')

                    .Position of the Clinician ('')

                    Using infrared goggles is preferred

                    .Before conducting positional tests, assess cervical ROM
                        • Only one case report (Moore P et al, 2018) in literature that Dix-Hallpike has resulted in symptoms consistent with Vertebral Basilar Insufficiency
                        • Tests for VBI are not reliable, but still a good idea to assess cervical ROM to see if you need to modify positioning
                        • If neck range of motion is limited, tilt head of table down

                    .Variations of the Dix Hallpike
                        • Head over pillow
                            • Sensitivity: 96%
                            • Specificity: 88%
                        • Loaded Dix Hallpike
                        • Sidelying test

                    .Loaded Dix Hallpike
                        • Head is turned 45 degrees to the side being tested
                        • Flex the head down by 30 degrees (loading the posterior canal)
                        • Then the clinician helps the patient into supine and extends the head 20-30 degrees
                        • Goal is to maximize the response of the otoconia moving through the canal

                    .Side-Lying Test
                        • Start in short sitting in the middle of a treatment table
                        • Turn the head 45 degrees away from the side being tested
                        • Help the patient into sidelying (this is the side you are testing)
                        • Observe for nystagmus
                        • Sensitivity: 90%
                        • Specificity: 75%

                    .Observing nystagmus
                        • In posterior canal BPPV, nystagmus is provoked following Dix Hallpike positioning with the affected ear down  
                        • Nystagmus will be torsional and upbeating

                    .Characteristics of the nystagmus in the Dix-Hallpike
                        • In posterior canal BPPV, torsional and upbeating nystagmus is provoked by the Dix-Hallpike test
                        • There is a latency period between assuming supine position and the onset of the nystagmus and vertigo symptoms
                        • The vertigo and nystagmus increase in severity and then resolve within 60 seconds of the onset (crescendo-decrescendo nystagmus)

                        • If the anterior canal is involved, can observe torsional downbeating nystagmus
                            HOWEVER: The observation of downbeating positional nystagmus requires careful assessment to rule out brainstem or cerebellar lesions

                    .Treatment for Posterior Canal BPPV
                        • Treat or refer to a clinician who can treat with a canalith repositioning maneuver
                            • Strong Recommendation by CPG
                        • These manuevers work by freeing the otoconia from the cupula (cupulolithiasis) and/or by moving the otoconia out of the involved semicircular canal back into the otolith organs
                            • Effective in 91% of cases (compared to sham maneuver 46% effective)
                        • Canalith Repositioning Maneuvers for Posterior Canal BPPV (!!E)
                            • Modified Epley Maneuver
                            • Semont Plus Maneuver
                            • Li Maneuver

                    .Epley maneuver and Modified Epley maneuver
                        • The Epley maneuver is no longer done as Epley described
                            • Original Epley included:
                            • Use of vibration
                            • Sitting almost upright in a chair and 
                            using a cervical collar for 48 hours 
                            post-maneuver
                            • Pre-medication using valium
                            • Evidence does not support this!

                        • Modified Epley Maneuver (!!E)
                            • Turn the head 45 degrees to the affected side
                            • Move the patient into supine and extend the head 20-30 degrees [Dix Hallpike]
                            • Wait until the nystagmus resolves plus 30 seconds
                            • Turn the head 90 degrees toward the unaffected side
                            • Wait until the nystagmus resolves plus 30 seconds
                            • Help the patient to roll onto the unaffected side with the head looking toward the floor
                            • Wait until the nystagmus resolves plus 30 seconds
                            • Carefully help the patient to sit up and HOLD ONTO THE PATIENT

                    .Semont Plus manuever (!!E)
                        (Strupp M et al, 2021)
                        • Start in short sitting in the middle of the bed
                        • Turn the head 45 degrees away from the affected side
                        • Help the patient to lay onto the affected side with the head extended over the bed 60 degrees
                        • Wait until nystagmus resolves plus 30 seconds
                        • Quickly move the patient from the affected side to the unaffected side (within 1.5 seconds)
                        • Wait until nystagmus resolves plus 30 seconds
                        • Slowly sit the patient up and hold on for safety
                        • No difference between treatment with the modified Epley maneuver vs the Semont plus maneuver

                    .Li Maneuver for Posterior Canal BPPV
                        • For right posterior canal BPPV (Li et al 2017)
                        • There was no difference between the Epley and the Li maneuver (n=120) in their randomized trial

                    .Summary
                        • The Dix-Hallpike or Side-lying test is the gold standard for the 
                        diagnosis of posterior canal BPPV
                        • Canalith repositioning maneuvers such as the modified Epley, the 
                        Semont plus, and the Li maneuver are supported by strong evidence 
                        for the treatment of posterior canal BPPV
