                .('39 Horizontal Canal BPPV.pdf')
                    .Examination and Treatment of Horizontal Canal BPPV

                    .Objectives
                        • Describe evidence-based tests used for the diagnosis of horizontal canal benign 
                        paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)
                        • Describe the procedure and indications for the Sit to Supine Test and Bow and 
                        Lean Test
                        • Describe evidence-based canalith repositioning maneuvers for horizontal canal 
                        canalithiasis and cupulolithiasis

                    .Horizontal canal BPPV
                        • Otoconia are displaced into the horizontal canal 
                        • Canalithiasis: otoconia are freely floating in the canal
                        • Cupulolithiasis: otoconia are adhered to the cupula within the canal
                        • Horizontal canal prevalence: 8-17% of BPPV cases

                    .Supine roll test
                        • If the history is consistent with BPPV and the Dix-Hallpike test exhibits horizontal or no nystagmus, the supine roll test should be performed to assess for lateral canal BPPV (Recommended by CPG)
                        • Position the patient in supine with head neutral
                        • Rotate the head 90 degrees to one side and observe for nystagmus
                        • Bring the head back to neutral and wait until nystagmus has subsided
                        • Rotate the head 90 degrees in the opposite direction and observe for nystagmus

                    .Horizontal Canal BPPV nystagmus characteristics
                        • Directional Changing Positional Nystagmus 
                        • Geotropic or ageotropic (apogeotropic) nystagmus associated with vertigo in the supine roll test (both sides)
                            • Geotropic: fast phase of the nystagmus beats toward the earth (typically transient) (!!E)
                            • Apogeotropic: fast phase of the nystagmus beats away from the earth (typically persistent) (!!E)

                    .Horizontal Canal BPPV - geotropic

                    .Horizontal Canal BPPV - apogeotropic

                    .Determining the affected side (!!E).Lv1.Q&A doc
                        • Geotropic type
                            • When rolling to the affected side, nystagmus (and symptoms) will be more intense
                            • When rolling to the unaffected side, nystagmus (and symptoms) will be less intense
                        • Apogeotropic type
                            • When rolling to the affected side, nystagmus (and symptoms) will be less intense
                            • When rolling to the unaffected side, nystagmus (and symptoms) will be more intense
                        • Sometimes it can be difficult to determine the intensity of nystagmus and symptoms

                    .Sit to supine test
                        (Nuti, 1996; Han, 2006; Asprella-Liberati, 2008) 
                        • PROCEDURE:
                            • Patient begins long sitting on mat
                            • Patient is quickly brought into the supine position with the head flexed 30°
                        • FINDINGS: (!!E).Lv1.Q&A doc (!!).Encara no ho entenc
                            • Evokes nystagmus towards the healthy side in geotropic forms (Geotropic=Good)
                            • Evokes nystagmus towards the affected side in apogeotropic forms Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences Vol. 1164, 1Basic and Clinical (Apogeotropic=Affected)

                    .Bow and Lean Test
                        Modified from: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences Vol. 1164, 1Basic and Clinical Aspects of Vertigo and 
                        Dizziness Pages: 316-323
                        Copyright © 2009 The New York Academy of Sciences

                        Sit erect (!!).No ho entenc; estic molt maretjat
                            • If geotropic, beats towards healthy ear (Geotropic=Good)
                            • If apogeotropic, beats towards affected ear (Apogeotropic=Affected)
                        Sit erect and bend head 60° forward
                            • If geotropic, beats towards affected ear
                            • If apogeotropic, beats 
                            towards healthy ear
                        Sit erect and bend head backwards  
                            • If geotropic, beats towards healthy ear (Geotropic=Good)
                            • If apogeotropic, beats towards affected ear (Apogeotropic=Affected)

                    .Treatment for HC BPPV
                        Geotropic Type 
                            • Gufoni (for geotropic)
                            • Li Quick
                            • Lempert (barbeque) Roll
                        Apogeotropic Type
                            • Gufoni (for apogeotropic)
                            • Kim

                    .Lempert (Barbeque) Roll maneuver (!!).No ho entenc; No se que passa amb l'otoconia
                        • Start in the supine position
                        • Rotate the head (or roll body) 90 degrees to the affected side
                        • Rotate back to supine head neutral
                        • Roll onto the unaffected side
                        • Roll into prone, head in neutral
                        • To resume sitting, the patient can either roll onto the affected side or sit up from prone
                        • Should wait until the nystagmus stops plus 30 seconds between each position

                        ('')
                            When it is determined to be horizontal canal BPPV affecting the right side, the patient is taken through a series of step-wise 90-degree tums away from the affected side in Steps 1 through 5, holding each position for 10 to 30 seconds. From Step 5, the patient positions his or her bod,' to the back (6) in preparation for the rapid and simultaneous movement from the eupire face up to tie sitting position (7).

                    .Gufoni Maneuver for Geotropic Type Horizontal Canal BPPV (!!).No ho entenc; No se que passa amb l'otoconia
                        • Start in a short sitting position in the center of a table
                        • The patient’s head is then quickly 
                        • Help the patient into sidelying onto the unaffected side (head neutral) for 30 seconds turned toward the ground 45-60 degrees
                        • Hold the position for 2 minutes
                        • Help the patient to sit up with the head turned toward the unaffected side
                        • Hold onto the patient for safety

                    .Geotropic HC BPPV double blind randomized trial
                        • In 10 nationwide dizziness clinics in Korea, 170 people with geotropic HC-
                        BPPV were randomly assigned to:
                        • Barbecue rotation (n = 56)
                        • Gufoni (n = 64)
                        • Sham maneuver (n = 50)
                        • An immediate response was determined within 1 hour after a maximum of 2 
                        trials of each maneuver on the visit day
                        • Saw them again in 1 month
                        • Barbecue roll (69%) and Gufoni (61%) maneuvers showed better responses 
                        than the sham maneuver (35%) 
                        • There was no difference between the barbecue rotation and Gufoni groups in 
                        terms of outcomes
                        Kim JS et al, Neurology, 2012

                    .Li Quick maneuver for HC BPPV (geotropic) (!!).No ho entenc; No se que passa amb l'otoconia
                        • Start in supine 
                        • Roll onto affected side and remain until symptoms stop
                        • Roll patient quickly to the unaffected sidelying position 
                        • Remain for 2 minutes
                        • Then bring them to sitting
                        • Total time: ~ 3 minutes
                        • In their study of 120 patients with HC BPPV, Li et al. found the Li Quick maneuver to have similar efficacy to the barbeque roll maneuver (93% vs 91% resolved in 1 week)

                    .Gufoni maneuver for Apogeotropic HC BPPV ('') (!!).No ho entenc; No se que passa amb l'otoconia

                    Appiani GC et al, Repositioning maneuver for the treatment of the apogeotropic
                    For right HC cupulolithaisis variant of horizontal canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. Oto Neurol, (26(2):257-60, 2005.

                    .Apogeotropic HC BPPV randomized trial
                    • 157 consecutive patients with apogeotropic HC-BPPV were randomized to:
                    • Gufoni (n = 52)
                    • Head-shaking (n = 54)
                    • Sham maneuver (n = 51)
                    • Gufoni maneuver (involved side-lying and upward head-turn)
                    • Gufoni (73%) and head-shaking (62%) showed better responses than the sham 
                    maneuver (35%)
                    • At one month, there was no difference between the outcomes from the Gufoni and the 
                    head shaking maneuver

                    Kim JS et al, Neurology, 2012

                    .Cupulolith Repositioning Maneuver for Apogeotropic HC BPPV ('') (!!).No ho entenc; No se que passa amb l'otoconia
                        (Kim, Jo, Chung, Byeon, and Lee, 2011) 
                        • Goal: 
                            • To move debris located on side of cupula adjacent to utricular vestibule (4th position) or to long arm (1st position) into the vestibule
                        • Procedure:
                            • Each position maintained 3 minutes.
                            • Vibration applied for 30s 1st and 4th position.
                            • Activity Restrictions: Sleep on uninvolved side
                        • Success Rate 97.4% (76/78) after 2 repetitions of maneuver

                    .Summary
                        • Geotropic nystagmus refers to nystagmus beating toward the earth and is 
                        a term generally used to describe nystagmus observed in horizontal canal 
                        canalithiasis
                        • Apogeotropic nystagmus refers to nystagmus beating away from the earth 
                        and is a term generally used to describe nystagmus observed in horizontal 
                        canal cupulolithiasis
                        • The roll test is commonly used to diagnose horizontal canal BPPV and the 
                        sit to supine and Bow and Lean tests can help to determine the involved 
                        side
                        • There are several evidence-based canalith repositioning maneuvers that 
                        are effective for horizontal canal BPPV (canalithiasis and cupulolithiasis)

                .('40 Treatment considerations.pdf')
                    .BPPV Treatment Considerations

                    .Objectives
                        • Describe treatment considerations for BPPV based on the best available 
                        evidence
                        • Identify contraindications to BPPV treatment
                        • Provide patient education for individuals with BPPV using recent literature 
                        findings
                        • Describe the consequences and implications for individuals with BPPV if left 
                        untreated

                    .Preparation for BPPV assessment and treatment
                        • Assess range of motion of the neck
                        • Remove glasses
                        • Remove large earrings, jewelry
                        • Remove hats
                        • Tuck in your tie
                        • Ask about motion sensitivity/sickness

                    .Head shaking during the Dix-Hallpike
                        • Can improve the chance of a positive Dix-Hallpike by 15% in posterior canal BPPV
                        • Consider as an option if all positional tests are negative but history strongly suggests BPPV
                        Kaplan DM et al, 2013

                    .Use of vibration during CRM
                        Do you need to use vibration during the repositioning?
                            • Hain et al (2000) reported that vibration did not affect the short- and long-term 
                            outcome of persons post repositioning with some followed up to 5 years (n=94; 
                            approximately half in each group)
                            • More studies are needed to determine the value/effectiveness during BPPV 
                            treatment 

                    .Timing and repetition of CRMs
                        • Gordon and Gadoth (2004) suggest that repeated repositioning within one session provides superior results to a single maneuver
                        • Repetition of CRM depends on:
                            • Response to treatment
                            • Patient tolerance
                            • Time constraints
                        • Timing between repetition may vary depending on patient response to treatment

                    .Multi-canal BPPV
                        • Can occur on both sides - primarily from head trauma (Katsarkas A, 1999)
                        • Can occur in multiple canals in the same side
                        • General rule is to treat one canal per visit

                    .Variability in anatomy of human semicircular canals ('')

                    .Vestibular agnosia: nystagmus without symptoms
                        • Not all patients say that they are spinning, even when you are seeing the 
                        nystagmus
                        • Post-TBI 
                        • Older adults
                        • Oghalai et al (2000) reported that in people who did not initially report 
                        dizziness to their PCP, 61% reported dizziness when asked, and 9% had 
                        BPPV
                        • Jumani et al (2017) 12 of the 40 people with nystagmus in the Dix-Hallpike 
                        did not report vertigo during the nystagmus
                        • Hawke et al (2024) found that 39% of older adults presenting to a falls 
                        clinic had BPPV (1 in 4 of them were not dizzy)

                        Harrell et al, 2023; Oghalai et al, 2000; Hawke et al, 2024

                    .Subjective BPPV: symptoms without nystagmus
                        • Haynes et al (2002) coined a term “subjective” BPPV 
                        • 91% of persons with “objective” BPPV improved and 87% of those 
                        with “subjective” BPPV improved
                        • Criteria: dizziness or vertigo triggered by a change of head position; 
                        no visible nystagmus; duration < 1 minute
                        • Among 50 participants over 65 years of age, there were significant 
                        differences in those treated versus not treated at 10 days

                        Uz U et al, 2019

                    .Conversion of probable to definitive BPPV
                        • Subjects (n=43; mean age=57) had typical BPPV symptoms within 
                        the past 4 weeks but a negative Dix-Hallpike test
                        • Followed them for 8 weeks
                        • Over the 8 weeks 25 (>50%) had positional vertigo and 8 had a 
                        subsequent positive Dix-Hallpike test

                        Van der Zag-Loonen H et al, 2018

                        Conversion of probable to definitive BPPV

                    .Post-repositioning instructions
                        • Original Epley maneuver included strict post-repositioning instructions
                        • However, there is now high levels of evidence that have found that post-repositioning instructions do not improve clinical outcomes
                        • Clinicians should NOT recommend postprocedural restrictions after CRM for BPPV (!!E)
                            • Strong recommendation by CPG
                        • Benefits of no post-repositioning instructions:
                            • Patient can return to normal lifestyle/activities
                            • Reduced anxiety
                            • Less sleep interruption
                            • More comfort/quality of life

                    .Conditions that require caution when performing the maneuvers
                        • Cervical stenosis
                        • Severe kyphoscoliosis
                        • Limited cervical ROM
                        • Down’s syndrome
                        • Severe rheumatoid arthritis
                        • Cervical radiculopathies
                        • Ankylosing spondylitis
                        • Low back dysfunction
                        • Spinal cord injuries
                        • Paget’s disease
                        • Morbid obesity
                        • Torn or detached retina
                        • Glaucoma
                        • Cognitive deficits
                        • Unstable cardiac conditions

                        When in doubt, get clearance from the physician 


                    .What happens if the symptoms do not resolve after CRM
                        • Try again – it is not uncommon to need more than 1 visit to be successful
                        • Try a different CRM if one is not successful
                        • Assess the other canals – could be multi-canal involvement
                        • Refer to a vestibular rehabilitation expert
                        • Refer back to physician if BPPV persists

                    .Falls and Vestibular Disorders
                        • Falls occur more frequently in persons with vestibular disorders than older adults living in the community 
                        • There is a 12-fold increase in reported falls in persons over the age of 40 who report dizziness (Agrawal et al, 2009)

                        (Herdman et al, 2000; Whitney et al, 2000; Marchetti & Whitney, 2005; Pothula, 2004; Gordon CR et al, 2004)

                    .CRMs decrease falls among those with BPPV
                        • In one study 120 individuals received the Epley and were followed for 12 months 
                        • The reduction in the number of reported falls was statistically significant (398 falls in the 12 months prior to the maneuver vs 139 in the 12 months after the maneuver)
                        • In another study, 40 people over the age of 65 were referred to a falls clinic in the UK who had BPPV
                        • Prior to the CRM, all patients had experienced a fall in the past 6 months
                        • 6 months after the CRM, 30 out of the 40 patients experienced a fall
                        • There was a decrease from 128 to 46 falls which was a 64% decrease in reported falls

                        Gananca FF et al, 2010; Jumani and Powell, 2017

                    .Why should you perform a CRM?
                        • Your patients will love you
                        • You can “fix” their problem with no medication/surgery (sometimes in one visit!)
                        • It could prevent a fall
                        • Your patient’s quality of life is enhanced

                    .What should NOT be done to treat BPPV
                        • Do not recommend radiographic testing (CT, MRI)
                        • Do not recommend vestibular testing (caloric, VEMP, etc)
                        • Do not prescribe vestibular suppressant medication
                        • It will sedate the person but will not “fix” the BPPV
                        • Do not provide strict instructions post-CRM

                    .Response to canalith repositioning maneuvers
                        • Canal conversion in 6-7% of posterior canal cases of BPPV treated with CRM
                        • Sensation of falling within 30 minutes of the maneuver
                        • Nausea, vomiting
                        • Postural instability that can last 24 hours

                    .Tumarkin-like phenomenon as a sign of therapeutic success in BPPV 
                        Maranhao et al, 2018

                    .Patterns of Recurrence in Idiopathic BPPV
                        • 15% recurrence rate per year 
                        • Only 24% of participants with BPPV 
                        showed recurrence in the same canal 
                        • The patterns of recurrences varies 
                        in patients with BPPV (n=224)
                        • “Instruction for self-administration 
                        of a specific CRP based on the 
                        previous type of BPPV may have a 
                        limited efficacy in this frequently 
                        recurrent disorder”

                        (Nunez et al, 2000; Kim and Kim, 2017)

                    .Systematic review and meta-analysis of BPPV outcomes in young versus older adults (Sim E et al, 2019)
                        • 35 studies met criteria using the Joanna Briggs Institute Critical Appraisal Checklists
                        • 3834 participants ranged from 32 to 74 years across studies
                        • Older adults often experienced greater:
                        • Residual dizziness
                        • Postural instability
                        • Dynamic imbalance
                        • Self-perceived handicap 
                        • Take home message: after you treat the BPPV, complete a thorough balance, gait, and functional assessment (particularly among older adults) (!!E)

                    .Patient Education after CRM
                        • Diagnosis of BPPV
                        • Common signs and symptoms of BPPV
                        • Even after successful treatment
                            • May experience imbalance after the repositioning
                            • May be sensitive to motion/movement after repositioning
                        • Follow-up in the clinic to reassess and further assess balance and gait
                        • BPPV recurrence
                        • Return to regular activities

                    .Conclusion
                    • BPPV occurs frequently and is a common complaint 
                    • Positional tests are safe to perform in order to make the 
                    diagnosis
                    • Recognizing and treating BPPV can decrease your patient’s 
                    risk of falling and improve their quality of life

            8.3. Example Videos: BPPV Tests and Measures and Evidence-Based Interventions
            //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
            //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

                Watch the video series to see examples of the tests and measures used to diagnose BPPV as well as evidence-based interventions used to treat BPPV. These will prepare you to complete your assignment this week and for immersion lab. 

                    .('Dix Hallpike.mp4') Dix Hallpike and variations (pillow, loaded, side lying)
                        (Γ)
                            ### Transcript for Video: Dix-Hallpike Test and Variations

                            #### Scene 1: Introduction
                            - Visual: The video opens with a title slide that reads "Dix-Hallpike Test and Variations" with the logo "Pitt SHRS" displayed.
                            - Narration: 
                              - "Welcome to this demonstration of the Dix-Hallpike Test and its variations. This test is used to assess for benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)."

                            #### Scene 2: Setup
                            - Visual: A therapist in a blue shirt and glasses is seen standing next to a patient who is seated on an examination table. The patient is wearing a blue polo shirt and khaki pants, with a face mask.
                            - Narration:
                              - "For this test, the patient will be positioned on the examination table. It's important to ensure the patient is comfortable and ready."

                            #### Scene 3: Performing the Dix-Hallpike Test
                            - Visual: The therapist stands behind the patient and gently supports the patient's head.
                            - Narration:
                              - "The Dix-Hallpike Test begins with the patient sitting upright on the edge of the table."
                              - "I will guide the patient to lie back quickly into a supine position with their head turned 45 degrees to one side."
                              - "The head will be extended slightly beyond the edge of the table."

                            #### Scene 4: Observing Symptoms
                            - Visual: The therapist observes the patient closely as they perform the maneuver.
                            - Narration:
                              - "We will watch for any signs of nystagmus or vertigo, which may indicate BPPV."
                              - "The patient should remain in this position for about 30 seconds to observe any symptoms."

                            #### Scene 5: Repeating the Maneuver
                            - Visual: The therapist helps the patient return to a seated position and then repeats the maneuver on the opposite side.
                            - Narration:
                              - "Now, we will repeat the maneuver on the other side to check for symptoms in both ears."
                              - "Again, we will observe for any signs of nystagmus or vertigo."

                            #### Scene 6: Variation with Pillow Support
                            - Visual: The therapist places pillows under the patient's shoulders to elevate the upper body.
                            - Narration:
                              - "For some patients, it may be more comfortable or effective to perform the test with the upper body elevated using pillows."
                              - "This can help in better isolating the ear being tested."

                            #### Scene 7: Observing Symptoms with Pillow Support
                            - Visual: The therapist performs the Dix-Hallpike maneuver again with the patient in the elevated position.
                            - Narration:
                              - "With the patient in this elevated position, we will once again observe for any signs of nystagmus or vertigo."

                            #### Scene 8: Conclusion
                            - Visual: The therapist assists the patient back into a seated position and discusses the findings.
                            - Narration:
                              - "After performing the Dix-Hallpike Test and its variations, we have observed the patient's responses."
                              - "Based on these observations, further treatment or referral may be recommended."
                              - "Thank you for watching this demonstration. If you have any questions, please consult with a healthcare professional."

                            #### Closing

            8.4. Diagnosis and Management of BPPV Interactive and Discussion

            ////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////// (!!Q)Final

                .Outpatient Clinic: Patient 1
                    ``A 65-year-old male comes to your outpatient clinic via direct access because he is experiencing dizziness. You start your examination by gathering initial information. Of the below information, select all items from the patient history that may indicate benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV).

                    .Items from the patient history that may indicate BPPV (Select all that apply)

                        The patient describes the dizziness as vertigo/room spinning
                        The dizziness occurs in brief episodes (30-60 seconds)
                        The dizziness occurs when the patient rolls over in bed and gets out of bed in the morning
                        The patient reports that he notices a gradual hearing loss as he gets older

                        The dizziness occurs when the patient rolls over in bed and gets out of bed in the morning

                    .From the patient history, your differential diagnoses includes BPPV. What is your first step in the neurologic PT exam after you assess vital signs?
                        Response 1
                        Conduct a cranial nerve exam/oculomotor exam to
                        identify potential red flags and/or potential central signs.
                            It is always important to assess cranial nerves in patients who are experiencing dizziness to identify any potential central causes of dizziness.

                        ✗Response 2
                        Assess positional tests first because you are fairly certain
                        the patient has BPPV.

                    .During a right Dix-Hallpike test, you observe the following. Watch the video below and answer the question that follows. ('Dix-Hallpike test.mp4')
                        Do the findings of your positional tests confirm or refute your hypothesis that the patient has BPPV?​

                        Response 1
                        Confirm
                            Correct! The presence of right torsional upbeating nystagmus in the right Dix-Hallpike position indicates that the patient has right posterior canal BPPV.​

                        ✗Response 2
                        Refute

                    .Given this information, what would you include in your plan of care and treatment for this patient?​
                        Response 1
                        Perform a canalith repositioning maneuver for the right posterior canal (modified Epley, Semont plus, or Li maneuver).
                            Correct! It is recommended by clinical practice guideline that BPPV should be treated with the appropriate canalith repositioning maneuver. In this case, you could elect to treat the patient with any of the maneuvers listed.

                        ✗Response 2
                        Perform VOR x 1 exercises to promote adaptation of the VOR.

                    .The nystagmus was more severe when the patient’s head was turned to which side?

                        Right
                            When the patient's head was turned to the right the nystagmus appeared to be more intense compared to when the head was turned to the left.

                        ✗Response 2
                        Left

                    .The presence of brief geotropic nystagmus observed during the Roll Test that is more intense on the right side indicates what specific diagnosis?
                        Response 1
                        Right horizontal canal canalithiasis (otoconia freely floating in the canal)
                            Brief geotropic nystagmus observed during the Roll Test indicates that the otoconia are freely floating in the canal whereas persistent apogeotropic indicate the otoconia may be adhered to the cupula in the horizontal canal. When geotropic nystagmus is observed, the affected side is the side that has more intense nystagmus and symptom provocation whereas when apogeotropic nystagmus is observed, the affected side is the side that has less intense nystagmus and symptom provocation.

                        ✗Response 2
                        Right horizontal canal cupulolithiasis (otoconia
                        adhered to the cupula)

                    .Given this information, what would you include in your plan of care and treatment for this patient?
                        ✗Response 1
                        Perform a canalith repositioning maneuver for the
                        right horizontal canal cupulolithiasis (Gufoni or Kim),
                        patient education

                        Response 2
                        Perform a canalith repositioning maneuver for the right horizontal canal canalithiasis (Gufoni, BBQ roll, or Li maneuver), patient education
                            Because the patient has brief geotropic nystagmus that is more intense on the right side, it is likely that they have right horizontal canal canalithiasis and should be treated with either the Gufoni, BBQ roll, or Li maneuvers for this specific type of BPPV.

            8.6. Module 8 Summary
            //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
            //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

                Well done! You have completed the third of six modules for Unit 2. Before moving on to the next module, remember to review these three key learnings:  

                Specific positional tests are used to diagnosed persons with posterior, horizontal, and/or anterior canal BPPV. 
                Canalith repositioning maneuvers are recommended by clinical practice guideline for treatment of persons with BPPV. 
                Patient education is essential before, during, and after treatment of persons with BPPV and should include education on the diagnosis, treatment/plan of care, and post-canalith repositioning maneuver information. 
                  

                Learning Outcomes
                After completing this module, you can now: 

                Perform appropriate treatment interventions for clients with benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV). 
                Perform appropriate patient education and follow up recommendations for persons with benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV).

Student inaccurately describes or fails to include multiple  essential elements of an abnormal test finding and/or impact on patient function.  Inclusion of most essential elements are severely lacking or unsafe.
                        Safety  Skill performance is safe for patient care  Skill performance is not safe for patient care.  
                        Note:  A ranking of unsafe in any of the above categories will result in submission of a new assignment.

                    Your video assignment is due in Module 8 by 11:59PM (EST) on Sunday, July 6.

                Assignment Details 
                    For these assignments, you will record yourself performing the selected skills on a subject of your choosing. 

                    Please take note of the following considerations when selecting a subject: 
                        -Make certain that the individual does not have any injury, condition, pain, or other problems that might be worsened by performing this particular skill. 
                        -Never assume this is the case and always ask specifically if the person is aware of “any problems in the body region that could potentially be aggravated.” If you live near to a classmate, this is an ideal choice of subject. 
                        -The subject should be dressed appropriately to allow proper performance of the skill and full viewing of the target area. 
                        -It is strongly recommended that you practice the skill several times before recording and to view your performance for quality prior to submitting. You may re-record the skill as many times as you like but once you submit the product is final. 

                    Please take note of the following considerations before recording: 
                        1.First state the name of the skill and the specific structure or body region that is being assessed.
                            For example: “This video will show a manual muscle test for the quadriceps muscles” or “I will now demonstrate a range of motion assessment on the hip.”
                        2.In layperson’s terms, explain to your model “patient” any brief instructions they need to know about what you are going to do and anything you need to tell them during performance of the skill. (In other words, speak to the subject as if they were your actual patient you are seeing in the clinic.)
                        3.Perform the skill in a manner that includes an adequate view of all needed components. While performing the skill, briefly describe what you are doing to the camera as if you were teaching someone to do this skill for the first time. Include a description of specific aspects of the skill that you have learned in this course are essential for effective performance.
                            -While you may have learned other approaches during your observational experiences, it is important that you demonstrate as you were taught in this program so that instructors can adequately assess your ability to internalize the information presented.
                            -Please assume that the patient requires close supervision so that we can appropriately grade your guarding and patient safety.
                        4.At the end of the video, please provide a brief description of an abnormal or significant test finding and how this might impact patient function per the rubric.
                        5.Keep each video as short as possible while including all needed elements. You should be able to do everything you need in 5 minutes or less.
                        6.Avoid long elaboration on what you are testing for and why, other extensive verbal explanations
                        7.If you are working with another student, each individual student will still need to submit their own video.
                        8.If you do not have all of the specific equipment that is necessary for the measure or intervention, that is OK. You can use materials that you have (be creative) and/or describe what equipment you would use if this were a clinical situation.
                        9.Please refer to the rubric to ensure that you include all required elements in your video.

                    In this module you will come to campus for on site Lab Immersion for Module 9. During the lab immersion, you will practice performing clinical tests and measures and intervention techniques used to evaluate and treat individuals with vestibular disorders. 

                    Learning Outcomes
                    By the end of this week, you will be able to: 

                    Select and perform appropriate tests and measures to determine baseline function for clients with balance and vestibular disorders. 
                    Evaluate data from the PT examination for persons with vestibular disorders to make clinical judgements regarding the care of clients that is patient–centered, evidence-based, and individualized. 
                    Perform appropriate treatment interventions for clients with central and peripheral vestibular disorders including benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV).

                                Clinical Exam Tests 3 

                                Nine Quadrant Test
                                The patient looks at a 9-point grid (high/middle/low X left/center/right) as the physical therapist (PT) 
                                moves a target (index finger). May need to lift eyelid for down gaze positions. The PT observes for  
                                nystagmus in any of the directions.

                                4

                                7

                                 5

                                4 Vestibular Lab Workbook

                                Gaze Holding Nystagmus
                                The PT asks the patient to look in eccentric gaze for up to 30 seconds while the PT observes for presence 
                                of nystagmus. The patient should look to the right about 30 degrees and hold that position, then switch to 
                                about 30 degrees to the left while looking at a target (such as the PT’s fingertip or a pen). The patient should 
                                also look up and down 30 degrees. This can be combined with eye movement range of motion testing.

                                1 2

                                3 4


                                Clinical Exam Tests 5 

                                VERTICAL

                                HORIZONTAL

                                Smooth Pursuit
                                The PT holds a target (fingertip) at a distance of 3 feet from 
                                the patient. The PT asks the patient to follow the target as 
                                the PT slowly moves the target left to right, then up and 
                                down. The PT does not exceed 30 degrees from the nose 
                                for each eye. The target should be moved at a rate requiring 
                                approximately 2 seconds to go from right to left, another 2 
                                seconds to go from left to right, and the same timing for  
                                up and down.

                                v

                                6 Vestibular Lab Workbook

                                HORIZONTAL VERTICAL

                                Horizontal and Vertical Saccades 
                                The PT holds two single points (fingertips) horizontal at a distance of 3 feet from the patient; 1.5 
                                feet to the right and 1.5 feet to the left of midline so that the patient must gaze 30 degrees to 
                                the left and 30 degrees to the right. The PT instructs the patient to move their eyes as quickly as 
                                possible from one point to the next. The same process is repeated up and down. 

                                1 1

                                2 2

                                3 3


                                Clinical Exam Tests 7 

                                Convergence
                                The PT holds up a stick that is marked with a 14 point font target in front of the patient. The PT 
                                instructs the patient to watch the target with both eyes as it comes toward the patient’s face and 
                                state when the target doubles. The PT records the distance from the patient’s nose to where the 
                                patient says the target doubled. Scores of ≤5 cm are considered normal. 

                                1a 2a

                                1b 2b


                                8 Vestibular Lab Workbook

                                Cover and Uncover Test
                                COVER (indicates tropia if positive): The patient is seated looking straight ahead at a target approximately 
                                10 feet away. The paddle (occluder) is placed over one eye and the PT observes for any eye movement of 
                                the uncovered eye. Note if the eye moves in or out, up or down. Then UNCOVER. Repeat for the other eye. 
                                If a corrective movement is seen, it means that a misalignment was present. Inward movement means 
                                that an exotropia was present and named for the eye that moved. Outward movement means that an 
                                esotropia was present. Downward movement means a hypertropia was present. Upward movement 
                                means a hypotropia was present. A tropia can be fixed or alternating. 

                                1 2

                                3 4


                                Clinical Exam Tests 9 

                                Cross-Cover Test 
                                CROSS COVER (indicates phoria, if COVER test is 
                                negative): The patient is seated looking straight ahead  
                                at a target approximately 10 feet away. The occluder  
                                is held over one eye for 3–4 seconds and it is then 
                                quickly placed over the other eye. Repeat for 3–4 cycles. 
                                The PT observes the eye that that is being uncovered 
                                and notes if it moves in or out, up or down. The same 
                                movement will be seen in both eyes, so phorias are not 
                                named by side. 
                                If a corrective movement is seen, it means that a 
                                misalignment was present. Inward movement means 
                                that an exophoria was present. Outward movement 
                                means that an esophoria was present. Downward 
                                movement means a hyperphoria was present. Upward 
                                movement means a hypophoria was present. 

                                1

                                2

                                3


                                10 Vestibular Lab Workbook

                                Head Impulse Test (Horizontal Canal)
                                The patient is instructed to look at a target in midline. The PT slowly moves the patient’s head in the yaw 
                                plane about 15–20 degrees and then quickly moves the patient’s head to midline (the impulse) while the 
                                patient attempts to keep their eyes on the target. The head is rapidly stopped, and the PT checks to see 
                                if the patient has a “catch-up” saccade that will refixate their eyes on the target. The head can be moved 
                                away from midline for the impulse, but it is better to move toward the midline. The movement must be 
                                fully stopped before doing the next impulse. 
                                A normal VOR response to rapid passive head rotation is that the patient is able to fixate on the central 
                                target without saccades. An abnormal response occurs when head is rotated to the side of the vestibular 
                                lesion and there is an inability to maintain fixation during rotation of the head requiring a corrective sac-
                                cade once the head has stopped moving. 

                                1 2

                                3 4


                                Clinical Exam Tests 11 

                                HINTS Exam
                                The HINTS exam can be used as a tool to identify a posterior circulation stroke. The cluster of tests 
                                includes Horizontal head Impulse Testing; Direction changing Nystagmus; Vertical Test of Skew. A 
                                single central finding on any of the three components rules in a posterior circulation stroke.

                                HI4 N1

                                Head Shake Test (Head Shaking Nystagmus) 
                                The PT tilts the patient’s head forward 20–30 degrees and shakes the head in the yaw plane with 
                                eyes closed for 20 cycles quickly. The PT has the patient open their eyes and observes for post 
                                shake nystagmus. Goggles are preferred for this test. 

                                1 1

                                2 2

                                3 3

                                WITH GOGGLES–PREFERRED WITHOUT GOGGLES


                                Clinical Exam Tests 13 

                                Dynamic Visual Acuity Test  
                                The patient sits at a distance that is marked at the top of the LogMAR Eye chart. The PT insturcts the 
                                patient to read the LogMAR Eye chart first with the head still, and notes the lowest complete line (Static 
                                Visual Acuity). The PT then shakes the patient’s head 20–30 degrees in the yaw plane with head flexed 30 
                                degrees at 2 Hz (240 beats on a metronome, head is in right or left position with each beat). The PT notes 
                                the lowest complete line (Dynamic Visual Acuity). A positive test occurs if the patient lost more than two 
                                lines while moving the head versus while the head is still and indicates a deficit in the functional VOR. 

                                1 2

                                3 4 5


                                14 Vestibular Lab Workbook

                                Vibration Induced Nystagmus 
                                While the patient is sitting with goggles donned, vibration with a frequency of 
                                100Hz is applied to the mastoid process. In someone with unilateral vestibular 
                                loss, the resulting nystagmus will beat away from the affected ear.  

                                1


                                Clinical Exam Tests 15 

                                Rinne and Weber Tests 
                                Rinne test: Used to discern sound transmitted through 
                                air versus bone and helps assess for unilateral hearing 
                                loss. Using a 512-Hz tuning fork, the PT strikes the 
                                fork inducing vibration. The stem of the tuning fork 
                                is placed on the mastoid process of the patient. The 
                                patient is then asked to cover their other ear with their 
                                hand. The patient informs the PT when the sound 
                                can no longer be heard. The process is then repeated 
                                with the tines of the tuning fork held near the external 
                                auditory canal and the patient again informs the 
                                examiner when the sound can no longer be heard.  
                                Results: Normal hearing is observed when the 
                                vibrating tuning fork positioned near the ear is louder 
                                and lasts twice as long compared to when placed on 
                                the mastoid.  
                                Abnormal: When the sound is at least equally loud 
                                or louder when the fork is placed on the mastoid 
                                compared to when it is held next to the ear.  
                                Weber test: Used to assess for a unilateral hearing loss 
                                and to characterize conductive versus sensorineural 
                                loss. Using a 512-Hz tuning fork, the PT strikes the fork 
                                tines to induce vibration. The stem of the tuning fork 
                                is then placed on the top of the patient’s head. The 
                                patient is asked “is the sound louder in your right ear, 
                                left ear, or the same in both?”
                                Results: Normal hearing is confirmed when the sound 
                                is heard midline and equally on both sides 
                                Unilateral sensorineural hearing loss is observed if 
                                the patient hears the sound louder (lateralizes) in the 
                                unaffected ear. 
                                Unilateral conductive hearing loss is observed if the 
                                patient hears the sound louder (lateralizes) in the 
                                affected ear. 
                                Symmertical conductive hearing loss is observed if the 
                                patient does not exhibit lateralization.

                                 

                                1

                                2

                                3


                                Clinical Treatment


                                Clinical Treatment 17 

                                VOR x1 (x1 viewing) 
                                The patient looks at a target about 18–24 inches away from their eyes. They are asked to move 
                                their head in either pitch or yaw planes while keeping the target in focus. A 14 point font is most 
                                commonly used for the 18 inch distance, and larger for farther away. The patient is instructed to 
                                move their head as quickly as possible but to keep the target in focus. The PT determines if the 
                                head movements increase their symptoms and at what speed. They should be able to move their 
                                head at about 100–120 beats per minute on a metronome without symptoms.  

                                HORIZONTAL VERTICAL
                                1 1

                                2 2

                                3 3


                                18 Vestibular Lab Workbook

                                VOR Cancellation (Visual Motion Sensitivity) 
                                The patient extends their arm directly in front of their body or clasps their hands together. The patient is 
                                instructed to visually fixate on the target and maintain fixation. The entire body is then rotated 80 degrees 
                                back and forth to each side at a comfortable speed for several cycles (use a metronome at 50 beats/
                                minute). May use a swivel chair/stool or the patient can twist from waist using a stationary seat or stand 
                                with feet apart. NOTE: Patient must keep the head, neck and shoulders moving together as a unit and 
                                their hands/thumbs straight out in front of their body. 
                                A normal response is when the eyes remain stationary and motionless throughout the test.

                                VOR Plus Vergence 
                                The PT instructs the patient to perform the VORx1 exercise while moving the target toward and

                                Head Impulse Exercise
                                The patient is seated and focusing on a target about  
                                3 feet from their nose. They quickly move their head 
                                about 15–20 degrees toward the affected side and then 
                                slowly move their head back to center. 

                                1

                                2

                                3


                                Clinical Treatment 21 

                                Eye Head Saccade Exercises 
                                This exercise is prescribed for patients with unilateral and bilateral loss but definitely for patients 
                                with bilateral loss. There are two targets in front of them at least 18 inches away at about a 30 
                                degree angle from their nose to the right and the left (or up and down). The patient is to look at 
                                one target, and then move their eyes ONLY to the second target, then move their head and repeat 
                                this in the opposite direction. The goal is to attempt to have the saccadic eye system help to 
                                compensate for the damage to the VOR. 

                                1 2

                                3 4


                                22 Vestibular Lab Workbook

                                Imaginary Targets (Remembered Targets) 
                                The PT has the patient look at a target directly in front of them. The PT instructs the patient to close their 
                                eyes and turn their head slightly in the yaw plane imagining that they are still looking at the target. The 
                                PT instructs the patient to open their eyes and see if they were able to keep their eyes on the target. The 
                                patient repeats the exercise in the opposite direction. The patient should NOT be holding the target. 

                                1 2

                                3 4


                                Clinical Treatment 23 

                                Brock String 
                                The patient holds one end of the Brock string at the 
                                tip of their nose and the other end is attached to a 
                                stationary object so that the string is taut. Move the 
                                nearest bead to the near point of convergence or just 
                                closer. Move the far bead to arm’s length and place 
                                the middle bead at the midpoint of the other two. The 
                                patient starts by focusing on the far bead and holds 
                                for 5–10 seconds. The patient should report seeing 
                                two lines diverging toward them like the letter A from 
                                the far bead. 
                                Next, the patient changes focus to the middle bead 
                                and holds for 5–10 seconds. The patient should report 
                                seeing two lines diverging toward and away from 
                                them like the letter X from the middle bead.
                                Then the patient changes focus to the close bead and 
                                holds for 5–10 seconds. The patient should report 
                                seeing two lines diverging away from them like the 
                                letter V from the close bead. 
                                Then the patient moves focus back to the middle 
                                bead and far bead, holding each for 5–10 seconds. 
                                This should be repeated until symptoms increase by 
                                several units or the patient needs to take a break. 
                                Progress by changing starting point, increasing reps, 
                                or adding more beads to the string.  

                                1

                                2


                                Posterior Canal BPPV  
                                Positional Tests


                                Posterior Canal BPPV Positional Tests 25 

                                Dix-Hallpike 
                                After checking cervical range of motion, with the patient in 
                                long-sitting position on a mat table, the PT places patient’s 
                                head in 45 degrees of yaw rotation. The PT quickly (1–2 
                                seconds) lowers the patient to supine position with head 
                                extended 30 degrees below the edge of the mat. The 
                                PT observes for nystagmus to become evident over 30 
                                seconds and notes the direction of the nystagmus. For 
                                posterior canal BPPV, nystagmus should be upbeating and 
                                torsional toward the tested side. Good body mechanics 
                                are utilized to avoid injury. The PT maintains contact with 
                                the patient after bringing the patient back up to the sitting 
                                posture and is careful throughout the maneuver to avoid 
                                neck or back pain for the patient and back pain for the PT.

                                2 2

                                3 3

                                WITHOUT GOGGLES


                                26 Vestibular Lab Workbook

                                Loaded Dix-Hallpike 
                                Perform the same as Dix-Hallpike, except begin with head rotated 45 degrees towards the side 
                                being texted, flexed 30 degrees to chest, and while in the long sitting position (i.e., pre-loading the 
                                head). Hold for 30 seconds before placing the patient in supine.

                                 

                                1 2

                                3 4


                                Posterior Canal BPPV Positional Tests 27 

                                Modified Dix-Hallpike Test With Head Over Pillow 
                                The patient, with their head rotated in yaw 45 degrees, is laid down in supine with their head 
                                extended over the edge of a pillow approximately 20–30 degrees in extension. Care must be taken 
                                to choose the correct pillow size in order to avoid excessive extension. 

                                1

                                2


                                28 Vestibular Lab Workbook

                                Sidelying Test 
                                The patient starts in sitting with legs resting over edge of table (hips/knees at 90 degrees). The 
                                PT has the patient turn their head 45 degrees away from the ear being tested and brings them 
                                rapidly down sidelying to the table on the side being tested, with the nose toward the ceiling. The 
                                PT observes for nystagmus to become evident over 30 seconds and notes the direction of the 
                                nystagmus. The PT understands what a positive test indicates when visualized. The PT brings the 
                                patient back up to sitting, taking care to hold onto the patient as they return to sitting and for about 
                                30 seconds to 1 minute after they have returned to sitting. 

                                1

                                2


                                Posterior Canal Canalith 
                                Repositioning Maneuvers


                                Posterior Canal Canalith Repositioning Maneuvers 31 

                                Modified Epley 
                                The PT instructs and demonstrates for the patient and explains the purpose of the maneuver.  
                                STEP 1: The PT seats the patient on the table in long sitting with the head in 45 degrees rotation toward the affected ear. 
                                The PT quickly lowers the patient to supine (1–2 seconds) so they may be taken back to the head-hanging position with 
                                the neck in slight extension (20–30 degrees of extension). The PT stabilizes the head with their hands and waits for the 
                                nystagmus to stop. The PT observes for eye movement in the head hanging position.   
                                STEP 2: The PT rotates the head 90 degrees towards the uninvolved side by turning the head toward opposite side. 
                                The PT observes the patient’s eyes and waits for nystagmus to stop. Keep the neck in extension during the turn to the 
                                opposite side and wait 30 seconds.  
                                STEP 3: Log roll patient onto unaffected side so that the head is turned to face ground. Hold and wait 30 seconds.  
                                STEP 4: The patient keeps their chin tucked towards their shoulder and rises to sitting while the PT HOLDS ON TO THE 
                                PATIENT with both hands. The PT slowly turns the patient’s head back to midline. The PT HOLDS ON TO THE PATIENT as 
                                they come to sitting and up to a minute or more after completion of the maneuver.

                                WITH GOGGLES–PREFERRED WITHOUT GOGGLES


                                32 Vestibular Lab Workbook

                                Semont
                                The PT rotates the patient’s head 45 degrees away from the affected side and quickly moves the patient 
                                into side-lie (head now facing up, image 3). Stay in this position for 1–2 minutes. Quickly, in one motion, sit 
                                up and move the patient onto the opposite side-lie (good side) without changing head position (nose now 
                                facing the ground, image 6). Stay in this position for 1–2 minutes. Remember that modeling suggests the 
                                ‘flip’ needs to be completed in <1.5 seconds. The PT then returns the patient slowly to sitting. If reversal of 
                                nystagmus occurs (or unsure), repeat up to three repetitions.

                                1

                                3

                                2

                                4 5

                                6 7


                                Posterior Canal Canalith Repositioning Maneuvers 33 

                                Semont Plus 
                                The patient begins sitting upright and facing forward, then the PT turns the patient’s head away from the affected ear. 
                                The PT quickly lays the patient down on the side of the involved ear, over the edge of the table about 20–30 degrees so 
                                that the patient’s dependent arm can abduct off the table and rest on the stool. The patient stays there until the vertigo 
                                passes. The PT QUICKLY sits the patient up and then lays them on their other side while KEEPING the patient’s head 
                                pointing over the shoulder the entire time (the orientation of the head should not change). This should be completed in 
                                one movement without stopping in the middle. The patient should be facing down toward the ground. Wait there until 
                                any vertigo/nystagmus passes. The PT then HOLDS ON TO THE PATIENT as they come to sitting, and continues holding 
                                onto them for up to a minute or more after completion of the maneuver.
