                        Vestibular Lab Skills Descriptions
                            .('36 Vestibular Lab Skills_2024.pdf')
                                Vestibular Lab Work Sheet

                                Observation of movement 
                                •   Observe how the person walks
                                o   are they veering to one side - may indicate unilateral vestibular loss 
                                o   are they ataxic- indicative of central disorder, motor, or sensory impairment.  
                                •   Observe their speech and facial symmetry when you first meet them.  
                                •   Observe them going from stand to sit if they walked into your clinic.  
                                •   Observe for any assistive devices or use of the wall or other person to assist them with locomotion.
                                History/patient/client Interview specific to vestibular disorders  
                                •   HPI, PMH, (including family hx and surgical hx), include questions about migraine, a history of strabismus, anxiety, depression, problems with sleep, past concussions, other psychiatric comorbidities)
                                •   Previous diagnostic testing
                                •   Previous treatment for their vestibular condition
                                •   Medications (esp. those that can interfere with vestibular testing results and with recovery) 
                                •   Reports of hearing loss, tinnitus and or visual disturbances 
                                •   Symptoms related to dizziness/vertigo/balance problems, e.g. onset, duration, frequency, intensity 
                                •   Information from self-reported questionnaires- what does the data tell you?  How will you use it in determining the PT diagnosis?
                                •   Description of movements or circumstances that exacerbate or decrease symptoms 
                                •   Report of falls or reports of imbalance or problems with movement 
                                •   Problems with activity and participation plus any environmental factors that affect movement
                                Systems Review: Screening 
                                Are there any red flags or any systems that warrant a more detailed examination? 
                                Is the patient’s condition:
                                •   Emergent:  Should I refer for medical interventions
                                •   Non-emergent: Initiate vestibular rehabilitation-but may want to refer the patient for additional medical intervention.
                                •   No need for other discipline involvement currently. Continue with vestibular rehabilitation 

                                As part of your evaluation process, you will need to determine if additional services are needed for optimal care.


                                 

                                Oculomotor Examination (all done with patient sitting)
                                Spontaneous nystagmus
                                The physical therapist should have the patient look at a white piece of paper with nothing on it and attempt to discern if there is any nystagmus. You may need to stabilize the head while you do this. Some hold the chin to make sure that there is no head movement. It is difficult to determine the direction of the fast phase when it is spontaneous nystagmus.

                                Eye Movement range of motion
                                The patient is to look at 9-point grid (high/middle/low X left/center/right) as physical therapist moves a target (index finger). May need to lift eyelid for down gaze positions. Does patient have full range of motion with both eyes? If not, may indicate nerve palsy. Also observe for nystagmus in any of the directions. 

                                Gaze-holding nystagmus
                                The physical therapist will ask the patient to look in eccentric gaze for up to 30 seconds to see if there is any nystagmus.  They should look to the right about 30 degrees and hold that position and then switch to about 30 degrees to the left while looking at your finger or a pen. You should see no nystagmus or drift. If they eye drifts to the middle (comes in towards their nose), it can indicate cerebellar dysfunction. This test can be combined with the eye movement range of motion. 

                                Smooth Pursuit
                                The physical therapist holds their fingertip at a distance of 3 ft from the patient.  The PT asks the patient to follow their finger (or a target) as they slowly move their finger left to right, then up and down.  The PT does not exceed 30° for each eye from the nose (target should be moved at a rate requiring approximately 2 seconds to go from right to left and another 2 seconds to go from left to right) and the same timing for up and down. 

                                Horizontal and vertical saccades
                                The physical therapist holds 2 single points (fingertips) horizontal. at distance of 3 ft from patient, and 1.5 ft to the right and 1.5 ft to the left of midline (so that the patient must gaze 30° to the left and 30° to the right). The PT instructs the patient to move her (his) eyes as quickly as possible from one point to the next. The same process is repeated up and down.

                                Convergence 
                                The PT asks the patient to bring a stick that has a target on it close to their eyes and the patient is to watch the target with both eyes as it comes in towards their face. When the patient says that is doubles or if the PT observes the eyes diverge, the therapist records the distance from the patient’s nose to where the target doubled or divergence occurred. Scores of ≤5 cm is considered normal.

                                Cover (Also called Cover-Uncover) Test
                                COVER (indicates tropia if positive): The paddle (occluder) is placed over one eye and the examiner observes for any movement of the uncovered eye. Note if the eye moves in or out, up or down. Then Uncover. Repeat for the other eye.

                                If a corrective movement is seen, it means that a misalignment was present. Inward movement means that an exotropia was present and named for the eye that moved. Outward movement means that an esotropia was present. Downward movement means a hypertropia was present. Upward movement means a hypotropia was present. A tropia can be fixed or alternating.

                                A vertical misalignment can occur from either peripheral or central disorders, but they are more common with central disorders, and should be investigated further. For instance, a skew deviation, consisting of vertical tropia, ocular counter-rolling and head tilt, is associated with a brain lesion.

                                Cross-Cover Test
                                CROSS COVER (indicates phoria, if COVER test is negative): The occluder is held over one eye for 3-4 seconds and it is then quickly placed over the other eye.  Repeat for 3 – 4 cycles. Observe the eye that that is being uncovered and note if it moves in or out, up or down. You will see the same movement in both eyes, so phorias are bilateral and not named by side.

                                If a corrective movement is seen, it means that a misalignment was present. Inward movement means that an exophoria was present. Outward movement means that an esophoria was present. Downward movement means a hyperphoria was present. Upward movement means a hypophoria was present.

                                 

                                Vestibular ocular reflex (VOR) testing (all done with patient sitting)
                                Head impulse test
                                The patient is to look at a target in midline. The PT flexes the head 20-30 degrees and slowly moves the patient’s head in the yaw plane about 15-20 degrees and then quickly moves the patient’s head to midline (the impulse) while the patient views the target.  The head is rapidly stopped, and the PT is to check to see if they have a “catch-up” saccade that will refixate their eyes on the target.  You can move the head away from looking straight ahead, but it is better to move toward center. Make sure to stop the movement fully before doing the next impulse.

                                A normal VOR response to rapid passive head rotation is that the patient is able to fixate on the central target without saccades. An abnormal response occurs when head is rotated to the side of the vestibular lesion and there is an inability to maintain fixation during rotation of the head requiring a corrective saccade once head has stopped moving.

                                VORx1 (x1 viewing)
                                The patient looks at a target about 18-24 inches away from their eyes.  They are asked to keep the target in focus and move their head in either pitch, yaw or roll planes while keeping the target in focus. Most use a 14-point font for the 18-inch target and larger for further away.  The patient is instructed to move their head as quickly as possible but to keep the target in focus.  The clinician determines if the head movements increase their symptoms and at what speed.  They should be able to move their head at about 100-120 beats per minute on a metronome without symptoms.   

                                Head shake Test (Head shaking nystagmus)
                                The physical therapist flexes the patient’s head forward 20-30° and shakes the head in the yaw plane with eyes closed for 20 cycles quickly.  The physical therapist has the patient open their eyes and observes for post shake nystagmus. More than 3 beats of nystagmus is considered to be a positive test and suggests a vestibular hypofunction. Freznel lenses are preferred for this test.

                                Dynamic Visual Acuity Test
                                The patient sits at a distance that is marked at the top of the LogMAR Eye chart. Have the patient read the LogMAR Eye chart first with head still and note the lowest complete line (Static Visual Acuity). Then shake patient’s head 20-30 deg in the yaw plane and head flexed 20-30 deg at 2 Hz (240 beats on a metronome, head is in right or left position with each beat).  Note the lowest complete line (Dynamic Visual Acuity). A positive test occurs if the patient lost more than 2 lines while moving head versus while the head is still and indicates a deficit in the functional VOR.

                                VOR cancellation (Visual Motion Sensitivity)- this cancels the VOR so it is not really a VOR test but it is included here
                                Patient is asked to extend their arm directly in front of their body or can clasp hands together. The patient is to visually fixate on their thumb(s) and maintain fixation; the entire body is then rotated 80 deg back and forth to each side at a comfortable speed for several cycles (use a metronome at 50 beats/min).  May use a swivel chair/stool or the patient can twist from waist using a stationary seat or stand with feet apart. NOTE: Patient must keep the head, neck and shoulders moving together as a unit and their hands/thumbs straight out in front of their body.

                                A normal response is when the eyes remain stationary and motionless throughout the test.  The physical therapist should understand that this test assesses the ability to inhibit vestibular-induced eye movements using vision.  

                                Note if the patient becomes symptomatic, however, symptom provocation does not indicate an abnormal test.


                                 
                                Posterior canal BPPV positional tests 
                                Dix-Hallpike
                                After checking cervical range of motion and stability, with patient in long-sitting position on a mat table, PT places patient’s head in 45 degrees of yaw rotation. PT quickly (1 -2 sec) lowers patient to supine position with head extended 30 degrees below the edge of the mat. The PT observes for nystagmus to become evident over 30 sec and notes the direction of the nystagmus. For posterior canal BPPV, nystagmus should be upbeating and torsional toward the tested side.  The PT understands what a positive Dix-Hallpike test indicates when visualized.  Good body mechanics are utilized to avoid injury to themselves.  The PT maintains contact with the patient after bringing the patient back up to the sitting posture and is careful throughout the maneuver to avoid neck or back pain for the patient and back pain for the PT.  

                                Loaded Dix-Hallpike
                                Perform the same as Dix-Hallpike, except begin with head rotated 45 deg and flexed 30 deg to chest and while in the long sitting position (i.e. pre-loading the head). Hold for 30 sec before placing patient in supine.

                                Modified Dix-Hallpike - Sidelying test
                                The patient starts in sitting with legs resting over edge (hips/knees at 90 deg).  The PT has the patient turn their head 45 deg away for the ear that they would like to test and brings them rapidly down sidelying to the table on the side you are testing, with the nose toward the ceiling. The PT observes for nystagmus to become evident over 30 sec and notes the direction of the nystagmus.  The PT understands what a positive test indicates when visualized.  Then bring the patient back up to sitting—hold onto the patient as they return to sitting and for about 30 sec to 1 minute after they have returned to sitting.

                                Modified Dix-Hallpike test with head over pillow
                                The patient with their head rotated in yaw 45 deg is laid down in supine onto a pillow extended over the edge of the pillow approximately 20-30 degrees in extension.  Care must be taken to choose the correct pillow size in order to avoid excessive extension.  The test is done with the head turned to the right and the left to test the right and left posterior canal.


                                 

                                Horizontal canal BPPV positional tests 
                                Perform in this order:
                                Bow and Lean Test
                                Patient is sitting.  
                                BOW: Patient to flex the torso to be parallel to floor and hold for 30 sec. Note the direction of nystagmus. If you see geotropic nystagmus with the roll test, the nystagmus will beat towards the affected ear. If you see ageotropic nystagmus with the roll test, the nystagmus will beat towards the healthy ear.

                                LEAN: Patient to extend head as if looking at ceiling for 30 sec. Note the direction of nystagmus, which should be opposite to what you saw in the BOW test. If you see geotropic nystagmus with the roll test, the nystagmus will beat towards the healthy ear. If you see ageotropic nystagmus with the roll test, the nystagmus will beat towards the affected ear. (Geotropic -> nystagmus beats toward Good, Ageotropic -> Affected)

                                Results from this test will be used to confirm the side of the affected ear if there is uncertainty about which ear had the greatest nystagmus/vertigo. Write down the results. In some cases, you will not see any nystagmus during this test.

                                Sit to Supine test (Similar to Lean Test)
                                The patient starts in long sitting and then moves to supine quickly and ends with them in about 30 degrees of neck flexion (on a pillow will usually work fine). Observe the eye movement if there is any. 
                                -If the roll test was positive for geotropic nystagmus, the nystagmus will beat away from the affected ear.  If the roll test was positive for ageotropic nystagmus, the nystagmus will beat towards the affected ear.   (Geotropic -> nystagmus beats toward Good, Ageotropic -> Affected)

                                Results from this test will be used to confirm the side of the affected ear if there is uncertainty about which ear had the greatest nystagmus/vertigo. Write down the results. In some cases, you will not see any nystagmus during this test.

                                Roll Test (Pagnini-McClure Roll Test)
                                This is the diagnostic test for horizontal canal BPPV. Patient begins in long sitting position on a mat table and head flexed in midline 20-30 degrees. PT lowers patient to supine (with head still flexed 20-30 deg above horizontal). PT quickly moves head to right and holds for 30 sec. The PT observes for nystagmus to become evident over 30 sec and notes the direction of the nystagmus.  The PT moves head back to midline and waits for 30 sec before quickly moving head to left and holding for 30 sec. The PT observes for nystagmus to become evident over 30 sec and notes the direction of the nystagmus.  If positive, you should see nystagmus beating towards the ground (geotropic), OR away from the ground (ageotropic), in both right and left head positions. PT asks the patient which side had the worst symptoms. The PT understands what a positive Roll test indicates when visualized.   The PT can recognize that the side with the worst symptoms is the side to be treated in geotropic nystagmus (toward Earth) and the opposite if ageotropic nystagmus (away from Earth). Geotropic nystagmus indicates free-floating otoconia (canalithiasis) versus apogeotropic nystagmus indicates otoconia stuck to the cupula (cupulolithiasis).



                                Canalith repositioning procedures (CRPs)  or Canalith repositioning maneuvers (CRMs) : Posterior Canal: 

                                Modified Epley (first choice)
                                The PT instructs and demonstrates for patient and explains the purpose to the patient.
                                STEP 1: Seat the patient on the table in long sitting with head in 45 degrees rotation toward the affected ear. Quickly lower to supine (1-2 sec) so they may be taken back to the head-hanging position with the neck in slight extension (20-30 degrees of extension). The PT stabilizes the head with hands and waits for the nystagmus to stop.  Observe for eye movement in the head hanging position. 
                                STEP 2:  Then rotate the head 90 deg towards the uninvolved side by turning the head toward opposite side - PT observes eyes- wait for nystagmus to stop. Keep neck in extension during the turn to the opposite side and wait 30 sec. 
                                STEP 3: Log roll patient onto unaffected side so that the head is turned to face ground- hold and wait 30 sec.  
                                STEP 4: Keep chin tucked towards their shoulder and have them rise to sitting but HOLD ON TO THEM when they sit up with both hands. Then slowly turn head back to midline. HOLD ON TO THEM when as they come to sitting and up to a minute or more after completion of the maneuver.

                                Li maneuver for the posterior canal
                                Start in sitting with legs hanging over edge of mat (hips/knees at 90 deg).  The PT moves the patient down quickly to their involved side with their nose forward while you hold their head (no turning of the head is required for this maneuver).  After 1 minute or after resolution of the nystagmus, rapidly move them 180 degrees with the healthy ear down on the mat with their nose facing forwards. Lie there for 4 minutes and then rapidly lift them back to sitting.  HOLD ON TO THEM for up to several minutes after completion of the Li maneuver.

                                Semont plus (from Strupp RCT)
                                The PT explains the purpose to the patient; the patient is rapidly moved from lying on one side to lying on the other. You can move the table up to a comfortable position for you and have a stool placed at the end of the table to which you will be moving patient first. Start sitting and turn the head away from the affected ear.  Then lie patient down on involved ear side quickly over the edge of the table about 20-30 degrees, so that their dependent arm can abduct off the table and rest on the stool. The patient is to stay there until the vertigo passes. The PT QUICKLY sits the patient up and then lays them on their other side but KEEPING the patient’s head pointing over the shoulder during the entire time (Do not change the orientation of the head). The patient should be facing down to the ground. Also do not stop in the middle of this movement.  Wait there until any vertigo/nystagmus passes. Then patient sits up and you must HOLD ON TO THEM when as they come to sitting and up to a minute or more after completion of the maneuver.


                                 


                                Canalith repositioning Procedures (CRPs): Horizontal Canal

                                Geotropic BPPV maneuvers

                                Gufoni maneuver for geotropic nystagmus (first choice)
                                Patient sits in the middle of a mat table with legs hanging over side and head in midline and is briskly brought down onto the UNAFFECTED side for 30 sec.  The head is then quickly turned down by 45 deg and held there for 2-3 minutes, then the patient is brought back into the sitting position.

                                Li quick repositioning maneuver for geotropic horizontal canal
                                Start in supine in the middle of a large bed.  Log roll patient 90 deg onto the affected side and wait until the symptoms resolve.  The clinician then is to stand behind the patient and grabs the patient’s hand on the involved side and QUICKLY log rolls them 180 deg onto their unaffected side.  Stay on the unaffected left side for 2 minutes and then bring the patient to sitting.  The maneuver takes approximately 3 minutes to perform.

                                Ageotropic BPPV maneuvers
                                Remember, affected side is opposite to the side which had most vertigo/nystagmus

                                Kim maneuver for ageotropic HC BPPV (first choice)
                                Starting in supine, log roll the patient 135 deg towards the affected side so that their nose is almost facing the floor. Put the vibrator over their mastoid of affected side for 30 sec; wait for the nystagmus to stop.  The do a series of log rolls away from affected ear and wait for 3 minutes in each position or until vertigo/nystagmus stop. Log roll them to back to side lying (90 deg from supine). Then log roll to supine nose up position.  Then log roll 90 deg to unaffected side and vibrate over the mastoid again for 30 sec. Finally log roll to prone.  The PT will move the patient carefully and ensure that they do not excessively pull on their cervical spine.

                                Gufoni maneuver for ageotropic nystagmus
                                Patient sits in the middle of a mat table with legs hanging over side and head in midline.  The PT will have the person look straight and then bring the patient down onto their AFFECTED side for 30 sec.  Then they will turn their head up towards the ceiling and let them rest in this position approximately 2 minutes. At the end of the 2 minutes, they should bring the subject back to sitting holding onto them throughout.  If this does not work, most of us will try the same maneuver but have the nose tilted down towards the floor.

                                Progressive gaze stability exercise (VOR adaptation)
                                VOR X1 (X1 viewing)
                                Patient is to focus on a target at about 3 feet from their nose and move their head to the right/left or up/down while moving as quickly as they can and still see the target clearly. The target must stay in focus. Progress speed with metronome.

                                VOR X2 (X2 viewing)
                                Patient’s head and eyes move in opposite directions as they focus on a target held in hand at arms distance.  As they move their head to the right, the target held in the hand that they are focusing on must move to the left and then they alternate directions. Perform in a small range of motion until the eyes get to end range.

                                VOR plus vergence
                                Have the patient do the VOR x 1 exercise but have the target comes towards their eyes and away from their eyes so that they are doing vergence and the VOR x 1 exercise simultaneously.  This has been shown recently to increase the gain of the VOR.


                                Unilateral self-initiated head impulses toward affected side
                                Patient is seated and focusing on a target at about 3 feet from their nose. They quickly move their head about 15-20 deg toward the affected side and then slowly move their head back to center.  

                                Substitution exercise
                                Imaginary targets (remembered targets)
                                The PT has the patient look at a target directly in front of them. The PT instructs the patient to close their eyes and turn head slightly in the yaw plane imagining that they are still looking at the target.  The PT instructs the patient to open their eyes and see if they were able to keep their eyes on the target.  The patient repeats the exercise in the opposite direction. The patient should NOT be holding the target.

                                Eye Head saccade exercises (saccadic corrections)
                                This exercise is prescribed for people with unilateral and bilateral loss but definitely for persons with bilateral loss.  They are 2 targets on a wall in front of them at least 18 inches away at about a 30-degree angle from their nose to the right and the left (or up and down). They are to look at one target, and then they are to move their eyes ONLY to the second target and then move their head and repeat this in the opposite direction. The goal is to attempt to have the saccadic eye system help to compensate for the damage to the VOR.

                                Habituation exercises (use them carefully and only in select patients):
                                Examples include:
                                •   VOR X1 with busy background in standing or walking
                                •   VOR Cancellation in sitting, standing and walking
                                •   Viewing a disco ball in sitting, standing and while moving the head or walking in various combinations
                                •   Moving the body to try to provoke symptoms repeatedly with the hope that they symptoms will decrease in intensity
                                Oculomotor exercises
                                Pencil Pushup
                                The patient is holding a pencil at arm’s length in midline and eye-level and focuses on a letter or other marking. They slowly move the pencil in toward their nose over a duration of 5 to 10 sec, until the target they are looking at just becomes double. Then they slowly move the pencil away at same speed until arm is fully extended. Repeat for a number of repetitions until symptoms increase by several units or they need to take a break. Progress by changing starting point or increasing reps.

                                Smooth Pursuits
                                The patient follows a moving target such as a tongue depressor or their finger as they slowly move their finger left to right, then up and down.  The PT does not exceed 30° for each eye from the nose (target should be moved at a rate requiring approximately 2 seconds to go from right to left and another 2 seconds to go from left to right) and the same timing for up and down. Progress by moving target in different directions such as diagonally, or using a visually complex background, or using different postures or walking.

                                Saccades
                                Place many different targets on a wall with a blank background, such as letters of the alphabet, or numbers, or pictures. Patient will quickly look to random targets using saccadic eye movements. Repeat for at least 30 sec and up to several minutes until symptoms increase by several units or they need to take a break. Progress by placing targets on more visually complex background, or moving to different head positions or different postures or walking. 

                                Brock String 
                                The patient is holding one end of the Brock string at the tip of their nose and the other end is attached to a stationary object so that the string is taut. Move the nearest bead to the Near point of Convergence or just closer. Move the far bead to arm’s length and place the middle bead at the midpoint of the other two. Start by focusing on the far bead and hold for 5 - 10 sec. The patient should report seeing two lines diverging toward them like the letter A from the far bead. Next, change focus to the middle bead and hold for 5 – 10 sec. The patient should report seeing two lines diverging toward and away from them like the letter X from the middle bead. Then change focus to the close bead and hold for 5 – 10 sec. The patient should report seeing two lines diverging away from them like the letter V from the close bead.  Then move back to the middle bead and far bead, holding each for 5 – 10 sec. Repeat for a number of repetitions until symptoms increase by several units or they need to take a break. Progress by changing starting point or increasing reps.

                                3-Dot Card 
                                The patient places the 3-Dot Card at eye level touching the tip of the nose. Using the same concept as the Brock String, alternate focus from far, to middle, to the close bead and back again, holding each position for 5 – 10 sec.

                                Static and dynamic standing balance and walking balance exercise
                                •   See Klatt BN, Carender W, Lin CC, Alsubaie SF, Kinnaird CR, Sienko KH, Whitney SL.  A conceptual framework for the progression of balance exercises in persons with balance and vestibular disorders.  Phys Med Rehabil, 2(4):1044, 2015 for ideas about exercise progression for persons with vestibular disorders

                    Vestibular Oculomotor Screening (VOMS) for concussion for concussion
                        .('43 voms-exam.pdf')
                            Mucha A, Collins MW, Elbin RJ, Furman JM, Troutman-Enseki C, DeWolf RM, Marchetti G, Kontos AP. A brief vestibular and 
                            ocular motor screening 
                            (VOMS) assessment to evaluate preliminary concussion: Preliminary findings. Am J Sports Med; in press. 

                             

                            Vestibular/Ocular-Motor Screening (VOMS) for Concussion 
                            Vestibular/Ocular Motor Test: Not 

                            Tested 

                            Headache 
                            0-10 

                            Dizziness 
                            0-10 

                            Nausea 
                            0-10 

                            Fogginess 
                            0-10

                            Saccades – Horizontal

                            Convergence (Near Point) (Near Point in cm): 
                            Measure 1: ______ 
                            Measure 2:______ 
                            Measure 3:______ 
                            VOR – Horizontal 
                            VOR – Vertical 
                            Visual Motion Sensitivity Test 
                            Instructions:  

                             

                            Interpretation:  This test is designed for use with subjects ages 9-40.  When used with patients 
                            outside this age range, interpretation may vary.  Abnormal findings or provocation of symptoms 
                            with any test may indicate dysfunction – and should trigger a referral to the appropriate health 
                            care professional for more detailed assessment and management. 
                            Equipment:  Tape measure (cm); Metronome; Target w/ 14 point font print.   

                             

                            Baseline Symptoms – Record: Headache, Dizziness, Nausea & Fogginess on 0-10 scale prior 
                            to beginning screening 

                             

                             Smooth Pursuits - Test the ability to follow a slowly moving target. The patient and the 
                            examiner are seated.  The examiner holds a fingertip at a distance of 3 ft. from the patient.  
                            The patient is instructed to maintain focus on the target as the examiner moves the target 
                            smoothly in the horizontal direction 1.5 ft. to the right and 1.5 ft. to the left of midline.  One 
                            repetition is complete when the target moves back and forth to the starting position, and 2 
                            repetitions are performed.  The target should be moved at a rate requiring approximately 2 
                            seconds to go fully from left to right and 2 seconds to go fully from right to left. The test is 
                            repeated with the examiner moving the target smoothly and slowly in the vertical direction 
                            1.5 ft. above and 1.5 ft. below midline for 2 complete repetitions up and down.  Again, the 
                            target should be moved at a rate requiring approximately 2 seconds to move the eyes fully 
                            upward and 2 seconds to move fully downward.  Record: Headache, Dizziness, Nausea & 
                            Fogginess ratings after the test. (Figure 1) 

                             

                             Saccades – Test the ability of the eyes to move quickly between targets. The patient and 
                            the examiner are seated.   
                             Horizontal Saccades: The examiner holds two single points (fingertips) horizontally 
                            at a distance of 3 ft. from the patient, and 1.5 ft. to the right and 1.5 ft. to the left of 
                            midline so that the patient must gaze 30 degrees to left and 30 degrees to the right.  
                            Instruct the patient to move their eyes as quickly as possible from point to point.  One 
                            repetition is complete when the eyes move back and forth to the starting position, 
                            and 10 repetitions are performed.  Record: Headache, Dizziness, Nausea & 
                            Fogginess ratings after the test. (Figure 2)  


                             

                            Mucha A, Collins MW, Elbin RJ, Furman JM, Troutman-Enseki C, DeWolf RM, Marchetti G, Kontos AP. A brief vestibular and 
                            ocular motor screening 
                            (VOMS) assessment to evaluate preliminary concussion: Preliminary findings. Am J Sports Med; in press. 

                             

                             Vertical Saccades: Repeat the test with 2 points held vertically at a distance of 3 ft. 
                            from the patient, and 1.5 feet above and 1.5 feet below midline so that the patient 
                            must gaze 30 degrees upward and 30 degrees downward. Instruct the patient to 
                            move their eyes as quickly as possible from point to point.  One repetition is 
                            complete when the eyes move up and down to the starting position, and 10 
                            repetitions are performed.  Record: Headache, Dizziness, Nausea & Fogginess 
                            ratings after the test.  (Figure 3) 

                             

                             Convergence – Measure the ability to view a near target without double vision. The patient 
                            is seated and wearing corrective lenses (if needed).  The examiner is seated front of the 
                            patient and observes their eye movement during this test.  The patient focuses on a small 
                            target (approximately 14 point font size) at arm’s length and slowly brings it toward the tip of 
                            their nose.  The patient is instructed to stop moving the target when they see two distinct 
                            images or when the examiner observes an outward deviation of one eye.  Blurring of the 
                            image is ignored.  The distance in cm. between target and the tip of nose is measured and 
                            recorded.  This is repeated a total of 3 times with measures recorded each time.  Record: 
                            Headache, Dizziness, Nausea & Fogginess ratings after the test.   Abnormal: Near Point of 
                            convergence ≥ 6 cm from the tip of the nose. (Figure 4) 

                             

                             Vestibular-Ocular Reflex (VOR) Test – Assess the ability to stabilize vision as the head 
                            moves.  The patient and the examiner are seated.  The examiner holds a target of 
                            approximately 14 point font size in front of the patient in midline at a distance of 3 ft.     
                             Horizontal VOR Test: The patient is asked to rotate their head horizontally while 
                            maintaining focus on the target.  The head is moved at an amplitude of 20 degrees to 
                            each side and a metronome is used to ensure the speed of rotation is maintained at 
                            180 beats/minute (one beat in each direction).  One repetition is complete when the 
                            head moves back and forth to the starting position, and 10 repetitions are performed.  
                            Record: Headache, Dizziness, Nausea and Fogginess ratings 10 sec after the test is 
                            completed.  (Figure 5) 
                             Vertical VOR Test: The test is repeated with the patient moving their head 
                            vertically.  The head is moved in an amplitude of 20 degrees up and 20 degrees 
                            down and a metronome is used to ensure the speed of movement is maintained at 
                            180 beats/minute (one beat in each direction).  One repetition is complete when the 
                            head moves up and down to the starting position, and 10 repetitions are performed. 
                            Record: Headache, Dizziness, Nausea and Fogginess ratings after the test.  (Figure 
                            6) 

                             

                             Visual Motion Sensitivity (VMS) Test – Test visual motion sensitivity and the ability to 
                            inhibit vestibular-induced eye movements using vision.  The patient stands with feet 
                            shoulder width apart, facing a busy area of the clinic. The examiner stands next to and 
                            slightly behind the patient, so that the patient is guarded but the movement can be 
                            performed freely.   The patient holds arm outstretched and focuses on their thumb.  
                            Maintaining focus on their thumb, the patient rotates, together as a unit, their head, eyes 
                            and trunk at an amplitude of 80 degrees to the right and 80 degrees to the left.  A 
                            metronome is used to ensure the speed of rotation is maintained at 50 beats/min (one beat 
                            in each direction).   One repetition is complete when the trunk rotates back and forth to the 
                            starting position, and 5 repetitions are performed.  Record: Headache, Dizziness, Nausea & 
                            Fogginess ratings after the test. (Figure 7)   

                    Dynamic Gait Index
                        .('44 Dynamic-Gait-Index.doc')

                            Dynamic Gait Index (original 8-item test) 



                            Description: 
                            Developed to assess the likelihood of falling in older adults.  Designed to test eight facets of gait.
                            Equipment needed:   Box (Shoebox), Cones (2), Stairs, 20’ walkway, 15” wide
                            Completion: 
                                Time:       15 minutes
                            Scoring:    A four-point ordinal scale, ranging from 0-3. “0” indicates the lowest level of function and “3” the highest level of function. 
                                        Total Score = 24
                            Interpretation: < 19/24 = predictive of falls risk in community dwelling elderly



                            1. Gait level surface _____
                            Instructions: Walk at your normal speed from here to the next mark (20’)
                            Grading: Mark the lowest category that applies.
                            (3)     Normal: Walks 20’, no assistive devices, good sped, no evidence for imbalance, normal gait pattern
                            (2)     Mild Impairment: Walks 20’, uses assistive devices, slower speed, mild gait deviations.
                            (1) Moderate Impairment: Walks 20’, slow speed, abnormal gait pattern, evidence for imbalance.
                            (0) Severe Impairment: Cannot walk 20’ without assistance, severe gait deviations or imbalance.


                            2. Change in gait speed _____
                            Instructions: Begin walking at your normal pace (for 5’), when I tell you “go,” walk as fast as you can (for 5’). When I tell you “slow,” walk as slowly as you can (for 5’).
                            Grading: Mark the lowest category that applies.
                            (3)     Normal: Able to smoothly change walking speed without loss of balance or gait deviation. Shows a significant difference in walking speeds between normal, fast and slow speeds.
                            (2)     Mild Impairment: Is able to change speed but demonstrates mild gait deviations, or not gait deviations but unable to achieve a significant change in velocity, or uses an assistive device.
                            (1) Moderate Impairment: Makes only minor adjustments to walking speed, or accomplishes a change in speed with significant gait deviations, or changes speed but has significant gait deviations, or changes speed but loses balance but is able to recover and continue walking.
                            (0) Severe Impairment: Cannot change speeds, or loses balance and has to reach for wall or be caught.



                            3. Gait with horizontal head turns _____
                            Instructions:  Begin walking at your normal pace. When I tell you to “look right,” keep walking straight, but turn your head to the right. Keep looking to the right until I tell you, “look left,” then keep walking straight and turn your head to the left. Keep your head to the left until I tell you “look straight,“ then keep walking straight, but return your head to the center.
                            Grading: Mark the lowest category that applies.
                            (3)     Normal: Performs head turns smoothly with no change in gait.
                            (2)     Mild Impairment: Performs head turns smoothly with slight change in gait velocity, i.e., minor disruption to smooth gait path or uses walking aid.
                            (1) Moderate Impairment: Performs head turns with moderate change in gait velocity, slows down, staggers but recovers, can continue to walk.
                            (0) Severe Impairment: Performs task with severe disruption of gait, i.e., staggers
                                    outside 15” path, loses balance, stops, reaches for wall.





                            4. Gait with vertical head turns _____
                            Instructions: Begin walking at your normal pace. When I tell you to “look up,” keep walking straight, but tip your head up. Keep looking up until I tell you, “look down,” then keep walking straight and tip your head down. Keep your head down until I tell you “look straight,“ then keep walking straight, but return your head to the center.
                            Grading: Mark the lowest category that applies.
                            (3)     Normal: Performs head turns smoothly with no change in gait.
                            (2) Mild Impairment: Performs head turns smoothly with slight change in gait velocity, i.e., minor disruption to smooth gait path or uses walking aid.
                            (1) Moderate Impairment: Performs head turns with moderate change in gait velocity, slows down, staggers but recovers, can continue to walk.
                            (0)     Severe Impairment: Performs task with severe disruption of gait, i.e., staggers
                                    outside 15” path, loses balance, stops, reaches for wall.

                            5. Gait and pivot turn _____
                            Instructions: Begin walking at your normal pace. When I tell you, “turn and stop,” turn as quickly as you can to face the opposite direction and stop.
                            Grading: Mark the lowest category that applies.
                            (3)     Normal: Pivot turns safely within 3 seconds and stops quickly with no loss of balance.
                            (2)     Mild Impairment: Pivot turns safely in > 3 seconds and stops with no loss of balance.
                            (1) Moderate Impairment: Turns slowly, requires verbal cueing, requires several small steps to catch balance following turn and stop.
                            (0) Severe Impairment: Cannot turn safely, requires assistance to turn and stop.

                            6. Step over obstacle ____
                            Instructions: Begin walking at your normal speed. When you come to the shoebox, step over it, not around it, and keep walking.
                            Grading: Mark the lowest category that applies.
                            (3)     Normal: Is able to step over the box without changing gait speed, no evidence of imbalance.
                            (2) Mild Impairment: Is able to step over box, but must slow down and adjust steps to clear box safely.
                            (1) Moderate Impairment: Is able to step over box but must stop, then step over. May require verbal cueing.
                            (0) Severe Impairment: Cannot perform without assistance.

                            7. Step around obstacles _____
                            Instructions: Begin walking at normal speed. When you come to the first cone (about 6’ away), walk around the right side of it. When you come to the second cone (6’ past first cone), walk around it to the left.
                            Grading: Mark the lowest category that applies.
                            (3) Normal: Is able to walk around cones safely without changing gait speed; no  evidence of imbalance.
                            (2) Mild Impairment: Is able to step around both cones, but must slow down and adjust steps to clear cones.
                            (1) Moderate Impairment: Is able to clear cones but must significantly slow, speed to accomplish task, or requires verbal cueing.
                            (0) Severe Impairment: Unable to clear cones, walks into one or both cones, or requires physical assistance.

                            8. Steps _____
                            Instructions: Walk up these stairs as you would at home, i.e., using the railing if necessary. At the top, turn around and walk down.
                            Grading: Mark the lowest category that applies.
                            (3)     Normal: Alternating feet, no rail.
                            (2)     Mild Impairment: Alternating feet, must use rail.
                            (1) Moderate Impairment: Two feet to a stair, must use rail.
                            (0)     Severe Impairment: Cannot do safely.

                    BPPV lab handout
                        .('46 BPPV Lab Handout_2023.docx')
                            Guide for Treatment of Persons with BPPV
                            Posterior Canal (PC) BPPV
                            Test to Identify PC BPPV    What does it mean?  Interventions
                            Dix-Hallpike1 

                            The head is rotated 45 deg and extended 20-30 deg over the edge of a bed.  You are expecting to see a torsional-upbeating nystagmus in BOTH eyes.  The torsion is beating down towards the affected ear. It is imperative that you hold the person by the shoulders when they come back to the long sit position. You will repeat the above test to the opposite side.      

                            If unilateral BPPV, you will observe torsional upbeating nystagmus when the head is turned to the affected side.  You would expect the nystagmus to have a latency, increase then decrease in intensity (crescendo-decrescendo), and then last under one minute and typically the person experiences vertigo. 

                            If they have bilateral BPPV, they will have torsional upbeating nystagmus on both sides.    

                            Preferred
                            Modified Epley2,3 (see pictures)
                            Li Maneuver4
                            Semont plus5

                            Alternates
                            Modified Epley with pillow under shoulders6
                            Brandt-Daroff

                            Modified Epley (first choice)
                            The PT instructs and demonstrates for patient and explains the purpose to the patient.
                            STEP 1: Seat the patient on the table in long sitting with head in 45 degrees rotation toward the affected ear. Quickly lower to supine (1-2 sec) so they may be taken back to the head-hanging position with the neck in slight extension (20-30 degrees of extension). The PT stabilizes the head with hands and waits for the nystagmus to stop.  Observe for eye movement in the head hanging position. 
                            STEP 2:  Then rotate the head 90 deg towards the uninvolved side by turning the head toward opposite side - PT observes eyes- wait for nystagmus to stop. Keep neck in extension during the turn to the opposite side and wait 30 sec. 
                            STEP 3: Log roll patient onto unaffected side so that the head is turned to face ground- hold and wait 30 sec.  
                            STEP 4: Keep chin tucked towards their shoulder and have them rise to sitting but HOLD ON TO THEM when they sit up with both hands. Then slowly turn head back to midline. HOLD ON TO THEM when as they come to sitting and up to a minute or more after completion of the maneuver.

                            Li maneuver for the posterior canal
                            Start in sitting with legs hanging over edge of mat (hips/knees at 90 deg).  The PT moves the patient down quickly to their involved side with their nose forward while you hold their head (no turning of the head is required for this maneuver).  After 1 minute or after resolution of the nystagmus, rapidly move them 180 degrees with the healthy ear down on the mat with their nose facing forwards. Lie there for 4 minutes and then rapidly lift them back to sitting.  HOLD ON TO THEM for up to several minutes after completion of the Li maneuver.

                            Semont plus (from Strupp RCT)
                            The PT explains the purpose to the patient; the patient is rapidly moved from lying on one side to lying on the other. You can move the table up to a comfortable position for you and have a stool placed at the end of the table to which you will be moving patient first. Start sitting and turn the head away from the affected ear.  Then lie patient down on involved ear side quickly over the edge of the table about 20-30 degrees, so that their dependent arm can abduct off the table and rest on the stool. The patient is to stay there until the vertigo passes. The PT QUICKLY sits the patient up and then lays them on their other side but KEEPING the patient’s head pointing over the shoulder during the entire time (Do not change the orientation of the head). The patient should be facing down to the ground. Also do not stop in the middle of this movement.  Wait there until any vertigo/nystagmus passes. Then patient sits up and you must HOLD ON TO THEM when as they come to sitting and up to a minute or more after completion of the maneuver.
                            Loaded Dix-Hallpike

                            The person’s head is rotated 45 degrees to the affected side and flexed forward 30 degrees in the plane of the posterior canal for 30 seconds, before placing patient in supine.

                                

                            This is a test for posterior canal BPPV but with the additional 30 degrees of flexion, it may result in longer duration of nystagmus and more intense symptoms, hopefully making the diagnosis easier for you to see.   
                            Modified Dix-Hallpike
                            Sidelying test7

                            The person is sitting on the edge of the bed.  To test the right posterior canal, the head is rotated 45 deg towards the left.  You then bring the patient down to the bed onto their right side with their head extended while maintaining the rotation.  Upon rising to sitting, hold the persons shoulders so that they do not fall back.  You will repeat the above test to the opposite side to test the L posterior canal.  If they have bilateral BPPV, they will become symptomatic to both sides.
                                


                            The patient should only have vertigo or nystagmus if the right ear is involved with the test when the person lays to the right.     
                            Modified Dix-Hallpike
                            Pillow under shoulders in supine8

                            Place the person in the middle of the bed. Turn their head 45 degrees and lie them over the pillow. The sensitivity of the test was 96% and the specificity was 88%8



                            It is comparable to the Dix-Hallpike test and provides another alternative for testing  

                             
                            Horizontal Canal (HC) BPPV
                            Test to Identify HC BPPV    What does it mean?  Interventions
                            Roll test (Pagnini-McClure diagnostic maneuver)

                            From the supine position with head flexed to 30 deg, move head to the right and wait for 30 sec. Then return to center and wait 30 sec or until nystagmus stops. Then roll head to the left and wait for 30 sec, and return to center. Observe the nystagmus throughout to determine which direction the nystagmus is beating (towards or away from earth). 
                                


                            Nystagmus beating towards earth is called “geotropic” nystagmus and if it beats away from earth it is called “ageotropic or apogeotropic” nystagmus.

                            If geotropic, you should see greater nystagmus on the affected side during the roll test. To confirm, you should have seen the nystagmus beat TOWARDS the good side in the sit to supine test.9

                            If ageotropic, you should see greater nystagmus on the unaffected side during the roll test. To confirm, you should have seen the nystagmus beat TOWARDS the affected side in the sit to supine test.9
                                Geotropic

                            Gufoni liberatory maneuver (GLM)10 

                            Patient sits in the middle of a bed and is briskly brought down onto the unaffected ear and held for 30 sec.  The head is then quickly turned down by 45 deg and held there for 2-3 minutes, then the patient is brought back into the sitting position.

                            Li quick repositioning maneuver11 (see picture) 
                            Start in supine in the middle of a large bed.  Log roll patient 90 deg onto the affected side and wait until the symptoms resolve.  The clinician then is to stand behind the patient grabs the patient’s hand on the involved side and QUICKLY log rolls them 180 deg onto their unaffected side.  Stay on the unaffected left side for 2 minutes and then bring the patient to sitting.  The maneuver takes approximately 3 minutes to perform.
                            Sit to Supine Test9
                            Flex the head to 30 deg and move from sitting to supine.  Observe if any nystagmus occurs immediately when the person is in supine with their head flexed the 30 deg.   
                            When you move the person from long sit to supine, look for nystagmus and record the direction of the nystagmus. Used to confirm side of affected ear if intensity of nystagmus/vertigo is uncertain during roll test.   
                            Bow and Lean test12-14(need to integrate the information from the roll test to make sense of this)

                            Person is sitting.  With neck flexion about 60 deg (the Bow), observe the nystagmus that occurs with the change of head position.



                            In long sitting, then extend the head about 60 deg from neutral (the Lean) and observe the nystagmus.


                             IMPORTANT: to optimize patient comfort and efficiency of testing, it is best to perform the horizontal canal BPPV tests in the following order:
                            1.  Bow and Lean
                            2.  Sit to supine
                            3.  Roll

                            Make sure to write down the findings in each position. You may not see anything with the bow and lean or long sit to supine tests.  



                            If geotropic during the roll test, with neck flexion the nystagmus should beat TOWARDS the affected side. With neck extension, the nystagmus should beat TOWARDS the good side.

                            If ageotropic, you should see greater nystagmus on the unaffected side during the roll test.  With neck extension, the nystagmus should beat TOWARDS the affected side.

                            Used to confirm side of affected ear if intensity of nystagmus/vertigo is uncertain during roll test.   Ageotropic

                            Kim maneuver (2012)- see attached

                            Starting in supine, log roll the patient 135 deg towards the affected side so that their nose is almost facing the floor. Put the vibrator over their mastoid of affected side for 30 sec; wait for the nystagmus to stop.  Then do a series of log rolls away from affected ear and wait for 3 minutes in each position or until vertigo/nystagmus stop. Log roll them back to side lying (90 deg from supine). Then log roll to supine nose up position.  Then log roll 90 deg to unaffected side and vibrate over the mastoid again for 30 sec. Finally log roll to prone.  The PT will move the patient carefully and ensure that they do not excessively pull on their cervical spine.

                            Gufoni liberatory maneuver (GLM)10 

                            Patient sits in the middle of a mat table with legs hanging over side and head in midline. The PT will have the person look straight and then bring the patient down onto their AFFECTED side.
                            After 30 sec, they will turn their head up towards the ceiling and let them rest in this position  approximately 2 minutes. At the end of the 2 minutes, they should bring the
                            subject back to sitting holding onto them throughout. If this does not work, most of us will try the same maneuver but have the nose tilted down towards the floor.



                             
                            Taken from:  Galgon, A. BPPV special edition newsletter, 2012 (Neurology Section, APTA)

                            You have a referral to evaluate and treat a person with dizziness with an onset 2 weeks ago. What would you look for in the history and what questions would you ask during the interview? What examination procedures would you want to perform?  

                            Practice these selected tests: 
                            •   Gaze holding
                            •   Visual tracking (smooth pursuits, saccades, convergence)
                            •   VORx1
                            •   Cover/uncover test

                            Vignette: In the primary position, you observe right-beating nystagmus which increases in intensity when the patient looks to the right and when she looks to the left the intensity of the nystagmus lessens, but the fast component is still towards the right (unidirectional nystagmus). Visual tracking and ocular alignment are normal, and patient’s symptoms increase with VOR x 1 at 90 bpm on metronome. 

                            What is your interpretation and what tests of VOR function do you want to perform?

                            Practice these selected tests: 
                            •   Head impulse test
                            •   Head shake test
                            •   Dynamic visual acuity
                            •   VOR cancellation (Visual Motion Sensitivity)

                            Vignette: Upon turning the patient’s head quickly to the left, you observe a corrective saccade back to right. A normal head impulse test was observed when turning the patient’s head to the right, where the patient was able to maintain focus on the target with no corrective saccade noted. You observe a persistent right beating nystagmus after completing the head shake test and the patient loses 5 lines on the clinical DVA. Given this information, what is the suspected diagnosis? Would you treat this patient or refer the patient to another provider?

                            How would you like to assess their balance? 

                            Practice these selected tests:

                            •   mCTSIB 
                            •   DGI 4-item
                            •   FGA

                            Vignette: The patient is unable to stand on foam with eyes closed without falling. They experience gait deviations and report dizziness when walking and turning their head. Based on findings from examination, what exercises would you like to prescribe for the patient. How would you dose the exercises? How would you measure the patient’s response to treatment and progress or regress based on their response?


                            Yellow Room : Vestibular Rehabilitation Treatment
                            Progressive gaze stability exercises (Vestibular adaptation)

                            Identify findings in your history and/or tests and measures that would indicate prescribing adaptation exercises for patients with vestibular disorders. Practice the following exercises and discuss how you would progress the exercises.

                            •   VORx1
                            •   VORx1 with vergence
                            •   VORx2

                            Substitution exercise:
                            Identify findings in your history and/or tests and measures that would indicate prescribing substitution exercises for patients with vestibular disorders. Practice the following exercises and discuss how you would progress the exercises.

                            •   Imaginary targets (remembered targets)
                            •   Eye-Head saccade exercises (saccadic corrections)

                            Habituation and optokinetic exercises for visual motion sensitivity
                            Identify findings in your history and/or tests and measures that would indicate prescribing habituation and/or optokinetic exercises for patients with vestibular disorders. Practice the following exercises and discuss how you would progress the exercises.

                            •   VOR cancellation in sitting and standing
                            •   Busy backgrounds
                            •   Computer videos
                            •   Optokinetic patterns (disco ball)
                            •   Virtual reality

                                    .Vestibular Hypofunction CPG Action Statement 6b
                                    OPTIMAL GAZE STABILIZATION EXERCISE DOSAGE OF TREATMENT IN 
                                    INDIVIDUALS WITH PERIPHERAL VESTIBULAR HYPOFUNCTION (UNILATERAL 
                                    AND BILATERAL)

                                    • (1) Clinicians may prescribe weekly clinic visits plus an HEP of GSE consisting of a 
                                    minimum of: 3 times per day for a total of at least 12 minutes daily for individuals with 
                                    acute/subacute UVH (evidence quality: II; recommendation strength: weak); 

                                    • (2) 3 to 5 times per day for at least 20 minutes daily for 4 to 6 weeks for individuals with 
                                    chronic UVH (evidence quality: II; recommendation strength: weak); 

                                    • (3) 3 to 5 times per day for a total of 20 to 40 minutes daily for approximately 5 to 7 
                                    weeks for individuals with BVH (evidence quality: III; recommendation strength: weak).

                                    .Vestibular Hypofunction CPG Action Statement 6a
                                    OPTIMAL BALANCE EXERCISE DOSE IN THE TREATMENT OF INDIVIDUALS
                                    WITH PERIPHERAL VESTIBULAR HYPOFUNCTION (UNILATERAL AND BILATERAL)
                                    • (1) Clinicians may prescribe static and dynamic balance exercises: for a minimum of 20 
                                    minutes daily for at least 4 to 6 weeks for individuals with chronic unilateral vestibular 
                                    hypofunction (evidence quality: II; recommendation strength: weak); 

                                    • (2) May consider prescribing static and dynamic balance exercises for individuals with 
                                    acute/subacute unilateral vestibular hypofunction; however, no specific dose 
                                    recommendations can be made at this time (evidence quality: II; recommendation 
                                    strength: expert opinion); 

                                    • (3) for 6 to 9 weeks for individuals with bilateral vestibular hypofunction (evidence 
                                    quality: III-IV; recommendation strength: expert opinion).

                                    .How to make the diagnosis of BPPV- history?
                                    • Questions to ask:
                                    • Do you get dizzy (spin) when you roll over in bed?
                                    • Do you get dizzy (spin) when you sit up in the morning or lie down at night?
                                    • Do you get dizzy (spin) when you look up or bend over?
                                    • Can you lie flat without a pillow?
                                    • How long do symptoms last?
                                    • Can you reproduce the symptoms?
                                    • Do you spin during the day?
                                    • Have you had this before (or any family member)?

                                    Introduction to Performance Improvement Project and Manual of Operations
                                    This manual of operations will be used as a guide for collection, analysis, and interpretation of 
                                    clinical outcomes data for our performance improvement project. Data will be collected over the first 
                                    three months of our terminal clinical experiences, then analyzed to identify opportunities to improve 
                                    clinical performance. We will be treating patients in outpatient physical therapy settings who have been 
                                    referred for treatment of concussion and vestibular related medical diagnoses and presentations. Patients 
                                    will be included in our project if they fit into any of our treatment-based classifications described in 
                                    Chapter 3.
                                    Chapter 1 outlines the primary outcomes which will be used to determine if a patient meets the 
                                    criteria for achieving meaningful change as described in the available research for the outcome measures. 
                                    An overview of the secondary outcomes and examination tools used in the treatment-based classifications 
                                    is explained in Chapter 2. These tests and measures will provide more specific details of change post- 
                                    physical therapy care and can be compared more directly to the classifications used and outlined in this 
                                    project. The criteria for the treatment-based classification system can be found in Chapter 3. Chapter 4 
                                    outlines which interventions should be provided according to each classification’s available literature , 
                                    followed by a summary of this material in Chapter 5.
                                    The final aspect of our manual of operations is the case report form which will be used to collect 
                                    data for each patient under our care who fits into any classification listed in this manual. This form will 
                                    utilize numbering patient’s IDs to maintain patient privacy as information is obtained about their history, 
                                    medical and physical therapy diagnoses, classifications which they fall under, duration of care, 
                                    interventions provided, and outcomes. These forms will be completed for each patient at the start of care, 
                                    every two weeks following, and at the end of care.

                                    TITLE OF 
                                    ASSESSMENT

                                    Dizziness Handicap Inventory (DHI)

                                    YEAR PUBLISHED 1990

                                    LAST UPDATED April 2023

                                    ACRONYM DHI

                                     

                                    PURPOSE The DHI is a 25-item patient-reported scale utilized to determine how much a 
                                    patient feels handicapped by their dizziness symptoms. 
                                    For the purposes of this project, the DHI will be used as a primary outcome 
                                    measure for both vestibular non-concussion and concussion populations to 
                                    determine meaningful change.

                                    LINK TO INSTRUMENT https://southampton.stonybrookmedicine.edu/sites/default/files/Dizziness%20H
                                    anicap%20Inventory%20-%20English.pdf
                                    INSTRUMENT IN PDF 
                                    FORMAT

                                    Dizziness Handicap Inventory

                                    ASSESSMENT TYPE Patient Reported Outcome Measure

                                    KEY DESCRIPTION

                                    25 items with response choices to include “Always”, “Sometimes”, or “No”. A 
                                    numerical equivalent is assigned to each response. No = 0, Sometimes = 2, 
                                    Yes = 4. A total score is calculated and expressed as a percentage of 100. The 
                                    higher the score, the greater the perceived handicap due to dizziness 
                                    symptoms. (Whitney, et al 2004)
                                     0 – 30 points indicate a mild handicap
                                     31 - 60 points indicate moderate handicap
                                     60 – 100 points indicate severe handicap.

                                    TIME TO ADMINISTER

                                    10 minutes

                                    EQUIPMENT 
                                    REQUIRED

                                    Pen and paper, or table


                                    4

                                    REQUIRED TRAINING No training
                                    AGE RANGE
                                    19 +

                                    individuals with vestibular disorders by Tray Rice, PT, MPH, NCS and Jenny 
                                    Fay, PT, DPT, NCS and the Vestibular EDGE task force of the Neurology 
                                    Section of the APTA (2013).

                                    - Excellent r= 0.97, df = 12, p <0.0001

                                    INTERRATER/
                                    INTRARATER 
                                    RELIABILITY

                                    N/A – Patient Reported Outcome 

                                    INTERNAL 
                                    CONSISTENCY

                                    Vestibular Disorder
                                    - Excellent internal consistency for total score (alpha = 0.89).

                                    CONSTRUCT VALIDITY 
                                    (CONVERGENT/
                                    DISCRIMINANT)

                                    Vestibular Disorder (Yorke, et al 2013). 
                                    There exists an adequate correlation between:
                                    - No. of dizzy spells/year and score on DHI (<12, >12, and permanent).
                                    - Adequate to excellent correlation of DHI vs. VAP (0.54 to 0.74).
                                    - Total score significantly poorer for patients reporting more frequent 
                                    dizziness symptoms or unsteadiness.

                                    CONTENT VALIDITY Vestibular Disorder
                                    - Bilateral peripheral vestibular loss is associated with lower self-
                                    perceived handicap in balance compared with individuals with balance 
                                    problems but normative balance tests.
                                    - Total score is poorer for patients reporting more frequent dizziness and 
                                    unsteadiness.
                                    Content validity of the DHI was determined by a panel of 6 experts in the fields 
                                    of Au.D, MD, and Education. The experts concluded that reporting the result of 
                                    a DHI with a total score is appropriate, and that there is statistical support for 
                                    the existence of three subscales: physical manifestations, impact, and 
                                    emotional impact of dizziness and vertigo. 
                                    (Van De Wyngaerde, et al. 2019).
                                    FLOOR/CEILING 
                                    EFFECTS N/A

                                    RESPONSIVENESS Vestibular Disorder
                                    - Responsiveness was reported in the DHI in subjects with a vestibular 
                                    disorder with a minimal important difference score of 1.66, with a 
                                    number needed to treat of 7.24 patients for detecting score change.
