                                    Canalith Repositioning - Canalith Repositioning Maneuvers (CRM)
                                    A group of procedures in which the patient moves through specific body positions designed to relocate 
                                    dislodged particles within the inner ear for the purpose of relieving symptoms of BPPV. The specific 
                                    CRM chosen relates to the type of BPPV diagnosed. Only one canal should be treated per treatment 
                                    session.
                                    Posterior Canal Repositioning Maneuvers: Repositioning maneuvers designed to relocate dislodged 
                                    particles within the posterior canal of the inner ear. The two most common posterior CRMs used are the 
                                    Modified Epley Maneuver and the Semont Maneuver and are described in detail below. Recent evidence 
                                    has described the Li Maneuver to have similar reliability as the Modified Epley Maneuver.
                                    Modified Epley 
                                    Maneuver

                                    1. The patient is placed in the upright position with the head turned 45° toward 
                                    the affected ear (the ear that was positive on the Dix-Hallpike testing).
                                    2. The patient is rapidly laid back to the supine head-hanging 20° position, which 
                                    is then maintained for 20-30 seconds.
                                    3. Next, the head is turned 90° toward the other (unaffected) side and held for 
                                    about 20 seconds.
                                    4. Following this, the head is turned a further 90° (usually necessitating the 
                                    patient’s body to also move from the supine position to the lateral decubitus 
                                    position) such that the patient’ head is nearly in the facedown position. This is 
                                    also held for 20-30 seconds.
                                    5. The patient is then brought into the upright sitting position, completing the 
                                    maneuver.

                                    Semont Plus 
                                    Maneuver

                                    1. Start with the patient sitting on a table or flat surface with the head turned 
                                    away from the affected side.
                                    2. Quickly put the patient into the side-lying position, toward the affected side, 
                                    with the head turned up and extended over the edge of the table by about 20-30 
                                    degrees. Nystagmus will occur shortly after arriving at the side-lying position. 
                                    Keep the patient in this position until at least 20 seconds after all nystagmus has 
                                    ceased.
                                    3. Quickly move the patient back up and through the sitting position so that he or 
                                    she is in the opposite side-lying position with the head facing down (head did not 
                                    turn during the position change). Keep the patient in this position for at least 30 
                                    seconds after nystagmus/symptoms resolve.
                                    4. At a normal or slow rate, bring the patient back up to the sitting position.

                                    Li Maneuver 
                                    (Posterior Canal)

                                    1. Start with the patient sitting with legs over the edge of the bed or table.
                                    2. Move patient down quickly towards involved side with head facing straight 
                                    toward. Hold the patient’s head in place.
                                    3. After 1 minute or resolution of nystagmus, rapidly move 180o away from 
                                    affected side, keeping the head facing forward.
                                    4. Hold for 4 minutes, then rapidly return to sitting position, stabilizing the 
                                    patient following the maneuver.


                                    58

                                    Horizontal Canal Repositioning Maneuvers: Repositioning maneuvers designed to relocate dislodged 
                                    particles within the horizontal canal of the inner ear.
                                    Geotropic:

                                    Apogeotropic:
                                    Kim Maneuver 1. Patient starts in supine position.
                                    2. Turn patient’s head 135 degrees towards the involved side while patient turns 
                                    into sidelying. Each position should be held for 3 minutes
                                    3. Apply vibration to mastoid process of involved ear for 30 sec.
                                    4. Remove vibration and bring head back so nose is parallel to ground.
                                    5. Return the patient to supine.
                                    6. Keeping head in line, roll patient 90 degrees in opposite direction.
                                    7. Applying vibration again to mastoid process closest to ceiling for 30 sec.
                                    8. Remove vibration and patient rolls to prone.
                                    9. Slowly sit up from this position.
                                    Gufoni Manuever 
                                    (Apogeotropic)

                                    1. Patient sits in the middle of the bed with legs hanging over the side.
                                    2. Therapist quickly brings the patient into side lying with the INVOLVED ear 
                                    closer to the ground and nose facing forward.
                                    3. Then turn the head towards the ceiling and stay in this position for 2-3 
                                    minutes
                                    4. Then bring patient back to a sitting position.
                                    5. If patient still reports symptoms, try maneuver over again but point nose 
                                    towards the ground instead of the ceiling.
                                    Additional Information
                                    Frequency: Therapists should perform the maneuver multiple times within a treatment session until the 
                                    patient is asymptomatic in a single treatment session. Current evidence indicates to perform the 
                                    maneuvers at least more than once to ensure their effectiveness. 31
                                    Considerations: Therapists should be mindful of the possibility for nausea, vomiting, fainting, and canal 
                                    conversion after performing the CRM.
                                    Exclusions: Therapists may need to reconsider or modify these maneuvers for patients at risk for stroke 
                                    or vascular injuries in the face of significant vascular disease, patients with cervical stenosis, severe 
                                    kyphoscoliosis, limited cervical range of motion, Down’s syndrome, severe rheumatoid arthritis, cervical 
                                    radiculopathies, Paget’s disease, ankylosing spondylitis, low back dysfunction, spinal cord injuries, and 
                                    morbid obesity. 30

                                    Gufoni Maneuver 
                                    (Geotropic)1

                                    1. The patient sits in the middle of the bed with legs hanging over the side.
                                    2. Therapist quickly brings the patient into side lying with the NON- 
                                    INVOLVED ear closer to the ground and nose facing forward.
                                    3. Turn the head towards the ground and stay in this position for 2-3 minutes.
                                    4. Bring patient back to a sitting position.

                                    Li Quick 
                                    Repositioning 
                                    Maneuver 

                                    1. Patient begins in supine position.
                                    2. Log roll patient 90o towards affected side and wait until symptoms resolve.
                                    3. Standing behind the patient, therapist quickly log rolls the patient 180o 
                                    towards the other side.
                                    4. Hold position on unaffected side for 2 minutes.
                                    5. Return patient to seated position.

                                    Summary of Evidence
                                    ● The clinical practice guideline for BPPV (Bhattacharyya et. al., 2017) strongly recommends the use of 
                                    repositioning procedures as initial therapy. These guidelines state that there is high-quality and 
                                    compelling evidence that patients diagnosed with posterior and horizontal canal BPPV should be initially 
                                    treated with repositioning maneuvers in attempt to promptly resolve symptoms and disability secondary 
                                    to BPPV. 
                                    ● In 2017, Kim et al. published a randomized controlled study investigating the effectiveness of various 
                                    treatments of apogeotropic HC BPPV. The maneuvers investigated were the Gufoni and mastoid 
                                    oscillation (Kim Maneuver) maneuvers. A total of 209 consecutive patients with confirmed apogeotropic 
                                    HC BPPV were recruited for the study and were randomly assigned to be treated with Gufoni, mastoid 
                                    oscillation, or a sham treatment. During short term follow-up, both the Gufoni and mastoid oscillation had 
                                    successful single treatment outcomes of 76.1% and 71.9% respectively compared to only 53.5% success 
                                    with only the sham. There was no significant difference between the Gufoni or mastoid oscillation 
                                    although the authors note that the Gufoni might be more effective at treating geotropic HC BPPV. In 
                                    conclusion, both Gufoni and Kim maneuver are both valid and effective ways to treat apogeotropic HC 
                                    BPPV. 2
                                    ● A randomized, prospective controlled trial by Kim et al studied the immediate and long-term therapeutic 
                                    efficacies of the barbecue rotation and Gufoni maneuvers for treating patients with geotropic horizontal 
                                    canal BPPV. 171 patients with geotropic HC BPPV were randomly assigned to the barbecue rotation 
                                    (n=56), Gufoni (n=64), or a sham maneuver (n=50). An immediate response to treatment was determined 
                                    within 1 hour after a maximum of two trials of the maneuver during the first visit. The long-term results 
                                    were determined during a follow-up with patients one month later. The results of this study found that the 
                                    barbecue rotation and Gufoni maneuvers were more effective than the sham maneuver in treating patients 
                                    with geotropic HC BPPV for immediate and long-term outcomes. However, therapeutic efficacy did not 
                                    differ between the barbecue rotation and Gufoni maneuvers.4
                                    ● In 2010, Casani et al. also investigated the effectiveness of the different treatments of geotropic HC 
                                    BPPV. They also investigated the barbecue roll + forced prolonged positioning compared to the Gufoni. 
                                    This study included 103 participants with geotropic HC BPPV. Upon follow up, they found the Gufoni 
                                    had better success than the barbecue roll (93% compared to 81%). Even though the above article (Kim et 
                                    al. 2012) discovered no difference between the two, this article demonstrates that even though both 
                                    maneuvers are effective, at least some evidence points towards the less complicated Gufoni to be an 
                                    appropriate first choice of treatment.5
                                    ● Helminski et al in 2010 published a systematic review of treatments for BPPV. Pertinent findings 
                                    included randomized control evidence that suggested the CRP was more effective than controls. There 
                                    were no significant differences between the use of the modified Epley or the Semont maneuver in the 
                                    treatment of PC BPPV. Finally, Brandt-Daroff exercises were proven the least effective self-administered 
                                    treatments.6
                                    ● A Cochrane Review in 2014 of 11 RCTs to assess the effectiveness of the Epley Maneuver in treating 
                                    posterior canal BPPV found the Epley more effective when compared to sham maneuvers or control 
                                    groups. Patients treated with the Epley showed significant improvement in terms of resolution of vertigo 
                                    (odds ratio (OR) 4.42) and a negative Dix-Hallpike Test (OR 9.62).7
                                    ● A double-blind randomized trial looked at short-term effectiveness of the Semont Maneuver compared to 
                                    a sham procedure. On the fourth day, 55 (84.62%) of 65 patients in the treatment group showed complete 
                                    resolution of symptoms compared with 9 (14.29%) of 63 patients in the control group.8

                                    Impaired balance (standing) - Standing Balance Training
                                    Standing balance is defined as the ability to maintain postural stability and orientation with center of mass 
                                    over the base of support and body at rest. Standing balance training aims to improve sensory integration, 
                                    anticipatory and reactive balance control, and habituation of symptoms of imbalance and dizziness. 
                                    Table 1. Standing Balance Exercises 1

                                    The above table was designed by Klatt et al.1 and outlines the various standing balance training exercises 
                                    that can be performed with a patient. The exercises are ranked from the easiest for the patient to perform 
                                    (1) to the hardest for the patient to perform (30). The following are variables that can be manipulated to 
                                    increase challenge for balance activities:
                                     Foot stance: stance difficulty is increased as the patient’s base of support narrows. Feet apart is 
                                    the easiest for the patient, followed by feet together, semi-tandem Romberg, tandem Romberg 
                                    and finally single-leg stance.
                                     Surface: Various studies show that balance is more challenged when standing on an unsteady 
                                    surface versus a firm surface. Additionally, an increase in slope of the surface can also increase 
                                    imbalance in the patient; specifically, downhill slopes are the most challenging for patients due to 
                                    increased friction force. In some studies, persons with bilateral vestibular loss demonstrated very 
                                    large and fast postural sway compared to individuals without vestibular deficits when standing on 
                                    an inclined surface with eyes closed. This reflects the difficulty that these patients have with 
                                    interpreting surface orientation based on solely somatosensory function. The following 
                                    progression ranks the various surfaces from easiest to hardest for the patient: firm, firm with 
                                    incline, firm with decline, and foam.
                                     Visual input: Having a patient stand with eyes closed results in increased postural sway because 
                                    the visual system is eliminated from the balance activity.
                                    Head movements: Patients with vestibular involvement demonstrate a decrease in visual acuity with 
                                    head movement, likely because the VOR cannot stabilize the patient’s gaze. These patients also 
                                    demonstrate greater difficulty with yaw head movements in comparison to pitch head movements. 
                                    Therefore, yaw movements with static balance are more difficult than pitch movements with static 
                                    balance in patients.


                                    63

                                    Movement Based Habituation Training
                                    Should patient’s symptoms occur with standing 
                                    balance, habituation training would be 
                                    performed with the goal of improving symptoms 
                                    tolerance with standing balance. 

                                    Repeated exposure to specific stimulus that 
                                    provokes dizziness; systemic repetition of 
                                    provocative movements reduces symptoms over 
                                    time; direction of motion, size/color of stimulus 
                                    and instructions to the patient

                                    Examples: Large amplitude, rapid cervical 
                                    rotation (horizontal or vertical) in standing 
                                    position; trunk flexion/extension in standing; 
                                    standing pivots
                                    Sensory Integration Exercises to incorporate sensory changes while 
                                    performing standing balance. 
                                    Examples: changing surfaces (concrete, foam, carpet, 
                                    etc.) addition of eyes closed, open, or changes in 
                                    lighting; addition of head movements.
                                    Anticipatory Balance Control Exercises to assist in controlling center of mass when 
                                    internal forces or voluntary movements result in a 
                                    change of balance. 
                                    Examples: stepping, weight shifting, throwing, reaching, 
                                    catching.  
                                    Reactive Balance Control Exercises of varying intensity that affect the patients 
                                    center of mass that include external forces that are 
                                    applied with the purpose of causing instability. 
                                    Examples: perturbations from a therapist in different 
                                    positions, catching, rolling platform.
                                    Summary of Evidence
                                    ● Following 6-weeks of habituation training, patients demonstrated overall improvement in DHI and both 
                                    active and passive DVA in patients with vestibular hypofunction.
                                    ● Hansson et al, conducted a randomized control study comparing people over the age of 50 with dizziness. 
                                    Their intervention group received balance training and vestibular rehabilitation over a six-week period 
                                    while the control group did not receive any type of intervention. While the study only found a significant 
                                    change in their standing on one leg with eyes closed (SONLEC) condition, their results demonstrated 
                                    improvements on all outcome measures for the intervention group, and a decline on most outcome 
                                    measures for the control group. This shows further evidential support for the efficacy of balance 
                                    training.6
                                    ● Mraz et al, conducted a small study evaluating the benefits of balance exercises in adults suffering from 
                                    systemic vestibular dysfunction. The study evaluated all participants (n=12) pre and post-intervention on 
                                    a force plate posturography system. After a 4-week progressive balance program, including 
                                    posturography, balance exercises and a home exercise program the participants showed a statistical 
                                    decrease in postural sway with eyes open, eyes closed and feedback. Their improvements demonstrate an 
                                    overall improvement in balance and postural control from their balance training.7
                                    ● Morisod et al, completed a retrospective review of patients with chronic subjective dizziness (CSD) that 
                                    underwent computerized dynamic posturography in their neurologic assessment. For patients that 
                                    benefited from vestibular rehabilitation, the researchers compared their pre- and post-rehabilitation 
                                    posturagraphies. The study found that only pathologic videonystagmography and a history of unilateral 
                                    vestibular dysfunction were significantly related to abnormal posturography. Patients with CSD have a 
                                    high rate of abnormal posturography but without a specific pattern. This review suggests that vestibular 
                                    rehab is an effective tool in therapeutic treatment in this patient population.8


                                    64

                                    Additional Information
                                    Exclusions/Considerations: In patients with bilateral vestibular loss, it’s important to note that 
                                    combining the conditions eyes closed on foam for balance activities is not recommended. Because these 
                                    patients have a non-functioning vestibular system, removing the visual and somatosensory systems 
                                    simultaneously can be dangerous and will likely cause the patient to fall. In patients that demonstrate 
                                    some sparing of the vestibular system, it is okay to remove the somatosensory and visual system 
                                    simultaneously if the patient has some remaining vestibular function.
                                    Summary of the evidence included with Dynamic Balance Training as both are commonly used in 
                                    conjunction during treatment.
                                    Additional information: Movement based habituation 
                                    Dosing/Frequency: patients may perform exercises 3x/day. Exercise dosing is dependent on patient 
                                    tolerance and symptomatic response to the exercise itself. Typically, patients are progressed to 
                                    completing the exercise for around a minute before progressing the exercise to a more challenging form. 
                                    Intensity: graded in intensity through manipulation of parameters such as velocity, number of repetitions 
                                    and duration

                                    Impaired balance (gait) - Gait Balance Training
                                    Dynamic balance is defined as the ability to maintain postural stability and orientation with the patient’s 
                                    center of mass over the base of support while the body parts are in motion.1 Dynamic balance training can 
                                    be completed in both standing and during gait. In standing, exercises can be done by completing weight 
                                    shifts in various directions and altering the patient’s center of gravity. Studies have shown that weight- 
                                    shifting in the medial-lateral direction in standing is easier for patients than weight-shifting in the
                                    anterior-posterior direction. The difference in difficulty is likely because weight-shifting in the medial- 
                                    lateral direction requires a larger base of support for the patient. Additionally, the hip muscles control 
                                    postural stability in the medial-lateral direction in comparison to the ankle stabilizers in the anterior- 
                                    posterior direction. In addition to weight-shifting, having the patient reach outside his or her base of 
                                    support can also make a static standing activity more dynamic. These exercises can include asking the 
                                    patient reach to grab an object a particular distance outside his or her base of support, having the patient 
                                    catch a ball thrown outside his or her base of support, and applying perturbations to the patient in static 
                                    standing.1
                                    Gait itself is considered a dynamic balance exercise. Completing gait activities with different tasks are all 
                                    effective ways to progress and challenge a patient’s dynamic balance with gait. The following are 
                                    examples of tasks to make balance more dynamic with gait for a patient:
                                     Reaching outside of base of support: ball tosses, reaching for objects placed outside of patient’s 
                                    base of support (on shelves, on ground, overhead, etc.)
                                     Head movements: pitch, yaw movements
                                     Dual tasking: naming words in a category, counting backwards, doing math, carrying an object, 
                                    etc.
                                     Environment variability: quiet or loud setting, empty or crowded setting, predictable or 
                                    unpredictable setting, surface (foam, carpet, outdoor, wood, etc.), lighting (natural light, dim 
                                    lighting, variable lighting, etc.)

                                    Gait Activities
                                    Purpose is to simulate gait in different environments that 
                                    may provoke a patient’s symptoms. 

                                    Gait training should consist of various functional aspects 
                                    of gait such as stepping over objects, backwards and 
                                    forwards walking, stair climbing, treadmill training, 
                                    walking on uneven surfaces. 

                                    Movement Based Habituation Training
                                    Should patient’s symptoms occur with dynamic 
                                    balance, habituation training would be 
                                    performed with the goal of improving symptoms 
                                    tolerance with gait balance activities. 

                                    Repeated exposure to specific stimulus that 
                                    provokes dizziness; systemic repetition of 
                                    provocative movements reduces symptoms over 
                                    time; direction of motion, size/color of stimulus 
                                    and instructions to the patient

                                    Examples: Head movements while walking, 
                                    reaching outside of base of support while 
                                    walking, tossing a ball while walking.


                                    66

                                    Additional Information
                                    Dosing/Frequency: For chronic vestibular hypofunction, complete static and dynamic balance exercises 
                                    20 minutes daily for at least 4-6 weeks if unilateral and at least 6-9 weeks if bilateral. For acute/subacute 
                                    vestibular hypofunction, static and dynamic balance can be prescribed but there are no specific 
                                    recommendations for dosing at this time.7 To dose both static and dynamic balance exercises, 30-second 
                                    training segments completed for 4-6 repetitions 2 to 3 times per week is recommended for healthy and 
                                    older adults1.
                                    Exclusions/Considerations: Careful observation for those patients with orthostatic hypotension or 
                                    weight-bearing precautions during upright activity.
                                    Summary of Evidence
                                    ● In the CPG for vestibular rehabilitation for peripheral vestibular hypofunction update in 2022, they found 
                                    that clinicians may prescribe static and dynamic balance exercises: (1) for a minimum of 20 minutes daily 
                                    for at least 4-6 weeks for individuals with chronic unilateral vestibular hypofunction (evidence quality: II; 
                                    recommendation strength: weak); may consider prescribing static and dynamic balance exercises (2) for 
                                    individuals with acute/subacute unilateral vestibular hypofunction; however, no specific dose 
                                    recommendations can be made at this time (evidence quality: II; recommendation strength: expert 
                                    opionin); and (3) for 6-9 weeks for individuals with bilateral vestibular hypofunction (evidence quality: 
                                    III-IV; recommendation strength: expert opinion).5
                                    ● A study by Marioni et al, enrolled 30 patients 2 weeks after acute unilateral vestibular hypofunction.2 
                                    Patients were randomized to a posturography-assisted vestibular exercises and home exercise program or 
                                    to a control group (spontaneous compensation). The vestibular group performed supervised vestibular 
                                    exercises during 30-minute sessions once a week plus a home exercise program three times per day for 5 
                                    weeks. After rehabilitation, posturography patients improved significantly in most sensory measures (eyes 
                                    open on foam and eyes closed on foam) and motor parameters (limits of stability) by comparison with 
                                    preliminary outcomes. Researchers also found there to be no significant difference in findings of the 
                                    mCTSIB and LOS findings between these patients and a subset of healthy volunteers.2
                                    ● Allum and Adkin conducted a study to track improvements in postural control during recovery from an 
                                    acute unilateral peripheral deficit and to determine if recovery rates were different for stance and gait 
                                    tasks.3 Postural control was quantified using simple measurements of trunk sway: amplitudes of trunk 
                                    sway angle and angular velocity, in the roll and pitch directions as well as task duration, were examined 
                                    for a battery of stance and gait tasks. The researchers found that trunk sway for the simple gait tasks was 
                                    within normal range at 3 months but task duration was still longer than normal. More complex gait tasks, 
                                    such as walking 8 tandem steps on foam or walking up and down stairs, showed no improvement in trunk 
                                    roll sway at 3 months. The results of this study suggest that recovery of normal trunk control during the 
                                    compensation process for unilateral vestibular hypofunction is more rapid for stance tasks than gait tasks. 
                                    The authors found that trunk sway for gait tasks provides a better insight into the remaining deficits in 
                                    balance control of vestibular-loss patients than the sway of stance tasks.3

                                    Impaired oculomotor function - Vergence Exercises, Smooth Pursuits, Saccades
                                    Convergence is the ability of the eyes to move medially in concert to fixate on objects within several 
                                    centimeters of the face in the midsagittal plane. Of the ocular deficits treated in concussion therapy, 
                                    convergence insufficiency is among the most common1. Convergence insufficiency is an impairment 
                                    identified by the occurrence of diplopia when fixating on target objects >5 cm from the tip of the patient’s 
                                    nose -- diplopia within 5 cm of the patient’s nose is considered normal2. Common interventions utilized 
                                    for correction of convergence insufficiency are pencil push-ups and brock string convergence exercises. 
                                    Smooth pursuit exercises9 work to improve the ability to follow a slowly moving target with your eyes 
                                    while the head remains stationary and can become a means of substitution for deficient VOR. Saccades 
                                    works to improve the ability of the eyes to quickly look between two objects when moving through 
                                    various environments in order to maintain focus on a given target.

                                    Pencil Push-ups Pencil push-ups utilize the basic testing format of near-point convergence 
                                    as a form of treatment3. To summarize, the patient holds a pencil at arm’s 
                                    length and positioned within the midsagittal plane between the eyes. They
                                    are then instructed to move the pencil toward their nose while attempting to 
                                    maintain a single image of the pencil. When they are no longer able to 
                                    maintain a single image of the pencil (i.e., diplopia occurs), the patient returns 
                                    the pencil to the closest point at which they can sustain the single image. One 
                                    such cycle is considered a repetition, and these repetitions can be repeated 
                                    with goal of lessening the distance from the nose at which the incidence of 
                                    diplopia occurs3.
                                    Brock String Exercises Brock string exercises4 employ the use of a string with a series of marble- 
                                    sized beads positioned along the length of the string. Patients hold one end 
                                    of the string to their nose, with the opposite end pinned at a height just 
                                    below held end. The beads are then placed at varying lengths from the nose 
                                    and the patient is instructed to direct their line of sight from the farthest 
                                    bead to the closest bead (in succession), thus challenging their convergence 
                                    at set and varying distances. Since binocular vision is employed, the patient 
                                    will perceive the string as two lines converging on the bead (like opposite 


                                    68

                                    sides of the road converging on the horizon, or an upside-down ‘V’). 
                                    Patients with normal convergence perceive the crossing of the string at each 
                                    bead whereas patients with convergence insufficiency may see the crossing 
                                    before or after the bead. Those with convergence insufficiency are 
                                    instructed to adjust their eyes so that string crosses at the bead for each 
                                    distance.
                                    Smooth Pursuits Patient instructed to follow target at a set distance from the tip of the 
                                    patient’s nose. The patient is instructed to maintain focus on the target as 
                                    it’s moved slowly in vertical direction. One repetition is complete when 
                                    the target moves back and forth to the starting position. The target should 
                                    be moving at a designated rate going fully upward and fully downward. 
                                    Repeated in horizontal direction.
                                    Can complete horizontal or vertical direction based on which movement 
                                    increases symptoms. Symptoms should be reported while completing to 
                                    track over time.
                                    Saccades Horizontal Saccades9: The examiner holds two single points (fingertips) 
                                    horizontally at a set distance from the patient to the right and left from 
                                    midline representing a gaze range of motion of about 30 degrees in each 
                                    direction. Instruct the patient to move their eyes as quickly as possible 
                                    from point to point. One repetition is complete when the eyes move back 
                                    and forth to the starting position.
                                    Vertical Saccades9: Repeat the test with 2 points held vertically at a set 
                                    distance and above and below midline to represent 30 degrees range of 
                                    motion in each direction. Instruct the patient to move their eyes as quickly 
                                    as possible from point to point. One repetition is complete when the eyes 
                                    move up and down to the starting position. 
                                    Can be completed in horizontal or vertical direction based on which 
                                    movement increases symptoms. Symptoms should be reported while 
                                    completing to track over time.


                                    69

                                    Summary of Evidence
                                    ● While dosing and intensity is largely variable, the use of vergence exercises to ameliorate convergence 
                                    insufficiency has been demonstrated as an effective treatment, especially in pediatric populations 
                                    undergoing return-to-learn protocols1. In addition to resolution of convergence insufficiency symptoms, 
                                    these protocols also demonstrated significant change in the correction of ocular misalignment3. These 
                                    exercises have been shown to be equally beneficial within a home-exercise program compared to office- 
                                    based vision therapy5.
                                    ● Though Brock string exercises are typically a progression exercise from pencil push-ups, both are 
                                    considered effective in eliciting meaningful change for both clinical and home-exercise programs4.
                                    ● Vision therapy and convergence exercises can improve NPC distance for those with a diagnosis of 
                                    chronic mTBI6, which is clinically relevant to patients and clinicians as convergence insufficiency has 
                                    been found in almost 50% of patients post-concussion7.
                                    ● Current research suggests that office-based vergence/accommodative therapy with home reinforcement is 
                                    more effective than home-based computer vergence/accommodative therapy for children. In adults, 
                                    evidence of effectiveness of various non-surgical interventions is less clear.8
                                    ● One study found that patients with a deficient vestibular system exhibited an enhancement in the pursuit 
                                    system, with open- and closed-loop pursuit gains that were about 9% higher than the control group10.
                                    ● Following oculomotor training for 10 minutes daily for 5 days, participants demonstrated a 25% 
                                    improvement in targeting saccade accuracy, and significant reduction in all neurobehavioral symptoms, 
                                    specifically affective and cognitive factors relating to poor saccades11.

                                    Impaired cervical function – Manual Therapy, Proprioception, Stretching, Strengthening, ROM
                                    Impaired cervical function may present alongside vestibular dysfunction or post-concussion depending on 
                                    the mechanism of injury. Based on the deficits present for each given patient, the following interventions 
                                    may be utilized. These descriptions and examples are not all inclusive.
                                    Manual therapy Graded joint mobilization/manipulation: Skilled thrust or non-thrust techniques 
                                    utilized on the cervical spine to improve cervical range of motion, tissue 
                                    extensibility, induce relaxation, modulate pain, and decrease restriction.
                                    Soft tissue mobilization: Manual therapy techniques on muscles, ligaments, or 
                                    fascia with the intent to break down nodules and
                                    optimize muscle function in patients with focal lesions or trigger points that are 
                                    tender to palpation.
                                    Sub-occipital release to cervical spine: with the patient in the supine position, 
                                    PT places fingers over suboccipital muscles around the level of C2 and takes 
                                    up the weight of the patient’s head. Slight traction is applied and held from 15
                                    seconds – 1 minute.
                                    Proprioception Head relocation practice I.e cervical joint position error: with a laser pointer 
                                    mounted on the patient’s head, they are asked to place the laser in the center of 
                                    the target placed on the wall. With the patient’s eyes closed, they are asked to 
                                    move their head in one plane of motion away from the target, then return to the 
                                    center of the target while their eyes remain closed. The patient should open 
                                    their eyes once they feel they have returned the laser pointer to the center of 
                                    the target5
                                    Eye-head coordination exercises: Eye-head coordination exercises are 
                                    performed to improve vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) gain adaptation and for 
                                    oculomotor re-education. These exercises include: VORx1, VORx2, VOR 
                                    cancellation, convergence, smooth pursuits, anticipatory gaze shifts, imagined 
                                    target, and saccades3
                                    Gaze stabilization exercises: A gaze stabilization exercise used to improve the 
                                    gain of the VOR. This exercise progression begins with the VOR X 1 viewing 
                                    paradigm involving the use of a stationary target at a distance of approximately 
                                    1 meter against a plain background while performing either pitch or yaw head 
                                    movements.1
                                    Instructions to patients: Keep your eyes on this target and move your head side 
                                    to side as quickly as you can keeping the letter clear and steady. May also 
                                    repeat by moving the head up and down.
                                    Stretching Static: holding end range position in maximally tolerated stretch for 15 
                                    seconds to 1 minute

                                    Dynamic: moving through active or active-assistive ranges of motion in order 
                                    to provide a stretch to soft tissue structures involved in that movement
                                    PNF techniques: stretching technique utilized to improve muscle elasticity 
                                    shown to improve active and passive ranges of motion6. This technique 
                                    combines joint mobilization, soft tissue stretching, and neuromuscular re-
                                    education in task-specific therapeutic activities to the patient


                                    72

                                    Strengthening Deep neck flexor strengthening: deep neck flexors are the main source of 
                                    proprioception afferents in the neck. Structural and functional changes in these
                                    muscles can alter the discharge of muscle spindles leading to changes in 
                                    proprioception.
                                    Range of motion 
                                    (ROM)

                                    Range of motion can be measured using an inclinometer and/or goniometer 
                                    and by the physical therapist visually assessing ROM asymmetry.
                                    Active: active neck flexion, extension, rotation, and side-bending motion
                                    Active assisted: cervical spine reaching end range flexion, extension, rotation, and 
                                    side-bending with outside force assist and the use of cervical musculature.
                                    Passive: cervical spine reaching end range flexion, extension, rotation, and side- 
                                    bending without the use of cervical musculature.

                                    Additional information
                                    Dosing/Frequency: The following guidelines are based on the 2017 Neck Pain Clinical Practice 
                                    Guidelines and associated references and should be changed and modified to meet the specific needs of 
                                    each patient. Low frequency exercise will be completed 1-2x per week, moderate frequency completed 
                                    approximately 4x per week, and high frequency completed 7 or greater times per week. Low intensity 
                                    exercise is force contraction approximately 10-30%max, moderate intensity is 40-60% max force of 
                                    contraction, and high intensity is 70-100% force of contraction. Dosage recommendations for cervical 
                                    manual therapy are 1-3x per week which will decrease over the plan of care, for 10-20 minutes, and grade 
                                    1-4.1
                                    Summary of Evidence
                                    ● Patients with acute neck pain with mobility deficits, stretching, strengthening, ROM /flexibility, and 
                                    relaxation exercise, are beneficial compared to soft tissue and cervical joint mobilization/manipulation 
                                    plus coordination, stabilization, and postural exercise.
                                    ● There is a benefit in using cervical mobilization and ipsilateral, but not contralateral, cervical 
                                    manipulation for reducing pain over the immediate term in patients with acute to subacute neck pain with 
                                    mobility deficits.
                                    ● For proprioception interventions, sensory input received from “passive” involuntary head movements 
                                    then corrective reflexes are initiated compared to active head movements resulting in reflexes 
                                    suppressed.

                                    Exercise intolerance (autonomic responses) – Graded Exercise Capacity Training
                                    Graded exercise capacity training involves regular and gradually increasing exercises. In which, exercise 
                                    capacity is the maximum amount of physical exertion a patient can endure.
                                    Graded exercise 
                                    capacity training

                                    Aerobic: stationary aerobic conditioning: outdoor walking, biking. Progress to 
                                    more dynamic aerobic conditioning: elliptical, treadmill, treadmill jogging, 
                                    agility drills, interval training, sport specific training3
                                    Anaerobic: exercises that limit head movements I.e. weight machines, 
                                    squats/lunges, core exercises. Resistance exercises with head movements:
                                    lateral squats with head movements, side planks with arm/head turn, Russian 
                                    twists, 3
                                    Movement based habituation training with the goal of increasing patients 
                                    tolerance to symptoms through exercise capacity training

                                    Additional information
                                    Considerations: Aerobic training performed on a treadmill and cycle is commonly used to measure the 
                                    work performed by each patient. Protocol methods differ in intensity, progression parameters, and 
                                    exertion duration across studies. Most common outcome measures assessed include heart rate, self- 
                                    reported symptoms, and blood pressure.1 This evidence is from UPMC Sport Medicine Concussion 
                                    program guidelines for post-concussion rehab.3
                                    Dosing/Frequency: Post-concussion patient’s exercise recommendations differ depending on current 
                                    rehabilitation stage. Recommendations for a patient’s target heart rate in stage 1 is 30-40% of maximal 
                                    exertion, stage 2 is 40-60% maximal exertion, stage 3 is 60-80% maximal exertion, stage 4 is 80% 
                                    maximal exertion, and stage 5 is full exertion. Aerobic conditioning recommendations for stage 1 are very 
                                    light, stage 2 are light to moderate, stage 3 is moderately aggressive, stage 4 is non-contact physical 
                                    training, and stage 5 is resume full physical training activities with contact. Anaerobic recommendations 
                                    include sub-max isometric strengthening and gentle isometrics for stage 1, light weight PRE’s in stage 2, 
                                    All forms of strength exercise at 80% max stage 3, aggressive strength exercise stage 4, and continued 
                                    aggressive strength/conditioning exercise stage 5.3
                                    Summary of Evidence
                                    ● Acutely concussed patients demonstrate impaired ability to shift from parasympathetic to sympathetic 
                                    control over heart rate at the onset of exercise.2

                                    Patient Education
                                    Patient education provides a mechanism for the patient to understand the etiology, course, and 
                                    rehabilitation potential of their injury. It is a crucial component of the rehabilitation process and 
                                    comforting for the patient to have a deeper understanding of their situation. Education can include, but not 
                                    be limited to, education about the vestibular system, symptoms associated with common vestibular 
                                    problems, treatment strategies, and prognosis for vestibular dysfunction. The specific patient education or 
                                    instruction depends largely on the individual patient’s diagnosis. Because vestibular/concussion issues are 
                                    a foreign concept to the majority of the population, education provides clarity and justification for the 
                                    treatment strategies.
                                    Additional Information
                                    Frequency: Patient education should be implemented with every patient encounter.
                                    Exclusions: Patient education is appropriate for all patients with vestibular dysfunction/concussion 
                                    regardless of pre-existing comorbidities and current health literacy. When appropriate, family education 
                                    may be incorporated as well.
                                    Summary of Evidence
                                    ● Evidence for patient education for a population suffering from vestibular disorders and concussions is 
                                    currently sparse. The current Clinical Practice Guideline for BPPV recommends based on observational 
                                    studies the use of patient education in the treatment of BPPV regarding the impact of BPPV on their 
                                    safety, the potential for disease recurrence, and the importance of follow-up.1
                                    ● An article written by Weightman et al, discusses the role of the evidence-based clinical management of 
                                    wounded soldiers with mild traumatic brain injuries. The importance of patient education using verbal 
                                    cues and handouts was recommended by the clinical experts for informing the soldiers of the common 
                                    symptoms of mild traumatic brain injuries along with vestibular rehabilitation, exercises and 
                                    balance/cognitive training.2

                                    Chapter 5: Summary of Interventions for Treatment Based Classification
                                    Head Movement Induced Dizziness
                                        complete one of the following intervention groups
                                    Gaze stabilization Adaptation exercises (retinal slip exercises)11: long-term changes in 
                                    neuronal response to head movements with goal of reducing symptoms and 
                                    normalizing gaze and postural stability; including:
                                    (1) VORx1: moving the head horizontally while keeping gaze on a 
                                    stationary target
                                    (2) VORx2: moving the head and target in opposite directions horizontally 
                                    or vertically while tracking the target with eyes
                                    (3) VOR adaptation with convergence: while completing VORx1 or 
                                    VORx2 as described above, addition of moving object closer to nose and 
                                    back out at varying speeds
                                    Substitution exercises Substitution exercises performed with goal of promoting alternative 
                                    strategies to substitute for missing vestibular function
                                    Enhancement of smooth pursuit movement: moving target horizontally 
                                    or vertically and tracking it with eyes while keeping the head still
                                    Use of central pre-programming in eye movements: perform anticipatory 
                                    eye-head movements
                                    Increase gain of cervico-ocular reflex: first fixate on target, then close 
                                    eyes while still visualizing target; rotate trunk/neck with eyes closed; open 
                                    eyes and eyes should be fixated on initial target
                                    Substitution or modification of saccades: use of saccadic eye movements 
                                    due to VOR inadequacy (ex: head-eye saccadic movements)
                                    Head movement 
                                    habituation exercises Includes repeated exposure to head movements to provoke symptoms 

                                    and reduce them over time with graded exposure and changes in 
                                    position, direction, and background stimuli. 
                                     (1): Head and neck flexion and extension
                                     (2): Cervical rotation
                                     (3): Cervical side-bending


                                    77

                                    Visually Induced Dizziness
                                    complete the following

                                    Visual habituation 
                                    training

                                    Repeated exposure to specific stimulus that provokes dizziness; systematic 
                                    repetition of provocative movements reduces symptoms over time; graded 
                                    in intensity through manipulation of parameters such as velocity, direction 
                                    of motion, size/color of stimulus, and instructions to patient
                                    Examples: optokinetic stimuli (use of repetitive moving patterns which 
                                    provoke symptoms), virtual reality environments, VORx1 with busy 
                                    background (standing or walking), VOR cancellation (sitting, standing, or 
                                    walking)

                                    Canalith Respositioning
                                    perform one of following the canalith repositioning maneuvers according to involved canal
                                    Posterior canal BPPV CRM Modified Epley, Semont Plus, Li Maneuver (posterior canal)
                                    Horizontal canal BPPV CRM Geotropic: Gufoni or Li Quick 
                                    Apogeotropic: Kim Maneuver or Gufoni

                                    Impaired Balance (Standing)
                                    select at least one of the following based on impairments
                                    Somatosensory changes Stance on firm surface, stance on foam, and/or stance on moving surface
                                    Changes to BOS Regular stance, Romberg, Tandem, and/or single-leg stance
                                    Altered visual condition Eyes open, eyes closed, and/or visual distraction
                                    Dual Tasking 
                                    variations

                                    Weight shifting, standing with head movement, throwing/catching ball, 
                                    and/or reaching outside center of gravity

                                    Voluntary and reactive 
                                    postural perturbations

                                    Anticipatory stepping, and/or external perturbations from therapist

                                    Movement based 
                                    habituation training

                                    Repeated exposure to specific stimulus that provokes dizziness; systematic 
                                    repetition of provocative movements reduces symptoms over time; graded 
                                    in intensity through manipulation of parameters such as velocity, direction 
                                    of motion, size/color of stimulus, and instructions to patient


                                    78

                                    Impaired Balance (Gait)
                                     perform at least one gait variations, progress with at least one dual-tasking variation
                                    Gait variations Walking on firm surface, walking on compliant surface, narrow-based 
                                    walking, figure-8 walking pattern, walking while stepping over/around 
                                    obstacles, walking at altered paces, and/or stair negotiation
                                    Dual tasking variations Walking while talking to PT, walking with head turns (vertical and 
                                    horizontal), walking while throwing/catching ball, and/or walking while 
                                    performing cognitive task (e.g. counting forwards/backwards)
                                    Movement based 
                                    habituation training

                                    Repeated exposure to specific stimulus that provokes dizziness; 
                                    systematic repetition of provocative movements reduces symptoms over 
                                    time; graded in intensity through manipulation of parameters such as 
                                    velocity, direction of motion, size/color of stimulus, and instructions to 
                                    patient

                                    Impaired Oculomotor Function
                                    perform one of the following
                                    Eye movement exercises Vergence, saccades, and/or smooth pursuits

                                    Impaired Cervical Function
                                    perform at least one of the following based on impairments
                                    Manual therapy Graded joint mobilization/manipulation, soft tissue mobilization, and/or 
                                    sub-occipital release to cervical and/or thoracic spine
                                    Proprioceptive Head relocation practice (i.e. cervical joint position error), eye-head 
                                    coordination exercises, gaze stability exercises
                                    Stretching Static, dynamic, and/or PNF techniques
                                    Strengthening Deep neck flexor strengthening
                                    Range of motion Active, active assisted, and/or passive
                                    Exercise Intolerance (Autonomic Responses)
                                    perform the following
                                    Graded exercise capacity 
                                    training

                                    Aerobic, and/or anaerobic

                                    Movement based 
                                    habituation training

                                    Repeated exposure to specific stimulus that provokes dizziness; 
                                    systematic repetition of provocative movements reduces symptoms over 
                                    time; graded in intensity through manipulation of parameters such as 
                                    velocity, direction of motion, size/color of stimulus, and instructions to 
                                    patient

                                    Psychologically informed 
                                    care

                                    Educational approach to help the patient better understand their 
                                    circumstances, increase self-efficacy, and compliance
                                    Open conversation between practitioner and patient working as a team 
                                    to reach a healthier mental state
                                    Patient education Associated HEP for each classification
                                    Weekly or frequent goal setting

                                    Criteria for Documenting Outcomes:
                                    DHI, PCSS, VOMS, GROC, FGA and ABC are the primary outcome measures. Record score of each test upon 
                                    administration every two weeks.
                                    DHI: Record Score (0-100)      PCSS: Record score (0-132)        ABC: Record score (0-100) 
                                    VOMS: Record each item score (0-40) based on patient’s reported symptoms of H/A, dizziness, nausea, & fogginess. Then sum up 
                                    the individual item scores and report as VOMS Total in SPSS.
                                    GROC: Record verbal response from measure. Measures will not be recorded at baseline.
                                    FGA: Record score (0-30).
                                    mCTSIB, Gait speed, NDI, VVAS, NPRS, BPPV Tests and/or EXIT Test will be performed as indicated by the patient’s 
                                    presentation as an adjunct to primary outcome measures every two weeks.
                                    m-CTSIB: Record performance time on each of the 4 categories           FGA: Record score (0-30) 
                                    Gait Speed: Record gait speed for 10-meter walk.
                                    EXIT test: Record Pass/Fail prior to anticipated discharge from therapy when applicable.
                                    NDI: Record score (0-100)           VVAS: Record score (0 – 10)             NPRS: Record score (0-10)
                                    DHP and Roll: 0 = negative, 1 = right, 2 = left, 3 = Bilateral, -9 = not tested. Mark which side is affected

                                    Diagnostic Criteria for Classification 
                                    Patient fits into classification if any one of the following diagnostic criteria is positive 
                                    Patient may fit into more than one classification
                                    1. Head movement induced dizziness
                                    o + Horizontal and/or vertical 
                                    VOR testing (increase of >2 
                                    points on symptom rating scale 
                                    compared to pre-assessment 
                                    rating)
                                    o + HIT in either direction 
                                    (inability to maintain fixation 
                                    during rotation of head requiring 
                                    corrective saccade, once the head 
                                    has stopped moving)
                                    o + DVA test (loss of 3 or more 
                                    lines)
                                    2. Visually induced dizziness
                                    o + Visual motion sensitivity test 
                                    (increase of >2 points on 
                                    symptom rating scale compared 
                                    to pre-assessment rating)
                                    o Visual Vertigo Analog Scale 
                                    (any rating of dizziness >0 on 2 
                                    or more items)
                                    3. Canalith Repositioning
                                    o Posterior Canal BPPV 
                                     + Dix-Hallpike 
                                    Maneuver (torsional 
                                    upbeating nystagmus 
                                    when head turned 
                                    towards affected side) 
                                    OR 
                                     + Subjective positional 
                                    vertigo with Dix-
                                    Hallpike Test
                                    o Horizontal Canal BPPV 
                                     + Roll Test 
                                    (cupulolithiasis when 
                                    nystagmus beating away 
                                    from the earth, 
                                    canalithiasis when 
                                    nystagmus beating 
                                    towards the earth; for 
                                    geotropic, greater 
                                    nystagmus and 
                                    symptoms on involved 
                                    side, for apogeotropic, 
                                    greater nystagmus and 
                                    symptoms on unaffected 
                                    side) OR
                                     + Subjective positional 
                                    vertigo with Roll Test

                                    5. Impaired balance (gait)
                                    o Gait speed <1.22 m/s
                                    o FGA </= 22
                                    o History of falls since the onset of 
                                    concussion/vestibular related 
                                    symptoms
                                    6. Impaired oculomotor function
                                    o + Near point of convergence (> 6

                                    pre-assessment rating)
                                    o + Smooth pursuits (increase of >2 
                                    points on symptom rating scale 
                                    compared to pre-assessment 
                                    rating)
                                    7. Impaired cervical function

            10.0. Module 10 Introduction
            //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
            //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

                Welcome to Module 10 of Unit 2. This week, you will learn about the evaluation and management of individuals with mild traumatic brain injury (concussion).  

                Learning Objectives
                By the end of this week, you will be able to: 

                Demonstrate a comprehensive examination to recognize concussion signs and symptoms in an adult population.   
                Understand and appreciate the interprofessional collaborations necessary to care for the client who has been concussed.   
                Discuss the most recent evidence for care in clinical practice for clients who have been concussed.
