                .('52 Concussion Background.pdf')
                    Neuromuscular PT 1

                    .Concussion Etiology, Pathophysiology, and Medical Management

                    University of Pittsburgh Department of Physical Therapy 

                    Pam Dunlap, PT, DPT, PhD

                   .Objectives
                    • Describe concussion etiology and pathophysiology
                    • Discuss medical management of concussion
                    • Identify risk factors for prolonged recovery after concussion

                    .What is a Concussion?
                    • A type of TBI induced by biomechanical forces that disrupts physiological brain 
                    function
                    • Results from a direct blow to the head, face or neck or an indirect force to the 
                    body that is transmitted to the head
                    • Functional disturbance to the CNS due to neurometabolic dysfunction, 
                    neurotransmitter disturbances, and/or microstructural changes
                    • Individuals may or may not experience a loss of consciousness of up to 30 minutes, altered mental state or post-traumatic amnesia for up to 24 hours post- injury (!!E)
                    • Glasgow Coma Scale 13-15
                    • Normal neuroimaging

                    .Epidemiology
                    • Estimated 1.6-3.8 million sports/recreation-related concussion annually in the US
                    • 8-23% of military personnel experience combat-related mTBI
                    • Other causes:
                    • Falls
                    • Motor vehicle accidents
                    • Assault
                    • Most individuals recover in 10-14 days (4 weeks for children) (!!E)
                    • However, it is estimated that up to 25% of individuals will go on to experience persistent post-concussion symptoms (!!E)

                    .Concussion Pathophysiology ('')
                    Giza CC, Hovda DA. The new neurometabolic cascade of concussion. Neurosurgery. 2014 Oct;75 Suppl 4(0 4):S24-33. 
                    doi: 10.1227/NEU.0000000000000505. PMID: 25232881; PMCID: PMC4479139.

                    .Clinical Correlates to Concussion Pathophysiology
                        ### 📋 Table Format

                        | Post-TBI pathophysiology                                                | Acute symptom / clinical correlate                         |
                        |-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------|
                        | Ionic flux                                                                  | Migraine headache, photophobia, phonophobia                   |
                        | Energy crisis                                                               | Vulnerability to second injury                                |
                        | Axonal injury                                                               | Impaired cognition, slowed processing, slowed reaction time   |
                        | Impaired neurotransmission                                                  | Impaired cognition, slowed processing, slowed reaction time   |
                        | Protease activation, altered cytoskeletal proteins, cell death              | Development of persistent impairments                         |

                        ---

                        ### 🧠 Outline Format

                        1. Post-TBI pathophysiology
                           - Ionic flux  
                             - Acute symptom / clinical correlate: migraine headache, photophobia, phonophobia
                           - Energy crisis  
                             - Acute symptom / clinical correlate: vulnerability to second injury
                           - Axonal injury  
                             - Acute symptom / clinical correlate: impaired cognition, slowed processing, slowed reaction time
                           - Impaired neurotransmission  
                             - Acute symptom / clinical correlate: impaired cognition, slowed processing, slowed reaction time
                           - Protease activation, altered cytoskeletal proteins, cell death  
                             - Acute symptom / clinical correlate: development of persistent impairments

                    .Concussion Sequelae
                    • Second Impact Syndrome
                    • < 24 years of age
                    • Occurs when a second concussion is sustained when still symptomatic from an 
                    earlier concussion (has occurred up to 28 days post-injury)
                    • Pathophysiology: loss of cerebral blood flow autoregulation, vascular swelling, 
                    increased ICP, brainstem herniation
                    • Mortality 50%; morbidity 100%
                    • Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy
                    • Neuropathological brain deterioration resulting from repeated head injuries
                    • Diagnosed via autopsy
                    • Post concussion syndrome (estimated 25% of people with concussion)
                    • Symptoms persist beyond the normal window of recovery
                    • >4 weeks; >3 months (varying definitions)

                    .Risk Factors for Prolonged Recovery
                    • Demographic characteristics
                    • Younger age/adolescents (sport)
                    • Older adults (non-sport)
                    • Female sex
                    • History of migraine
                    • History of anxiety or depression
                    • Post-injury characteristics
                    • Dizziness
                    • Continued play
                    • Prolonged rest following injury
                    • Post-traumatic migraine
                    • Psychiatric factors post-concussion

                    • Not associated with recovery or mixed 
                    findings
                    • Type of hit
                    • Loss of consciousness
                    • History of learning disability
                    • History of previous concussion(s)

                    .Medical Diagnosis of Concussion
                    • Clinical Exam
                    • History/mechanism of injury
                    • Symptom assessment
                    • Important to screen for red flags indicating more serious injury
                    • Declining consciousness
                    • Pupillary asymmetry
                    • Seizures
                    • Persistent vomiting
                    • Progressing neurologic signs
                    • Cervical instability

                    .Medical Management of Concussion
                    • Acute management
                    • Remove from play
                    • Identify needs for imaging (head/spine)
                    • Prohibit activities that are associated with risk of concussion
                    • 24-48 hours of “relative rest”
                    • Ensure follow-up care
                    • Follow-up management
                    • May need to modify activities (school, work, high intensity exertion) BUT 
                    should still participate in activities (exposure/recovery model)
                    • Monitor symptoms and recovery
                    • Follow guidelines for return to play/sport/combat (review state laws)

                    .Clinical Examination
                    • History and symptom assessment
                    • Post-Concussion Symptom Scale
                    • Post-Concussion Symptom Inventory
                    • Graded Symptom Checklist
                    • Rivermead Post-Concussion Symptoms Questionnaire
                    • Neurocognitive testing
                    • Confirm diagnosis and consider profile
                    • Identify needs for additional therapies
                    • Screen balance, vestibular/ocular (VOMS), cervical spine
                    • Pharmacological needs
                    • Counseling/therapy

                    .Post-concussion Symptoms
                        #### Physical Symptoms
                        - Headache  
                        - Dizziness  
                        - Balance deficits  
                        - Nausea  
                        - Fatigue  
                        - Sleep disturbance  
                        - Visual disturbance  
                        - Sensitivity to light  
                        - Sensitivity to noise  
                        - Tinnitus  
                        - Hearing loss  

                        #### Cognitive Symptoms
                        - Impaired attention  
                        - Impaired concentration  
                        - Impaired memory  
                        - Impaired processing speed  
                        - Impaired judgement  
                        - Impaired executive function  
                        - Impaired speech/language  
                        - Impaired visuospatial function  

                        #### Behavioral/Emotional Symptoms
                        - Depression  
                        - Anxiety  
                        - Agitation  
                        - Irritability  
                        - Impulsivity  
                        - Aggression  

                    .Symptom Profiles
                        ### 🧾 Outline

                        - Symptom Profiles  
                          - Vestibular  
                          - Ocular  
                          - Cognitive  
                          - Post-Traumatic Migraine  
                          - Cervical  
                          - Sleep  
                          - Concussion

                        - UPMC Concussion Program

                    .Multidisciplinary Approach to Management
                    • MD
                    • Neuropsychology
                    • Psychiatry/Psychology
                    • PT
                    • OT
                    • SLP
                    • ATC
                    • Neuro-optometry/Neuro-ophthalmology


                    .Return to School, Work, and/or Sport
                        Here’s the word-for-word transcription in both formats from the image showing the graduated return-to-sport strategy following concussion recovery:

                        ---

                        ### 📋 Table Format

                        | Stage | Aim                        | Activity                                                                 | Goal of each step                                              |
                        |-----------|--------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------|
                        | 1         | Symptom-limited activity       | Daily activities that do not provoke symptoms                               | Gradual reintroduction of work/school activities                   |
                        | 2         | Light aerobic exercise         | Walking or stationary cycling at slow to medium pace. No resistance training | Increase heart rate                                                |
                        | 3         | Sport-specific exercise        | Running or skating drills. No head impact activities                         | Add movement                                                       |
                        | 4         | Non-contact training drills    | Harder training drills, eg. passing drills. May start progressive resistance training | Exercise, coordination and increased thinking                      |
                        | 5         | Full contact practice          | Following medical clearance, participate in normal training activities       | Restore confidence and assess functional skills by coaching staff |
                        | 6         | Return to sport                | Normal game play                                                             | (no explicit goal listed)                                        |

                        ---

                        ### 🧾 Outline Format

                        1. Stage 1
                           - Aim: Symptom-limited activity  
                           - Activity: Daily activities that do not provoke symptoms  
                           - Goal of each step: Gradual reintroduction of work/school activities  

                        2. Stage 2
                           - Aim: Light aerobic exercise  
                           - Activity: Walking or stationary cycling at slow to medium pace. No resistance training  
                           - Goal of each step: Increase heart rate  

                        3. Stage 3
                           - Aim: Sport-specific exercise  
                           - Activity: Running or skating drills. No head impact activities  
                           - Goal of each step: Add movement  

                        4. Stage 4
                           - Aim: Non-contact training drills  
                           - Activity: Harder training drills, eg. passing drills. May start progressive resistance training  
                           - Goal of each step: Exercise, coordination and increased thinking  

                        5. Stage 5
                           - Aim: Full contact practice  
                           - Activity: Following medical clearance, participate in normal training activities  
                           - Goal of each step: Restore confidence and assess functional skills by coaching staff  

                        6. Stage 6
                           - Aim: Return to sport  
                           - Activity: Normal game play

                    .PT Role in Management of Concussion
                    • Screening
                    • Treatment
                    • Vestibular/ocular
                    • Balance
                    • Cervical
                    • Autonomic/Exertion
                    • Involved in return to play decision-making

                    1:18

                    1:34

                    1:56

                    2:00

                    2:04

                    2:17

                    2:20

                    2:26

                    2:31

                    2:37

                    2:42

                    2:44

                    2:49
                    and an influx of sodium and calcium at the cellular level.
                    2:53
                    This ionic flux causes depolarization,
                    2:57
                    which can lead to a diffuse spreading depression like state.
                    3:00
                    In an effort to restore homeostasis,
                    3:03
                    ion pumps shift into overdrive,
                    3:06
                    which depletes intracellular energy,
                    3:08
                    resulting in a mismatch between energy supply and demand.
                    3:11
                    The intracellular calcium flux occurs early
                    3:15
                    and may persist longer than the other ionic disturbances,
                    3:19
                    and glucose metabolic rates can be impaired for up to 7-10 days in adult animals.
                    3:23
                    This is associated with behavioral impairments in spatial learning.
                    3:29
                    Biomechanical forces on neurons and glia can also damage microstructural components,
                    3:33
                    resulting in the loss of structural integrity in axons.
                    3:40
                    This can lead to diminished neurotransmission and,
                    3:44
                    in severe cases, potential axonal disconnection.
                    3:47
                    This table is adapted from the same article,
                    3:53
                    which outlines the clinical correlates to some of
                    3:57
                    the pathophysiological changes that are seen after a concussion.
                    4:00
                    The widespread ionic flux that is seen after concussion
                    4:04
                    can be correlated to migraine headache-like symptoms,
                    4:07
                    inclusive of photophobia and phonophobia.
                    4:11
                    The energy crisis that occurs immediately after injury leads to biologic vulnerability,
                    4:15
                    which likely plays into the increased risk of
                    4:21
                    secondary injury within the first 10 days after sustaining a concussion.
                    4:24
                    This risk can be reduced by delaying return to risk activities,
                    4:30
                    things like delaying return to sport,
                    4:36
                    work, or active duty.
                    4:39
                    From studies of moderate to severe traumatic brain injuries,
                    4:41
                    we know that cognitive deficits can occur even in the absence of overt cell death,
                    4:46
                    leading us to believe that axonal injury after
                    4:51
                    mild traumatic brain injury can be associated
                    4:54
                    with variable degrees of neurobehavioral impairments.
                    4:57
                    Similarly, the impaired neurotransmission that can occur after
                    5:01
                    concussion can also lead to impaired cognition and behavioral deficits.
                    5:05
                    From studies of brains of individuals that have experienced repeated injury,
                    5:11
                    it is likely that the occurrence of
                    5:16
                    repeated mild traumatic brain injury prior to
                    5:18
                    full recovery from a prior injury can result in
                    5:21
                    more lasting metabolic dysfunction that may trigger activation of
                    5:25

                    5:29
                    One of the most serious sequela of concussion is second impact syndrome.
                    5:34

                    5:40

                    5:44

                    5:48

                    5:52

                    5:56

                    6:03

                    6:09

                    6:17

                    6:24

                    6:30

                    6:33

                    6:39

                    6:52

                    6:59

                    7:50

                    8:04

                    8:11

                    Sleep dysfunction is a common symptom following concussion and
                    14:56
                    can range from reduced ability to fall asleep or stay asleep,
                    15:01
                    or sleeping too much and feeling sleepy throughout the day.
                    15:05
                    Sleep is included as a modifier for the symptom profiles because it can modify or have
                    15:09
                    reciprocal relationships between many of the other signs
                    15:14
                    and symptoms included in the clinical profiles.
                    15:18
                    For example, sleep disturbances are related to emotional symptoms,
                    15:21
                    greater reports of migraine symptoms,
                    15:25
                    cognitive symptoms, dizziness, and oculomotor dysfunction.
                    15:27
                    Concussion can often involve a cervical injury as well,
                    15:31
                    and therefore, cervical symptoms are also included as a modifier.
                    15:36
                    Several symptoms can be impacted by cervical spine dysfunction including dizziness,
                    15:41
                    headache, and sleep dysregulation.
                    15:46
                    Concussion care is often a multidisciplinary approach,
                    15:50
                    including a variety of healthcare providers.
                    15:54
                    A primary care physician, neurologist,
                    15:57
                    or PM&R physician may be coordinating the care of the individual.
                    16:00
                    There may be neuropsychology or psychiatry,
                    16:05
                    and psychology that may be involved.
                    16:09
                    PTOT and speech can provide various forms of rehabilitation,
                    16:12
                    including vestibular rehab, vision care,
                    16:17
                    cognitive training, exertion training, and orthopedic care.
                    16:20
                    Athletic trainers may be involved,
                    16:25
                    particularly if it is a sport-related concussion,
                    16:27
                    and neurooptometry or neurophthalmology may be included in
                    16:32
                    the team as well if oculomotor and vision problems are present.
                    16:36
                    This certainly isn't an exhaustive list.
                    16:41
                    There may be other providers that are also included in the management.
                    16:43
                    The decision about return to school or work,
                    16:50
                    or sport is often made as a team.
                    16:53
                    The decision will be guided by symptom monitoring over time,
                    16:56
                    the results of the clinical examination and/or neuropsychological tests,
                    17:00
                    the results of a graded exertion test,
                    17:06
                    as well as using published guidelines.
                    17:09
                    Here you can see the recommendations for return to
                    17:12
                    sport from a consensus statement on concussion in sport.
                    17:15
                    As you can see, moving from one stage to the
                    17:20
                    next depends on symptom report and patient tolerance.
                    17:23
                    The return to sport process may occur gradually,
                    17:27
                    or they may move through each stage relatively quickly,
                    17:31
                    depending on the individual and the symptoms that they are experiencing.
                    17:35
                    If you, as a physical therapist,
                    17:39
                    are involved in return to sport decisions,
                    17:41
                    you should check with your state guidelines as well as
                    17:44
                    any published guidelines that are provided by your program and or team.
                    17:47
                    Physical therapists can have varying roles in concussion management.
                    17:54
                    They may be involved in the screening process
                    18:00
                    and identifying needs for further evaluation or treatments.
                    18:02
                    They may be involved in treating specific signs and symptoms following concussion,
                    18:06
                    such as vestibulo-ocular dysfunction, balance impairments,
                    18:11
                    cervical spine dysfunction, and autonomic or exertion therapies.
                    18:15
                    Physical therapists may also be involved in the return to sport decision making.
                    18:20
                    But again, this decision is usually made as a multidisciplinary team.
                    18:27

                .('53 Concussion PT Examination.pdf')
                    Neuromuscular PT 1

                    .Physical Therapy Examination for Persons with Concussion

                    University of Pittsburgh Department of Physical Therapy 

                    Pam Dunlap, PT, DPT, PhD

                    .Objectives
                    • Identify components of the neurologic PT exam to prioritize for individuals 
                    diagnosed with concussion
                    • Demonstrate the components of the Vestibular/Ocular Motor Screening (VOMS)
                    • Describe important considerations when conducting a PT examination for 
                    individuals with concussion

                    .Organization of PT Exam
                        From Clinical Practice Guideline:
                        Physical therapy evaluation and 
                        treatment after concussion/mild 
                        traumatic brain injury

                        - Organization of PT Exam
                          - From Clinical Practice Guideline: Physical therapy evaluation and treatment after concussion/mild traumatic brain injury
                          - Physical Therapy Examination and Evaluation Processes for Patients Who Have Experienced a Concussive Event
                            - Patient appropriate for physical therapy examination
                              - Determine probable movement-related impairments (sidebar 1) and levels of irritability (sidebar 2)
                              - Strategically plan and sequence examination procedures based on symptom types and levels of irritability
                              - Reports neck pain at rest or with movement?
                                - Yes
                                  - Examine for cervical musculoskeletal impairments
                                  - Provide basic interventions as indicated for pain relief to support additional testing
                                  - Proceed with additional tests as indicated and tolerated
                                - No
                                  - Reports dizziness and/or headache at rest or with movement?
                                    - Yes
                                      - Examine/evaluate for cervical musculoskeletal, vestibulo-oculomotor, and orthostatic hypotension/autonomic impairments that may contribute to dizziness and/or headache, in order from the anticipated least to most irritable
                                      - Provide basic interventions as indicated for symptom relief to support additional testing
                                      - Delay tests until future session as needed according to patient tolerance
                                      - Proceed with assessment of motor function impairments per patient tolerance
                                    - No
                                      - Examine any movement-related impairment domains (sidebar 1) and administer selected outcome measures not yet examined or administered and sequence based on:
                                        - Levels of irritability and disability (sidebar 2)
                                        - Patient’s needs and preferences
                                        - Patient’s ability to tolerate tests
                                      - Determine and document:
                                        - Patient’s impairments and irritability levels (sidebars 1 and 2)
                                        - Potential headache type in accordance with the International Classification of Headache Disorders
                                        - Self-management capabilities and other psychological and sociological factors for recovery
                                        - Need for follow-up testing
                                        - Plan for outcome measure administration
                                      - Proceed to physical therapy plan of care and implementation decision tree (FIGURE 3)

                        ---

                        ### 🧩 Sidebar 1: Impairment Domains
                        - Cervical musculoskeletal impairments  
                        - Vestibulo-oculomotor impairments  
                        - Autonomic dysfunction/exertional tolerance impairments  
                        - Motor function impairments  

                        ---

                        ### 🔥 Sidebar 2: Irritability Considerations
                        - Frequency of symptom provocation  
                        - Vigor of movement required to reproduce symptom(s)  
                        - Severity of symptoms once provoked  
                        - How quickly and easily symptoms are provoked  
                        - Which factors ease the symptoms  
                        - How much, how quickly, and how easily the symptoms resolve

                    .Summary of Recommendations from CPG related to Examination
                    • PTs must screen individuals who have experienced a potential concussion and 
                    document impairments as well as screen for emergent conditions
                    • PTs should screen those diagnosed with a concussion for mental health, cognitive 
                    impairment, and other diagnoses and make appropriate referrals
                    • PTs must conduct and document a comprehensive intake
                    • PTs should test for orthostatic hypotension and autonomic dysfunction by evaluating HR 
                    and BP in supine, sitting, and standing
                    • PT Examination should include cervical musculoskeletal function, vestibulo-oculomotor 
                    function, autonomic dysfunction/exertional tolerance, and motor function
                    • PTs should examine patients who have experienced a concussive event for motor 
                    function impairments, motor coordination and control, including static/dynamic balance, 
                    and multitasking


                    .PT Exam – History and Mental Status

                    • History, Observation, Review of Systems
                    • Mechanism and timing of injury
                    • Follow-up imaging and care
                    • PMH: prior concussion, migraine, anxiety, depression
                    • Symptoms
                    • Prior level of function and work/leisure activities, goals
                    • Systems screen:
                    • Vitals
                    • Cervical spine
                    • Mental health
                    • Mental status
                    • Screen or prioritize, depending on presentation and symptom report
                    • Review neuropsychological test results if available


                    .PT Exam – Cranial Nerves

                    • Vestibulo-oculomotor examination is 
                    indicated for those who report:
                    • Headache
                    • Dizziness
                    • Vertigo
                    • Nausea
                    • Fatigue
                    • Balance problems
                    • Visual motion sensitivity
                    • Blurred vision
                    • Difficulty focusing on stable or moving 
                    objects

                    • Oculomotor Assessment
                    • Ocular ROM
                    • Smooth pursuit
                    • Saccades
                    • Vergence and accommodation
                    • Ocular alignment
                    • Vestibular Assessment
                    • Gaze stability
                    • Dynamic visual acuity
                    • Visual motion sensitivity
                    • Screen for BPPV: Positional tests
                    • Screen for orthostatic hypotension
                    • PROM: Dizziness Handicap Inventory


                    .Vestibular/Ocular Motor Screening (VOMS)

                    • VOMS symptom scores >2 over baseline and NPC distance >5cm represent clinically useful cut-offs
                    • 3 VOMS items (VOR, VMS, NPC distance) resulted in 89% accuracy for identifying patients with concussion


                    .PT Exam – Sensory and Motor

                    • Sensory (not usually a priority)
                    • Motor
                    • Cervical assessment (screen should occur in systems screen)
                    • Indicated for those with neck pain, headache, dizziness, fatigue, balance 
                    problems, or difficulty with visually focusing on a target
                    • Exam components
                    • ROM
                    • Strength and endurance
                    • Palpation of cervical and scapulothoracic muscles
                    • Joint mobility
                    • Joint position error
                    • PROM: Neck Disability Index (NDI)


                    .PT Exam – Coordination and Balance

                    • Coordination (screen)
                    • Balance
                    • Static and dynamic balance
                    • Sensory organization test
                    • Balance Error Scoring System (BESS)
                    • Dynamic gait assessments: FGA, DGI, MiniBEST
                    • Dual task assessment
                    • PROM: Activities-Specific Balance Confidence Scale


                    .PT Exam - Function

                    • Functional movements
                    • Motor control and coordination
                    • Symptom provocation
                    • Autonomic and exertional tolerance
                    • PTs should conduct a symptom-guided, graded exertional tolerance test for 
                    those who report exertional intolerance, dizziness, headache, and/or desire to 
                    return to high-level exertional activities
                    • Buffalo Concussion Treadmill/Bike Test
                    • Dynamic Exertion Test


                    .Buffalo Concussion Treadmill Test

                    • Obtain resting HR
                    • Start treadmill at 3.2-3.6mph at 0 incline
                    • The incline is increased by 1 every 1 minute
                    • Symptoms, RPE and HR are measured at each stage
                    • Discontinue if symptom report is >3 from rest, HR is >90% of calculated Hrmax, 
                    RPE >17, or the patient requests to stop

                    • Buffalo Concussion Treadmill Test 


                    .Dynamic Exertion Test (EXIT)
                    • Cardiovascular fitness assessment
                    • Aerobic exertion
                    • Dynamic Circuit
                    • Functional Testing
                    • Agility tasks
                    • Sport-specific drills

                    Kochick V, Sinnott AM, Eagle SR, et al. The Dynamic Exertion Test for Sport-Related Concussion: A 
                    Comparison of Athletes at Return-to-Play and Healthy Controls. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2022;17(6):834-
                    843. doi:10.1123/ijspp.2021-0258


                    .May Classify Exam Findings into Clinical Profiles

                    Cervical

                    Sleep

                    Concussion

                    Vestibular Ocular

                    Cognitive

                    Post-
                    Traumatic 
                    Migraine 

                    Anxiety/
                    Mood


                    .Exam Considerations

                    • Communicate with team
                    • Symptom provocation
                    • Monitor throughout
                    • Provide breaks as needed
                    • Consider the order of the exam
                    • Consider completing part of the exam today and part next visit

                    ('BUFFALO CONCUSSION TREADMILL TEST.pdf')


                        BUFFALO CONCUSSION TREADMILL TEST (BCTT) – INSTRUCTION MANUAL 
                        John J Leddy, Mohammad N Haider, Barry S Willer 

                         

                        Purpose 

                         

                        • To assess the degree of exercise tolerance in patients with concussion. 
                        • To identify the heart rate (HR) at which concussion-specific symptom exacerbation occurs (i.e. the Heart 
                        Rate Threshold [HRt]). 
                        • To help establish a safe level of exercise for treatment of concussion. 
                        • To help differentiate between concussion and other possible diagnoses for concussive symptoms (e.g. 
                        cervicogenic post-traumatic disorder). 
                        • To identify physiological variables associated with exacerbation of symptoms, and the patient’s level of 
                        recovery. 

                         

                        Caution 

                         

                        • The BCTT alone should never been used to make a diagnosis of concussion or clearance to begin 
                        the return-to-play protocol. The BCTT is a supplementary test and should be interpreted 
                        alongside a complete history and physical examination. 
                        Eligibility 

                         

                        • Do not perform the BCTT if the patient is experiencing such cervical dysfunction that motion while walking 
                        on a treadmill could cause considerable pain or harm, is experiencing vestibular/balance issues that 
                        would impair the ability to safely walk on a treadmill, or has a lower extremity or spinal orthopedic injury 
                        that compromises safe walking. 
                        • Before beginning the BCTT, participants should be evaluated for any contraindications to exercise 
                        testing. The AHA Guidelines contraindications to exercise testing are as follows: 

                         

                        Absolute Contraindications 
                        • Acute myocardial infarction (within 2 days) 
                        • High-risk unstable angina 
                        • Uncontrolled cardiac arrhythmias causing symptoms or hemodynamic compromise 
                        • Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis 
                        • Uncontrolled symptomatic heart failure 
                        • Acute pulmonary embolus or infarction 
                        • Acute myocarditis or pericarditis 
                        • Acute aortic dissection 
                        Relative Contraindications 
                        • Left main coronary stenosis 
                        • Moderate stenotic valvular heart disease 
                        • Electrolyte imbalance 
                        • Severe arterial hypertension (>200 mmHg systolic or >110 mmHg diastolic) 
                        • Tachyarrhythmia or bradyarrhythmia 
                        • Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and other forms of outflow tract obstruction 
                        • Mental or physical impairment leading to inability to exercise adequately 
                        • High-degree atrioventricular block 

                         

                        • The BCTT is not recommended within 24 hours of concussive brain injury or if the patient is too 
                        symptomatic (symptom severity 7/10 or more). 

                         

                        Safety Considerations 

                         


                         

                        • While testing, participants must be dressed for exercise (comfortable clothing, running shoes), wearing 
                        any vision or hearing aids (glasses, etc.), and should be hydrated. 
                        • It is suggested that 2 persons assist in conducting the BCTT in order to assure safety of the participant, 
                        with 1 examiner positioned behind the patient (at back of the treadmill) at all times while test is in progress. 
                        • It is important to engage in casual conversation with the patient during the exercise test to assess his/her 
                        confidence level as well as any changes in cognitive and communicative functioning. As exercise 
                        intensifies, note if patient seems to have difficulty communicating, looks suddenly pale or withdrawn, or 
                        otherwise appears to be masking serious discomfort. 
                        • Be aware of postural and structural changes (slouching, rounding the back, leaning head) since noting 
                        the patient’s thoracic and cervical posture can offer clues on the etiology of the injury. 

                         

                        Equipment Requirements 

                         

                        • Treadmill with capacity to reach 15 degrees of incline 
                        • HR monitor (Polar OH arm band or chest band is recommended) 
                        • BCTT Assessment Form for monitoring HR, symptom severity, RPE and relevant observations – See 
                        form attached 
                        • Visual Analogue Scale (VAS): Can be explained to patients as a measure of “how bad their concussion-
                        specific symptoms are”. It should be clarified that getting tired from walking on a treadmill is not a 
                        concussion-specific symptom and should be reported in the next scale - See form attached 
                        • Borg Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE): Can be explained to patients as a measure of “how hard you 
                        feel like you’re working out”. The scale ranges from 6 – 20, 6 being no exertion and 20 being the maximum 
                        they can ever do. Descriptors of each exercise intensity level should be pointed out and patient should 
                        be allowed to read through it before the test begins.- See form attached 
                        • Chair, water and towel for patient recovery after exercise. 

                         

                        Setup 

                         

                        • Attach HR monitoring device according to manufacturer’s instructions. 
                        • Place RPE and VAS scales within comfortable viewing distance of participant while on treadmill (it is 
                        suggested that participants should not have to turn head to view scales). 

                         

                        Test Protocol 

                         

                        1) Inform patient about test procedures and what to expect during the BCTT. 
                        2) Explain and demonstrate the VAS and RPE scales and obtain resting scores. Remind participant that he/she 
                        will be asked to rate symptom severity and exertion each minute during exercise. 
                        3) Obtain resting HR after 2-minute seated position before getting the patient on the treadmill. 
                        4) Patient should begin by standing on the sides of the treadmill while the treadmill is turned on. The 
                        experimenter should set treadmill at a speed of 3.2mph for patients up to 5’10”, and 3.6mph for those 5’10” 
                        and above. Starting incline is 0 degrees. Speed can be adjusted depending on athletic status or overall 
                        comfort of treadmill speed – patients should be moving at a brisk walking pace. The HR at Stage 0 is the HR 
                        when the patient is standing on the treadmill before starting the BCTT and not during the 2-minute seated 
                        rest. 
                        5) After 1 minute at this pace, treadmill incline is increased by 1 degree and patient is asked to rate their 
                        symptom severity and RPE at the beginning of each stage. HR in bpm are also recorded at the beginning of 
                        each stage. Examiner should also record general observations as the test progresses if needed. This 
                        procedure is repeated each minute while treadmill incline is raised at a rate of 1 degree/minute. 
                        Changes to VAS rating should be specifically clarified/noted, for example, if the rating moves from 2 to 3, it 
                        should be clarified if this reflects the addition of a new symptom and/or increased severity of an existing 
                        symptom. 1-point is given for any worsening of a symptom and 1-point for the addition of a new symptom, 
                        for example, if the patient reports symptom severity change from 2/10 to 3/10 and reports slight increase of 
                        headache and onset of light sensitivity, then this should be considered a 2-point increase to 4/10. Once 
                        treadmill reaches maximum incline (15 degrees), speed is increased by 0.4 mph each minute in lieu of 
                        increased incline. 


                         

                        6) Once test is terminated (see Stopping Criteria below), speed is reduced to 2.0 mph and incline reduced back 
                        to 0 for a 2-minute cool down (if patient is able). HR, RPE, VAS plus any additional comments (if needed) 
                        are recorded after the 2-minute cool down. 
                        7) Patient is allowed to rest on a chair in a quiet environment until symptom severity returns to pre-BCTT value 
                        or patient feels like they are able to continue with remainder of the clinical visit. 

                         

                        Stopping Criteria 

                         

                        The BCTT is terminated based on the following criteria: 
                        1) Symptom exacerbation - defined as an increase of 3 or more points on the VAS scale from resting VAS 
                        score. 
                        2) Voluntary exhaustion – defined as an RPE of > 17 without significant symptom exacerbation. If the patient 
                        has not reached at least 80% of age predicted maximum (calculated as 220 – age), the examiner should 
                        encourage the patient to try and keep going but should not push the patient if they are too exhausted. 
                        3) Examiner notes a rapid progression of complaints (pressure in head to searing focal headache) or patient 
                        appears faint or has stopped communicating or continuing the test constitutes a significant health risk for 
                        the patient. 
                        4) Patient has reached 90% or more of age predicted maximum without any increase in symptoms and still 
                        reporting low RPE. The RPE scale should be discussed with the patient at this time to make sure they 
                        accurately understand it before we begin the cool down period. 
                        5) Patient requests to stop for any reason. The reason for stopping, other than the above mentioned, should 
                        be recorded in the BCTT Assessment Form.  

                         

                        Interpretation 

                         

                        • The maximum HR achieved on the BCTT at symptom exacerbation is called the Heart Rate threshold 
                        (HRt) and a safe level of exercise is considered to be below 90% of HRt. 
                        • If the patient is able to exercise to voluntary exhaustion without any increase in symptoms (i.e. does not 
                        have symptom-limited exercise intolerance) but is not cleared to return-to-play because of symptoms at 
                        rest or physical examination impairments, then the patient can perform aerobic exercise at any HR up to 
                        the maximum achieved or at 85% of age appropriate maximum. 
                        • Patients who have symptoms at rest, but do not have a physiologic threshold (can exercise to max without 
                        increase in concussion-specific symptoms) should be evaluated for dysfunction of the cervical spine, 
                        vestibular system or temporomandibular region. 

                         

                         

                         

                        For more information, please visit concussion.ubmd.com

                    .Physical Therapy Management Post-Concussion

                    University of Pittsburgh Department of Physical Therapy 

                    Pam Dunlap, DPT, PhD

                    .Objectives
                    • Identify concussion management practices supported by clinical practice

                    • Compare and contrast intervention strategies based on concussion clinical

                    • Describe special considerations for working with individuals post-concussion

                    .Interventions supported by CPG

                        ### 🧾 Outline Format

                        1. Communication and Education  
                           - Must  
                        2. Interventions for Movement-related impairments

                    .Concussion: no two are the same

                    • Create a personalized plan for those who have experienced a concussion
                    • Consider clinical profiles when developing treatment plan
                    • Consider patient goals, prior level of function, activity and participation (work, 
                    school, sport)
                    • Align interventions with the patient’s identified impairments, functional limitations, 
                    participation restrictions, self-management capabilities, and levels of irritability
                    • Multidisciplinary management is best – identify needs for additional referrals to 
                    other team members


                    .Communication and Education

                    • Education on the typical symptoms and functional impairments and their recovery
                    • Educate patients and caregivers that most people recover well and do not 
                    typically have difficulties more than 1-3 months post injury
                    • Avoid activities that place the individual at a high risk for a second concussion
                    • Gradually resume normal activity after a period of rest for 24-48 hours post-injury 
                    (relative rest and NOT strict rest)
                    • Lifestyle and self-management of symptoms to improve quality of life during 
                    recovery
                    • Progressive re-engagement in activities
                    • Sleep hygiene
                    • Nutrition, hydration
                    • Return to activity and pacing
                    • Follow up with care team


                    .Interventions for Cervical Spine Impairments

                    • Address cervical and thoracic spine impairments
                    • Strength training
                    • Range of motion
                    • Postural positioning
                    • Sensorimotor control
                    • Manual therapy


                    .Oculomotor Interventions

                    • Common symptom report
                    • Headaches or pressure
                    • Blurry vision
                    • Double vision
                    • Difficulty focusing
                    • Eye strain
                    • Difficulty with work/school/reading
                    • Common exam findings
                    • Convergence insufficiency
                    • Ocular misalignment
                    • Accommodative dysfunction
                    • Smooth pursuit or saccade impairment

                    • Intervention strategies
                    • Oculomotor training
                    • Smooth pursuits
                    • Saccades
                    • Vergence exercises
                    • Consider needs for referral to neuro-
                    optometry or neuro-ophthalmology


                    .Oculomotor training

                    Brock string exercise for convergence insufficiency Smooth pursuit activity


                    .Vestibular Rehabilitation

                    • Common symptom report
                    • Dizziness
                    • Motion sensitivity
                    • Intolerance to busy environments
                    • Imbalance
                    • Common exam findings
                    • Symptom provocation with VOR, VMS
                    • VOR impairment
                    • Balance impairment
                    • Positive positional testing (BPPV)

                    • Intervention strategies
                    • VOR exercise
                    • VMS exercise
                    • Balance exercise
                    • Canalith repositioning maneuvers 
                    (BPPV)
                    • Consider needs for referral to ENT, oto-
                    neurology
                    • Also consider non-vestibular causes of 
                    dizziness
                    • Autonomic
                    • Oculomotor
                    • Cervical


                    .Vestibular & Balance Training ('')

                    This Photo by Unknown Author is licensed under CC BY-NC-ND

                    This Photo by Unknown Author is licensed under CC BY


                    .Exertional Tolerance Training

                    • Principles
                    • Exposure/recovery model
                    • Progressive training
                    • Patient-specific (may be general aerobic activity vs. sport-specific)
                    • Monitor using symptom report, RPE, and HR
                    • Can be beneficial across clinical profiles
                    • Goals
                    • Maintain physical fitness and wellness during recovery
                    • For athletes, progress toward return to play
                    • Condition those who are deconditioned due to injury


                    .Exertional Tolerance Training ('')

                    This Photo by Unknown Author is licensed under CC BY


                    .Motor Function Interventions

                    • Static balance activities
                    • Dynamic balance activities
                    • Motor coordination and control
                    • Dual task/Multi-task
                    • Task-specific training

                    This Photo by Unknown Author is licensed under CC BY-NC-ND


                    .Monitor and Progress

                    • Monitor and document symptoms, functional impairments
                    • Administer outcome measures
                    • Symptom checklist/inventory
                    • Cervical spine ROM, muscle strength, joint position error, self-report 
                    measures
                    • Vestibular and oculomotor tests (VOMS), self-report
                    • Graded exertion test
                    • Functional measures (mCTSIB, FGA)
                    • Self-management assessment


                    .Return to work/school/play

                    • Address any impairments related to work/school/sport tasks early
                    • Graded return to high intensity activities
                    • No activities with risk of concussion prior to medical clearance
                    • Example: Return to football
                    • Initially, no practice or contact activities
                    • Start with walking and daily activities and monitor tolerance
                    • Implement light aerobic activity (stationary bike)
                    • Sport-specific exercises in supervised setting
                    • Return to non-contact training drills with team
                    • Full contact practice (after medical clearance)
                    • Return to play

                .Question 1
                Which of the following should physical therapists include in their examination of patients who report dizziness, vertigo, and/or headache after a concussive event? 

                Cervical and thoracic spine function only
                Vestibular and oculomotor function only
                Cervical/thoracic spine, vestibular/oculomotor, and autonomic function
                Mental health status and sleep disturbances

                Cervical/thoracic spine, vestibular/oculomotor, and autonomic function 
                 
                .Question 2
                What is the recommended approach to aerobic exercise for patients with concussion who exhibit exertional intolerance? 

                Begin a symptom-guided, progressive aerobic exercise program
                Ask the patient to completely rest until all symptoms resolve
                Avoid all exercise until symptoms resolve
                Progressive strength training

                Begin a symptom-guided, progressive aerobic exercise program 
                 
                .Question 3

                Relative rest followed by progressive re-engagement in activity
                Avoid any activity that results in symptom provocation

                .Question 4
                Please utilize the following case scenario for the next two questions. A 17-year-old high school soccer player presents to physical therapy for evaluation 10 days after a concussive event. She reports persistent dizziness when turning her head quickly and in busy environments (school, stores). Her medical history is unremarkable, and she has not previously had a concussion. During the examination, the patient becomes light-headed during a sit to stand transition. What is the most appropriate next step? 

                Initiate ROM and strength training for the cervical spine
                Refer the patient to a cardiologist
                Provide VOR exercises for dizziness
                Perform an assessment for orthostatic hypotension and autonomic dysfunction

                Perform an assessment for orthostatic hypotension and autonomic dysfunction

                     Importance of Sleep with Individuals with Dizziness 

                     

                     Lisa Heusel-Gillig, PT, DPT, NCS

                    a component of 

                     

                    Produced by 

                    Patient 
                    Fact Sheet  

                    Difficulty sleeping is common in people with diagnoses including cancer, diabetes, 
                    weight gain, and heart disease. Keeping a regular sleep routine is also important for 
                    individuals with inner ear problems and dizziness. Lack of sleep is a major trigger for 
                    migraines including vestibular (inner ear) migraines. Those who have concussions 
                    also have difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep, which can make their dizziness 
                    worse. Adults with positional vertigo (BPPV) may not have good quality sleep 
                    because they are either afraid to move in bed or use extra pillows to prevent 
                    dizziness. Eight hours of sleep is suggested for maximum benefit.   
                    Tips for Good Sleep Hygiene 
                    1. Keep a regular sleep routine, even on weekends and vacations 
                    2. Don’t exercise too late in the day 
                    3. Avoid caffeine and nicotine before bed 
                    4. Avoid alcoholic drinks before bed 
                    5. Avoid heavy meals and beverages before bed 
                    6. Avoid medicines that delay or disrupt your sleep 
                    7. Don’t nap after 3 PM 
                    8. Make sure you leave time to relax before bed; as well as turn off 
                    bright lights or electronic devices at least 30-60 minutes before 
                    bedtime 
                    9. Take a hot bath before bed 
                    10. Make sure your bedroom is dark and the room temperature is cool 
                    11. Get  plenty of sunlight exposure during the day 
                    12. Don’t stay in bed if you cannot sleep- get up and read, draw, or do 
                    any other calming activity in low light 
                    13. Do not use your bed for watching TV or activities on your 
                    computer/phone 
                    14. Exercise and physical activity during the day can help the quality of 
                    your sleep 

                     

                     Gadgets such as cell phones and computers can give off light that can 
                    decrease the melatonin in the brain which helps sleep/wake cycles. You can 
                    set your computer or phone to use the night light or blue light filter setting 
                    to prevent dizziness and sleep loss 
                    Reference: 
                     https://fastlifehacks.com/matthew-walker-12-tips-for-good-sleep/

                Well done! You have completed the fifth of six modules for Unit 2. Before moving on to the next module, remember to review these four key learnings: 

                Concussions are the most common type of traumatic brain injury, typically resulting in functional, rather than structural deficits 
                Physical therapists play an integral role in the evaluation and management of individuals with concussion 
                Vestibular dysfunction following concussion can cause problems with VOR function, visual motion sensitivity, balance, and/or BPPV 
                Exertion testing is a necessary part of formal clearance post-concussion 
                Learning Outcomes
                After completing this module, you can now: 

                Demonstrate a comprehensive examination to recognize concussion signs and symptoms in an adult population.   
                Understand and appreciate the interprofessional collaborations necessary to care for the client who has been concussed.   
                Discuss the most recent evidence for care in clinical practice for clients who have been concussed.
